CLAUDE HOWARD MORRISON

Grand Master
1943

Our seventy-seventh Grand Master was born in Pontiac, Illinois, July
10, 1887. .He is the son of Samuel L. and Jessie E. Morrison. His father
passed on in 1941. His mother resides in San Diego, having recently
passed her eighty-first birthday. Brother Morrison received his schooling
in Pontiac, Illinois, and graduated from Lake Forest College, Lake Forest,
Illinois, in 1910. He moved to San Diego in 1911 and was employed by
the County Tax Collector temporarily. On Dec. 8th, 1911, Brother Morri~on
joined the staff of the First National Bank of San Diego (now the First
National Trust and Savings Bank) and has been connected with that institution continuously since, being now Cashier, arriving at that responsible position in 1937 after serving as Auditor, Comptroller, etc., for a number
of years; and has served as Chairman of the Committee on Banking Practice
of the California Bankers' Association for two years, 1941 to 1943.
Pontiac Lodge No. 294 initiated Claude Morrison on February 14,
1911, passed him on February 21, and raised him on February 23. His
Masonic progress and career since that time has been an eventful and a
busy one. Demitting to San °D iego No. 35 in November of 1921, he was
appointed Junior \l\Tarden in May of 1922, to fill an unexpired term: Served
as Master in 1924, in the usual course of events, marshal from 1925 to
1930, treasurer 1930 to 1940. Appointed Grand Standard Bearer 1930,
member of the Grand Lodge Committee on Policy and General Purposes
1931 to 1933, and member of the important Finance Committee for Grand
Lodge from 1934 to 1940. He was elected and served as Junior Grand
Warden in 1941, Senior Grand Warden in 1942, Deputy Grand Master in
1943, and was elected and installed Most \ l\Torshipful Grand M aster on
October 15; 1943.
This constitutes but a part of Brother Morrison's service to Masonry.
A member of the Scottish Rite Bodies since 1912, and of the Mystic Shrine
since 1913 (charter member ) he has served well and faithfully as presiding officer of both, 10 terms as master of the various Scottish Rite Bodies,
Potentate of Al Bahr Temple in 1938. Elected Knight Commander of the
Court of Honor, A. A. S. R., 1919, and a 33rd degree Mason since 1925.
Member of San Diego Chapter, Council and Commandery of the York
Rite, Sovereign, San Diego Conclave Red Cross of Constantine, and in
addition to his other duties, served for many years as representative in
San Diego of the Inspectors General for the Scottish Rite, Trustee of Al
Bahr Temple, and member of the Advisory Council, Order of De Molay.
Brother Morrison and Daisy Bentley, who was a graduate of Northwestern University, were married on July 3rd, 1913, and have since then
reared a family in San Diego consisting of three lovely daughters and two
fine sons. The daughters are Mrs. Allen C. Keller of Compton, California,
and Mrs. Roderick C. Steddom and Miss Charlotte A. Morrison of San
Diego. The sons are Sergeant Allen H. Morrison who is now serving in
the Army Air Forces and George S. Morrison who is at Claremont. On
August 2nd, 1943, their first grandson, Clark Morrison Steddom, arrived.
Brother Morrison is a member of the First Methodist Church and, at
present, is Chairman of the Finance Committee and Secretary of the Board
of Trustees. He is,also a member of the University Club.,
The above is but a brief outline of this brother's useful, active life,
truly an example worthy of emulation.

DEVOTIONAL SERVICES
The Very .Rev: .Grand Chaplain, George A. V.,Tarmer, con?ucted a most mspmng and thought-provoking devotional service on the theme "Supreme Grand Master of the Universe."
Most Worshipful Grand Master, Distinguished G1tests, Officers of. the Grand
Lodge, and Masons entitled to be in the Grand Lodge of California:
We have purposely this year, through the executive orders of our
Grand Officers and our Grand Master, curtailed the amount of hours to
be c~nsumed by the Grand Lodge; and consequently I wish to abide by
the time schedule and try to bring us up to date through this period.
There is a phrase very much used by Masons into which I would like
to build som~ c?.ntent and out of wpich we iii·a y gather a bit of° instruction.
That phrase is Supreme Grand Master of the Universe."

As we use that ph<ase, let us recognize that there are two things
involved in it ; first, a vast amount of space and second, a tremendous
amount of time. When men first thought · of the universe in a reflective
way, •(jf course, they looked around iibout them and discovered that they
)lad their feet upon that _which they could stand with security and stability,
so they centered their universe in this very out of the way planet. Then
they had to find some way by which they could make this planet adequate,
and so they built a firmament and studded it with stars. The stars were
the windows of the universe, the windows through which the waters came
to water the thirsty earth. They suspended the planet upon the back of
Atlas, and then, not wanting to leave man in an impossible position, they
put him on the back of an elephant, the largest creature on the face of
the earth; and then, realizing that this huge creature could not swim, so
burdened, they put the elephant upon the back of a turtle and left it to
make what progress was possible with such a tremendous overload. It
didn't take very much of a Supreme Architect of the Universe to build
that sort of a world. Most anybody could conceive as much as that, but
a little over three hundred years ago men began to inquire with eyes more
than human. They lengthened their sight through the telescope and
brought to themselves lengthened understanding. Finally the distances
became so magnificent that they had to talk about them in light years and
a light year is a distance of five trillion eight hundred seventy billi.on miles.
Now, even when the national debt wants to come up to about 350 billion
dollars, you can still multiply it by two and have five trillion, 170 billion
left. And then, if you multiply that by thousands and tens of·.thous;i.nds,
you still have not gotten out to the end of space, and the Supreme
Architect of the Universe, is still manager and puts the billions of suns to
bed on time each night. The job that Aristotle assigned him with 4,000
observable stars was not much of a task, by comparison. Such magnificent space keeps the sense of wonder alive and the exclamation point
central in our thought world. That is a great and important thing.
There is in this planet upon which we dwell an hour glass and with
that hour glass is coming to us some illumination concerning the amount
of time that has been consumed by the Supreme Grand Master of th e
Universe in building this planet. He worked it out as His own dream
and hunted it out objectively so that mankind can. come into intimate touch
with it. Those who are skilled in the sciences, tell us that the basic metal
of uranium decomposes at a very slow rate, and when it throws off three
atoms of helium it becomes radium. As radium releases the alpha, beta
and gamma rays it becomes lead. This is the process. How important it
is as a time revealer is just dawning upon it. You have a vast territory
of this uranium in Australia and in Canada, and the hour glass of the
world has been ticking away until we now know that God has been working on our planet at least 1260 million years to produce what He has and
to give us a sense of at-homeness in our field of operations.
There have been those who have said that man does not amount to
much, .that man came late, that he was at th e end of a great process, and
that whether he was important so far as his planet is concerned, did not
ma!<.e .hi~ ·v:'ery imeg~tant s,q_ f~r .a~ the universe is concefr1ed; his planet
. is insignificarit in ari out-of-the-way corner of a great universe which _is
one of the littlt; particles hurleq off by one of the great si.ms: These men
have sa1d, . "Well, it doesn't make 'much difference. Astronomically speaking, irra."K.is' not important." But one of the great outstanding minds of
our gen~ration said, " Man may "be on an insignificant planet, he may be in
a faraway corner of' die universe; he,may be crushed by the ·powers around

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

him, but still you have to say: Man conceives the universe; man thinks
the universe into existence; man understands the laws by which it operates and man, gathering those laws to himself, as they operate, achieves
for himself distinction and purpose and cooperates with the best and the
highest and the noblest, the most honorable and most significant. Man is
the astronomer, man is the geologist, man is the physicist, man is the
chemist, man is the fraternal spirit, man is the religious genius, man has
the creative instinct, man is the only being that understands the perfect
plan of the Supreme Architect of the Universe, men have great possibilities ·
for good. The up thrust of life through the aeons of time has always been
the result of an urge to more adequately adjust life to its environment."
That was a tremendous time in animal history, when the fishes got together, as the lakes and seas were drying up, and, after due consideration,
passed a resolution that instead of having fins they would have feet;
instead of gills they would have lungs, and out of their determination they
did that very thing and became amphibious beings. Henceforth they were
to have life both in and out of the water, a clearly significant demonstration. Equally important was the hour when the reptiles of this planet got
together and said, "We are bogged down, our method of locomotion is too
slow. V.le crawl instead of walk. Our vision is too limited. A motion
was made to pass a resolution to grow feathers and develop wings to improve the situation. As a result, reptiles became birds. That's what
happened.

The first manifestation of life was a one celled microscopic animal with
only one nerve. They call it the amoeba. One day the amoeba talked
with itself and said, "I don't have to remain as I am, so he doubled and
had two nerves. Sometimes we have too many nerves so that we are all
nervous about things that are not tremendously important. You don't
get mad at the thing that is pressing upon you with great reality. Two
men meet on a battlefield and they are not mad at one another. They
have a desperate thing to do. But if either, after coming back to camp
keeps sticking pins into the other, he will get mad as blazes. We don't
get mad over big things but we do get mad over the little things when
our nerves are out of order. The up thrust of life gives us awareness of
the great and magnificent-the things that we can build into our experience. I had a visit with a Chaplain in the Armed Forces last night. He
told me a story of a young woman who went into a store in California and
she was waiting and waiting, as we all do these times, because of the
shortage of manpower. And finally some one was loose and came up and
said to her, "What do you want?" just like as though she was a most unreasonable of persons. She said, "I would like to have" so and so; and the
clerk said, "Well, you can't get" so and so, "don't you know there's a
war on?" She had complete control, she had suffered enough to understand,
and so she said, "Is that so? My husband has been away in the South
Seas for two and a half years. Maybe that is what he is doing."

10

In the total scheme of things the Supreme Grand Master of the
Universe was trying out of this whole experimentation to develop a being
worthy of Himself, one through whom His own purposes might be
accomplished, one that would seek fellowship with the creator in the days
that were ahead. Man is that being seeking such fellowship. Isn't there
something tremendously dignifying about the recognition that we are the
only beings ii]. the total universe, so far as we know, that can grasp the
mind that is behind the scheme that is working in the universe in which
we live and that we can grow to such fullness and stature as to fellowship
with the Supreme Architect of the Universe? Like the baby that comes
into your hands impressionless but impressionable who can grow until he
has fellowship with you, so you may grow until you have fellowship with
Infinite Reality in the universe in which you live. That fellowship will not
have meaning merely to you, but as the fellowship of the growing child
gives satisfaction to the mind and heart of the father, so the fellowship of
the adult man, grown tall, who sees things as they are may in the counsels
of God give satisfaction to the Supreme Grand Master of the Universe as
the eternal ages roll on. There are three great things in Masonry that
aid this upsurge of life: First, we believe in God-no man comes into
Masonry who does not--; Second, we believe in the inter-relatedness
of life, that there is such a thing as the common good--; and third, that
death is just experience, but life is reality. In this time when eternity
presses upon us, the idea of eternal life must find its rightful place in our
social procedures.
·
Men are being ruthlessly destroyed in our social procedures in vast
numbers. There is a good deal of satisfaction to know that even if your
body is destroyed, death is only an experience. There is an up thrust of
life, an awakening to reality.
·
,
The second thing I would like to say is like unto the first, and that is
that as we move through life there must arise an increasing awareness.
The fact is the up thrust of life is not merely in the organism, but appears
in •an increasing of nervous responsiveness and a development of control.

11

You know there is a book that came out of the Enterprise, that illfated carrier, which tells the story of a young lad from Guam who was on
that boat and a bomb burst and water came into his compartment, and
when he was rescued at long last some one said to him, "How about it?"
"Well," he said, "at first I was worried and then," he said, "for six hours
I was scared perpetual. In the beginning I prayed to God in English, then
I prayed to Saint George and all the other saints I knew, and when that
didn't do any good I just talked direct to God myself." I am trying to talk
about the awareness-how the Supreme Grand Master of the Universe
has to use tremendous.methods in order that he may make contact with
mortals such as ourselves, in order that he may function some of his
purpose or plan through our tiny lives.
My closing word is this: Not only is there an up thrust of life that
identifies us with our environment and that makes us aware of the things
that are about us, but the high duties of life arise out of moral quality, not
physical quantity. They tell us when the bloody commune of France was
on and they had turned out the king and run him through the guillotine,
and also the queen,' they came to the little Dauphin. They wanted to kill
him also because they desired destruction of the whole royal line. Historians differ; one says that there came a diabolical cry from the mob,
"Don't kill him, he is a kid; turn him over to Old Meg. If you kill him you
will send him to Heaven; if you turn him over to Old Meg you will damn
his soul to hell." This historian says that they did turn this child over to Old
Meg and ·when she was attempting to teach this little lad something
different and more bestial than anything that had happened in his experience before, he would clench his little royal fist and stamp his little
royal foot and say, "I will not do it. I will not do it. I was born to be
a king and I will not do it." And I am wondering, in a time like this if we
could not rise to that same height as we think of the magnificence of the
total scheme of the Supreme Grand Master of the Universe who is
attempting to unfold a loftier plan of things. Why not clench our little
royal fists and stamp our little royal feet and declare, "I will not do it, I
was born to be a child of God, I will not do it," as things are being done

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

13

around us that would hold life at its best from full expression. Why not
determine that "we shall not go through this kind of chaos again," and
demand of ourselves that we build a world in which a baby shall have an
opportunity for development, in which youth and in which mankind may
choose life, not be forced to death, shall come to be all that God planned,
when He created us in His own image, and challenged us to come into the
fullness of the stature of His Son. Why not clench our royal fist, because
we belong to the high royal family? Why not stamp our royal feet because we are children of the Infinite? 'And when the world presses on
us in ways that would destroy inen, why can we not, as the child in the
French royal family, cry out in the very face of the forces which oppress
us, " I was born to be a child . of God·. I will not do it." Let us all think
God into our experience in all His . follness, and accept the challenge to
live His life-find His way.

In my report as Grand Treasurer for the year ending July 31 1943
I_ referred to changes in the law essential to orderly and careful tr'ansac~
hons respecting securities and funds. Further consideration has resulted
in .suggested amendments which have been sub~itted to ·p_ G. M. Dana
R. 'Yeller~ chairman of the Committee on Jurispruaence, for preliminary
con~1derahon. The amendments are believed to be essential to completely
clarify fiscal procedure, with particular regard to safeguarding Grand
Lodg~.
Suggestions affecting the Grand Sec_retary have been submitted
af~er conference with our Brother Grand Secretary. Also, in collaboration
with the Grand Secretary, it is contemplated that remittances received by
him will be transmitted direct to the Grand Treasurer for deposit and distribution.
There is some difficulty with respect to signatures by reason of nonresidence of appropriate officials. Where two signatures are required it
is not satisfying at all for one signatory to affix his signature other than
concurrently with that of the other signatory.
It is manifest that there is great fiduciary responsibility reposed in
the Gra'.1~ Treasurer. For that reason, consideration must be given to
such rev1s1ons of fiscal procedure as may be offered Grand Lodge for consideration.
Suggestions have been made with the intent of enlarging the powers
of the Committee on Investment of Endowment Funds to include consideration and approval of sale and exchange of securities.
In consonance with suggestions made in the annual report of the
Grand Treasurer at the Ninety-fourth Annual Communication of Grand
~odge of 1943, the Grand Treasurer, being aware of the prevalent very
high prices of municipal and similar securities, requested a study to be
made by Mr. Paul B. Kelly of the Bond Department of the Anglo California National Bank, long-time custodian of securities in Grand Lodge
and Masonic Homes portfolios..
As a result, in March, 1944,_ a draft of a study was submitted by the
Bond Department, setting forth market values of such securities in those
portfolios and various trust funds established for the benefit of the Homes,
also the yield at market to maturity or earlier date of retirement. Subsequently, cost prices of securities were inserted for the purpose of comparison with market prices which, in the very nature of the study, were
only approximate. Market values were so far in excess of cost which
in turn was in excess of par value, that it was impressive of the n~cessity
of determining policy in keeping with responsibility to Grand Lodge. Fortunately, the funds of Grand Lodge and income therefrom are not taxable.
Therefore, no tax is applicable to profit and it was determined that
advantage should be taken 0£ that fact.

It must be borne in mind that amortization based on cost will not
protect a portfolio against potential loss when market exceeds cost.
Probably for the information of members of Grand Lodge who are not
familiar with securities transactions, it would be well to explain the meaning of amortization. We are immediately concerned with bonds bought at
a premium or price in excess of par. The coupon or rate of interest is
based on par.· That rate in dollars and cents is a lower percentage of cost
of bonds bought at a price above par. The amount in addition to par is
capital and if the bonds were sold the profit or loss would depend upon
whether the price were higher or lower than the cost, not par. For that
reason, the amount in excess of par of any security must be recovered by
maturity or call or optional date, if' any, or it will be lost if the coupon
rate is used a& income. In order to protect against that, the real_ percentage of earning is calculated and that is regarded as income and the
balance is accumulated to equal the amount above par paid for the security.
This is amortization in case of securities purchased at a premium or at a
price abov~ par. · Book value thus far reflects cost in case of purchases,
or indicated value of time of acquisition, in case of donations.
It was determined to authorize sale of the securities in the Endowment Fund yielding less than approximately 2 ~% to maturity or call
or optional date, if any, and also a few selected securi~ies from F lint Trust,
Patton Fund and Wadleigh Endowment F und (see Exhibit I.) In accordance with these conclusions, the Bond Department of the Anglo California
National Bank was authorized to submit the same for bids. A copy of
the bid form and instructions is appended as Exhibit I I. T he securities
were submitted to nine responsible bidders who had been currently active
in the market for municipals and similar types of securities being currently
offered. One house did not bid. The municipals were sold to the highest
bidder on June 27, 1944, yielding $439,781.50 (not including accrued interest
on such securities as follows: Endowment Fund, $4,991.91 , Patton Fund,
$9.75, Wadleigh Endowment, $48.89·; totaling $5,050.55), as compared with
th e March 14th valuation of $438,862.40. Deducting the cost thereof
amounting to $375,838.67, from sale price, namely, $439,781.50, develops
a profit of $63,942.83.
The foregoing figures do not reflect results from the sale of items in

In 1920 a total of 29,786 degrees was conferred on our own members
and the net gain for the year was 8,983. In the year just closed 35,286
degrees were conferred on our own members and there was a net gain
of 9,228. This great volume of work by the Lodges, when considered with
the other business of Grand Lodge, makes it evident why we have handled
through the Grand Lodge office this year approximately 26,000 pieces of
incoming mail.
The peak of membership growth was reached in 1931, with a total
membership of 142,422. The total membership as of July 31, 1944 was
138,738.
With the war continuing as it is and the interest apparently remaining
at a high point it is to be expected that great growth will be experienced
for the next two or three years. One of the best figures in this year's
report is in relation to restoration and shows that during the year 1,057
members were reinstated.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the Most W orshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The crescendo of conflict and the tempo of war have _b~en stepped. up,
but now it is the bastions of our enemies that are r ece1vmg the weight
of hot steel and the rending by high explosives. Fortress. Europe ~as been
comp~essed to Fortress Germany and every rampart of its walls is under
the assault of encircling Allied arms.
In the Pacific the Japanese fist has been pried from off the ~yriad
of islands seized in her first aggressive rush. Our .fleets of t~e air and
of the sea range at will, bringing destruction to he~ every citadel and
blasting the factories of her very homeland. . Now .m b~th theaters of
strife, it is only a question of when, not how, this conflict will end.. Tho~gh
the way be tong and the road ahead exceedingly rough, the route 1s plainly
marked and we all go forward together in confidence.

To achieve this superiority of arms, to bring this g oal within ou_r sight ;
has required the united effcirt.s of all ~u~ ci~izens-e con~mic curtailments,
temporary surrender of freedoms, hm1tat1ons of action, work under
pressure but never under duress. It has all been volunta~y-a free c?un;ry
operating in a free way for Freedom's sake. Even th is Con:mumcat1on
of the Grand Lodge in keeping with the hour, has shortened its assemblage to accomplish its necessary labors within a minimum of time.
This report shall likewise be limited ; terse perhaps, but sufficient in
words, I hope, that he who in future chances to read, may comprehend

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

not only our workings but may also find mirrored in Masonry a reflection
of the times.

To the Assistant Grand Lecturers: Obed W. Carr, Sidney K. Lehman, Charles A. Schwartz and Arthur M. W arren, my thanks and appreciation for their splendid accomplishments. They. have take_n from me t?e
burdens and responsibilities of this office, leavmg only its honor~, its
benefits and its privileges. They are a grand team whose comradeship, as
well as their work, is a joy and pleasure to me.
Finally let me pay my respects to the unofficial member of the Ritual
Committee.' The present system of teaching the work was inaugurated
in 1934 under the order of Brother James B. Gist, then Grand Master.
During the past decade ten brethren in all h.ave. occupie~ th.e fi_ve places on
the reorganized committee. During all this time, by mv1tation, Br~ther
Dana R. Weller, Past Grand Master, has regularly attended our me~tmgs,
three, four, even fi ve meetings a year, missing none, save one when _illness
intervened. From 1910 until we younger fellows were entrusted with the
work Dana with Thomas J. Baker as. Grand Lecturer, and one other constitut~d the' Ritual Committee. Both had received their work directly
from William H . Edwards, the previous Grand Lecturer. T he new pla.n
was Dal)-p,'s._ He has watched over. it and guid.ed 1;1s. His wisdom, his
knowledge ·c,r the work, his enthusiasm and his kmd~ess have been a
flaming torch for our enlightment. If we who sit at his feet have been
able to improve the for m and the standard of the work in California, (and
I believe we have); if we have been able, with the fine as sist~~ce of the
Inspectors, to hold the Craft to that standard under war cond1tions, (and
I know we have), then to him the honor and the glory and. these few words
are for him a very meager though justly deserved encomium.

28

We are having our usual experiences under war conditions. Officers
of our Lodges continue to ~urrender their places to enter the armed forces
or to move to locations of endeavor directly connected -w ith war production. Fortunately, Past Masters, or other well trained brethren, are
stepping into the vacancies and our work is going on without retrogression.
Membership attendance at Lodge meetings is being adversely affected
in many localities by gasoline rationing and also by the weariness of
strenuous production endeavors. For similar reasons our Inspectors are
having difficulties with their Schools of Instuction and the 'supervision of
their Lodges. The appointment of Lodge officers' coaches, under recommendations made in previous years, has been an especial boone under the
circ.u mstances, alleviating conditions that might otherwise have produced
serious resu Its. ·
During the past year, in connection with other duties, it has been
my privilege to meet with our bret_h ren in many places. Your Grand
Lecturer has attended not only tli.e · usual Masonic assemblages, but also
has visited many of the Schools of Instruction held by the Assistants in
their Divisions and by the. Inspectors in their Districts, as well as
numerous Lodges 'whe_n -$i~ ·ptesence was unexpected. · Thus he has
observed the actual work of the brethren not only in cities arid 't owns, but
also in t_h e villages and hamlets. From these personal experiences I can
assure this Grand Lodge that throughout the State uniform work is being
splendidly done and that the base of ritualistic perfection has been so
broadened that no brother need err in his work because of a lack of
authoritative sources near at hand. .
Under war time prosperity applications for degrees have assumed
dangerous proportions. With the exception of nine Lodges in our mountain areas who had no applicants, all Lodges have far exceeded their
normal quota of candidates. Four Lodges have conferred more than 300
degrees each. Two hundred degrees, or even a hundred, in a single Lodge
in a single year means lengthy Lodge meetings and several meetings a
week. "Therein lies the danger. Line officers become satiated and lose
their enthusiasm. Members become bored and stay at home. This bodes
ill_for the future for it is hard to reestablish enthusiasms and the habit of
non-attendance is difficult to overcome. Remember that Lodge meetings
are primarily for the benefit of the members, not the candidate; Masonry.
is a privilege, not a right; candidates should be made to await the convenience of the Lodge· and work conferred with thoughtful care and expression will make more real Masons than a candidates' degree mill can
ever produce.
Though there be an abundance in the quarry, let us shape each ashlar
well that the future edifice have no faulty blocks.
The amendments to our esoteric work authorized last year by this
Grand Lodge have been received with enthusiasm by the Craft as needed
improvements in our ritual. Uncertainties, if any there be remaining, will
be eliminated at the School of Instruction for Inspectors to be held this
evening. Tomorrow evening, if the time is not required for a session of
the Grand Lodge, will be devoted to instruction in the candidates' lectures.
All interested brethren of the Craft are invited to attend at that time.
To the In's pectors of the several Masonic Districts my congratulations
and my thanks. They are achieving excellent results, though greatly
hampered by the times.

29

Thanks again for the privilege of serving.
Respectfully submitted,
CHESTER H. WARLOW ,
Grand L ecturer.

Referred to Committee on Segregation.

ILLINOISTOWN LODGE N O. 51
August 4, 1944.

To the M. W. Grand Lodge of California:
Greetings:
It is the sincere wish of Illinoistown Lodge No. 51, after due deliberation, that Grand Lodge go back to the policy of "Full time Grand Lecturer."

a year and more often when possible, especially the districts of the small
country Lodges.
L ESTER R. STARR,
Secretary.

RESOLUTION
WHEREAS, It has been the practice of the Masonic bodies in this jurisdiction and throughout the United States, that no person shall draw double
expenses for attendance at any mee'ting or the taking of any trip for
attendance upon two or more concurrent meetings.
Now, THEREFORE, in conformity to said practice, BE IT HEREBY RESOLVED,
By the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the
State of California that the Ordinances of said Grand Lodge be, and are
hereby amended by adding thereto a section to be designated as Section 680,
reading as follows :
"Extraordinary expenses of officers and members of Grand Lodge.
"Sec. 680. No officer or member of Grand Lodge shall receive any
reimbursement from Grand Lodge for any part of the expenses of any trip
taken by him as an officer or member of Grand Lodge or for attendance at
any meeting, if, in connection therewith, such officer or member is entitled
to reimbursement from any other . organization for expenses ·connected with
such trip or· for attendance at an:y meeting connected or concurrent with the
trip or meeting at which ·expenses otherwise would be paid from the funds
of Grand Lodge."
Proposed by

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE
To ·the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California.:
When you elected me as your Grand Master a year ago, and appointed
me to act in your place until the next Annual Communication, you placed
a very heavy responsibility upon me. The world was torn asunder by
war. While we thought that we would win eventually we did not then
have that certainty of complete victory which we have now. In this
year we have come to realize what war means. True, we have been
spared from bombing and invasion, and as civilians our sacrifices have
been largely nominal; but we have had constantly before us the everwidening battle front; we have had in mind the more than ten thousand
California Masons now in the service of their country; and there is
scarcely one of us here whose family is not represented by someone in
uniform. The ever increasing casualty lists bring home to us the horrible
waste and tragedy of it all.
Now, with peace a nearer certainty, the great problems of the industrial
transition from war to peace, rehabilitation of our soldiers and the greatly
transcending problems as to how to accomplish a lasting peace which
will preserve our own national standards, and at the same time help to
raise those of many needy nations, face us with the grim, inexorable
necessity of succeeding in these tasks, the failure of which might spell
disaster.
During this period of hope, faith, and yet foreboding, Masonry has
carried on. As is usual in times of war, men are thinking more seriously,
and many who heretofore have 'not considered Masonry favora~ly have
entered our portals, and many more are taking advantage of this brief
period of prosperity to achieve what they have always desired-to be a
Mason.
While it was a difficult task which you assigned to me, it was a very
pleasant one. I shall never cease to be grateful for this opportunity to
serve you, and to meet and work with so many fine, loyal citizens of
our country, carrying on our work throughout the jurisdiction, and in
other jurisdictions, as well. And as I report to you my official acts, the

38

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

results o.f my administration, I hope that you will realize that, while I am
speaking to you as your Grand Master, I am also trying to speak for every
Master Mason in this great jurisdiction, having at heart the welfare and
future usefulness of our iQstitution.

Change in Annual Communication
At the very beginning of this report to you of my official acts and
activities during the past year, I want to make special mention of the
change which I made in the dates of this communication.
Before I had been in office very long I realized that railroad travel
was becoming more and more difficult, and that this applied especially
to coastwise travel. Hotel facilities in the larger cities in· California likewise were becoming more and more strained. It did not take very much
imagination on my part to 'picture the situation which might prevail in
October 1944 if these conditions continued, and of the abnormal congestion that might prevail if the European war should end suddenly and
many of our forces should be moved across the country to embark at
Pacific Coast ports for the Japanese war area.
I realized that to carry out our program according to our constitution
it would be necessary for many of our members, particularly those in
Southern California, to crowd the trains on two week ends, and also to
strain the hotel facilities of San Francisco. If this came to pass I felt
that we as patriotic citizens would regret that we had not foreseen this
emergency and taken steps to avert this congestion, and that the public
might not view with favor an institution which so openly flouted the
public welfare by insisting on conducting a leisurely session in these war
times. I felt also that most of the members of the Grand Lodge, being
very busy men, would welcome the opportunity to leave their work later
and return earlier than under ordinary conditions.
I am not a person who would lightly set aside established practices
and customs, and I know that a deviation from the provisions of our
constitution, while not without precedent, should not be undertaken without very q.reful consideration. I therefore asked the Grand Secretary
to plan a tentative program for a three-day session, and he was of the
opinion that our essential business could be conducted in that time without
slighting any part of it. I then consulted with many of our officers and
Past Grand Masters, and all approved my plan. Thereupon I caused the
following notice to be sent to the constituent Lodges:
To the Members of Grand Lodge:
I have been giving considerable consideration to our next Annual
Communication, which by our Constitution is set for October 9th to 13th
inclusive. The request of the Office of Defense Transportation, that all
conventions and conferences be eliminated or curtailed, is in line with
the increasing flow of military personnel and equipment up and down
our State and through our ports.
While I do not think that our Annual Communication should be considered as an ordinary convention, but as a strictly business session, we
should eliminate all other activities, and in a spirit of cooperation transact
our business within a shorter period. The purposes which I would like
to achieve by holding a shorter session are:
(a) Elimination of week-end travel. (b) Decreased individual
demands on hotel service. (c) Elimination of group demands
upon hotel service.

GRA~D

LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

39

I feel that we can achieve these objectives only by shortening our session,
and I am therefore taking it upon myself to set the dates for the next
Annual Communication of Grand Lodge as October 10th, 11th and 12th.
In accordance with this schedule I make the following proposals and ask
that all officers and members of Grand Lodge cooperate with me to the
fullest in making the plan successful.
We will therefore,
1. Convene at 10 :00 A. M. on Tuesday, October 10th, and at 9 :30
A. M. on Wednesday, October 11th, and Thursday, October 12th.
In each case the entire day will be given over to business sessions.
2. The evenings, with the exception of the Inspectors' School of Instruction, will be kept open for business sessions if required.

3. All entertainment features, such as the Get-together Dinner, etc.,
will be eliminated.
4. Committee reports heretofore printed and distributed separately
will be printed well in advance, combined into one volume, and
distributed at the close of the morning session on Tuesday.
5. Reports which must of necessity be made during the business sessions will be brief and reliance for detail will be had in the printed
report.
6. Registration will be conducted as usual on Sunday in order that
those who reside near San Francisco may register and avoid as
nearly as possible confusion on Monday and early Tuesday morning
when out-of-town members will be arriving and registering.
As- soon as Grand Lodge opens it will be necessary to seek approval
of what has been done and to ask for unanimous consent to elect and
install officers on Thursday at 2 :00 P. M.
I dislike very much to urge any member of Grand Lodge to refrain
from attending this Annual Communication. I do not feel that it is
incumbent upon me to request Lodges to limit their representation. I do
feel, however, that every member who is planning to attend the Communication should consider very carefully whether it is necessary, that
those who have had the privilege of attending our Communications in
the past should defer to those who are new in Grand Lodge and may
not have an opportunity to attend in the future, and that the representation of the Lodges should be cut to the lowest possible level.
I believe that this plan is for the best interest of all concerned and
in line with the patriotic cooperation of our war effort, and I sincerely
trust that it will have your cooperation and unqualified approval.
Dated at San Francisco, this 12th day of June, 1944.
CLAUDE H. MORRISON, Grand Master.
Attest: LLOYD E. WILSON, Grand Secretary.
That railroad and hotel accommodations are more congested than they
were at the time this notice was sent i~ evidenced by the fact that the
members of a great Order are having difficulty in securing reservations
for a meeting to be held in this city next week. I am sure that you will
agree with me that we have done our utmost to cooperate with the war
effort and at the same time carry on our Annual Communication though
on a restricted basis.
If any of you feel that the session is to6 short, and that we may not

which may be controversial, let me assure you that this is exclusively a

Official Visitations
At the beginning of the year I had no idea as to how much time I
could devote to making official visits to our Lodges, and therefore made
no schedules for such visits. Those which I have made were undertaken upon short notice but by this method, and with the kind cooperation
of the Inspectors and Masters of Lodges, I have covered most sections
of the State, except in the North.
I have been very cordially received by the officers and members of the
various Lodges, and the attendance at the meetings, generally, has been
very flattering. I find that the attendance in the smaller districts, proportionately, is larger than in the city districts, and in fact in one case
in a large center the attendance was frankly disappointing, being limited
to less than half of the total of the number of officers of the Lodges repre. sented. While I am not concerned with numbers, I do feel that the visit
of a Grand Master should be a stimulus for the attendance of all of the
officers of the Lodges.
Inasmuch as I am the first Grand Master to come from San Diego
I felt that I owed it to the Lodges of my own community to pay them
special visits, and consequently I have made a number of official visits
to single Lodges in Sap Diego County. In the other parts of the State,
I visited districts or groups of districts. In this way I estimate that I
have visited three-quarters of the Lodges in our jurisdiction, my official
visits totalling fifty-five.
·
I presume that every Grand Master has been impressed, as I was, with
the bigness of California. In geography, in resources and in men our
great jurisdiction is so vast that the privilege of visiting in community
after community makes one very proud and very humble.
The spirit prevailing in the Lodges is truly Masonic. Under stress of
war-time conditions, our Lodges are carrying on, and the loyalty and
unselfish devotion of our officers and faithful workers is greatly to be
commended, and brings us to the realization of "How good and how
pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity."
Breakfasts

In accordance with the practice followed by Grand Masters in the last
few years, I attended the breakfasts given in the larger communities in
the jurisdiction.
Starting with the very fine breakfast tendered me immediately following
my installation in October, by the brethren of San Francisco, I attended
the Board of Relief and Emplorment Service breakfasts at Los Angeles,
Long Beach, and Sacramento; the Masters and Wardens Assoeiation
breakfasts at Oakland, and Fresno; the Flag Day breakfast given by the
Officers' Association in San Diegp; and the St. John's Day breakfast given
by Anchor Lodge No. 273, at Compton.
At each of these breakfasts I gave the principal address, and in that
way was able to reach many more Masons than was possible through the
ordinary official visits.
The Los Angeles breakfast was outstanding, not only because of the
large attendance of seventeen hundred Masons, in spite of the fact that
no breakfast was .served, but that each of the brethren present paid sixty-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

41

five cents to defray the expenses of the meeting, thus affording themselves
the privilege of applauding the fine work of the Board of Relief and Employment Service .in this city.
At the Sacramento breakfast I had the honor of having in attendance
two outstanding Governors and Masons-our own Most Worshipful Earl
Warren, P. G. M., and Brother John W. Bricker, Governor of the State
of Ohio.
Inter-Jurisdictional Visits
We were fortunate in being able to have our Grand Lodge represented
at more than the usual number of Grand Lodge Communications this year.
The Annual Communications of our neighboring Grand Lodges occurred
at times when it was inconvenient for me to be present. Therefore,. I
asked R. W. Lawrence C. Kelley, Senior Grand Warden, to represent us
at the annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Arizona, in April;
R. W. Arthur W. Brouillet, J;.mior Grand Warden, to represent us at the
Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Nevada, in June; and R. W.
Gilbert C. De Forest, Deputy Grand Master, to represent us at the Annual
Communications of the Grand Lodges of Oregon and Washington, in June.
We were especially favored this year, also, in having Worshipful George
Frampton, Grand Bible Bearer, represent us at the Annual Communication
of the Grand Lodge of Idaho, in September. Brother Frampton's father
was a member of one of the Lodges in that Grand Jurisdiction.
In company with the Grand Secretary, M. W. Lloyd E. Wilson, I
attended the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Kansas, in
February, a.n d on the same trip we visited the headquarters of the Grand
Lodges of Missouri, New York and Louisiana.
In June, Mrs. Morrison and I went to Cedar Rapids for the purpose
of attending the Centennial Observance of the Grand Lodge of Iowa, and
on the same trip I spent one day at the Centennial Observance of the
Grand Lodge of Wisconsin, at Milwaukee.
The Observance of the Grand Lodge of Iowa was a very unusual event,
the whole program being in keeping with the fine traditions of this great
Jurisdiction. Representatives were present from most of the Grand Jurisdictions of the United States and Canada, and fifteen Jurisdictions were
represented by their Grand Masters. One of the interesting features of
the celebration was the Centennial Banquet, at which representatives of
those Grand Lodges from which the Grand Lodge of Iowa came; namely,
¥issouri, Tennessee and North Carolina, presented their felicitations, and
were followed by representatives of those Grand Jurisdictions which had
come directly from the Grand Lodge of Iowa; namely, North Dakota and
South Dakota. The fine hospitality and cordial good-will of our Iowa
brethren and their ladies will be one of our outstanding memories of this
year.
Grand Masters' Conference
·1n company with Lloyd E. Wilson, Grand Secretary, I attended the
Grand Masters' Conference in Washington, D. C., February 23rd and 24th.
The Grand Masters of most of the jurisdictions of the United States
and Canada were present, and the opportunity of meeting the leaders of
so many Grand Lodges was very welcome. At the annual banquet the
guests of honor included Brother General George C. Marshall, and Brother
Admiral Ernest J. King.
It was unfortunate that the program prepared for this Conference was
not one which had a universal appeal. While the papers presented were

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

well prepared, and showed much study of the various subjects on th~ part
of the Grand Masters who presented them, most of them were topics on
which each Grand Lodge has taken definite action and not much progress
can be made toward uniformity. Such live subjects as the large influx
of applicants, the program of Masonry toward our service men, our attitude
toward foreign Grand Lodges, if presented at all, elicited only perfunctory
interest and led to the conclusion on my part that while attendance at
these ~eetings is very desirable and worth-while from m:1:ny standpoints,
we still must rely for leadership and constructive thinking upon the many
fine men whom we are proud to call members of this Grand Jurisdiction.

Charles A. Shepherd, Inspector of the 102nd District, is able to be present
at this Annual Communication. We are glad, however, that W. Clair R.
Weaver, Master of Schofield Lodge No. 443, is with us today. We remember with interest the graphic picture of the Masonic activities in ·that great
fortress of offense and defense given us by Brother Potts last year. It is
difficult, however, to realize how zealous has been the devotion of our
Brethren in the Islands. Holding their meetings under wartime conditions,
which meant that for a portion of the time they must be off the streets
by eight o'clock, their Members burdened with the duties of civilian defense as well as those of their own jobs, these Masons have made an
outstanding record for themselves. Since Pearl Harbor the net membership in the two' Districts has increased about twenty-nine per cent. This
indicates, of course, that the actual conferring of degrees has been burdensome, and in addition it has been very difficult for some of the officers to
perform their duties. During that time they have contributed over three

D ispensation s
There have been many requests for special dispensations. Most of these
have been made for the purpose of receiving applications from men in
military service who did not possess the necessary residential qualifications,
and a few have been received for the purpose of balloting without reference
to a committee.
Upon the assurance of the Masters of the Lodges that proper investigations were being conducted I granted most of the former requests. I
granted some requests to ballot without reference to investigating committees in cases of yotmg men in the military service who had recently
reached their majority, and consequently had not previously had the opportunity to apply for the degrees of Masonry, and who had grown up in
the community and were therefore very well known to members of the
Lodge. In most of these cases these men had a few days at home and
could take their first steps in Masonry in their own Lodges. I declined
to honor other requests of this nature, as I have felt that no one would be
injured by following the regular procedure.
I have approved many changes in the by-laws of Lodges, most of them
being for increases in fees, and many amendments to life membership
resolutions providing for higher fees.
Growth in Membership
The report of the Grand Secretary will give you an idea as to the
growth in membership during the past year, a growth unparalleled in any
previous year.
As I have visited the various Lodges I have met many of the new
men who have come into our institution and I have been very highly
impressed with them. I find that in most cases the officers of the Lodges
are taking this growth in a very philosophical way, are investigating the
applicants very carefully and probably will feel no ill-effects from this war
flurry in after years.
Of course one wonders how effectively the investigating committees
are functioning in those Lodges which are having large influxes ot members, and only time will tell. However, we may get some idea of the
trend in the individual Lodge by comparing its rejections with its initiations. It is only reasonable to suppose that any Lodge which is alive to

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA
/

44

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

the situation will reject a certain number of applicants. What that percentage should be is open to conjecture. However, I think you will agree
that a Lodge which rejects twenty per cent of its applicants- over a period
of a year, and these are actual cases, probably is taking care of itself very
well, and that a Lodge which rejects only two per cent of its applicants
is piling up trouble for itself in the future. This is more significant when
we realize that in the first case the applications accepted represent a twenty
per cent ratio to the membership, and a forty per cent ratio in the latter
case. I am the last person to place implicit reliance in ratios or trends
of this kind, but I do suggest to the Masters and Wardens here today
that if you are not rejecting a reasonable number of the "applications submitted to you, your Lodge is either very fortunate, or somewhat careless.
A great many Lodges are using Personnel Committees with very
effective results. These committees openly interview the applicants and ·
determine, themselves, whether or not they seem to be imbued with the
ideals which will make them good Masons. Such committees of course
should function only after receipt of the application, and are not in lieu
of the secret Investigating Committees required by our Constitution. And,
to place additional emphasis on our responsibility, listen to this quotation
from the ceremonies of instituting a Lodge : "It does not follow that a
member of a Masonic Lodge is justified in giving his recommendation to
one who has signified a desire for the degrees of Masonry merely because
he knows nothing detrimental to his character. Something more than this
is required for the proper discharge of duty devolving upon him as a
Mason." The recommenders of an applicant for the degrees of Masonry
have a very serious responsibility. ·
Courtesy Degrees
We continue to confer more courtesy degrees than we request of other
Grand Lodges. Approximately three degrees a~e conferred in California
for each degree which we request to be conferred in other jurisdictions.
The loyalty of our Inspectors, and the consideration shown by the
officers of our Lodges, to those candidates whose degrees are requested
by other jurisdictions has been unfailing, and is highly appreciated, when
we realize that many of the officers are making real sacrifices to attend
many extra meetings for the purpose of conferring degrees on their own
candidates as well as those of other jurisdictions.
As the requests for courtesy degrees in other jurisdictions have passed
over my desk it has been interesting to note how widely scattered are
our men. We have requested degrees to be conferred in Australia, New
Caledonia and New Zealand, in England and in the Holy Land. Truly,
the outreach of Masonry augurs well for future peace, and better understanding in the world.

George Washington Masonic Memorial
While 'in Washington, the Grand Secretary and I attended the annual
meeting of the George Washington Masonic Memorial Association, of
which Brother Wilson, our Grand Secretary, is a Director.
·
This meeting was held in the Memorial at Alexandri·a, Virginia, this
being the first occasion I had had to see it in its present state of completion. I hope that every one of you who has the opportunity will not
neglect to visit this fine memorial to the Father of our Country. It is
not only a tribute to him, but to Masonry as well, and it is very inspiring
when viewed from the Washington Monument to see it loom up as one
of the outstanding structures of the surrounding country in a city of outstanding buildings.
Two interesting features are the Lodge room which is ready for use,
and the replica of the original Lodge hall in Alexandria which will be
used to house the priceless Washington relics which are now stored in
the basement of the Memorial.
To date approximately four and one-half million dollars have been
expended; this has come from Grand Lodges, other Masonic bodies, and
individual Masons all over the country. The Memorial is not completed.
Several rooms cannot be finished until after the war, and even then there
may not be sufficient funds on hand, although the Association has a substantial amount to be used for the necessary labor and material. And, of
course, after the Memorial is completed there will be a continuing annual
expense for maintenance.
Our Grand Lodge and the Masons of California have donated approximately $171,000 to this project, the last payment by Grand Lodge having
been ma'de in 1932. By some standards this is sufficient, and by other
standards we have not done enough. Some Grand Lodges are charging
a dollar a member for each new initiate, and others are making annual
contributions from their current funds. While I am proud of what we
have done, I felt somewhat concerned when I saw the enthusiasm of the
visiting Grand Masters, most of them representing Grand Lodges smaller
than ours, as they ma'de substantial contributions.
I recognize that some of our brethren feel that mistakes have been
made; that a less pretentious structure might have sufficed. That, however, is in the past. Having done nothing for twelve years we should now
determine whether or not we wish to be a continuing part of this great
project.
Therefore, upon my return from Washington, I appointed a special
committee on the George Washington Masonic Memorial, and have
requested this committee to study the subject and make recommendations
at this annual communication. The members of this committee are : M. W.
William B. Ogden, Past Grand Master; M. W . Leslie E . Wood, Past Grand
Master, and W. Samuel E . Dollar, Inspector 6lst District.
When this committee makes its report and recommendations, I trust
that you will give them your sympathetic consideration.

of any ~o~mittee to which this matter might be referred during this
commu111cat10n to ask them to approve any suggestions when they have

Q ualifying E xamin ation s for Secretaries
.At the !~st annual communication Grand Lodge approved Section 187a
which provides that a secretary-elect must, before being installed as such
produce to the installing officer a certificate of proficiency in those portion~
of our law relating to his duties and to the government of a lodge.
. I · do not wish to put myself in the position of disagreeing with the.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

51

However, I do feel that I should report the reaction among the secretaries
of the jurisdiction as I have found it.
A number of the Associations of Secretaries throughout the State have
gone on record as objecting to the procedure, and ask that steps be taken
to rescind the legislation.
Individual secretaries, generally, have not object~d to the examination
except that in most cases they thought it was unnecessary on the grounds
that a secretary who had been in office for a great many years was familiar
with his duties and the law and did not need an annual examination to
qualify him.
One Association of Secretaries in presenting the matter to me suggested that the legislation might be changed to require the examinations
of new secretaries only, and that if a secretary had once qualified it would
not be necessary for him to be re-examined before being re-installed.
I recognize that there is much merit in bringing up new questions in
the examinations every year, and that many of the secretaries might well
profit by being required to search the constitution for the answers to those
questions.
However, we must have real reasons for imposing additional burdens
on our officers, and these examinations make more work, not only for the
officers who take them, but for the Inspectors and the Grand Lodge
officers.
I recommend, therefore, that this question be re-examined, and that
consideration be given to modifying the terms of the legislation so that
examination of Secretaries previously qualified may be waived by the
Inspector.
Government of Lodges
I have been well impressed with the ability and sincerity of the Masters
of our Lodges ; I have met most of them personally and have corresponded
with others. In these difficult times they are guiding their Lodges with
intelligence and fraternal understanding. ·
From time to time reports have come to me as to this or that violation
of our law by some Masters. In these cases I have tried to avoid disciplinary measures. Sometimes I have asked Inspectors to correct the matters,
or I have written to the offending parties, making suggestions for improvement. In all cases I have received whole-hearted cooperation, making me realize more than ever that ours is a voluntary association of who
best can work and best agree.
Decisions
A great many questions on law and procedure have been submitted to
me. In some cases they have been asked informally, and in others a
formal reply has been requested. Sometimes a reference to the law has
been sufficient. However, I am reporting as "Decisions" those rulings
which I have made which I beli.eve may serve to clarify certain points in
our law, even though the rulings themselves may not make any important
addition.
In most cases I have declined to rule on the eligibility of liquor dealers because sufficient facts were not submitted, and I have held that t he
matter of deciding as to the eligibility of a person engaged in the liquor
business rested with the discretion of the Lodge. However, I had a series
of questions submitted to me on which I made a ruling which may or
may not add to the sum total of the law on the subject. I quote:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

"A restaurant operates in conjunction with a bar, or cocktail lounge,
in the following manner:
a. Patrons of the restaurant may order drinks with their meals, but
are not required to do so.
b. Patrons of the bar may order meals with their drinks, but are
not required to do so.
c. All liquor is served from the bar to either bar patrons or restaurant patrons; and
all food is served from the restaurant to either bar or restaurant
patrons.
d. At present, bar and restaurant are under common ownership and
management.

If the owner of such a restaurant applie.d for membership, does the mere fact that drinks are served without
food in the bar make him ineligible?
2. If a Mason buys the above described place, does he make
himself liable to charges of unMasonic conduct?

1.

Following is my reply:
"Section 210 of the Constitution reads as follows:
'No Lodge shall receive an application for the degrees of Masonry or
for affiliation, from any one who is engaged either as principal, agent or
employe in the saloon business (except in connection with and as part of
the operation of a bona fide hotel or restaurant), or who is a barkeeper;
and any Mason who may hereafter enter upon and engage in the saloon
business, whether as owner, agent or employe, except in connection with
and as part of the operation of a bona fide hotel or restaurant or who
shall become a barkeeper shall be deemed guilty of ~nmasonic' conduct,
and shall, upon due trial and conviction of said offense, forfeit all Masonic
rights and privileges, including membership in any lodge.'
This legislation was adopted in 1912, and is the same today as when
it was adopted. At that time we had saloons and barkeepers, and the
intention of the legislation seems to be very clear. It might be well to
recall the definition of a saloon as given by Grand Master Bledsoe in 1915:
'The Century Dictionary defines a saloon as a place where intoxicating
liquors are sold and drunk-a grog shop,' and he added 'and evidently the
Grand Lodge in enacting Section 129 (now Section 210) merely intended
to exclude from membership those who handled liquors in small qu,antities
usually found in connection with and to be consumed at a bar.'
Now, however, saloons as referred to above have disapp eared, but we
still have "places where intoxicating liquors are sold and drunk-grog
shops." I think that there is no question that the owner of such a place,
or a barkeeper therein, is ineligible to apply for degrees of Masonry.
There is, however, certain qualifying language in the original legislation; namely, "except in connection with and as part of the operation of .a
bona fide hotel or restaurant."
You do not state in your question whether or not the restaurant you
have in mind is a bona fide restaurant, and I believe that the answer to
your question hinges largely upon that point.
We know that hundreds, or possibly thousands, of hotels and restaurants operating in California today also operate cocktail bars, or saloons,
to use the old-fashioned name; many of these were in business during
prohibition and had no connection whatever with the liquor traffic at that

53

time. When prohibition ended they began serving liquor a~ .an adjun~t
to their hotel or restaurant business as a result of compet1t1on, and tn
many cases now operate cocktail bars, or saloons, separately, but in connection with the restaurant business, the restaurant part being the more
~ubstantial part of the business. In most of these cases undoubtedly the
restaurant is bona fide, and the engaging in such liquor business would not
even if drinks are served separately, in my opinion, operate as a bar to
lhe owner's applying for the degrees of Masonry, although a person employed exclusively in the cocktail bar should be classed as a barkeeper
and consequently ineligible to apply for the degrees.
If however a restaurant operates merely as a screen for the operation
of a ~ocktail b;r, and where the sale of liquor seems to be the major portion of the business, it could not be classed as a bona fide restaurant, and
the owner should be held ineligible to apply.
Between these two extremes fall many border line cases, and the
determination as to whether each case makes for eligibility or ineligibility
is very difficult without a complete examination of the facts, and .must of
necessity rest with the sound discretion of the Lodge. Ho~ever, 1f a particular case is resolved in favor of eligibility when an application is received the members of the Lodge must then decide whether or not the
applic~nt has those high qualities of character and sufficient standing in
the community which will make him a credit to the Lodge and to the
institution of Masonry in spite of the business in which he is engaged.
If this decision can be made in advance, honestly and sincerely, not much
time or sentiment will be wasted in the determination of eligibility or
ineligibility.
The answer to the second question hinges also upon the determination
of border line cases. A study of the character of the place which is operated by a Mason should determine whether or not it is the duty of the
Master or other officer of the lodge to prefer charges against him.
As long as we have the present system of retail liquor sales in California these will continue to be troublesome questions. However, they
should not be difficult if the welfare of Masonry is placed paramount to
all other interests.''

2
The matter of procedure in receiving applications for restoration to
membership after suspension for non-payment of dues seems to puzzle
some of our officers.
I held that no formal application is required, but that it could be in
the form of a letter. In making this statement, however, I pointed out to
the Lodge that the absence of a formal application does not relieve the
Lodge of the duty and responsibility of ascertaining by any means of investigation available whether or not the applicant is a worthy subject for
restoration.
On several occasions I have heard of Lodges which, for restoration of
suspended members, have charged the dues a~crued during .the tim.e of
suspension as well as the amounts due at the time of suspension. This of
course is in the province of the Lodge, although a portion, or all of the
accrued dues may be remitted by action of the Lodge. However, in one
particular case a suspended member whose accrued dues amounted to
something over $200.00 applied to the Lodge for restoration and .offe~ed
approximately $100.00 in settlement. The secretary, under the direction
of the Master, refused to present the application to the Lodge stating that

54

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

it would not consider the matter unless a check for the full amount of
arrearages acc.ompanied the application.
Section 260 of our Ordinances seems to provide that the matter of
restoration is one to be considered by the Lodge in all of its phases including that of payments of all or a portion of the arrearages.
'
It seems unfair to require payment in full, in advance, when the Lodge
its judgment may decide to remit a portion of the accrued dues; also,
1t does not seem consistent with the spirit of Masonry for a Lodge to require payment of dues over a long period when the suspended member
has had no benefit during that time. Such a procedure may restore· members, but does not extend a cordial welcome to one who desires to be restored.
I therefore advised this particular Master that in my judgment he had
no right to refuse to present an application for restoration to the Lodge,
regardless of whether or not it was accompanied by the fee; that a restoration could not be effective until the amount fixed by the Lodge had been
paid, and that the Lodge could act upon an application for restoration in
the absence of payment. I stated furthermore that if an applicant for
restoration enclosed a check for less than the amount of the arrearages
that act in itself should be considered an application for remission of the
balance of arrearages. In making this statement I did not in any way wish
to restrict the authority of the Lodge to act according to its best judgment
but I d.i d want to point out that a suspended member has certain rights:
one of which is to communicate directly with the Lodge from which he has
been suspended.

Public Schools Week
Over a period of twenty-five years our Committee on Public Schools
Week had grown from a few members until at the end of the 1943 communication it consisted of over thirty members. These members had been

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

56

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

selected principally from school men all over the State, and the responsibility for the Masonic observance of Public Schools Week was largely
left with these school officials.
I felt that there were several good reasons for appointing a smaller
Committee. There is a tendency on the part of the Masters and other
officers of the Lodges to throw the burden of arrangements on the public
schools and thus escape themselves the responsibility for a successful celebration. A smaller committee could place the responsibility for the Masonic participation of Public Schools Week on the Masters and officers
of the Lodges and thus attempt to get more universal support of this great
project. While we are enthusiastic supporters of the Public Schools we
should always reserve the right to make such constructive criticisms of
schools as seem proper at the time, and we would be in a better position
to do this were we not so closely affiliated with the schools by having so
many school men on the Public Schools Wec;k Committee.
Consequently, I limited the Committee to five men, with a secretary,
not one of whom is connected with the schools, and you will hear the
report from .the Chairman of the Committee.
I cannot pass this ' subject, however, without commenting upon the
attitude of many of our Masters toward Public Schools Week. I received
a number of requests to permit the conferring of degrees during this week,
all of which were refused. In one large city Public Schools Week was
observed in advance of the time set by Grand Lodge, and I a~ still waiting
for a report from the Chairman of that local committee explaining to me
the extent of the Masonic participation in that celebration.
The public schools, my brethren, are one of the most vital forces in
our present form of National existence. They are always in danger.
Selfishness and ambition are always seeking to make them into something
that they were not intended to be. While we are not political in any sense,
participation in Public School affairs is not political, and we are missing
a marvelous opportunity if we do not participate whole-heartedly in Public
Schools Week, bringing out to the public the weaknesses as well as the
strength of this great system of public instruction.
We should look with suspicion upon attempts to subsidize our schools
from outside sources and gradually remove them more and more from
local control.
We want to make every Mason Public School minded, so that ail will
join with gratitude and enthusiasm in bringing before the public the value
and necessity of this great cornerstone of our National life.
Masonic Homes and the Endowment Fund
One of the greatest projects in our Grand Lodge program is maintenance and security of our Masonic Homes. As I have appeared before
various meetings during the year I have felt it my duty to emphasize to
the brethren the fine work that is being done by Superintendents Eubanks
and Downen and the personnel at Decoto and Covina. One has but to
visit either of the Homes to assure himself that the welfare of our old
people and children is in safe hands.
The Board of Trustees is to be commended for its unflagging devotion
to the in.terests of the Homes. Meeting regularly in groups in San Francisco · and Los Angeles they pass on all applications for admission, and
on all policy matters in connection with the operation of our Homes. I
know tha; you will listen with interest to its report.
You will note that the population of the Children's Home at Covina

57

is at less than half of capacity. This is in line with the experience of all
Masonic Children's Homes at present. It is likely, however, that as the
tragic results of the war become more real there may be a greater ~eed
for our facilities. In the meantime, we have a fine plant only partially
used. In order to make the best use of this plant it might be well to relax
our entrance requirements for the time being or to enter into reciprocal
arrangements with other Grand Lodges for the care of children living in
California.
We are trying to insure the future of the Homes by building up the
Endowment fund. Great credit must be given Most Worshipful Frank
M. Smith, Past Grand Master, for the constructive and pioneering work
he has done in the past, and in the last two years in particular we have
begun to see the results of his fine work. Unfortunately, it became necessary for him to resign from the Chairmanship of the Board, and I asked
Worshipful Brother Ernest G. Bashor to take his place as Chairman.
The work has been carried on uninterruptedly, and I am sure that when
you hear the report you will agree with me that the Endowment Board
is to be commended, and that many Lodges are worthy of recognition for
the improvement they are making in supporting this great enterprise.
Constitution Month Observance
Like the observance of Public Schools Week, this is a program which
has been endorsed by Grand Lodge.
At the Grand Masters' Conference in Washington we were addressed
on the Constitution by Samuel B. Pettengill, who retired recently as
Deputy Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Indiana. In the course of
his remarks he stated that he felt that every Grand Lodge ought to institute an annual observance of the adoption of the Constitution. I was
very proud to be able to tell him that our Grand Lodge had had such an
observance for a number of years.
Headed for many years by Past Grand Master Robert B. Gaylord, and
this year by Leo E . Anderson, our Committees through many local observances have brought to the Masons of California the significance of our
Constitution, and the necessity of preserving the spirit of it.
I cannot commend too highly this project of Grand Lodge which tie:;
the ideals of Masonry into the application of practical citizenship.
Employment and Relief
Under the supervision of the Board of Control our Boards of Relief
and Employment Service are doing workmanlike jobs under war-time
conditions. While the figures indicate a falling off in requests, both for
relief and for jobs, there is no indications of a slackening of the work
done by these fine agencies of Masonry. While the number of jobs secured this year was considerably less than last year, the cost per job remains substantially the same. There is no doubt in my mind that during
the next few years we shall come to regard the work of these agencies
as probably the most important phase of all Masonic work.
California faces some tremendous problems in the post-war period. The
demobilization of war industries, combined with the needs of returning
soldiers, will test these organizations in a way that they have never been
tested before. The Board of Control and the various Employment and
Relief Boards deserve the sympathetic support of this Grand Lodge.

War Activities
We have continued to follow the standards respecting War Activities
which were outlined by Grand Master Wilson in 1941, and amplified by
Grand Master Smith in 1942 following the disaster at Pe~rl Harbor.
That policy has been continued except that we did not attempt to add
to our war fund, only in those cases in which Lodges had not reached their
quotas. Also, we attempted to coordinate the work under one committee
and Past Grand Master Leslie E. Wood consented to act as Chairman of
that committee. It must be borne in mind that this committee did not
and does not plan to institute service men's activities, or any other projects, in communities served by Lodges. In some cases it is assisting the
work of local Lodges, and at all times stands ready to supplement the
service which the Lodges are giving.
It is my belief, and I think that I speak for the committee when I say
that no activity for the service men in any community will be successful
unless it has the enthusiastic and continued support of the Lodge or
Lodges in that particular community, and that to be worthwhile such work
must be initiated by responsible Masons who are on the ground and know
the conditions in their particular com!Ilunities.
We are proud of the ten thousand Masons belonging to California
Lodges who have responded to the call of duty. Some of them have paid
the supreme s.a crifice, some will come back broken in body or in spirit.
Even with the advent of peace the important work of this committee
should be supported by Grand Lodge in an effort to inspire in all Masons
the determination to cushion the effects of the transformation from war to
peace, and to do our utmost to care for those who have suffered from the
effects of war. We must not overlook our individual responsibilities in
this war. By urging support of the Red Cross, the War Chests, the Blood
Banks and the War Bond Campaigns this committee has done constructive
service.
Masonic Information
Under the Chairmanship of Worshipful Reynold E. Blight, the Committee on Masonic Information continues to render very effective service.
The questionnaires which it has sent out periodically are calculated to
cover a wide range of subjects and consequently to interest a large proportion of those attending our meetings. So far as I can learn they have
met with great favor in our Lodges. This committee should assume a
greater importance as we approach the post-war era. Thousands of our
new members have had the opportunity to receive only the degrees and
necessary instruction. To provide more practical instruction for our
returning members, and then to integrate them successfully into the work
of our Lodges, should continue for this committee a very fertile field of
endeavor.

Investment Committee
I have only the highest regard for the members of the Investment
Committee, and we are fortunate that at the present time several of its
members are men who are skilled in the investment field. However, it is
an ex-officio committee, consisting of the chairman of various committees
and boards, and there is no reason to believe that in the future the chairmen of those committees and boards will possess the same investment
skill as the present members. Obviously it would be most unwise to make
any change at pre·s ent, but I believe that this provision is wrong. With
the increase in our Endowment ·Fund, and the growing importance of our
Grand Lodge funds, we should have the best investment advice available.
While I make no recommendation at present, eventually the Constitution
should be changed to provide that the members of the investment committee shall be chosen with due regard to their experience in investments,
that they shall have supervision over all the investments of Grand Lodge,
and its subsidiaries, and that they shall have the authority to employ such
trained assistance as may be neeessary.
