The Future
No review of the activities of the year is complete without giving some
consideration to what lies beyond us. We should not be so immersed
with the immediate work of Masonry that we cannot lift our eyes to the
ever-widening horizon of the future, and discover there· greater possibilities for usefulness and happiness through the teachings and influence of
our craft. We cannot imagine that the tragic lessons of this war will be
forgotten and that there will not ensue a new era ·o f progress and improvement, and we will not have learned the lessons of war if that era
does not produce much that shall encourage peace and understanding between men and nations, and as we are men of goodwill we should enter
this new era boldly, and with a determination to diffuse the principles of
peace anti understanding and toleration among all men, as well as among
Masons.
And, my brethren, there are certain fundamentals in our institution
that we should consider very carefully as we stand on the threshold of that
new era. There are those who feel that Masonry is entirely an individual
matter, that by means of instruction in our ritual we point out to the
individual great lessons in morality, belief in and understanding of God,
responsibilities to his brethren, and humanity, and the ever-impressive
duties of citizenship, and having pointed out those lessons the individual
is left to carve out his own Masonic career. Generally, this has been the
position of our Grand Lodge. We have not given much leadership in the
realm of Masonic thought. We have, however, deviated somewhat from
that policy by instituting Public Schools Week, and Constitution Observance Month, and by the collective ability of many able men have aided
the Lodges in bringing home to the individual member his civic responsibilities in these respects. While we should never lose sight of the primary
purpose of Masonry-to make better men-we must not neglect the potentialities of Grand Lodge.
Bearing in mind that we are having the largest influx of Masons in
our history, that many of them have received their degrees in other places,
that due to lack of time the instruction of most of them has been elementary, it stands to reason that the responsibility of integrating this
vast army of men into the ranks of Masonry must be shared by the Grand
Lodge with the individual Lodges, and in order to do this we must first
raise our sights, so far as Grand Lodge is concerned.
I do not think that we place sufficient emphasis upon Grand Lodge.
Ranking with the oldest and the best, and with potentialities far greater
than any, we must convince ourselves of our own dignity and importance.
We have certain responsibilities to our constituent Lodges, and to other
Grand Lodges, and we must discharge these responsibilities in a fitting and
dignified manner.
·
And as I direct your thinking into the channels of the future I want
you to know that I am serious in these proposals. Some of them may
appear to be trivial, and some revolutionary. We are not ready for the
adoption of any of them, and they are not presented for that purpose.

Several years ago the Grand Secretary',s o_ffice w~s refi~t~d with fu_rniture and furnishings in keeping with the d1gmty of his position. I believe
that as soon as the necessary materials are available we should extend
these improvements to all of the rooms occupied by the Grand Lodge.
The office set aside for use of the Grand Master is not _in any s.ense
modern and while seldom used should on necess.ary oc.cas1ons be such
as refle~ts the dignity of our institution. So far as is possible our quarters
should rank with the best in modern business offices.
Our Centennial
While it is too early to plan definitely for an observance. which wi_ll
not occur for six years, I feel that some attention should be given to this
subject in the not-too-distant future.
It will be remembered, of course, that our Cent~nnia.1 will fall in the
same year as the Centennial of th~ Statehood of. Cab for ma. Undoubtedly
much will be made of this celebration. At that time, also, v:e should r~nk
very high in the list of Grand Lodges of the world. A fitting celebration
of our Centennial should draw representatives from most of the Grand
Lodges of the country,' and prove very beneficial to our craft.
Finances
I am n~t certain that we are sufficiently ~nanced. _For a number of
years it has been our policy to levy a per capita tax which would i;iay the
expenses of the Grand Lodge, and keep our reserves at approximat ely

$250,000.00.

.

.h

In the meantime our Grand Lodge has assumed an importance wit
relation to other Grand Lodges much greater than in for~er years. We
are now the fifth in membership of all the Grand Lodges in the country.
It is not out of reason to feel that while our present rate of growth may
not continue we will have a very satisfactory increase in membership for
a number of years in the post-war period. It seems to me th~ part of
wisdom to consider whether or not our reserves should not be increased
in order that we may be better prepared for any unforeseen emergency.
While it is true that we can always raise the per capita tax, the money
can be well spared by most of the Lodges now, and it might be well during
these good times to build up our reserves. It seems to me t~at .a Grand
Lodge of our size should consider half a millic;in dollars an o~iective. for a
reserve fund. I do not feel that we should raise our per ca~1ta tax 1~ t~1e
Lodges but that in these t imes of activity we should keep it where it 1s,
and let' the Lodges assist in increasing our reserves when they can best
afford it.
Planning
" All of our committees of Grand Lodge function for the purpose. of
present expediency, their functions being generall~ to recommend or reiect
whatever matters are brought before them. As time goes on, as we grow
larger, and our problems become more complic~ted, and ~s the ~ime .of our
Grand Masters is taken up more and more with executive duties, it. ~ay
be of advantage to have a Planning ~ommittee for th~ purpose of assisting
the Grand Master, and for formulating recommendations to. Grand Lodge,
having future accomplishments in mind, these recommemiahons, of course,
to be submitted to the proper Constitutional Committees.

Whether or not this should be a Constitutional Committee is questionable as the Grand Master always has the privilege of calling on anyone
to serve on any committee. However, should such a committee be established, it should include the Deputv Grand Master, and the Senior and
Junior Grand Wardens, and thus make for continuity of policy and operation in our Grand Lodge affairs.

Communications

Program for Lodges

Except for a fow short bulletins sent in the last few years Grand Lodge
has never adopted any means of communicating with the membership of
its Lodges. The Masons of our jurisdiction receive only such bulletins
and messages as are sent to them by their own Lodges. No · attempt has
been made to coordinate the information and editorial matter that is given
our members. Some Lodges have pretentious papers and bulletins, some
give only the notices of meetings.

I believe that a program should be established which would tend to
maintain a closer relationship between the Grand Master and the constituent Lodges. While the Grand Lecturer and his assistants, the Inspectors, the various committees and boards all function well, I think that
much improvement could be made in coordinating all of the work of Grand
Lodge relating to the individual Lodges. The Lodges receive too much
material from too many sources.

If we a're to keep our members informed of the program and problems
of Masonry, consideration should be given to sending a Grand Lodge
bulletin direct to every member of our jurisdiction. Such a bulletin should
be prepared by an able editor and should represent the best thought of
Grand Lodge. Inasmuch as such a program would represent a considerable outlay it should be considered only when the results would justify the
cost in money, time and effort.

There would be considerable time saving if 'at the beginning of each
year a handbook could be prepared outlining the program of Grand Lodge
for the coming year. It would contain the dates of Public Schools Week,
Constitution Month Observance, Endowment Fund Month, and suggestions for the appointments of local committees early in the year. It would
contain also suggestions as to how material furnished by the Committee
on Masonic Information, or speakers furnished by.the History Committee,
could be used during the year.

With the continued popularity of radio and the imminent probability
of widespread use of television, we should not ignore the potentialities of
communicating with our brethren and enlightening them on Masonic questions through. the use of radio. It .is not beyond the realm of possibility
that Grand Masters, on important occaGions, may address Masons in their
Lodges and in their homes, and that the committee on Masonic Information, or other committees, may rely on the radio to bring to Masons information and instruction which will make them more keenly alive to the
privileges . and responsibilities of Masonry. It is quite possible that new
Masons may obtain information on Masonic subjects by the use of the
radio. It is not too radical a departure from our accepted practices to
envision the time when monthly or quarterly programs will be broadcast
to all Masons, particularly to new Masons, and that •listening to this program may · form as important a part in their final instructions as taking
their proficiency examinations, and that proficiency certificates might be
issued on the basis of general Masonic information as well as on ritualistic
attainment.

Presented to the incoming Masters at the time they are. making up
their programs for the year such a handbook would be of vast assistance
to theip, and would tend to make them more conscious of their responsibilities to an integ.r ated Grand Lodge program.
Order of De Molay
The relationship of Grand Lodge to De Molay has been settled for
many years. It is in no sense a part of Masonry, and yet the relationship
is very close. Many fine Masons are devoting untold hours to the training of youth through the ideals of De Molay. It requires tact, patience
and an understanding of youth to head a De Molay Chapter. To the
extent th~t the Advisory Councils function well, Masonry reflects the
credit, and to the extent that our De Molay advisors are short-sighted and
constantly at friction with the members of the Chapters, Masonry is
blamed.
I feel that we are too close to this subject to ignore il. I do not feel
that any of. us know enough about the subject to make any recommendations. However, I think that Masonry must assume at least part of the
responsibility for curbing the juvenile delinquency which is rampant in
this State, and that possibly more progress may be made by taking a
more constructive attitude toward the Order of De Molay.
Within the next few years thousands of young men will be looking
for places to work in Masonry. Many of them will be war heroes and
capable of leading youth through the ideals of De Molay. It is not too
early for us to start thinking of this, and by means of special committees,
or other means, study this problem in order that the greatest good may
come from this great Order.
Any committee investigating the Order of De Molay should consider
very carefully the national organization of the Order, and before making
any recommendation which would give us a more definite relationship,
assure itself as to the soundness of its national leadership.

The first thought that occurs to you as you listen to these comments
is the same that occurs to me--who is going to do this work? Where are
we to find the men with the ability and enthusiasm to lead us into new
fields of Masonic endeavor? They are here, my brethren. We have
them in our Lodges, and many more are coming in, but they are not attending our Lodges because they are not interested in the things that we
do there. Many of them have found activities more to their liking in
the collateral bodies of Masonry, and many of them are engaged in civrc
and welfare affairs. When we provide the program the men wiil be
available.
We should always bear in mind that we can lead only so far as men are
able to follow; that the level of human ability, interest and loyalty can be
raised only gradually.
In Conclusion
We should not forget the continued fulfillment of the purpose for which
we became Masons. While this varies with each individual Mason, it is
connected with the well-being and improvement of mankind through the
application of the principle of good to the individual man.
In a world torn with prejudice and ill will we can and should be known
as men of goodwill. When others scoff at this or that creed, race or sect,
we should, with the tolerance of perfect understanding, assist the world ·

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAN D LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

to a better understanding. We should hate nothing but hatred and intolerance.
We must respect our individual personalities, we must support our
rights as individuals, but in supporting those rights we must accept the
responsibilities which go with those rights, and those responsibilities can
Oest be discharged by that service which comes from loyal enthusiasm and
clear, unbiased thinking.
Such is. the program of Masonry. The development of the individual
by the combined, intellectual and material resources of his Lodge and
Grand Lodge, and with it all the nuturing of faith, a faith that enables him
to look to the future with confidence, a faith born of belief in God.
I am wondering if · you see the picture as I see it. We have a great
institution, rich with the traditions of the past, and bright with the potentialities of the future. This institution can never rise above the sincerity,
the ability and enthusiasm of the men who compose it. The primary purpose of Masonry is to make better men, and if we are to accomplish this
purpose we must not only invoke the aid of the traditions of the past, but
take advantage of all of the help that modern science can give us.
They say that the soldiers and sailors in the field, on and under the .
water, and in the air, have a special kind of faith. It is not a blind faith,
nor a faith born of fatalism. It rises above danger, and continues firm
w:hen their comrades do not return. They implement their faith with action, and make .those actions count against their enemies whose faith is
blind' and born of hatred.
My br.ethren, .our battle is one of peace. Our enemies are intolerance
and ' ig~obn~e. . ···bur weapons are intelligence and understanding and love.
By in:iple~ehting our faith with action 'may we encourage and incite all
Masons to ri~e 'to higher levels of..interest and accomplishment, and thus
speed the real V-Day when ignpra'iice and' misunderstanding are no more.

REPORT OF COMM ITT E E ON CONSTITUTION
MONTH OBSE.RV ANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Mast.er and Brethren of the Grand Lodge of
the liwisdiction of California:

Your Committee on Constitution Month Observance reports as
follows:
'
'
This report will be divided into three sections to cover, first, . the
organization of the committee, second, results of the observance, and
third, the purposes of the committee.
Immediately following the appointment of the committee, we set about
to organize the work of the committee members in such a way that all
·the Lodges could be divided by areas and a member of the committee
selected to represent .. that . area on the committee. Past Grand Master
rJan:w.s -T:· !lf.!'as.e r was assigned the northern area of California, including
distric;ts. ,1.•,9. Brothe.r~ Albert C. Wo11en.l;>erg an.d Brother Hanns H.
'S\ratmann, both o.~ San Francisco, were assigned the districts in the San

6i

Each member of the committee was furnished vyith the names and
addresses of the inspectors of the districts within his respective area and
requested to keep in touch with the Lodges and Inspectors, to be of whatever assistance possible in carrying on the activities of Constitution 01;>servance Month. The first letter sent to the Lodges and Inspectors in
May by the committee, specified the areas as cletermjned by the committee so that each I~_spector and each Lodge would know immediately
which member of the committee should be contacted for information,
assistance and material. The second letter of the committee was sent out
in August AS a final reminder of the necessity for holding an observance of
the adoption of our federal Constitution, with a short form of report to
be filed with the Grand Secretary by each Lodge.
We have gone into the organization of the committee in considerable
detail in order that the committee which will assume the responsibility for
the activities of Constitution Month Observance next year will have the
benefit of our experience, and we believe th e method of organization was
extremely helpful in carrying out the work of the committee. We knew
that a meeting of the committee as a whole should be avoided, if possible,
because of the difficulties of travel, securing hotel reservations and taking
the necessary time from our usual activities to travel from one end of the
state to the other. Accordingly, the committee's activities w ere carried
on entirely by correspondence and we are very happy to report that so
far as we have been able to ascertain, the observance was almost universal
and carried out smoothly and without confusion. Many members of the
committee are to be particularly congratulated upon the thorough job
they did in handling their areas. Many members of the committee made
a personal contact with every Inspector and every Lodge within the area
in addition to the letter which was sent out by the committee and followed up by reporting to the chairman of the committee the activities of
the various Lodges in detail. One member of the committee, J udge William R. McKay of Los Angeles, in addition to the work we ·have previously
outlined, addressed ten separate observances, addressing over 625 persons
who attended these meetings. The reports of meetings were a ll forwarded
to the Grand Secretary, who in his usual efficient manner, caused the results to be tabulated.
Reports have been received by .the Grand Secretary from 324 Lodges
of a ·total of 582. From the reporting Lodges we find that 274 meetings·
were held, with a tota l attendance of 18,447. Assuming that t he reports
from other Lodges, most of whom held meetings, would maintain the·
average attendance. of the reporting Lodges, we are th en ab le to report

68

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

that 35,733 attended the meetings sponsored by the Lodges this year.
When we realize that each person who attended any of these meetings
was reminded of the historical background of our Constitution, its benefits
and its accomplishments, and undoubtedly gained some new knowledge,
we see that the work of the committee and of the Inspectors and of the
officers of the Lodges has . not been in vain but, on the contrary, has
accomplished the important objective of keeping before the people of
California the importance of zealously guarding the American system of
representative government and freedom of opportunity.
We are pleased also to report that although $500 was budgeted for the
expenses of the Constitution Month Observance Committee, only $165.83
has been expended and those expenditures were for printing and mailing
the notices to the Lodges-a very small expenditure .for a very large
service.
Our sole regret is that not all of the Lodges held an observance of
Constitution Month and in many cases not enough interest was shown
in the observance to make it a success. For example, ten Lodges joined
together for the observance of Constitution Month and even though there
were ten Lodges involved, only 70 persons were present, 28 of whom
were women and children and 5 were not members of the fraternity. In
other words, only 37 Masons, representing 10 Lodges, were sufficiently
interested to attend the meeting. If we contrast this meeting with another
meeting held in one of our smaller cities, sponsored by one Lodge, at
which 225 persons were present, we believe you will see that one meeting
was enthusiastically supported while the other was not given the necessary
support to secure the attendance of even the officers of the Lodges involved. We are happy to report that in almost all instances a fine attendance was present, but a few cases, s1,1ch as the one we have cited, illustrate
the necessity for the officers of the Lodges to look upon the Constitution
Month Observance as an opportunity to do something to support and
perpetuate our Constitution rather than as a duty which must be performed with as little effort and attention as possible. The Masonic fraternity has a great .stake in our Constitution, not only because it embodies
the principles of freedom and representative government toward which
mankind has been struggling for ages, but also because that Constitution
has, in 157 years, given to the people of these United States more opportunity and a better way of life than any other gqvernmental document in
history. Some of you have heard this said before, but it will bear repeating. History shows that in most instances the things which w,e receive
by inheritance, by gift and without any effort on our part are lightly regarded and soon dissipated, wasted or lost. The things we work the
hardest for are the things we cherish and keep. That ·same lesson applies
to our Constitution . . We inherited it from our forefathers, many of whom
gave their lives to secure the freedom and the opportunity which our
Constitution represents. We are very likely to treat this great heritage
lightly and if we do, we are apt to lose it. We hope that our Lodges who
did not consider Constitution Observance of sufficient importance to
themselves, their families and their country to put forth a real effort to
bring the message of the Constitution to as many people as possible will
make certain that the observance next year will be a credit to the Lodge,
to the fraternity and of real benefit to the nation. Our boys in all corners
of the globe are fighting to preserve freedom. The least we at home can
do is to preserve it here.
We respectfully urge that the committee be continued with an appropriate budget and that you brethren in attendance at Grand Lodge

GRANO LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

each make it your individual project to make next year's observance
bigger and better. In closing, may we remind you that this is an election
year, that the results of the election may have a far-reaching effect upon
our future. It is our duty as Masons and as Americans to vote and to
see that our friends and families also vote.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK COMMITTEE
To .the M . W. Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
It is impossible, of course, in such a report as this to even refer to,
much less make adequate mention of, the many outstanding local observances, and of the fine work responsible for them. Our treatment must
be of the observance generally. And perhaps as concise and yet comprehensive an account as could be given appears in a letter to our Committee
from the Superintendent of a very large city school system from which
we quote :
" Public Schools Week has come and gone. In the few weeks
since that event was celebrated, reactions have come to this office
and we can now look at the occasion in perspective. I am very
glad to give you the following comments:
"1. Practically all Public Schools Week activities, this year,
were carried on at schools. A few meetings were held in lodge
halls where school pupils presented programs.
"2. All schools in - - - observed the entire week doing the
following:
a. Maintaining open house-welcoming visitors and displaying
pupils' work.
b. Performing community services-sending g roups of pupils
to service clubs, churches, w;omen's clubs, etc.
c. All Parent-Teacher Association activities centered around
Public Schools Week purposes.

71

d. Youth activity groups such as the Scouts and Campfire
Girls and youth work agencies such as the · Woodcraft
Rangers and the Y. M. C. A., all conducted special activities at schools in the community they serve.
e: Community newspapers and community business houses
cooperated by using special news releases, posters, and
reports prepared at schools.
"3. The theme of Public Schools Week this year was threefold :
a. Youth activities and constructive services which will counteract destructive habits.
b. Paµ-iotism and loyalty to our country, the particular pupil
habits and activities which make for good citizenship.
c. An emphasis upon spiritual and cultural values, so that in
a war period and at a time when materials and production
are so important, there will not be overlooked the fine,
human, spiritual needs by which man always lives.
"4. This year Public Schools Week was more successful than
ever :
a. There was more intelligent visiting of schools.
b. There was more expression of desire to cooperate with
schools.
c. '.Ihere we.re more parent and child activities conducted together than any ·time heretofore.
d. There were more discussion groups and question· and
answer meetings where the real interests of those anxious
to help their children were served.
e. This year, more than ever before, we were successful in
having the cooperation of other civic groups, such as the
Housing Authorities, the City and County Health Service,
the Playground Department, service clubs, youth service
agencies, and better than ever the Parent-Teacher Association."
.Anotl\er Superintendent of a large school system wrote the local Comm'ittee· as follows :
"I have no hesitancy in reporting to you that the Twenty-fifth
Observance of Public Schools W eek, under the guidance of
Masonic officials in "this area, has been the most successful and
the m:ost satisfactory of any observance that we have had in this
community in my recollection.
"Certainly this year's observance has demonstrated that individual Masons have a sincere and intelligent interest in the
schools, and that they are willing to sacrifice their time in order
to manifest this interest and to aid the schools."
Reports were received from many communities indicating that in spite
of wartime conditions and restrictions the Twenty-fifth Observance of
Public Schools Week was one of the n:iost successful eyer held. Typical
of these was this we quote:
"We have just concluded what I am sure was a most successful Public Schools Week. There were thousands of visitors to
the schools throughout the entire week and the major evening
meetings enjoyed overflow houses. At - - - High School in my
own neighborhood it was necessary to close the doors of the

the grounds while the auditorium program was in progress. I
think it may be said that this was a fair sample of the attendance
throughout the week at the ·other meetings."

This was especially gratifying, and somewhat surprising in the case of
the newspapers because of war-time limitations on their space. In addition tq the news stories, there were editorial~, cartoons and special articles

In addition to the other war conditions with which we were confronted last year, and which had not become very much, if any, better,
there were this year two big handicaps to be overcome for a successful
observance of Public Schools Week.

There. was, one editorial (a long one in a large metropolitan. newspaper)
which seems to call for some mention. It was one of the clippings
attached to the report of an observance in which the service clubs of
the community appear to have played an important part. From other
attached newspaper clippings it appears that local school officials had
announced that the nation's schools are facing a financial crisis; and that
here in California although the expense of maintaining the schools has
materially increased, the allotment from the State has remained unchanged
and that an ever increasing burden is being placed on the local districts.
The local Committee of Arrangements therefore decided that ·during
Public Schools Week it would be well to have the people acquainted with
the way in which the cost of the schools is financed by having talks made
before meetings of the' service clubs and at the public meeting which
would be held. Now, of course, this is just exactly one of the things
the people should know; and it would seem that Public Schools Week,

The other handicap was the situation of the school people in communities where there had been either a material increase in the number
of pupils, or a decrease in the number of teachers-or perhaps both. This
meant, of course, increased and extraordinary demands upon the time
and energy and patience of the teachers still in service. They could
hardly be expected to grow enthusiastic over suggested plaris for entertaining visitors.
That both these handicaps were overcome is in itself a tribute Jo the
school people and to organized Masonry. But even the zeal, industry
and intelligence with which they arranged and carried out the program
would not, alone, account for the success that was achieved. What
assured success was the public support which resulted, in part at least,
from the cooperation of those organizations on which we have come to
·
confidently rely.
This year in addition to the proclamations by the Governor and by
the Mayors of many of our municipalities, and the calls and notices
issued by the heads of the cooperating agencies which have so willingly
and enthusiastically joined with us in the observance of Public Schools
Week, there were two other notable proclamations; one was by the President of the California State Federation of Labor and the other was by
the President of the California C. I. 0. Council. Both urged the members
of their respective organizations to participate in the observance by visiting
the schools and thus become acquainted with their problems and "to
make whatever criticisms may come to mind."
As indicating the extent to which the community is now represente'd

"Let us not devote Public Schools Week to a study of school
taxation. The subject of taxation is a shifting thing. We cannot
tell today what our taxation plan or foundation will be tomorrow."

- - - high school curriculum, a student Public Schools Week
survey shows.
"Science classes are training microscopes on possible new
sources of war-short chemicals and foods; learning basic principles of aeronautics and navigation; drilling prospective army,
navy and merchant marine officer candidates in mathematics and
technical subjects.
"Food classes are learning to can and dehydrate food, juggle
ration points; clothing classes are making over garments and
becoming textile wise.
"Social studies and English classes are figuring out what we
are fighting for and why, with heavy accent on European history,
geography and American life and institutions, and the home
front's place in total war.
"In the thick of war work are the high school shops, which
work for the coast guard and the Red Cross and lend their facilities to these agencies after school hours.
"The commercial department, besides placing students in war
jobs, is tutoring them in payroll procedure, taxes, rationing and
price control; wartime selling and advertising; while the health
department has gone in for 'commando' physical training."
There were many reports of programs through which the extracurricula war activities in which the pupils had engaged were brought to
the attention of the public. Usually this was done throug·h the medium
of printed or mimeographed material distributed to visitors. But this
was only one of the methods pursued; and the contribution to the war
effort made by their respective schools was the subject of some of the talks
made by student speakers at meetings of clubs and other organizations to
which they had been invited. There were also stage representations of
various sorts. One of the most interesting of those reported was a meeting
of the student council presented as a feature of the program of a junior
high school. The council is composed of representatives of thirty-two
"home rooms" and the heads of all the activity groups, with the President
of the Student Association as the presiding officer. Reports were received
from each of the activity groups and then discussed by the council.
That the schools and the school children of California have made and
are making a material contribution to the war effort there can be no doubt.
Not only have they engaged in campaigns for the sale of war stamps and
war bonds, and for the planting of victory gardens, and in salvage work,
and the collection of books and magazines for military camps and for the
Red Cross, but through the 4-4 plan of four hours in school and four
hours in useful work they have materially helped in relieving the shortage
of manpower. And in the shops and in the trade schools they have made
stretchers and stretcher stands, operating tables, air raid cushions, and
useful articles of various sorts for the comfort of service men a11d of their
families.
The sale of war bonds is not ordinarily a part of the observance of
Public Schools Week. But there was a report this year of a "War Bond
Auction" which was a novel feature of a program presented in the auditorium of a union high school. A seven months old purebred registered
Holstein bull calf had been donated by the owner of the herd to be given
to the largest war bond purchaser. The President of the Lions Club acted
as auctioneer and the auction was made an amusing, as well as a most
interesting, feature of an open house that was described by · a local paper
as "an outstanding success."

In connection with this r.eference to a particular community; mention
should be perhaps here made of the fact that the Twenty-fifth Observance
of Public Schools Week was held under conditions almost identical with
those which prevailed during the first observance, and which furnished
the reason for the institution of th~ movement. Now, as was the case
then, a crisis confronts our public schools; and it is said by competent
authorities that California is face to face with the threat of a serious
breakdown in educational standards and of closed schools in some areas.
Again there is a dearth of competent teachers; and in order to prevent
schools in certain rural areas from being closed, it has become necessary
to lower the high credential standards maintained in California and issue
emergency credentials to teachers whose qualifications are not up to
our normal standards. A report from the Chief of the Sta.te Division
of Elementary Schools discloses that 1906 elementary emergency credentials have been issued to teachers now employed in rural districts, and
that many schools would have been closed if this had not been done.
As was also the case when our first observance was held, what is
proposed as a remedial measure in the form of an amendment to the
State Constitution will be submitted to the people at the general election
to be held this year.
If this amendment has not already been, it undoubtedly will be, called
to the attention of the brethren in their respective localities by either
those who favor, or those who oppose it-perhaps, by both. It would
not be appropriate to here make further reference to it because organized
Masonry does not, nor should Masons as ~uch, give support, nor offer
opposition, to any pending legislation or any measure to be passed upon
by all the people. It is, however, assumed that because of the professions
we as Masons make with respect to our public schools each one of us
as an individual citizen will make himself familiar with the provisions
of the proposed amendment and then vote as his conscience dictates.

somewhat critical of the work of the schools. The complaint m6st often
voiced was that "the fundamentals" are being neglected and that there
has been a general deterioration of school standards in America. It is

urged to avail themselves of· the opportunity offered by Public. Schools
Week to find answers to the questions that were being asked.

Again this year "open house" at .the schools was the dominant feature
of most of the local observances. · There are, however, communities in
which the week is observed by a public meeting with visits to the schools
as merely incidental. Until precluded by war conditions, there were several
places in which each of several district schools held its own observance
and then joined with all the others in a night meeting. And even this
year the Master of one· of our Lodges reported that they had ten schools
in their district and· had had a meeting in each school with a big meeting
in the union high school on the last night.

The service clubs seem to have been especially active this year. Many
held their regular weekly luncheon meeting in a school cafeteria with a .
school man, or in some instances a student, as the speaker. They not
only sponsored essay, poster, and other student contests, and donated
valuable prizes, but they also furnished teams to compete against student
teams in spelling bees and quiz contests of various sorts. This year a
Soroptimist Club was among the service clubs holding noonday· meetings
in school cafeterias.

76

Of course a personal visit to the school and a talk with teachers and
administrators is the best way to find out just what our schools are doing,
and why it is being done. But this does not mean there should be no
night meetings, with properly arranged programs. The ideal observance
combines both methods, and is indicated in the following brief quotation
from a splendid report of an observance held in one of our large cities:
"Practically every school in - · - - had a program for the week.
The elementary schools maintained open house and classroom
demonstrations during the week. Some of the element;iry schools
had prepared assembly programs. The junior high schools with
adequate auditoriums put on evening programs. The senior high
schools cooperated in the opening program on Monday evening.
The Junior college had a special assembly. The trades school and
adult education classes maintained open house duripg the week.
Programs were planned for each evening during the entire: week."
As perhaps was to be expected more attention than ever before was
this year given to the trade and vocational schools where they are maintained. Here visitors saw demonstrations and exhibits of courses in boat
building, carpentry, dental assistants, industrial electricity, acetylene welding, electric welding, machine shop, radio and electronics, sheetmetal,
upholstery, millinery, power sewing, dressmaking and alterations, drafting,
steamfitting, plumbing and tool and die making.
These schools also furnished extremely interestin.g exhibits for the
store window displays which were made possible through the courtesy
of merchants who donated the space. And most interesting of course
were the so-called "live exhibits" where students were at work in the
window just as they would be in their classes at school. In passing,
mention should be made of the fact that not only was window space
made available, but there were reports of the use of entire floors of vacant
buildings having been obtained for exhibits and demonstrations of school
work.
One of the most gratifying developments disclosed by the reports was
the increase in the number of programs evidently arranged with the idea
of conveying information rather than for mere entertainment. Forums
and panel discussions were largely used for that purpose, with adults or
advanced students participating. But in at least one instance the children
of a first grade explained to visitors how they learn to read.
This modern method of learning to read used in some schools is
frequently referred to in newspaper clippings attached to reports of
observances. One of these clippings shows a photograph of five first
graders listening to their t eacher as she points out phrases in a reading
lesson; and in an adjoining column headed "Reverse System in Reading
Study': is a very interesting description of the method in which sentences,
phrases, words, syllables and then letters are the steps in learning to read.
Incidentally visitors to that school saw the abacus being used to teach

77

An interesting, and a very significant, development of Public Schools
Week, particularly noticeable this year, is the extent to which the week
is observed by clubs and other organizations not acting in conjunction
with the local committee of arrangements, nor even, in some instances,
with its knowledge.
One of these observances this year was by a lodge of E lks with a
meeting in its lodge room, at which there was presented a program entitled
" Education for Today." And there were several Shrine clubs which made
their luncheon meetings during that week a "Public Schools Week" meeting, with either a school man or a student as the speaker, and a program
furnished by the pupils of the local schools. And in at least one instance
where a Shrine Club did not devote its luncheon meeting exclusively to
the observance, it recognized it by having the local school aut horities as
its guests, and formally introducing them to the audience.
There were also events for which the arrangements had been independently made by local units of such organizations as League of Women
Voters, Parent-Teacher Associations and American University Women,
but which were included in the official program of the community observance. Among the most interesting of these reported was a Forum
sponsored by a center of California League of Women Voters, the ParentTeacher Association of the school in which it was held, and a local Public
Education Society. The subject was "T h e Truth About Your Elementary
Schools"; and there appears to have been a very thorough and animated
discussion of the scope and aims of the elementary school and of the
curriculum and methods of instruction. It was an ideal program.
The success of one observance was said to have been due to the fact
that public interest reached an all-time high because the people of that
community had become "very school conscious." Now that is just what
accounts for the success of the observance generally in spite of the wartime conditions which would seem to militate against it. The people of
California have indeed become "very school conscious"; and the increase
of public interest in our annual observance is the best evidence of just
how close the schools are to the people of California, and how close the
people, in turn, are to our schools-the most cherished of our American
institutions.
All of which is respectfully s4bmitted,

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California herewith present
the fifty-second annual report, for the year ending July 31, 1944, togeth.er
with the reports of the Superintendents of our Homes, and the financial
reports of the Secretary and Treasurer.
The Board of Trustees met on October 15, 1943, after the adjournment
of Grand Lodge with the following members present:
Samuel E. Burke (term expires 1944) .
Chas. Albert Adams (term expires 1945) .
Charles M. Wollenberg (term expires 1946).
James B. Gist (term expires 1947).
Gilbert C. DeForest, Deputy Grand Master.
Lawrence C. Kelley, Senior Grand Warden.
Arthur W. Brouillet, Junior Grand Warden.
The reappointment of Past Grand Master, James B. Gist, to the Board
of Trustees for a four-year term commencing October 15, 1943, and the
election of Gilbert C. DeForest, Deputy Grand Master; Lawrence C.
Kelley, Senior Grand Warden; Arthur W. Brouillet, Junior Grand Warden, were formally reported to the Board.
The board then organized for the ensuing year by electing the following officers:.
Charles M. Wollenberg, president.
Jam es B. Gist, vice-president.
By Virtue of his office as Grand Treasurer of th.e Grand Lodge, F. &
A. M. of California, Past Grand Master Francis V. Keesling is Treasurer
of the Masonic Homes of California.
By virtue of his office as Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge, F, &
A. M. of California, Past Grand Master Lloyd E. Wilson is Secr.e~ary
of the Masoni~ Homes, of California.

Meetings
For many years, it has been the custom to hold a number of gener~l
meetings of the entire board .throughout the year, but due to war. conditions and the difficulties of travel, there have been but two meetmgs of
the entire board held during the year since the Organization Meeting
at the close of Grand Lodge. The general meetings are of real value
and should be resumed as conditions permit. The weekly meetings of
the Northern members of the Board held ·each Friday in San Francisco,
and those of the Southern members. of the Board held each Tuesday in
Los Angeles have been held 'regula.rly throughout the year.
Population
As might be expected with the present conditions of employment and
prosperity prevailing, t~ere . has been a decrease in the number of ~es!­
dents at both of our Howes. The decrease has not been great and 1t 1s
not believed that it repres.e nts any permanent trend.
Like all other organizations and i11~.titutions ·in the State of California,
a real problem has developed in the matter of maintaining an adequate
staff at each of the Homes. The lure of defense work with high :-vages
has taken many employees both from Decoto and Covina during the year,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

79

and as a result, both Homes have been forced to operate with inadequate
staffs.
The loyalty and efficiency of the employees who have remained has
been very much appreciated and has been a real factor in carrying forward
the work on the present high plane. Too much praise cannot be given
our two Superintendents, John M. Downen at Covina, and James R.
Eubanks at Decoto, for the splendid manner in which they have carried
on and administered their work under these trying conditions.
Old Age Assistance
For a': number of years, the question of what to do with Old Age
Assistance for our residents at Decoto .has been an increasing problem.
The practical question which confr6nts ' the Board is whether or not the
residents of Decoto should be permitted to apply for Old Age Assistance.
Under the law, they would be entitled to it, but the Trustees have
constantly discouraged any of our residents applying for this assistance,
because if the money received by them from the State were turned over·
to the Masonic Homes, it would mean that in effect we would be operating
a boarding house and not a home for brother Masons; furthermore, if the
money received as a pension was not collected for room, and board and
shelter, it would mean that they were accepting money from the state for
food, shelter and the necessities of life which in actual practice is being provided by their •Masonit brethren.
Since ·it is the desire of the Masons of 'California fo provide a Home
for their brethren, the Trustees have deemed it wise to discourage the
acceptance of Old Age Assistance by the residents at Decoto.

Summer Camp
The changing character of the area adjacent to our summer camp at
Balboa has been a matter of concern to the Trustees for some years, and
they have felt that the development of the area made impossible the
continuance of a proper summer program at that location for-the children
from Covina. The sale of the Balboa property has been discussed from
time to time without any action being taken until during the present year
an offer was received of $25,000 cash for the property. After giving
serious consideration to the matter from every standpoint, the Trustees
accepted the offer and the total sum realized from this sale has been
placed in a special Fund for the development of a summer camp at a ·
different location after the war.
Scholarship
Another· indication of the current availability of employment and the
general prosperity of the times is shown by the fact that but one scholarship
request was made during the year. Miss J ewe! Bottger (Hermann Lodge
No. 127) desired to continue with advanced training and on the recommendation of Superintendent Downen, the Trustees being convinced that
the applicant was serious about the continuance of her education, granted
$500.00 to her from the S1=holarship' Fund for the year.
Alumni in the Armed Forces
In addition to those women mentioned by Superintendent Downen
as being in the armed services, it was my experience a few weeks ago
to visit the Hammond General Hospital at Modesto where I found Mary
Raffety, who was from the Home and who for some years was secretary
of the School Board of the City of Covina. She had given up a $300
p~sition as secretary to the general manager of an aircraft plant in Southern California to become a hospital social worker and if you had seen
the faces of the bedfast men in this military hospital light up as she
appeared in the ward you would realize that although she does not wear
the uniform ·of one of our armed forces she is doing her bit in this
emergency.
Many letters have been received from our alumni on the fighting
fronts. Time will not permit the reading of but two excerpts but we
are sure you will find them of interest. Others are to be found in
Superintendent Downen's report.
''Life is really a subject, when you get right down to it. I've seen
the precious candle of life burning at its fullest in our 'ready room'
where we have our talk and receive our orders, and then within ten
minutes see it snuffed out so quick you can't seem to realize it. Why?Who knows- things just happen and I guess it will always be that way."
GEORGE Pr.ASTER, u. s. N.

Finances
The financial situation of the Homes has been given serious consideration.
The auditor's report reveals cash on hand July 31, 1944 of $141,628.92.·
The funds received by the Homes with the annual returns total $214,846.00,
thus making cash available for fiscal year August 1, 1944-July 31, 1945,
'
$356,474.00.
In the light of this favorable financial situation, the Trustees have
decided upon the following program:
1. To transfer from the present cash available, the sum of $100,000.00
to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund.
2. To use the cash on hand for the operation and maintenance of the
Masonic Homes of California, during the current fiscal year.
3. To request no per c;apita assessment for the fiscal year August 1,
1944 to July 31 , 1945, other than the constitutional per capita tax provided
in Section 99.
Aside from other considerations, a ver~ practical and constructive
effect of this program will be to place the Masonic Homes on the same
basis as Grand Lodge, namely, to have on hand at the annual communication of Grand Lodge the necessary funds for the operation of the Homes
during the fiscal year in which the Grand Lodge session is held,

Our previous report indicated that at the close of the fiscal year of
1943, there were 283 members enjoying the comfort and protection of the
Home.
During the year, we have lost by death 19 women, their average age
was 80.47, and 18 men, their average age 76.61; 15 women were admitted;
average age 74.47, and 17 men, their average age was 75.64, and 1 man
was withdrawn by his Lodge and returned to his family. Most of those
admitted during the year came to us in a rather frail physical condition.
The end of the year leaves us with 148 women and 129 men, including
13 married couples; of this number there are 2 women and 5 men out
on extended leaves, contributing to the war efforts.

Grand Matron, Dr. Francis J. Herz, Worothy Grand Patron, and their
corps of Grand Officers of the Grand Chapter 0. E. S. were introduced.
Piano selections rendered by Mrs. Herbert Harris, Grand Organist, and
Mrs. Evelyn Taulbee, and vocal solos by Mrs. Virginia Lord, our Matron,
and Mrs. Ruth Hunter, added much pleasure and enjoyment to the program.
The East Bay Masters' and Wardens' Association, under the able
leadership of their President Alvin A. Harwege, made their visit on
August 27, and presented the residents of our Home with an excellent
show. The occasion offered a splendid opportunity for the members
of the Association and their families to visit the Home, fraternize with
and becQJll~ b,e tter acquainted with the family.
Jmi.ior Grand Warden Arthur W. Brouillet and Grand Secretary Lloyd
E. Wilson made very interesting addresses.
Other programs which have ·been presented during the year were made
by R. K. 0., Columbia Pictures, United Artists, Warner Brothers. and
Twentieth Century Fox, film distributing companies of San Francisco.
These film distributing companies furnish the Home gratis each Thursday
evening a complete moving picture program.
The Ministerial Association of Southern Alameda County, consisting
of Rev. John W. Winkley, Rev. Wilder V. Immel, Rev. 0. D. Ironmonger and Rev. Thos. C. Harris of Hayward and Rev. Hoyt J . Hamilton
of Ashland, have been conducting our Sunday devotional services. The
members of the Home are very grateful to these gentleman for the fine
messages they bring to them each week.
·
Our library is kept well supplied with books, magazines a nd periodicals
by friends and members of the Fraternity. These contributions provide
our members with many hours of enjoyable reading and enable them to
keep up to date on current events.
Other Grand Lodge officers who have visited the Home during the
year in addition to our Grand Secretary and our Junior Grand Warden,
which I have mentioned above, were Past Grand Master Charles Wollenberg, Past Grand Master Charles Albert Adams, Senior Grand Warden
Lawrence C. Kelley and Most Worshipful Grand Master Claude H .
Morrison.

Morrison and his · good wife personally greeted and shook hands with
each member of the Home.

Age groups of the residents are as follows:
5 between the ages of 50 and 60 years,
45 between the ages of 60 and 70 years,
126 between the ages of 70 and 80 years,
89 between the ages of 80 and 90 years,
12 between the ages of 90 and 100 years..
The average age for women, 76.06 and for men 77 years.
The health condition of the residents at the Home during the past
year has been very good, considering the advanced ages which the above
table indicates.
Miss Esther G. Payne is still supervising the work in the hospital,
where about 45 of our members are being cared for.
It is difficult, due to our inability to secure enough competent help,
to maintain the high standard which has always been maintained in the
hospital department. However, I am pleased to say that Miss Payne
and Dr. McWhirter, handicapped as· they are, are doing a very fine job.
Mrs. Virginia Lord, our Matron, is having the same difficulty in the
Home. In both cases many of the members are assisting; their assistance
is invaluable. With the help of our members, we are able to keep the
Home and hospital presentable, and the grounds also present a fairly
pleas~i;ig appearance.
. ·Many repairs and much painting should be done. As soon as· we areable to get the material and labor, these matters will be taken care of>
and when the work is completed will add much to the appearance of the
Home.
A very good showing has been made- on the small portion of land
which is retained by the Home.
Our records indicate that the value of the poultry and eggs was $542.13,
pork $827.40 and fruits and vegetables $1192.37, or a total of $2561.90.
Due to transp9.~_tation conditions, we have not had as many entertainments this Y.e ar as we have had in past years; however, those that
were presented were excellent, and thoroughly enjoyed by our family.
The two outstanding programs of the year were the East Bay Past
Matrons' Association and the East Bay Masters' and Wardens' Association.
The East Bay Past Matrons' Association made their annual visit on
August 19 and presented the Home with a goodly supply of jams, jellies,
and many useful articles such as nightgowns, bureau scarfs, hospital
gowns and quilts. A complete list of these articles will be found in
anothe.r part of our report~

Report of Superintendent-Covina Home

To the Trustees of the M asonic H omes of California:
'rn submitting my annual reports for the past two years, I commented
upon the decreasing enrollment at the Covina Home, the turnover in

our employed staff, the need to raise salaries in many instances to retain
good employees, the rise in prices of all commodities, and the influence

to rise. During the year 1943-44 these same conditions have prevailed.

In thinking of the reduction in population in the Covina Home year
by year for the last twelve years, its significance can be estimated only
in the light of the population trends of other Masonic Homes. We find
that our reduction in enrollment is similar to that of the other twent~·
Masonic Homes in the United States. There is a marked relationship
between the lessening populations of Masonic Homes on the one hand,
and the general improvement in employment opportunities for boys and
girls on the other hand. As times got better the call on the Masonic
Homes for their services got less; this is norrrial and to be expected.
We know that as a child gets older he is likely to become more impatient to escape the restr.ictions of group living. The youngster of sixteen
or seventeen sees real money in his pockets and more freedom to go
and do as he pleases on the outside than he can be allowed when in the
Home. This is a result of more employment opportunities, more chances
to make money in larger quantities than he can have in the Home. However, under our money earning system in the Home older boys and girls
have been able to earn a modest sum each week with which to defray
certain items charged against them.

101

. The thing th_e child cannot see is that the restrictions imposed upon
him at the Covina Home are all for his benefit, and that his earnings
at the Home should not be compared with what he mig ht earn outside.
. An illustrative case is that of three brothers, each of whom has exerted
himself at the age of about sixteen to win his independence from the
Home; in each case it has been thought better to discharge the boy. The
third one of these boys is now in foster care outside the H ome, and we
have recently had letters from the other two (both now enlisted in the
service) asking us to exert all our influence with the third boy to persuade
him to do wha_t we failed in persuading them to do, namely: to stay in
school. We will, of course, keep trying with this one, but do not have
much hope of success.
The inability of adolescent children to see the necessity for restraint
is a large fact; it is part of the condition of being adolescent that the
child going through this period cannot be made to see its symptoms. Our
present chaotic economic situation tends to exaggerate these symptoms.
In many cases adolescent children have perception enough to know how
much money the;v could earn on the outside and not enough perception
to know how this would figure out by the time their expenses on the
outside are paid. . When by dint of teasing and wheedling they finally
ge_t a parent. to g1v~ in to their request, it is usually too late to do any~hing a_bout 1t.. ,It 1~ only when they have profited by a little experience
in a wider community that they begin to reflect on what they so stubbornly refused to accept as a better preparation for adult life. The following excerpt from a letter written by an alumnus of 1942 is illustrative:
" Remember the little redheaded boy who didn't give a care
for anything and was trying his best to get out of school as soon
as possible? Well, he hasn't changed much, from an outside
appearance, but he sure has some different viewpoints on life now.
I can remember one statement he always used to make, and that
was, 'When I get out of school I'll never wish I was back.'
BUT! Oh, how I wish I could live those days over again. Yes,
this is really me saying that . .. ."
. Health of Children-We have been able to retain the competent services of our nurse who has been with us for seven years. In that time
she has come to know well the children in the Home and their health
needs. Through her capable management, in spite of limited medical
service, the health of the children has been unusually good. The daily
average number of patients in the hospital during the year has been
only 2.02.
Summer Camp-Without the camp at Balboa, the summer recreational
program threatened to be a problem. A n SOS was sent out and Miss
Dorothy Barcus, of the University of Redlands, picked up our call and
came to the rescue. Under her guidance the children have enjoyed trips
to Po_mo_na for horseback riding, bowling and roller skating. We have
had picnic suppers on the grounds, a 4th of July Picnic at Covina Park
and watermelon parties and wienie roasts. Movies on Friday at Covina'.
Our regular S~turday ?ight shows in our own auditorium, usually followed by dancing at either the girls' building or the beys.' The pool
has been busy every day, and a water carnival was a Saturday afternoon
feature. Special all-day be~ch trips were enjoyed and a bus load of boys
attend~d the Aquacade-Sw1m Meet at the Coliseum. Twelve boys and
four girls attended c~mp through opportunities afforded by the Y. M.
C. A., Boy Scouts, Girl Scouts, etc. All in all. it. has been a good sum-

102

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

mer, and now we are ready to return to classes on September 11 when
schools reopen for the fall session.
Orthodontia Treatment-We have now six children who are under
orthodontia treatment in Los Angeles. These are only our worst cases.
We have some children, who by lack of orthodontia treatment will suffer
throughout their lives those social and physical disabilities' which are
sequela of neglected treatment. Expense involved in the treatment of
these six children is being taken care of otherwise than through regular
funds, by special donations which have been given for this purpose.
Repairs to Buildings and Equipment--In undertaking repairs to buildings and equipment, our•thought has been chiefly to prevent deterioration
of a serious nature. We recognize that a number of r)!pairs and replacements to both buildings and equipment will be necessary in the coming
months, such as roofing, painting, and plumbing replacements.
Alumni in the Armed Forces- Last yea'r the panel in the hallway of
the Administration Building at the Covina Home contained the names
of 126 of its alumni who are in the Armed Forces of the United States.
Now this number has increased to 159.
Eight of our young women graduates are in the Armed Forces:
Georgiana Davis, Tujunga Lodge No. 592, left the Home in 1935, and
is a private in the Women's Army Corps; Corporal Rosetta Lewin Los
Angeles Lodge No. 42, left the Home in 1938; Private Marian Hass', San
Francisco Lodge No. 360, left the Home in 1940; and Private Dorothy
Jordan, Justice Lodge No. 549, left the Home in 1940-all are in the
~arine Corps. In the Waves, U. S. Navy, are: Helen Hass, San Francisco Lodge No. 360, left the Home in 1939; Alice Parbery, Excelsior
Lodge No. 166, left the Home in 1942, and Betty Richards, Monte Vista
Lodge No. 655, left the Home in 1940. Helen Schulte, Hermann Lodge
No. 127, left the Home in 1936, is a Second Lieutenant in the U. S. Army
Nursing Corps and is at present on foreign service.
Eight boys have given their lives in their country's service: Walter
Anderson (Apollo Lodge No. 396), U. S. Navy; Walter Smith (Ocean
Park Lodge No. 369), U. S. Navy; Second Lieutenant Melvin R. Rouch
(T~a".er Lodge No. 294), U. S. Army, killed piloting a plane in Africa;
Aviation Cadet Ralph E. Peterson (Victorville Lodge No. 634) U. S.
Army, killed in training at Williams Field, Arizona ; First Li~utenant
Lawrence S. Myers (University Lodge No. 394), U. S. Army, killed in
action in the Southwest Pacific; Fred E. Kathan (Security Lodge No.
581), U . S. Ma~ine Corps, died in line of duty, Southwest Pacific; Jack
Gorbett (Ontario Lodge No. 301), U. S. Army, died in line of duty
Mediterranean area; Fred Burgen (Alhambra Lodge No. 322) U.
Army, killed in action, Biak Island.

A year ago the number of Masonic Home Alumni who had received
commissions as officers was twenty; this number has now been increased
to thirty-two, or 21 % of the total number of Alumni serving their country.
T~ey repr~sent:. one Colonel, two Lieutenant-Commanders, two Captains,
thirteen First Lieutenants, eleven Second Lieutenants and three Ensigns.

Relationship of Home Personnel and Children to the Military Alumni
-A great deal of time and attention is being given to our Alumni in
service. They write frequent letters to members of our staff as well
as to Superintendent and Mrs. Downen. Their expressions mak~ it clear
that letters from the Home family are eagerly awaited and are a great
encouragement to those who are in faraway places.
At present we are finishing .a very considerable work in getting out
another Newsletter of twenty-eight pages. It will have a mailing list of
475, including not ·o nly the military boys but also all alumni of either sex.
One of the boys who received the last issue, March, 1944, wrote back
from New Guinea, and his expression is typical:
·
"I just received the Newsletter and do appreciate it a lot. I
have written about twenty letters out of it so far. Page 4 was
missing from my copy of the Newsletter. Would you please send
me the sheet containing pages 3 and 4 as they are about the most
interesting of the letter. I almost cried when I read it and
thought it over."
The sheet containing pages 3 and 4 was the little article entitled
"Meandering" and told about an imaginary trip through the Home by
an alumnus comfog back after years of absence.
. A month or so after writing this letter, Fred Burgen met his fate on
B1ak Island. One of the fine things connected with this boy's service
and its end is indicated in a letter written to Fred's mother by General
MacArthur, as follows:
"I cannot express to you the poignancy of my regrets at the
death of your son, Cpl. Fred A. Burgen. His service under me
was characterized by his complete devotion to our beloved country and his noble death integrates him with its imperishable glory.
I have lost a gallant comrade in arms and with you mourn a
splendid gentleman."
There is something poignant that inheres in these letters from alumni
especially since we know that some of them will not come back.
'

GRAND LODGE OF CALI FORNIA

107

Boys often seem to want to visit the "old" home, "just to see the
old place once more"; it has for them significant memories which a mere
visit seems to satisfy. They come to the Home as to a shrine and absorb
impressions which they wish to cherish for a long time. T hey go away
not laughing, but solemn.
Among letters recently received were those from a boy we will call
Bill Smith. He wrote Mother's Day letters to several of our women
employees. To one he expressed himself as follows:
"Do you remember our talks about everything from politics
to flowers? It was stamp collecting and our club on · Friday
nights. It was Christmas, the presents, and the train in the
library on Sunday afternoons. There were our exhibitions of
magic in the basement .a nd our 'Camp Crumbs' at Balboa, and
our dramatic stunts and skits-I shall pever forget it.
"It's things like these that make me feel fortunate that I knew
you. Your kindness toward me in all those years, your neverfailing faith and trust, your smile, and your laughter; your
buoyant, happy atti tude, your love of all good things. So I'm
proud this Mother' s Day that I know you, and that I can sign
this as Your Son-Bill."
Entertainments, Visitations, Donations--Since transportation has become so restricted, visitations by Lodges and interested individuals to
the Home have become less and less. We look forward · to the time
when these visits may be renewed.
Through the interest and generous contributions of the Beverly Management Corporation, we have been ab le to do many things for the
children which are not included in regular operating expense. During
summer vacation, twenty-one children had an opportunity to spend from
one to two weeks at summer camps operated by Boy Scouts, Girl Scouts,
Camp Fire Girls, Y. W. C. A.
Carrying out its custom of many years, Monrovia L~dge No. 308,
gave a delightful Christmas Party for the children at Monrovia. This
party is an annual highlight in lives of the children, and they usually
start talking about it long before the holiday season.
Several years ago we had in the Home a group of four boys, now
in their early twenties, who formed a little special "secret" club which
they called the "TST." These boys are now scattered far a nd wide,
three of them are now commissioned officers, one is a civilian employee
of the Hindustan Aircraft, Ltd., in India. Not long ago Superintendent
Downen received a letter from one of the boys enclosing two $50.00 War
Bonds. He said, "These are the first annual contributions from Philip
and myself to the TST Post War Fund. We are planning to collect
a fund which will some day be large enough to· draw on to s·end a
deserving child or children from the Home to college. We have only
a rough draft plan which we will whip into shape during our first reunion.
We want you to be our strong box for the duration. Will you kindly
handle this for the TST and be prepared to receive more contributions
as we send them."
]ORN

M. DowNEN, Superintetideut.

REPORT OF MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT
BOARD
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
It is with ~leasure that we present herewith the twelfth annual report
of the Masonic Homes Endowment Board, covering the period from
August 1st, 1943 to July 31st, 1944, inclusive:
~he Board was created by action of Grand Lodge (Constitution ~nd
Ordinances, Art. V) and consists of fifteen members. The personnel of
the present Board is as follows:

1944
Ernest G. Bashor
Raymond Taylor
Louis C. Drapeau
James T. Fraser
Ira D. Wheeler

1945
Wm. Rhodes Hervey
Robert B. Gaylord
Edmund A. 'Lockett
Henry G. Hill
Frank M. Smith

1946
Reynold E. Blight
Harry F. White
Carl E . Miller
Rollie W. Miller
Orno E. Tyler

The officers of the Board are :
Ernest G. Bashor, Chairman
Wm. Rhodes Hervey, Vice-Chairman
Robert B. Gaylord, Vice-Chairman
Francis V. Keesling, Treasurer
Lloyd E. Wilson, Secretary

119

The purpose of the Board is to "study, devise, and carry out plans for
the securing of adequate endowment for the Masonic Homes of Californi<L." To that end and in keeping with the policy of previous Boards,
it has been our aim to stimulate interest in our two Homes among the
Lodges and membership within our jurisdiction.
We believe our program is a long range educational one. The ultimate
purpose is to secure a sufficient endowment from which the monies obtained will properly maintain our Homes. This is not impossible or just
theoretical, but it may take many years to reach such a goal. When we
realize the rapid strides that have been made in the few short years of our
endeavor, and the splendid response attained, we are encouraged to greater
efforts. Most gratifying is the larger number of brethren that are participating. In the 1943 report some 12,000 individuals mq.de contributions.
During the past fiscal year, more than 25,000 had a share in this activity.
Such response is heartwarming to your Board, and makes us realize that
more than twice as many Masons have had a share in the support of
our guest Homes during 1943-44.
Some changes have been instituted during the past year, mainly in the
collection of moneys and handling the details in the business affairs of
the Board. The reaction of the Lodges leads us to conclude these have
served a useful purpose and are appreciated. The cost of collecting and
operating the fund is very low and the centralization of business operations has proved economical and efficient . It has been advisable to operate
on· a fiscal year basis, in accord with the Grand Lodge financial program.
This may seem to work a hardship on some Lodges as to reporting their
total contributions this year, but an additional list is appended herewith,
showing total collections up to September 25th, 1944. It is believed that
next year's report will not necessitate this additional list, as the change,
by that ti!Ile, will be thorough ly established.
In a separat.e pamphlet is shown the auditor's statement, with the
essential facts which should be of interest to the brethren.
A special committee was appointed from the Board with instructions
to ascertain from the honor roll Lodges the methods that were used and
the one that gave the most satisfactory results. The committee concluded
that no one plan is applicable to all L odges, large and small, nor to any
definite part of the jurisdiction, but the interest shown and the many
inquiries, have led your Board to believe that certain information in a
condensed form should be gathered and made accessible for use by the
Masters, Secretaries, Special Committeemen, and others who have so
valiantly been carrying on this work. To that end, a pamphlet of information is being prepared, and should be available in the near future.
This report must include a word of sincere appreciation and thanks
to the many who have given their time and their talents in carrying on
this important and vital Masonic program and, without whose cooperation
and support, little could have been accomplished. First, our special thanks
and appreciation to the Grand Master for his continuous and untiring
efforts throughout the year and on every occasion where it was appropriate he has, in a most forceful manner, presented the cause of our
Homes to the brethren. His splendid Proclamation designating the month
of May as Masonic Homes Endowment month brought to the Craft
throughout the jurisdiction the importance of the work, the opportunity
of service, and the significance of this Masonic accomplishment. To those
splendid men, our Inspectors, we are grateful for their support. To all
the officers of Grand Lodge, and to the fine group of Masters, Secretaries,

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Committee Chairmen, and the many brethren who have rallied tb our
aid, we are deeply grateful, and commend to you continued interest and
effort until a complete realization of our program may be effected.
The Chairman, Secretary, and other members of your Board, have
made an honest effort to answer all correspondence, which has been multitudinous in nature; have responded to requests where personal appearance
was desired; and have endeavored to cooperate to the fullest ex.tent with
your individual Lodge activities al~ng this line.
It is a great personal satisfaction to every one of us to see our Fund
accumulate and grow progressively toward a satisfactory goal. We are
sure your personal pride and satisfaction to this end will be a stimulus
for your continued and greater support.

Adopted and referred to the Committee on Finance.

This is believed to be the largest increase in membership in Grand
Lodge history. We are nearly back to the year 1931 when we reported
142,422 members, the highest in our history.
The withdrawals increased only 16 over last year.
The suspensions for non-payment of dues dropped from 997 to 629.
The losses from death increased 135 over last year. During the past
ten years the deaths have increased from 1,905 to 2,433, a yearly average
gain of 53.
We congratulate Grand Lodge on the year's activities. We are not
unmindful of the depression years that followed World War I. Let us
plan our future so we may not suffer the great losses in membership in
the years that follow World War II.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History begs leave to submit the following report, together with its recommendations :
We are in full accord with. expressed desire of the Grand Master that
reports of committees at this communication be curtailed to a minimum.
Therefore, we will refrain from our annual custom of enumerating in
detail in this report the many highly interesting Masonic stories collected
during the past year, and also a recital of the work and activities of the
Committee and its individual members.
We feel that this Committee should be continued for the ensuing year,
and the sum of $100.00 be appropriated and set aside for its use, and we
so recommend.

REPORT OF TRUSTEES OF THE MASONIC CLUBHOUSE AT U. C. L. A.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Board of Directors of Masonic Clubhouse U. C. L. A. presents
the following report for the year just closed:
It will be rem.e mbered that the University of California took over our
property May 1, 1943 for use as a Mess Hall for Army Cadets· and we
moved our Club activities to space which we rented in ·the Y. W. C. A.
Bldg.

This arrangement continued until April 30th of this year, on which
date the University vacated the property, the Army having previously
withdrawn all Cadets from the University.
The Los Angeles Chapter of the American Red Cross, being badly
hampered in its work in this important district because of lack of suitable
housing for its several functions, requested the use of our property where
all of its work could be coordinated.
After careful consideration on the part of our young people, and our
Board of Directors, it was the unanimous opinion . that we would greatly
assist the war effort by complying with the .request. Negotiations culminated in bur leasing the property to ·t~e Los Angeles Chapter of the American Red Cross for a period beginning June 1, 1944 and expiring September
1, 1945 at a monthly rental of $250.00, which sum, it is estimated, will be
sufficient to meet our "out of pocket" expenses chargeable to the Clubhouse.
The activities continue at the Y. W. C. A. building as before. Although
our membership is much reduced, we continue to be the best organized
and the strongest group on the campus.
As contemplated in our report last year, we have paid all expenses out
of rentals and still have impounded the sum of $3,096.99 of Grand Lodge
funds which we ~ad on hand when the University took over the property.
The budget for the ensuing Masonic year divides itself into two parts
as before-the expense of carrying on the limited activities of the Club
itself amounting to $1,825.00 for the year, and the expense of the Clubhouse property, an amount of $4,020.00.
A complete statement of our financial condition is reflected by Brother
Reynold E. Blight's audit report which is attached hereto and made a part
hereof.
