REPORT OF WAR ACTIVITIES COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
I have the pleasure of presenting, for your consideration, the report of
the War Activities Committee, in which we attempt to outline the work
of this Grand Lodge in behalf of the members in the service of their
country and their families.
Early in the year, the Grand Master directed a questionnaire to the
Masters of the constituent Lodges in which he asked questions pertinent
to the subject of partici!'ation of the Lodges in war work activities. The
majority of the answers showed a desire on the part of the Masters to
have their Lodges play a part in this program. Many of them asked this
committee for suggestions, with the result that, on March 1, 1944 a folder
was mailed to the Lodges, outlining, what this committee believed to be a
well rounded program, and one which could be followed in whole or in
part by all Lodges. It was suggested that a war activities committee be
appointed in each Lodge 't o have charge of the work. From the many
letters received from Masters and committee chairmen, we believe that the
majority of the Lodges have an adequate war program and are carrying
on this activity in spite of the unprecedented amount of degree work,
naturally· brought about by war conditions.
Hospital Section
Under this heading the War Activities Committee is effectively carrying on the work established by Grand Lodge more than a year ago.
The yeat has seen continue.<;! expansion of both Army and Navy hospitals in this state; those und~r construction last year are now in full operation, and others have been expanded to take care of additional beds.
b~e to transportation difficulties, it has been impossible for the chairman of this section to visit each of the hospitals this year as was done last
year. However, practically all the hospitals in the northern part of the
state have been visited and through correspondence, we have been able
to keep in touch with the commanding officers and our representatives in
those hospitals we were unable to visit.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFO~NIA

The year has been one of many changes in personnel.- Some of the
commanding officers, with whom we have worked, have been assigned to
other areas, while several of the men who acted as our representatives
have been transferred to other duties. However, in each of these instances,
we have been able to arrange for the appointment of a new representative.
In passing, it is interesting to note that, of the eighteen men who act as
our representatives, only four are members of California Lodges; the
others are from jurisdictions all over the country. These men have
rendered a valuable service to California Masonry, they have been ever
willing to go out of their way to obtain for us information about the men
in their respective hospitals, which we could not have obtained through
any other source. We acknowledge this service and regret, that for
reasons of security, we cannot make their names public at this time.

the leyel; where he could read or write that letter home amid quiet surroimdings; where he might feel that he is wanted and made to feel at
home. No attempt has been made to duplicate the work of the U.S.0. or
other existing agencies, but rather to supplement their efforts with a
service they cannot perform for our members.
In the Palm Springs area we found an encampment of approximately
200,000 men, with no Masonic Lodge in the vici~ity. Your committee
felt that in this particular instance, it would be advisable to open a clubroom, with writing tables, rest room and showers available. This project
becaine so popular with our service men and the requests were so numerous for its continuance, that after the six months' trial period had elapsed,
it was decided to continue the clubroom as long as there is an apparent
need for it.
Lodge Activities Section

126

Almost two hundred requests for information about 'men in the hospitals have been received this year, and as a result of our efforts and the
help of our representatives, we have been able to bring cheer and comfort
to the folk back home, by getting first-hand information concerning their
loved ones, and when requested, doing for them those things which can
be done only by a Masonic organization.
There have been few cases of relief in the hospitals. This is due partly.
to the fact that sick and injured men are rapidly removed from this area.
Men in the hospitals are receiving the best possible medical attention.
Many famous doctors and surgeons are members of the various hospital
staffs. Every effort is being made to prepare those seriously injured, to
care for themselves after being discharged and elaborate rehabilitation
schools have been set up to put into effect the provisions of the . G. I. Bill,
We feel that it is impossible to make a word picture clear enough to
properly portray the valuable w()rk . which has been accomplished in the
hospitals. We can only say that every case which has come to our attention has received the consideration which one might expect Masonry to
give to one of its members in distress.
Camp Service Section
This section of the committee has endeavored to stimulate the activities
of those Lodges situated close to military encampments. Unfortunately,
many large camps have been established within a few miles of some of
the smaller Lodges. Despite their small membership these Lodi'es are
performing a fine Masonic service to their brethren in uniform, making
them feel at home in the Lodge, and performing those acts of brotherly
love, which only a Masonic Lodge can extend to a brother Mason. The
true spirit of these Lodges is best shown by the fact that, although the
ente~tainment of these visiting brethren has, in many instances, been a
financial burden, with two exceptions they have refused reimbursement
from the War Fund of. this Grand Lodge.
Under the instruction of Grand Lodge, this committee has not attempted to establish club rooms in any of our California cities. If . this
work. is to be attempted, it must be initiated by those Lodges which feel
that a Masonic Club is needed in their city. The War Fund would have
to be many times its present size if this activity were to be undertaken by
a committee of Grand Lodge. We could not erect a club in one city and
deny that privilege to another. We have, however, urged those Lodges
which are in a position to do so, to open a room in their Temple"s for the
use of service men. A place where the Mason in uniform could be surrounded by a Masonic atmosphere; where he could meet his brethren on

127

It has been the aim of this section to encourage Lodges in their individual war activities. The effectiveness of this work is demonstrated by
the great number of Lodges which have set up programs to keep in touch
with their members in the armed forces, particularly those serving outside
the continental United States; also keeping in touch with the families
here at home, rendering them every Masonic service which they may
require.
The purchase of War Bonds, donations to the Red Cross, the War
Chest and the Blood Bank on the part of individual members have been
stressed by this committee. The majority of Lodges have made this a
part of their regular war program.
Relief and Employment Section
So far the demands made upon the Lodges have been limited. However wha't the future may bring,_ no man can foresee. Many complicated
and 'gigantic problems may present themselves without warning. In this
respect the committee has leaned rather heavily on the several Boards of
Relief and Employment Services and the Board of Control.
So far our problem has been that of service to the men in the armed
forces and their families. Now, with thousands of men being discharged
from service and with the conditions which will follow the war we must
give careful thought to the rehabilitation of our members and to the
placement of thousands of men in jobs. Our task will be to aid in this
re-adjust171ent and in the many problems that are apt to arise. Employers
will look with favor upon our employment service because our Managers
have performed such a splendid job in helping them during peace times
and during this present period of labor shortage.
Our Boards of Relief have worked quietly and thus are little known
outside the fraternity. During the present emergency this has somewhat
changed, due to frequent contacts ~ith the hospitals and the many bases
of the armed forces.
One of the problems which may become serious in our jurisdiction was
pointed out to us by the Secretary of the Board in one of our southern
cities. They have thirteen Masonic Lodges with a membership of thirtyeight hundred. A survey shows that twenty thousand sojourning Masons
are residing within the city. This condition is not peculiar to that city
alone. With the great influx of war workers to our state and with the
tens of thousands of service men passing through or located here for
the duration, many of them with their families, we are going to experience
a substantial increase in population. Many of these men will be Masons

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

from other jurisdictions and doubtless will seek our services. How are we
to meet this condition?
We must have unity in America and among ourselves if we are going
to solve the problems of unemployment, free enterprise, freedom of choice,
of individual initiative and freedom of opportunity. Business must be
encouraged to expand in order to abso~b all available labor. Financial
institutions must aid in the establishment of new enterprises and the expansion and improvement of those existing businesses which may desire
such assistance. The younger men and women must be encouraged t<;>
continue their education to prepare them for useful and fruitful lives and
thus remove them from the immediate ranks of job seekers. The physically
handicapped must be given a place in the field of useful workers. Some
vocations ar already opening for them. Insurance companies are advertising the fact that these men can be put on the payroll and. share under compensation insurance, regardless of their handicap.
To carry oi.it the program to anything like a successful conclusion, we
must ask the aid of every California Mason. Carry back to your Lodges
the message that "every Mason must help by ~eing a job hunter for a
Brother Mason." List your jobs with your Employment Manager or
your local committee. Without your help, no program can succeed. Help
us to re-establish our Brothers in the American way of life.

. Wilson, Grand Secretary, who has acted as Secretary to this committee,
we feel deeply indebted.
Our thanks'also are expressed to the members of the Board of Control,
the Boards of Relief and Employment Services, the brethren who are serving as our representatives in the several hospitals and. to the Lodges and
Masons of California, who have made this work possible.
Respe<.".tfully submitted,
LESLIE E. WOOD, Chairman,

The vast majority of cases coming before our Lodges and committees
are stories of service and brotherly affection that may never be told. As
an example may we tell the story of a young man, about nineteen or
twenty years of age, who had served at Pearl Harbor and had taken part
in many of the Pacific engagements and was finally given a discharge on
account qLmental disability, with a rating of sixty percent disability?
He was on his way from Seattle to Tucson, Arizona, where he was ·
to join his father. At Portland he was delayed for eighteen hours, waiting
for a bus. At Sacramento, which is another bus stop, he was again delayed. He was without funds and was in no condition, mentally or
physically to stand the long delays. He appealed to the representative of
the Travelers Aid for help, but when financial assistance was offered him,
he declined because he said it would be charity. He did not wish to wire
his father for money, knowing that his father was in no condition to help
him. He was asked if his father belonged to the Masons, whereupon he
produced a card from the Grand Lodge of Illinois, certifying that he was
the son of a Mason in good standing. He was informed that the Grand
Lodge of California would help him and a member of this committee was
contacted by the Travelers Aid, with the result that the committeeman
talked with the boy, took care of his needs and with the help of the
Travelers Aid representative succeeded in getting the boy on 'the first bus,
ahead of all other passengers. The record of these many cases will perhaps
go unrecorded, but they will not soon be forgotten by those we have
helped and they give California Masonry the right to look with pride upon
what is being done for those who are doing so nµich for us.
Conclusion
In closing this brief report, we express our appreciation to the Most
Worshipful Claude H. Morrison, Grand Master, who has been in attendance at all of the committee meetings ; to the Deputy Grand Master and
the Senior and Junior Grand Wardens who have accompanied him. Their
counsel and advice have been most helpful. To Most Worshipful Lloyd E.

REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES OF THE MASONIC CLUBHOUSE, U. C. AT BERKELEY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California :
The Board of Directors of the Masonic Club of the University of
California, Inc., .presents this its. annual report, covering the fiscal year
ending September 30, 1944, which fiscal year substantially coincides with
the past Masonic year of this Body.
Property Maintenance and Financial Affairs
The Clubhouse Trustees have presented to the Finance Committee in
its usual form their audited and certified financial report for the period
under review. The total income was $7,522.00 of which this Grand Lodge
contributed $7,500.00; also, a special fund ~f $1,500.00 to assist the students
in c,arrying on their social affairs during the emergencies created by the
war. Total maintenance charges aggregated $6,860.92. Total charges
against the special fund referred to were $476.06. There was transferred
to the Insurance and General Reserve Fund $1,117.53. These reserve funds
stood, at the end of the year, as follows:
Special Reserve War Emergency....:.........................$1..023.94
Insurance Reserve Fund ............................................ 131,84
General Reserve Fund ................................................ 5,130.68
Total ................ :.................................:.............$6,286.46
All of this sum was on deposit with a savings bank in Berkeley on
September 30, 1944.
The building and its. furnishings are in good condition. A total of
$278.02 was expended for repairs and replacements during the past year.
At s'ome indefinite, but not remote period, we will obviously have to spend
a considerable amount in replacement of furnishings. At the present time
we find one of our pianos in quite bad condition.
The Effect of War Upon the Clubhouse
The shock of war during the past year has be~n. severe, but not so
severe on our activities, as had been feared a year ago, when our last
report to this Body was presented. Then we. anticipated that the membership of the student organization would not exceed 50. As a matter of
fact, the lowest figure reached, and that during the summer period when
the college enrollment is' least, was 113.

occasions held during the period up to August 26, 1944. These aggregate .
6347 persons, 3119 of whom were service men. This is, of course, in addition to our ordinary day-to-day attendance.
The black oxen press on. Our new hostess, Mrs. Morton, seems to
be giving general satisfaction, alike to students and trustees. Attached
hereto is a statement from her which I think you will find interesting as
showing her sincere devotion to the welfare of the organization. Other

The Trustees believe that the Clubhouse has successfully carried out the

the war.

Dear Sir:
This being my seventh month as hostess of the Masonic Club of the
University of California, may I express to you my appreciation of what it
means and has meant to all who have, even in a small way, been privileged
to enjoy its hospitality and uplifting protection. Yes, I mean literally, the
protection one feels in the atmosphere of this beautiful building.
I have had many visitors, Masons from other states, past members,
some now located in far away places, come in, introduce themselves, say,
"Just came around to see if the good old Masonic Club is still here. Yes
it's just the same." They all say that they look back now and truly ap~

132

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

preciate their very great privilege in having had such a wonderful club
home. ·
Many of our present members. live rather far from campus. Because
of difficult transportation, speeded up programs, and added work, they use
the Club as a home for study, relaxation, and play. Many have told me
they didn't know what they would do if it weren't for the Club, as home
was much too far to go between classes.
I feel that the fine association and friendships formed in the right
atmosphere have a far reaching effect for good.
Although our membership is not as large as it once was, due to the
small enrollment at the University, we are very proud of our one hundred
and fifteen members, and they are very proud and appreciative of their
Club.
.
•
The students and myself, wish to thank you for the hallowed background and sense of security you have made possible through Masonry.
Respectfully and fraternally yours,
EDNA H. MORTON.

REPORT OF WAR RELIEF FUND COMMITTEE
By HON. EARL WARREN.
Most W orshipfut Grand Master, Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
I am somewhat embarrassed to make this prosaic report that I mu~t
make to you, after that presentation by the Grand Master. However, in
reporting on the committee on the War Relief Fund I can report progress
-not sufficient progress to bring satisfaction, but still enough progress
to indicate that this obligation of allocating a War Relief Fund is still on
the conscience of those Lodges that have not fully complied with the
request of the Grand Mast.e r three years ago. In the 1943 proceedings
we reported 352 Lodges had made their quotas and we had collected
$131,810.19. At this time we report that 386 Lodges have made their quotas
for a total of $149,120.31. That represents a net gain of $17,310.12 for the
year.

we

have used no pressure methods during the year to augment this
fund. We have asked the Secretary to call to the attention of the Lodges
that have not made their quotas the fact that it is in the interest of our
craft to have them do so. It i~ our opinion that the same gentle urging
should continue until the work of the committee has been completed. I
think' we are often inclined to forget that the worst part of this war is still
ahead of us, and I think that those who read the daily papers and who see
what is happening on the fi_e ld of battle each day will realize that is the
fact.
Only a few weeks ago we saw that the casualties in the Army and
Navy and Air Forces amounted to 300,000. Just a few days ago it was
announced that the casualty list at that time was 500,000. We still have
to go through that wall in Germany; we still have to go through all those
islands in the vast Pacific before we get at Tokio. That is going to mean
great suffering, great hardship on these boys across the sea. We have
to realize that all the suffering and hardship is not confined to the field
of battle. We are going to live with this war throughout the rest of our

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

lives; and most of th.e hardship is going to be when these boys come home.
There will be service-connected disabilities, service-connected cases and
hardship all over this nation just as long as we live. We have in the
State of California over 10,000 of our brothers in this war. Many of them
will come back hardship cases; their families will need the relief that the
Lodges are accustomed to giving; and just because of the service that
these boys are giving in the war. I believe every Mason in this jurisdiction
would like to feel that he has done a small part to take care of that work.
We are proud, of course, of those Lodges that have made their quotas;
but we are still more proud of those Lodges who have made their quotas
through the contribution of every member of the Lqdge. We are sincerely hopeful that within the next year all of the Lodges will have measused up to their quotas.
I know when the boys come home from the service you would like
to have them look at the records of your Lodge and feel that while they
were away you were willing to contribute something to a fund that would
protect them and their families in the event they are obliged to suffer
~ardship as a result of the war when they return.
I recommend that there should be no pressure methods used to augment this fund, but keep gently reminding the Lodges in th_e jurisdiction
that they have a duty to perform and that there may be need for this fund
in the future.

ANNUAL ORATION
By WILLIAM J. CoURTIOUR, Grand Orator
THE MASTER
Most Worshipful Grand Master, Distinguished Visitors, and tnembers vf th~
Grand Lodge:
.
For many years I have been privileged to attend the Grand Lodge
communications, and with many of you I have looked forward with great
eagerness and anticipation to the hour of 10 :30 o'clock when the grand
oration would be delivered before a group of good men, such as are
gathered here today: Masters and Wardens of Lodges; men from every
walk in life; the professional men; the mechanics; men from the farms;
truly ·a cross section of the great American public, who meet together
once a year with the end in view, "of benefiting orfe another, and being of
service to humanity, and as we have listened to the men who have preceded me on this platform, and from whose lips have fallen oratory that
has made deep and lasting impressions upon our hearts and minds.
Surely Longfellow was right when he wrote the words:
"Lives of great men oft r emind us,
We can make our lives sublime.
And departing leave behind us, .
Footprints on the sands of time."
For these_men have left behind them footprints on the sands of time.
For they have given to the craft, beautiful expressions, gems of thought,
priceless treasures that you and I can read and enjoy at our leisure.
And it is with a feeling of deep humility that I stand before you, "a
humble servant of the craft," praying that some word of mine might find
an abiding place in your hearts and be an inspiration to you in the great
work of reconstruction and the rehabilitation of men in the years that
lie before us. For the Temples of Masonry, in many parts of the world,
have been destroyed, our working tools beaten into implements of war,
our Bibles and our .altars burned, our young men taken from us, and

137

For the lapse of time, the ruthless hand of ignorance, and the devastation of wars have laid waste and destroyed many valuable monuments
of antiquity upon which the utmost exertions of human genius were
employed. Not only the Temple of Solomon, but many of the great
temples and cathedrals of Europe, so spacious and magnificent, and constructed by so many celebrated artists, escaped not the unsparing ravages
of barbarous force. Freemasonry, notwithstanding, still survives, and will
survive, because it is not built of material things which are subject to the
will of man. Freemasonry is embedded in the hearts of men. Men like
DeMolay, Latimer, and the many martyrs, whose bones were broken on
the rack, whose bodies burnt to the stake because they were true to a
trust. The fires kindled around those great men are never extinguish.e d,
for today they burn in the hearts of men and boys-fires of love, hate,
and patriotism.
Men who all through the ages have been willing to sacrifice and die
for a just and righteous cause; freedom of speech, freedom of religion,
freedom of the press, free enterprise, free to act . in accordance with
the dictates of his own conscience-real Master Masons.
But my subject must be of a Masonic nature, and so a little of its
history will be in order.
In the book of human history, Freemasonry has a chapter of its own.
In all ages and in all lands men have forlll&d secret societies, made use
of ceremonies of initiation, employed symbols, emblems and means of
recognition. When Freemasonry came into existence, nobody knows how
many centuries ago, it inherited much from such societies.
The oldest existing written record of our craft is a manuscript written
by some unknown brother in Engl~d, about 1390, nearly six centuries
ago. At the time this document was written all Freemasons were operatives, that is, they were workers engaged on buildings. There were many
kinds of Masons,' but the evidence indicates that Freemasons were those
builders of a superior type, who designed, supervis·ed, and erected the ·
great cathedrals and other marvelous structures in the Gothic style of
architecture.
·
Operative Freemasons designed the buildings; dressed the stone from
the quarries and laid it in the walls; set up arches, pillars, columns and
buttresses; laid the floor and built the roof; carved out the decorations;
made and fitted the stained-glass windows into place; and produced the
sculptures. Their work was difficult, called for a high degree of skill
and genius, and required much knowledge of mechanics and geometry
as well ~s of stone masonry.
·
. They were the great artists or masters of the Middle Ages.
Training men for such work called for a long period of severe discipline. Boys sound in body, keen in mind, and of good reputation, at the
age of twelve, were apprenticed to some Master Mason for a number of
years, usually seven. This Master Mason was such a boy's tutor, his
mentor, his guide, who taught him both the theories and practices of the
craft. At the end of his apprenticeship the youth was required to submit
to exacting tests of his profidency before being accepted into full membership in the craft.
·
When a number of Freemasons worked together on a building over
a period of years they organized a Lodge, which might meet in a tern-

'

PROCEEDINGs__ OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

porary building or in one of the rooms of the uncompleted structure.
Such a Lodge "was governed by a Master, assisted by Wardens; it had
a Secretary to keep its books; a Treasurer to keep and to disperse its
funds; a charity chest from which to dispense relief to the members in
accident, sickness, or distress, and to widows and orphans of Master
Masons. It met in regular communication, divided its membership into
grades, admitted members by initiation ; in short, it was in essentials what
a Masonic Lodge is today.
The beginner in the builders' art was called an appre11tice. After
he had served as such a sufficient time to give evidence of his fitness,
his name was entered in the Lodge books, after which he was called an
Entered Apprentice. At the end of his seven years of apprenticeship
·he was called into open Lodge, his conduct was reported, and he then
had to prove his skill by producing what was called a " Master's piece."
Hitherto he had been on probation. If he passed his test satisfactorily he was made a full member of the craft. Then he stood on an
equality of duty, rights, and privileges with others, a Fell6w of the craft
-the word "Fellow" meaning full membership. In the sense that he
had now mastered the theories, practices, rules, secrets, and tools of his
trade, he was called a Master Mason.
Completing their work in one community, the Freemasons would move
to another setting up their Lodges wherever they met. Other types of
Masons w~re compelled to live and work in the same community year
in and year out, and under local restrictions. A number of our historia.ns
believe that it may have bet:n because they were free from such restnctions that the Gothic builders were called Freemasons.
Such was the fraternity in its op~rative l'leriod, and as such it flourished
for generations. Then came a great change in its fortunes. Euclid's
geometry was re-discovered and published, thereby giving to the public
many of the · Masons' trade secrets.'
The Reformation came and the Gothic style of architecture began .to
die out. Social conditions underwent a revolution-laws were changedthese and other factors brought about a decline in the craft. During the
sixteenth and seventeenth centuries Freemasons became so few in number
that only a small Lodge here and there clung to a precarious existence.
To recruit their numbers Freemasons adopted a new practice-they began
to accept non-operative' members. In the old days only an operative
Mason in the literal sense, could become a member, but during the two
centur{es of the transition period, gentlemen with no intention to become
builders, and out of curiosity, for social reasons, or from interest in the
craft's ancient customs, were received as "accepted Masons." At first there
were few of these, but as time passed their number increased, until. by
the early part of the eighteenth century they were more numerous than
the operatives and were more influential.
The craft then took a step destined to revolutionize it and to set it
on a new path of power and magnitude. On St. John, the Baptist's day,
"June 24th, 1717, four or more old Lodges of London and Westminster
met in London and organized a Grand Lodge and on the same day selected
.their first Grand Master: M. W . Anthony ·Sayer.
·
.
Within a few years of that date the craft had "completed the transformation of an , 0 perative body into a speculative fraternity ; reorganized
the two old degrees into three degrees of Entered Apprentice, Fellowcraft,
and Master Mason; collected and collated the old Masonic manuscripts;
produced the first books of Constitutions ; and was chartering Lodges in

many countries, including our own, to take care of the fraternity's membership, which began rapidly to increase shortly after the organization
of the Mother Grand Lodge.
This was the beginning of organized Speculative Freemasonry as we
know it.
American Lodges, of which the earliest with authentic historical records was "The First Lodge at Boston" (1733), were under the charge of
Provincial Grand Lodges, which were ruled by Provincial Grand Masters
appointed by the Grand Lodges in England, or in Scotland, or in Ir.eland.
As a result of the Revolution, one after another American Grand
Lodges became sovereign and independent. The guestion arose at that
time whether there should be one Grand Lodge for the whole of the
United States, but the wisdom of the craft prevailed and the scheme was
abandoned.
. As the years passed, one Grand Lodge was organized in each state,
sovereign within its own limits, no other Grand Lodge having any right
to control Masonic affairs under its jurisdiction. Today, in the United
States, are forty-nine Grand Lodges, one for each state a nd one for the
District of Columbia-and on their rolls over three million members.
Speculative Freemasonry did not spring full-formed o ut of nothing in
1717, but came as a gradual development of Operative Masonry. Through
an unbroken line we can trace our lineage back to those builders of the
early Middle Ages. We are Masons, yea we are Masters too, except that
where they erected buildings, we build manhood; their tools we have
transf.ormed "into emblems of moral and spiritual laws and forces; their
practices and secrets we have embodied in the royal art of Brotherly
Love, Relief and Truth ; their ritua ls-m e llow~d, enriched, a nd made mere
beautiful with the passing of time-we em ploy in the entering, passing,
and raising of our candidates. All that was living and permanent in
their craft we have preserved to u se in behalf of good will, kindliness,
charity, and brotherhood among men.
Surely the lines have fallen to us in pleasant places and we have a
goodly heritage. Such is our history, and we must preserve it.
The same forces that sought to destroy al\ that was good, noble and
fr'ee in the past is still abroad in the world, and the Master is still needed
to eradicate the old abuses, to protect and safeguard our landmarks, and
to promote the .:irtues of brotherly love, relief and truth.
Entered Apprentices assembled on the ground floor. Many of our
members never get beyond the Ground Floor, content to pay their dues,
and, wear the pin-moving and being swayed with the crowd-just a
member. A few advance a little higher in thought, read a nd study a
little more, and progress as far as the middle chamber. B ut only those
who become real Masters have the privilege of meeting in the sanctum
sanctorum, finding in fraternal associations the fellowship which none can
find alone.

Who is the Master?
• He is the man who draws the designs upon the trestle. board at the
commencement of the day. Whether he be doctor, lawyer, or builder,
plans must be made so that there will be no confusion among the workmen.
Who is the Master?
I see him in the character of that one who could not. be bought with

gold--,a seemingly insignificant character in our degree work, but in that
man I find the real Master as he answers, "Then you cannot go for it is
strictly forbidden"-the man that could not be bribed. He had mastered
self.
I find him in the mountains of · the southland-a great naturalist; a
member of the craft; giving to the world, by his writings, the beauties of
nature; finding the sa.nctum sanctorum in God's great cathedral, the great
outdoors.

only the best should be allowed to enter our doors, for the good name of

I ~it with him in his cabin as he pens the words:
Not what seems fair, but what is true.
'Not as we dream but the good we do.
These are the things that shine like gems,
Like jewels in royal diadems.
Not as we take, but as we give.
Not as we pray, but as we live.
These are the things which make for peace,
Both now and after time shall cease.
Who is the Master?
I find him in the foxholes in the South Pacific and the battlefields of
Europe, forgetting his own wounds, and going on foot and out of his
way to assist his buddies. I see the Master workman in the field hospital.
Those doctors bending over our boys from morning far into the night
to alleviate their pain and suffering. These men have the satisfaction of
meeting with the Masters. They have served as Apprentices. They have
enjoyed their meetings in the middle chambers. But the real joy comes
as they meet with the Masters, practicing the virtues and studying the
philosophies inculcated in the degr.ees of our order.
It is the Master .•who can say, when assailed by the enemies of right
and truth, "I can not, I will not, I shall not."
Lincoln once said:
"Stand with anybody that stands right;
Stand with him while he is right,
And part with him,
When he goes wrong."
The world is always looking for men who are not for sale. Men who
are honest, sound from center to circumference, true to the ~eart's core,
whose consciences are as steady as the North Pole; men who stand for
right if the heavens totter and fall; men who will tell the truth and look
the world right in the eye; men that neither brag nor run; men that
neither flag nor flinch; men who know their message and tell it; men
who know their business and attend to it; men who will not lie, shirk
nor dodge; me.n who are not too lazy to work and not too proud to be
poor; men who are not afraid to say "No" with the emphasis.
Freemasonry is an exclusive institution. Guard well your doors.
Beware of the Cowans and imposters who seek admission, those meh who
have not learned to build fairly and squarely with all men.
Frederick Daleo, tliat great Masonic S>Cholar and gentleman, once said:
"Let down the bars, and you will soon have the birds· roosting in your
rafters, and the cobwebs hanging over your doors."
Freemasonry. expects from . its mem~rs, the noblest and the best, and

141

It was Sh~kespeare who wrote:
"He that stealeth my purse stealeth trash,
'Tis something, 'tis nothing, 'tis his, 'tis mine,
But he who filches from me, my good name,
Robs me of that, which not enriches him,
But leaves me poor indeed."
"A good name is better to be chosen than great riches."
The eyes of the world are upon the Masters. The Master is some
boy's ideal. It may be his own son, the neighbor's boy, or the boy down
the street. Some boy somewhere is watching your life. He is shaping
his own after some ideal, just as you did when you were a boy.
A prize was once offered for the best picture representing "peace."
One artist painted a picture of a beautiful lake, not a ripple anywhere,
not a movement in the trees, the animals peacefully grazing in the
meadow:> It was a beautiful picture, and in the corner he wrote, "Peace."
But the prize was won by the artist who painted a picture of a storm;
the lake covered with whitecaps; the trees swaying from side to side; the
sky covered with black clouds; lightning striking across the horizon.
Perched among the branches of one of the trees was a nest with a bird
setting on its eggs, peaceful and secure. Underneath he penned the word,
"peace."
The Master is the man that can be calm when the battle rages, when
misfortune and difficulties arise.
My Brethren, our advancement in Masonry takes us through the state
of an apprentice, into the field of education as a fellowcraft, to the stern
realities of our responsibilities as citizens, to the beauties and satisfaction
of a Master, and as we journey along its pathway we find it inexhaustible
in its interest, lifelong in its appeal, a power within us to enrich, · to ennoble, and to inspire.

REPORT ON PHILIPPINE ISLANDS LODGES
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
Our enemies are still in possession of the Philippine Islands. The
little information that has reached us from the Islands in the past year
has come from three sources: Radio Tokyo, in which little or no confidence can be placed: the international Red Cross, which informs us that
some supplies from the United States are now reaching the Ameris;an
prisoners of war still held in the Islands, and a report on the physical
condition l!>f a few of our brethren who are civilian internees in the camps
at Santo Tomas and Los Banos.
Brother ]. C. Klasson, formerly of Manila and now a resident of Los
Angeles, was an exchange civilian aboard the S. S. Gripsholm which
reached New York last December, after the exchange of prisoners with

all our brethren interned at Santo Tomas and Los Banos were in good

The Grand Master in the course of his travels visited the Grand Lodge
of Kansas. In his address to that body he gave in detail the methods
adopted by the Grand Lodge of California for the benefit of our brethren
of the Philippine Lodges. After his address Eric S. Kintsel, Grand Master
of the Grand Lodge of New Mexico, inquired of him if he had any
knowledge of the whereabouts of John McFie, Past Grand Master of the
Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands and a native of New Mexico.
Brother Roy G. Shearer, Abilene, Kansas, Representative of the Grand
Lodge of the Philippine Islands near the Grand Lodge of Kansas, asked
if the Grand Lodge of California could supply him with information
relative .to Masonry in the Islands. Brother A. J. Ross, Topeka, Kansas,
asked if any information could be furnished regarding his son Irvin C.
Ross, Past Master of Manila Lodge No. 1. The Grand Master forwarded
these inquiries to me and I am very happy to report that the information
desired by these brethren was furnished.
On August 1, 1944, at Saranac Lake, New York, one; of the most co1orful chara'cters of this era passed. Manuel Quezon, 65, exiled President of
the Philippine Commonwealth and Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of
the Philippine Islands 1918-19, died of pulmonary tuberculosis. At the
bedside were members of his official family and his widow, two daughters
and a son, all of whom escaped with the President from Corregidor in a
submarine February 20, 1942. As· a synopsis of his life was given in my
report of last year it will not be repeated here. His body was placed in a
crypt in Arlington National Cemetery until recapture of tqe Islands permits removal there for permanent burial.
·
The collection of dues of members of Philippine Lodges continues to
be an important function of our Grand Lodge, and at the moment there
is in the trust fund held by us for the benefit of the Grand Lodge of the
Philippine Islands $13,248.37. There are 71 cases pending; 574 members
have paid dues for more than one year.
How soon the defeat of Japan will come no man can say, but the handwriting is on the wall; her defeat is inevitable.· What the peace terms will
be we do not know, but we can reasonably assume that she will be stripped
of all _her military power. There will, however, be left in her hands one
very potent weapon, the removal of which will require all the tact, diplom~cy and statesmanship of which the Western World is capable. Her
weapon will be racial agitation.
At the outbreak of the Philippine Insurrection, 1899, Rudyard Kipling
the English poet and member of the Fraternity, wrote a satirical poe~
dedicated to. the United States and the Philippioe Islands, entitled "The
White Man's Burden." This poem deals with the price of empire that
must be paid in blood and treasure. The Western Powers with interests
in the Orient readily accepted the title of this poem as proof of sacrifice
on ,their part, but did not comorehend that the Oriental Nations also had
a problem and that that problem was the white man. Japan had this in
mind when, she called the Pan-Asiatic Congress at Nagasa"ki in 1926, at
whi~h meetiqg a constitution of a Lelague of Asiatic Peoples was adopted.
In no other period of history have the people of this troubled world
been so conscious of race, color and religion as they are at this monl.ent.
Had not Japan attacked China and thus convinced most of the Orient that

Before World War I all Asia was restless. Two great religious movements, both with a political tinge, were slowly gaining mom entum; The
Pan-Islam bloc composed of Northwestern India, A fghanistan, Persia,
Turkey, Irac, Arabia and Egypt. The Pan-Buddhist bloc consisting of
much of India. Japan, China, Siam, Cambodia, Java, Burma, Tibet and
Ceylon. Both these movements are dormant at the moment. The PanIslam movement was delayed by the action of Kemal Pash a, P resident of
Turkey, who abolished the Caliphate thereby leaving Islam without a
leader and also by the Pan-Arab movement which is purely political. The
Pan-Buddhist movement was interrupted by the brutal actions of Japan
toward the conquered people of the same faith ..
The White man's superiority in the Orient has been due to his inventive
genius, particularly as it applied to instruments of destruction. In recent
years th~ Oriental Nations have been taught not only how to use these instruments but how to manufacture them as well. Today the best minds
of the East and the West are convinced that if an understanding cannot
be .reached between the Occident and the Orient at the end of the present
conflict, then it is only a question o f time until the teeming millions of
the East will challenge the supremacy of the West. Should that tragedy
occur all the horror and suffering of past wars will sink into insignificance
by comparison.
Important steps have already been taken by the Western Powers in
i:egard to China. January 11, 1943, the U nited States and Great Britain
signed treaties with China abolishing their extraterritorial privileges, treaty
ports, and other limitations on Chinese domestic sovereignty. Only four
countries . (Switzerland, Sweden, Portugal and the Netherlands) still hold
special rights in China, and negotiations are now proceeding amicably toward the abolition of these.
·
Many problems remain unsolved. The British Empire has the problem
of India, Burma and Malaya. The Netherlands has its problems in the
East Indies. France has her problems in lndo-China. P r esent indications
are that the United States and the P hilippine Islands have complete under~
standing and no great difficulties will arise between them.
The political problems of the reconstruction period we leave to the
duly accredited representatives of the various nations and to those who
are well versed in political science. But the question of understanding,
tolerance and brotherly love offers a wonderful opportunity to Freemasonry. It is well known that Amity Lodge No. 106 of Shanghai China a
Lodge under the jurisdictien of the Grand Lodge of the Philippi~e Islands,
was chartered primarily for the purpose of furthering better understandi ng between the Chinese, the Filipinos and the Americans of that city.
Masonic Lodges are situated throughout the width and breadth of the
Orient, and it is no exaggeration to say that the actions of the Grand
Lodge of California in behalf of Philippine Masonry and its unselfish interest in issuing a dispensation for a L o dge in the war torn city of Chungking are matters that will in time be know n to every Mason from Cairo to
Canton and from Singapore to Samarkand. This action on the part of
California Masonry will have its effect upon untold numbers of people.

association for the purpose of erecting a memorial to Washington, the Mason.
The relics were to be housed in that Memorial. The meeting in 1910 indorsed
the proposal and at meetings in 1911 and 1912 plans for raising funds were
developed and a Constituti-0n and by-laws were adopted .
Like most projects of the sort, it became a very ambitious one and instead
of a mere fireproof structure on the old Lodge site, a monumental structure
was planned and proceeded with, without however, being assured of the funds
adequate for its completion. As. the years passed and greater interest throughout the country was manifested, it became the ·fixed idea of the Directors
of the Association and Masons, generally, that the .Washington Memorial
offered :m opportunity of a monument to Freemasonry itself and to the
influence it had exerted in the foundation and preservation <if our free government.
.
.
Meetings were held annually thereafter on Washington's birthday until at
the twelfth annual meeting en February 22, 1922, the Treasurer's . report showed
a cash fund on hand of $688;332.85. This sum had been contributed from the
forty-nine g.rand jurisdictions, the Lodges in Alaska, Canal Zone, Puerto Rico
and the Philippine Islands; the Grand Encampment, Knights Templar ; the
General Grand Council, Royal and Select Masters ; the General Grand Chapter,
Royal Arch Masons; the Supreme Councils, Ancient and Accepted Scottish
Rite; the Imperial Council of the Shrine ; the ~upreme Council of the Grotto
and miscellaneous contributions.
At th~ meeting on February 22, 1922, plans were adopted and the work
ordered to proceed. The estimated cost was $2,100,000. Ground was broken
on June 5, 1922, and the cornerstone was laid on November 1, 1923.
It has been an invariable rule of the association to let no contract until
the money was in hand to pay for work and materials, and consequently the
work has progressed slowly. Could the structure have been completed within
a reasonably short time after it was commenced doubtless the total cost as
estimated by the architects might have been approximated. H owever, over
the years, the cost of materials and labor has increased enormously. Some
changes in the plans were made from time to time that may have added somewhat to the total cost but not greatly. T he increase in cost may be said
to be due almost wholly to rising costs.
In round numbers, $4,500,000 has been expended and the Memorial is not
completed. On February 1, 1944, the treasury of the association showed a
cash balance of approximately $150,000 in the Building Fund and $58,836.74
in the Endowment Fund.
For many years after the completion of the exterior of the structure in
1931, ·by reason of the unfinished state of the grounds and approaches (as
well as the like condition of the interior for those who could be induced to
enter), the Memorial left a very bad impression on the visitor, whether
Masonic or profane. This is somewhat alleviated at the present time. The
grounds are landscaped, the granite steps installed and to outward appearance
the work of completion is nearing an end. But the Memorial is not completed.
As you will- observe by the cut of the Memorial, the ground floor is a base
for the tower containing eight , more floors below the finial. None of the
interior work above the first floor is done, nor have the elevators been installed.
From the entrance beneath the facade of pillars in the front of the structure,
one enters the great Memorial Ball which is completed except for the statue
of Washington and the mural decorations. The statue of Washington will
be the gift of the Order of De Molay. On this floor too is the replica of
the original Lodge room where George Washington presided as Master and
which is completely finished and furnished, but the relics will not be installed
until the war is over; they are safely stored in a safety deposit vault in the
second basement of the Memorial.

WASHINGTON MASONIC NATIONAL
MEMORIAL ASSOCIATION
Most W arshipf11l Grand Ma.rt er and Members of Grand Lodge :
The Most Worshipful Grand Master shortly after his return from the
Conference of Grand Masters in Washington City in February .of this year
appoint~ this committee to make a study of- the financial situation of the
George Washington Masonic National Memorial Association and the state of
the Memorial that for many years has been in course of construction at
Alexandria, Virginia, and of the ciuesfion of the desirability of our grand
jurisdiction again participating in the work, and, if recommended, then to
suggest a plan or program for such participation.
The Committee has gathered all the information touching the history of
the Memorial, its cost to date, its present state of construction, its fin:inces,
and probable future requirements .to complete the project, et cetera, that was
made available to it, or 'it could assemble, and has given the same its earnest
consideration.
The Memorial stands on Shooter's Hill across the Potomac froin Washington and on a line extended passing through the United States Capitol, the
Washington Monument and the Lincoln Memorial. The architecture · is· Grecian
and consists o f a ground floor which forms the base of a tower inset at three
levels beneath the finial ancl containing eight floors. The main entrance embraces six great columns and faces East. The tower is finished with a beacon
light and rises to a height of several hundred feet. It is of reinforced concrete
and faced with granite. The site embraces ap11roximat~ly 40 acres.
California should perhaps have a somewhat augmented interest in this
project since our own Senior Past Grand Master, then Junior Grand Warden,
was among those assembled in Alexandria-Washington Lodge room in 1907
and urged the necessity of providing a suitable structure, substantial and fireproof, for· the preservation of the mementos appertaining to the connection
and .s~r.vice of George Washington in that Lodge, and of which he served as
Worshipful Master while also serving as President of the United States.

a meeting held at .Alexandria on the invitation of the Grand Master of
Virginia .on February 22,' 1910, when a number of Grand Masters and representatives of Grand Masters took preliminary steps to organize a national

The Auditorium, which was the first room to be completed, is also on this
first floor. This was completely finished and furnished at the time of the
dedication during National Masonic Week in 1932. The· Blue Lodge Room,
Banquet Room and appurtenances were completed and furnished last year, with
the exception of the kitchen, the directors deeming bids received for furnishing
the kitch~n as being out of all reason. Thus the first floor of the Memorial
is nearly completed.
The rooms in the tower above the first floor are intended to be finished
as "Memorial" Rooms, Library, Offices, et cetera. The nucleus of a great
Masonic Library is already possessed by the Association and it is hoped that
the Memorial may eventually become a mecca for students of Masonic history
and teachings.
·
Toward this work, our jurisdiction has contributed the sum . of $.171,467.30,
and of this sum our Grand Lodge has contributed the sum of $138,434.20, the
remaining $33,033.10 having been given by other organizations and individuals,
resident in California and therefore credited to this jurisdiction.
It was originally thought that the sum of $1.00 per member from each
of the forty-nine grand jurisdictions of the United States would' be ample
fo finance the project. In 1932 when Grand Lodge completed its contributions
the California membership was 142,422, so it will be seen that California
responded in its usual generous fashion by contributing $1.20 per member.
Grand Lodge. made its last contribution in October, 1932. It was that year
that sober after judgment recognized that a dollar per member would be
insufficient. The Grand Lodge of New York then pledged a total gift of
$600,000, bringing its contribution up to $1.70 per member and the other grand
jurisdictions represented at the annual meeting agreed to make every effort
to attain a similar per capita. Only eighteen of the jurisdictions have reached
the goal. On the first of FebruaTy of this year California was 32nd on the
list, expressed in percentages ; however, in amount contributed, only six jurisdictions have exceeded us. These are New York, $636,717; Pennsylvania,
$399,519; Indiana, $232,608; Massachusetts, $223,408; OhiJ, $214,559, and New
Jersey, $195,783.
To bring the contribution of this jurisdiction up to the sum of $1.70 based
e n the membership of 1932 would require further contributions on our part
equalling the sum of $70,650.10. This is a sizable sum of money and needless
to say should not be expended without due and careful consideration. The
committee has given it that consideration and has also consulted and advised
with many of the brethren and it seems to be .the opinion of those consulted,
with . one or two exceptions, that California should do its part. There, of
course, arises the question of what our part should be. 'There is, also, some
divergence of opinion as to how the money should be raised; the three methods
considered being (a) by Grand Lodge appropriations, (b) by assessments upon
the membership, and (c) by voluntary subscriptions; and the three methods
were supported by those consulted in the order named. ·
Before passing on the question of contribution, your committee believes
that Grand Lodge should know something of the ultimate cost of construction
and of the maintenance of the structure after completion. As we have before
stated, the George Washington Masonic National Memorial Association has
no debts. The entire building so far as it has progressed is paid for and there
remains approximately $200,000 in the Building Fund. Importuned by the
chairman .for a statement as to the cost of completion of the Memorial, the
officers of the association explained that it was impossible to obtain a firm bid
for completion, except for immediate construction and that the association
was not in a position to let a contract at this time; that no contractor with
rising prices such as they are would feel safe in making a bid for construction
that would involve work to be done at some indefinite time in the future; that

on February 22, 1910, and ~ith the power to look into the. future and fee the
things that were to be, your Committee would have viewed this matter in an
entirely different manner than it seems possible to assume at this time. Here
there is no alternative. Masonry has no choice. We .have put our hands to
the plow and we cannot turn back.
As is not infrequently the case with enterprises of this nature, the size
of the monument was over emphasized and the .necessity for and expense of
perpetual maintenance not .given the consideration which it might well have
received. We might well say that a more modest Memorial might well have
served the .p.urpose of preserving the spiritual and material relics of him to
whom we would do honor.
It was quite natural, however, having in mind the pre-eminent character
and qualities of the man by whose memory it was inspired, that the project
should have been an ambitious one. It is, however, now an obligation of the
fraternity arid must be accepted as it is and dealt witl:i accordingly.
The Memorial is a fact and not a theory. Not something that we may
debate pro and con as tD whether it ought to be undertaken. It has been
undertak.m by M aso11ry and it must be finished by Masonry in a manner
creditable to the great instit1ttion which has undertaken it, and the Man and
Mason whose 11ame it bears.
Now more than at any time in the nation's history, is it important that
the place of George Washington should not be permitted to fade. Those who
have been privileged to visit Alexandria-Washington Lodge and examine the
Register will not soon forget the thrill that came on observing the names of
Washington, Lafayette, Franklin, Rochambeau and other names of historical
significance closely associated with the Revolution, and recalling in a most
vivid manner the part played by the fraternity in the establishment of our
national union.
Your Committee, therefore, recommends that this Grand Lodge and grand
Jurisdiction do resume its contributions to the George Washington Masonic
National Memorial Association and that to that end:
1. That there be appropriated f~om the general fund of Grand Lodge the
sum of $70,650.15. for the Building Fund of the Association, to be paid to the
said Association in three annual payments of $23,550.05 each, commencing at
the annual meeting of the Association in February, 1945, and annually thereafter until fully paid.
2. . We further recommend that the question of uniting in the general plan
of contributing annually the sum of one dollar for each Master Mason raised
in this jurisdiction to augment the Endowment Fund of the Association be
considered at the Communication of Grand Lodge holden in October, 1945, at
which time your Committee hopes to have more information in hand upon
which to base a recommendation.
3. We further recommend that no assessment be laid upon the constituent
Lodges, and that no drives be made for subscriptions among the members,
for any purpose connected 1'.erewith.
4. We further recommend that the Committee be continued with directions
to report progress of the Memorial and make such recommendations as may
be warranted by conditions from time to time in the future.
Fraternally submitted,

consistent with sound financing. Lodges have been most courteous and cooperative.
There have been frequent inquiries with respect to advantages. or ~isa~­
vantages of vesting title in a corpor~tion over the J?eth?d of holdmg title m
the names of the trustees of· a Lodge. Where title 1s held and ~rop~rty
operated by trustees, individual members of a Lod~e, in .cas~ of financial d1ffi,
culty, will be jointly and severally liable for unpaid obhgat10ns.
The committee lias uniformly recommended the organization of corporations for the purpose, and that it is advisable that the corporation~ be st?ck
corporations rather than membership corpora~ions, in order to ~votd poss1~le
confusion. It is not essential that a corporation be a membership ~orporat1on
to be entitled to classification as a nonprofit corporation, because it becomes

no profit inures or may inure to any individual.

The Grand Master referred to the chairman the unsatisfactory financial

years ago with the owner of its temple property for the payment to him and
his wife during their lives of a stipulated sum, the Lodge to become owner
of the property upon the de.ath of both. Investigation was made and several
conferences held and on September 1, 1943, the surviving beneficiary (the

faith, and provided for an annuity of $225 per month, there was both a
legal and moral obligation to perform, and as the revision .proposed was
eminently fair, the chairman unhesitatingly recommended that the adjustment
be made. The Lodge had become financially embarrassed and could not pay
that amount. The Grand Master approved the recommendation and authorized
temporary assistance. Subsequently, the Finance Committee of Grand Lodge
recommended approval of the new arrangements and appropriation from Grand
Lodge funds of necessary amount, which recommendation was approved by
Grand Lodge.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON GRIEVANCES
Chairman Frank B. Belcher, before presenting the report of
the Committee ori Grievances, read the following tribute to
Brother Olin L. Berry, who served for so many years on the
Committee on Grievances.
As the members of the Committee on Grievances were gathering on Monday of this week for their first meeting, we were advised that Brother Olin
Berry, for 14 years a member of this Committee, was ill at his home and
unable to meet with us. Within the hour, we received the saddening news
that his earthly toil had ended.
Olin Berry was an accomplished lawyer, a real gentleman, a fine Mason,
and a loyal brother. We will miss-we have missed-his wise and sympathetic
counsel.
The members of this Committee wish to pay this brief tribute to his ·
memory, and M. W. Grand Master, if there be no objection, may this statement be incorporated in the Minutes of the Proceedings of this Communication
of Grand Lodge.
FRANK B. BELCHER,
Lours C. DRAPEAU,
HERBERT A. HUEBNER,

Committee.

Chairman Belcher presented the Omnibus Report of the
Grievance Committee covering the following cases :
To the M. W. Grand Lodge of California:
To your committee on Grievances there have been referred one Petition
for Restoration and eighteen Trial Records.
The Petition for Restoration and six of · the Trial Records will be reported
to you by separate opinions.
Only one matter would seem to merit special mention in this report. We
note that some Lodges in proceedings under Section 332 of our Ordinances,
which deals with automatic expulsions, do not make use of the forms outlined
in Section 334. Many of the steps prescribed by Section 332 are jurisdictional
in character. Unless strictly complied with an expulsion can not be permitted
to stand. We, therefore, strongly urge that where resort is had to the provisions of Section 332, all Lodges should make use of the prescribed forms.
In the twelve Trial ~ecords dealt with herein, your committee purposes
to recommend affirmance in each instance. These records are:
1027-Meridian Lodge No. 667.
1030-Ascot Lodge No. 538.
1032-Fraternity Lodge No. 399.
1033-George Washington Lodge No. 525.
1034-,).Sanger Lodge No. 316.
1036-Ionic Lodge No. 520.
1037-Porterville Lodge No. 303.
1038-Far West Lodge No. 673.

1039-La Parfaite Union Lodge No. 17.
Tried by Starr King Lodge No. 344.
1040-Menorah Lodge No. 623.
·
1042-Crockett Lodge No. 139.
1043-Union Lodge No. 58.
We have carefully examined the Records enumerated above. In each of
them there has been a sufficient compliance with the procedural requirements
of our Ordinances-. The evidence in each instance is ample to uphold the
findings and conclusions·of the ' respective Trial Commissions. In the unanimous
opinion of your Committee, substantial justice, in accordance with Masonic
law, has been accomplished in every instance.
We, therefore, offer the following' resolution, and move its adoption:
RESOLVED that in the'twelve Trial Records enumerated above the findings
of the respective Trial Commissions and the penalties fixed therein be and
the same hereby are approvtd, ratified and affirmed.

Adopted.
Trial Record No. 1029

To the M. W. Grand lodge of California:
Trial Record No. 1029 from Blackmer Lodge No. 442 has ~een referred
to your Committee on Grievances. This record involves one L. 0 . S. who
petitioned this Lodge for the degrees of Masonry. He was elected to receive
the degrees and was made an Entered Apprentice Mason. Thereupon, and
before receiving. any further degrees, charges were preferred, a trial had with
the penalty fixed at expulsion. Specification one alleges that the accused was
guilty of misrepresentation and falsehood in his application in that, he answered
"None" to question 12 which reads: "Do you know of any physical, legal
or moral reason which would prevent you from becoming a Free Mason?
State particularly any physical deformity or defect"; whereas, in fact, he had
been twice convicted of felonies and had served two terms in the Missouri
State· penitentiary and, in addition, had some five arrests in San Diego on
various misdemeanor charges involving drunkenness or disorderly conduct.
The second specification charges that when this matter was being investigated he threatened to cause publicity in newspapers if he was prevented from
going forward with the degrees. We attach no importance whatsoever to this
second specification and, in our opinion, the evidence does not warrant the Trial
Commission's finding of guilty thereon.
It appears without question that in 1922, some 21 years before .the accused
filed his application for tl).e degrees of Masonry and when he was 21 years
of age he was convi<;ted of breaking into a store and ste.aling 12 dozen eggs,
4 Rhode Island Red chickens, 80 pennies, all of the total value of $10.00; and
that, in 1917, when he was 18 years old, he was convicted of breaking into a
store and stealing 200 pennies, 24 packages of Camels, 24 packages of Fatimas,
24 packages of Chesterfields, all of the total value of $5.60. After serving
his two sentences in the Missouri Penitentiary, he received a pardon from
the Governor of that illustrious State. On his five arrests in San Diego
there were three dismissals and fines were imposed in two.
Your Committee does not approve of the form of question 12 which
appears in the application blank. This question calls for a conclusion and not
for facts; it places on an applicant the burden of drawing such conclusion
on matters concerning which he knows little,' if anything. Outside of age
and residence, what legal reasons are there which would prevent an applicant

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

156

from becoming a Free Mason? What moral reasons may so operate?, Would
not the Lodge have had a perfect right to elect applicant to receive the degrees
if all of these facts had been known'? No showing is made that any inquiry
on these matters was made by the investigating committee prior to applicant
being elected to receive the degrees of Masonry. In the light of these circumstances, a very grave question exists as to whether applicant was in fact
guilty of any fraud or deceit. Yet, the thought of receiving such an applicant
into Masonry without all of these matters being known is abhorrent and
shocks our sensibilities. This is true even though we might readily conclude
that the investigating committee of the Lodge had been extremely derelict
in its duty.
We would be inclined to recomm~nd a revision of question 12 were it not
for the fact that we are advised that the form of our application blanks is
now under consideration by members of Grand Lodge. We hope changes
will be made by which an applicant will be called upon to disclose specific
facts and not merely to express a conclusion.
Th~ penalty in this case was fixed at expulsion. With .that, your Committee does not agree. It has been the practice of Grand Lodge in cases
involving misrepresentation in applications to uniformly fix such penalties at
suspension. This is for the reason that an opP,ortunity is then given for a
petition to the Lodge to lift such suspension, if it so desires, after all the
pertinent facts are known. If, in this case investigation should disclose that
this applicant has been completely rehabilitated, that he is now of good moral
character, that he has atoned for his past transgressions, then the Lodge
could legally restore 4irn. to membership and he could proceed with the degrees.
We do not suggest . that this should be done but we do believe that the matter
should be left in -such conditions that the Lodge may pass thereon should it
be presented.
'
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
RESOLVED that the penalty of expulsion,' as fixed by the Lodge in this matter,
be modified and the penalty be fixed at suspension.

Adopted.

Trial Record No. 1028

To the M. W. Grand Lodge of California:
The accused was charged in the civil courts with the offense of maintaining
a place where bets were made on horse races. He pleaded not guilty, was

157

tried by jury, convicted and sentenced to six months in the county jail. While
the crime may be a felony, except iq aggravated cases, trial judges generally
pronounces sentences in the county jail, which reduces the offense to a misdemeanor.
The individual who actually made the bets and kept the "book" pleaded
guilty and was let off with a fine.
Masonic charges were filed against the accused, he was brought before a
trial commission, convicted on a specification charging him with maintaining
a place where bets were made, and the penalty of suspension adjudged. But
the trial commissi9n made no finding of his guilt or innocence of unmasonic
conduct.
In Masonic jurisprudence it has been the rule from time immemorial that
before a Master Mason may be suspended or expelled he must be convicted
(a) of a specification or specifications of wrongdoing, and (b) a determination that such wrongdoing constituted unmasonic conduct. (Ordinances 322.)
It is entirely logical that this rule should be applied in the case of this, accused
because when the trial commission found he maintained a place where bets
were made, the essential finding of guilty knowledge on his part which would
have been included in a finding of unmasonic conduct is left undetermined.
Therefore your Committee proposes the following resolution:
REsoLVED, that, tP~ l\Ction of the Trial Commission in suspending the accused
be and the same is hereby reversed and set aside, and remanded for new trial.

Adopted.

The procedure in this case was for automatic expulsion under the provisions of Section 332 of the Constitution and Ordinances which provide that
in the event that any Mason who is a member of a· Lodge under the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge .shall suffer 'a final conviction of a crime classified
as a felony, and shall be imprisoned in pursuance thereof ; that., a certified
copy of 5uch judgment shall be procured and filed in the records of the ,Lodge,
and (quoting)
"T1'ereupon sixty days' notice in writing shall be given to such Mason by
registe~ed mail, forwarded to his last known place of address, potifying such
Mason of the filing of such record of conviction in such Lo9,ge and requ~r,ing
such Mason within such period of sixty days to elect in writing, if he so
desires, to have a trial in such Lodge on the charge of unmasonic conduct
based on the offense, or offenses, of which he has been convicted in a court
of the land."
The requirement of Section 332 just quoted that the notice therein provided
for shall be forwarded by registered mail to the accused at his last known
place of aduress, has been consistently held by this Grand Lodge to be jurisdictional, and failure to comply therewith has resulted in reversal of the
judgment of the Lodge.
In this case the record shows that the accused H. L. R. on the 27th day of
September, 1943, entered pleas of guilty to two counts of felony, and was
thereafter, on the 2d day of November, 1943, committed to the California
State Prison; and pursuant thereto was imprisoned in the State Prison. The
1ecord further shows that although at the time of the maiting of the notice
to the accused on April 10, 1944, he was confined in 'the State _P rison, the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

notice was sent by registered mail to 4-02 H Street, Modesto, California, which
·
was plainly ryot his last known address.
Your Committei;, therefore, consistently with the many former rulings of
Grand Lodge in such cases, recommends the adoption of the following resolution :
RESOLVED: That the action of Stanislaus Lodge No.. 206 in expelling Brother
H . L. R. from all the rights and privileges of Masonry be and the same is
hereby reversed and set aside, and the matter remanded to said Lodge for
further action in compliance with the provisions of Section 332, Constitution
and Ordinances.

Trial R ecord No. 1031

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
There has been referred to the Grievance Committee Trial Record No.
1031. In this record A. L. M. is charged with unmasonic conduct under
specification which in brief states:
That Brother A. L. M., an Entered Apprentice Mason of Ashlar Lodge
No. 306, at Colton, California, did on or about the first day of October, 1943,
unlawfully reveal the secrets of the Entered Apprentice degree of Masonry.
.The record shows that the Trial Commission voted "guilty" on the specification and also on the charge of unmasonic conduct, fixing the penalty at
expulsion.
·
It' appears from the record that the accused, after having received the
Entered Apprentice degree in Ashlar Lodge in Colton, moved to Tulare, California. Olive Branch Lodge No. 269 was then requested by Ashlar Lodge to
confer upon him the second and third degrees of Masonry. This request
brought to light the fact that the -accused was reputed to have made certain
statements after he had taken up his residence at Tulare. The matter was
called to the attention of Ashlar Lodge through the medium of correspondence.
Upon the trial of the case, the only evidence which was introduced before
the Trial Commission were letters chiefly between the officers of the two

PROCEEDI NGS OF THE

160

Lodges. No witnesses were called and no direct evidence was introduced .that
the accused had made the statements set forth in the charges. The accused
was unable to attend the trial, and was not represented by counsel.
The record further shows that the alleged statements were 'made to a
certain unnamed pe.r son; that this unnamed person was interrogated by the
Master of Olive Branch Lodge, the latter setting forth in a letter to Ashlar
Lodge, the substance of his interview with the non-Mason.
This type of evidence is purely of a hearsay nature. Section 319 of the
Constitution and Ordinances of this Grand Lodge provides "The ordinary
~ules of evidence employed in the courts of California shall be followed as
nearly as the circumstances shall permit." Also in the same section appea~s '
the following "Hearsay evidence ,is not admissable." Hearsay evidence of this
sort is not permitted in the courts of California, and is specifically forbidden
by our own Constitution and Ordinances.
It also appears from the record that the Trial Commission voted "guilty"
on the specification, "guilty" on the charge of unmasonic con9uct; ,and that
it voted ..aye" on the question " Shall the accused be expeJled ?" The number
of the Trial Commission so voting is not disclosed. While this matter, standing alon~, might not be sufficient to warrant reversal · of this expulsion, we
.calf attention to it for the purpose of emphasizing that records transmitted
to Grand Lodge should disclose the numerical standing of the Trial Commission in their votes upon the .specifications, th,e charge, and the penalty. (Section
323, Constitution and Ordin?-nces.)
The record shows the accused to be a resident of Tulare. The Masonic
offense set forth in the charges was committed, if at all, in Tulare. All witnesses who might be called against the accused likewise reside in that community. Your Committee i~ impressed with the idea that the convenience of
the accused and of the witnesses would be best served if the re-trial of this
matter were transferred to some Lodge in the Tula.re district. This would
enable the accused to be personally present, the witnesses tci appear. and testify
in person, and would avoid the expense of depositfons or the possible travel
of the accused and the witnesses from Tulare to Colton. This is permii.ted
in our laws in Paragraph 9th of Section 34 of the Constitution. (See also
Sections 942 and 943 of Ross Digest.)
We offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
RESOLVED, That the finding of "guilty" and fixing of the penalty of exp,ulsion in Trial Record No. 1031 be and the same is hereby reversed and set
aside and the matter remanded for a new trial.
RESOLVED FURTHER, That it is ·recommended that the Grand Master transfer
the trial of this matter from Ashlar Lodge in Colton to some Lodge in the
vicinity of Tulare.

Adopted.

Adopted and referred to the. Committee on Finance.
To the M. W . .Grand Lodge, F. & A. M.:
Your Committee on Masonic Information has prepared and published four
Quiz Programs on Masonic subjects during the past year. These programs
were most favorably received and letters of appreciation have been received
from all parts of the Grand jurisdiction. The Masters assert that there is a
widespr.ead interest in Masonic topics and with the raising of so· many new
candidates there is a universal demand for Masonic information.
In many instances the Masters made the questions part of the dinner
program before the Lodge opened. In other instances the guestions were
discussed informally at the refreshment table after the Lodge meeting.. Many
Masters utilize them in regular Lodge meeting ; somdimes as a special order
of business and sometimes at special times, such as while the Stewards are
preparing the candidate. In some Lodges the Quiz Program occupied a whole
cv.ening, the brethren assigned to answer the questions amplifying the answers
from their own research and experience. But wherever used the questions
and answers made a wide appeal.
The Committee has had extensive correspondence with Masters and
brethren who submitted special questions, some of which were incorporated
in later programs.
lt is interesting to note that many Grand Lodges are using the Quiz Program , technique in extending Masonic education and are finding .it most
eiiecti've.
At the last communication of Grand Lodge an appropriation of $750 was
made for the work of this Committee, of which an amount of $465.69 was
disbursed for printing, pastage and stenographic services, which includes an
invoice of $.100.64 .for printing brought forward from the preceding year.
Your Committee recommends that its work be continued and that an appropriation of $750 be approved for its activities during the year 1944-5.
It would seem that the time has arrived for the p.reparation of a Manual
of Instruction designed for the use of coaches and others, consisting of
information for the instruction of candidates regarding the Masonic degrees.
The. Committee plans during the coming year to gather' appropriate data for
the compilation of such a manual, subject to the approval of the Grand Master
and such other officials as he may designate.
