REPORT OF SPECIAL TAXATION COMMITTEE
To the Most .W orshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Special Taxation Committee has continued to funttion during the
year 1944 without any change in membership.
Meetings of the Committee have been held as formerly and many inquiries
from the constituent Lodges have been answered by letter. .
The Committee also made an interim report to the Grand Master on July
25, 1944, in which it reported that the new Federal Revenue Act did not
require a Lodge to make a return of its financial status to the United States
Collector of Internal Revenue. This report was published and sent to the
Lodges by the Grand Secretary, and a copy is attached hereto.
Reporting further on the status of Grand Lodge in its relationship to the
State Unemployment Reserves Tax, the committee reports that p;rsuant to
the authorization at the last communication, it engaged tax counsel to represent it .i.nd arrangements were made with the State Commission to withhold
any action or decision ort Grand Lodge status until an authoritative decision
could be secured from the United States Department of Internal Revenue.
This action was taken on the theory that the Federal Government would have
to first establish the status of Grand Lodge before the State Commission
could properly act.
·
After cortsiderable investigation, two petitions were filed with the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, and he has filed decisions on both petitions.
The general import of the holding of the Feder.al Government is to exempt
the Grand Lodge from responsibility for the Boards of Relief and for the .
Employment Offices, but to hold Grand Lodge liable for tax on all of its
office employees, including the Grand Tyler, the Grand Master, the Grand
Treasurer, and the Chairman of the Correspondence Committee, in so far as
any of them received any Grand Lodge payments in e'xcess of $45.00 per calendar quarter that were not solely for reimbursement of expense and for
which expense vouchers were submitted. In addition, the holding is that all
clerical help engaged by the Masonic Homes Endowment Board must be classed
as employees of Grand Lodge.
·
We will now take up with the State Commission the application of these
rulings to the computation of the State Unemployment Tax.
During the year, the State Unemployment Commission also made demand
for current and all back taxes against the Masonic Homes. The Committee
was able to give some aid to the trustees of the homes in presenting a claim
for exemption to the California Commission, which claim was allowed. This
resulted in a saving of a very large amount of taxes that would otherwise
have been assessed against the homes.
We have recommended to the Finance Committee that a suitable reserve
be set up for the payment of any possible taxes 'that may now be assessed
against Grand Lodge and also that $1,500 be set aside for possible legal
expenses.
Respectfully submitted,
}AMES E. HAMMOND,
' WALTER PERRY JOHNSON,
R. P. WISECARVER,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CLANDESTINE

Right on the heels of the initial report of the foregoing incident, the
secretary of another of our regular Lodges passed along the report from one
of its members that a man taking the degrees in this same spurious lodge
had been coached by one of our regular Masons. This has been discontinued.
Tq_ date the committee has not been advised of the Mason guilty of the
infraction, but that information has been promised. It is desi red only to
emphasize the need of thorough investigation upon the part of regular Masons
as to who they recognize as such. Let this be another example to the craft
that vigilance and the keeping of vows is needed.
·
'
puring the year there came to the .attention of the committee a pamphlet
entitled "A Resurgence of Clandestinism" published by the Supreme Council
of the Scottish Rite for the Northern Jurisdiction of the United States.
Because this document correctly sets forth the point at which regular Masonry
should concern itself with the activities of clandestinism established as 't he
policy of this co~mittee, announced in its previous reports, a brief digest
of that document 1s here recorded.
·
A bill in equity was filed by the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania against a
spurious blue lodge operating in Allentown. A second bill by the Supreme
Council of the Scottish R ite of the Northern Jurisdiction was filed at the
s~me time against a spurious Scottish Rite body operated by the same individuals. Reputable business men of the community to a considerable number
had been duped by this racket. Both bills were tried before a judge who
was not a Mason. The history of regular Masonry was traced in the testimony of the officers given in court and some thirty witnesses testified to the
manner of their being made Masons by one individual in · their own homes
by the use .of a Bible. The fees were traced to the pockets of the spurious
Masons which was the only treasury so far as could be ascertained. Decrees
in equity were rendered in each case confiscating the so-called charters of
these spurious bodies, perpetually enjoining the individuals from all representation and solicitation in the name of Masonry and from the use of the
~a?1e,. and effecting rest?~ation as far as could be done in that particular
htigahon. Here the activity had invaded the field of regular Masonry and
good men had been duped. T hose circumstances called for action.
. Clandestinism is not general throughout California. Its activity is principally confined to certain areas. This committee is composed of only a few
members. While . it believes its reports previously given have correctly set
fo~th the extent of the activity of clandestinism it believes that a questionnaire to be approved by the Grand Master should be sent to the secretaries of
al~ the lfidges of this jurisdiction to enable the committee to definitely determine the extent and situs of the activity and the proper education of the
cr~ft. T~e tabulation of the results and the scope of the future activity of
this committee could best be determined by ·such a questionnaire.
No appropriation has ever before been asked by this committee. It is
however, the request ~f thi> com~ttee that the sum of $500 be appropriated
from the funds of this Grand Lodge for the purpose of this questionnaire,

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
· ' Your Committee on Clandestine Mason.ty begs leave t o report as follows :
The policy of this committee in not naming the Grand Lodges and constituent Lodges of· clandestine organiz~tions is bearing good fruit. This year,·
for the first time, so far as the committee is advised, there have been · no
articles reach the regular Masonic press, which have paraded this activity
as regular. The two previous reports recounted incidents of this kind. We
trust that such errors have been permanently discouraged.
The only bit of appreciable publicity coming to the attention of the committee during the year was the presentation of a charter to ·a new clandestine
Filipino Lodge as ~eported in the lay press. This appeared in a single small
town newspaper and so far as we are advised, was not picked up by any others.
As reported last year, the financial prosperity of all working classes is
enabling these organizations to revive themselves after approaching close to
the point ·of extinction two years ago. However, as yet, with the single
exception hereafter recited there has been no invasion of our regular Masonic
field. Their activities are being confined to a scope that does not interfere
with the growth of recognized Masonry.
The one new activity during the year was the incorporation of a new
Negro Grand Lodge with headquarters in San Francisco. No activities of
this particular body have come to the attention of the committee. The Articles
of · Incorporation of that organization were filed in the office of the Secretary
of State shortly after the last communication of this Grand Lodge and contained the use of the initials "F. & A. M." in the name· of the organization.
This has provoked an investigation of both the right of our own Grand
Lodge to make a filing and the policy involved 'in it t~at would forestall the
recurrence of a subsequent filing of a similar kind. There is no question
of the right iii equity of this Grand Lodge to enjoin the use of . the term
"F. & A. M." by any other group in California. The policy of dignifying
nothing as something by such an action is the real question. Until the activity
approaches the proportions of . another later reported herein, there seems to
be no occasion for decision or action.
A few weeks ago the . secretary of one of our regular Lodges called the
attention of the committee to the activity of one of these clandestine organizations in the south in obtaining as a member a man who thought he was joining
Masonry. After considerable correspondence and telephoning the man was
interviewed. He was told his mistake and advised that if he was desirous
of becoming a Mason, his only recourse was to resign from this spurious
organization, repudiate it entirely, arid petition for the degrees in a regular
Lodge. He was further told that if he did this he must be sure to disclose
in his petition his experience and the fact that he repudiated completely this
false Masonry. He was further advised that he was entitled to receive back the
money he had paid, including dues of $1.50 per month from the time he took
his first degree; and that if that was refused, and he himself desired to resort
to law to recover it, suitable advice and guidance would be furnished him.
At the time of this report the committee has not been informed of his
decision. From the committee's interview and investigation this is the only
instance coming to our attention where a man of apparent Masonic caliber
has been duped by these organizations, although one of the members of the
committee piloted another victim through this same course in 1914 resulting
in a conviction. It also resulted in ending the racket of that defendant.
This is the only effective method of curbing the activities of clandestinism
and the cooperation of our entire craft and all officers in it toward this
objective is urged.

Respectfully submitted,

many Americans, but since the cessation of the American oil industry in
Mexico the number of Lodges and membership have dwindled very much;
and it is possible that some arrangements may be made in Mexico in matters
Masonic that will relieve us of any embarrassment in the matter of recognitions there.
In the Latin countries we find a people who do not understand majority
· rult, either in Masonry or in government ; and when the minority loses they
just begin to fight and for that reason Masonry is not so stable in some Latin
countries as it would be in an Anglo-Saxon country, an English-speaking
country. We find the same trouble to a certain extent in Europe. So those
matters will be continued.
Now with ' reference to the general state of Masonry in the world, I am
happy to inform you that so far as I know there is not a ripple of discord
or lack of harmony in any English-speaking Grand Lodge. The Grand Lodges
of Denmark, Norway, Holland, Belgium, the Orient of France, of Italy, of
Spain, of Greece, the Gran:l Lodges of Germany and of Austria, of Poland,
of Czecho_-Slovakia, of Yugo-Sill.via and of Roumania have all gone out of
existence. Masonry still lives there in the hearts and minds of our brethren,
but the organization was banned by Mr. Hitler and Mr. Mussolini and Mr.
Franco and those who had military force to support their ideas on the subject.
However, I am creditably informed that the Grand Orient of Italy is now
again in Rome. I know that the Grand Orient of France is again in Paris,
and I doubt not that King Christian in Denmark can resume his Masonic
labors in rather a short time, likwise the brethren in Norway. As the Fascists
and Nazis are cleared out, Masonry wilf be reestablished in all the European
countries.
A number Off Grand Lodges were in exile. The Grand Orient of Italy
was in exile in Santiago, Chile. The Grand Orient of France was in exile
in Lim::i., Peru, Czecho-Slovakia in exile in London and perhaps some of the
others. The largest of the German Grand Lodges are in exile on King
David Street in Jerusalem. So the organization, in one form or the. other,
is still alive. Masonry is to be found in every clime and in every country
and will be reestablished in a reasonably short time, we all hope.

The Charters Committee proposed that a photostatic copy or a duplicate
original of the charter of a Lodge be used, except at the installation of
officers, in lieu of .a charter kept in a place of safekeeping.

Your committee thinks that the proposal of having a photostatic copy

your committee recommends the adoption of a.policy that upon the request
of a Lodge a full sized photostatic copy of its charter be made and certified
to be a true copy by the Grand Secretary, and the negative of such photostat be lodged with the Grand Secretary.
Your committee recommends the adoption of such policy and that the

Uniform Accounting System
A resolution has been introduced proposing that all The con~tituent
·Lotlges keep their books and records in a uniform ·hstem as prepared by
the Grand Secr!!tary, or , ~s may hereafter be prescribed .by Grand Lodge;
provided, ho~ever, that the reso,lutjon shall not apply to Lodges which,
in the opinion of the . l!lspector, have complete, adequate and satisfactory
books and records. Your committee has made a careful examination of
the subject matter and is of the opinion that the Grand Secretary is successfolly introducing a uniform system of records in the Lodges, and that
no legislation on the subject is appropriate at the present time. Therefore
your committee recommends that the resolution be not adopted.

Adopted.
Remission of Dues of Men in the Armed Forces

'A resolution.
"
has been adopted proposing an amendment to Se.c tion 255,
Article 6, of the Constitution and Ordinances having the effect ·to exempt
in advance or otherwise, by special resolution, the dues of those 'who shall
be in the armed forces of the United States of America in the time of war.
Your committee is of the opinion that every Mason according to his ability
should contribute to the support of Masonry and that an exemption of a
large class, without regard to their ability is unwarranted: Many Masons
in the armed services are well able to pay dues to their Lodges, and
your committee thinks that no Lodge would refuse to remit the dues of
a member, whether a soldier or otherwise, where the circumstances warranted such action. Your committee . therefore recommends that the resolution be not adopted.

·Adopted.

" Death is only an old door,
Set in a garden wall,
On gentle hinges it gives at dusk
When the thrushes call.
Along the lintel are green leaves,
Beyond the lights lie still,
Very weary and willing feet,
Go over that sill.
There is nothing to trouble any heart,
Nothing to hurt at all,
Death is only a quiet door,
In an old wall."
-Nancy Byrd T11rner.
Death is th.e universal decree of all who live and move in material
form. The earth itself is one vast mausoleum. The very rocks and hills
that wall us in are but the dusty archives of life that throbbed in dead
and forgotten ages.
Henry Ward Beecher often spoke .of .death as a coronation, and so it
is. Henceforth when we speak of it, let it be only as the pathway to a
nobler life. Let us strip it of its awful significance and think of it only
'as the working of God's infinite mercy and goodness.
So let us live in faith and hope and join in that spirit of unselfish service
which animated the lives of those whom we here honor.
I know of no better manner of concluding this rep·ort than by leaving
with you the following quotation. These words were spoken by a man of
God at the bier of a loved one and might be termed a vision of the passage
from life to light eternal. I quote :
"I am standing on the sea shore. A ship at my side· spreads her
white sails to the morning breeze and heads for the blue ocean. She

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

174

is an object of beauty and strength and I stand and watch her until at
length she hangs like a speck of white cloud just where the sea and
sky come to mingle with each other. Then someone at my side says,
'There, she's gone.' Gone where? Gone from ·my sight that is all.
She is just as large in mast and hull and spar as she was when she
left my side, and just as able to bear her load of living freight to the
place of destination. Her diminished size· is in me, not in her; and
just at the moment when someone at my side says, 'There, she's gone,'
there are other eyes watching her approach from another shore and
other voices read.Y to take ·up the glad shout, 'There she comes.'"
EULOGY

Ellsworth Meyer

I

TIME and CHANGE
ELLSWORTH MEYER

. In these moments of meditation and memory, well may we say with th~
poet Whittier:
" Look where we may the wide earth o'er ·
Those fighted faces shine no more.
We turn the pages that they read,
Their written words we linger o'er
But in the sun they cast no shade,
No voice is heard, no sign is made,
No step is on the conscious floor.
Alas fo~ him who never sees
The stars shine through his cypress-trees
Who, hopeless, lays his .dead away
Nor looks to see the breaking day
Across · the mournful marbles play."
Many of those lighted faces we knew, nevermore shall shine upon these
communications; nevermore . shall we see their signs made, their steps
taken upon this conscious fioor, but through the eyes of faith and hope we
do see the breaking day.
'
Our poet · spoke of ;Time and Change-and in these moments we s~nse
how swiftly time does flow into. the sea of eternity. Verily, we can see the
stream of history, now in channels so deep and straight that there is
scarcely a ripple upon the velvety surface, now racing the rapids to pound
against great rocks which "obskuct its course, but whether we see it
meandering through sun-lit fields ainid the sweet sounds of peace or
storming through gorges where glooiny light makes little of the day and
much of the night, ever we see the current seeking the sea, responsive to
some Divine Command.
Time and Change-we cannot think of life or death without a consciousness of many changes, day by day, year by year, and· in this hour
we stand face to face with the most dramatic change of all.
Though each of our departed brethren .is entitled to a separate eulogy,
for we recognize no distinction save only that of goodness, we can but
speak of two and in our words must be found the eulogium of all.
Our eldest, James, silver-crowned, full of days, has reached the earthly

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

175

bounds which he could not pass. The number of his months was determined but they made more than four score and ten year.s. When first he
saw the light of day, old Zachary Taylor was President, there was yet no
Grand Lodge of California and the eastern seaboard still rang with hue
and cry of a new El Dorado by the Pacific shore. The eyes of adventurers
and psalm-singers alike were turned toward the gold at the end of the
rainbow which arched the vast plains and the Sierra Nevadas to touch a
soil christened with odd Spanish names. There were no speeding trains
to swiftly bear a man to this new Promised Land, he must sit and sway
many a day behind plodding oxen and risk death on parched lands or at
the point of some swift-winging arrow to reach the rainbow's end. There
were no bright shining wires to carry his voice or news across a continent.
All these and more were yet to come-J am"es was de.s tined for a part in
their building.
When first our brother saw the light of day, storm clouds were gathering above the nation, but men had not yet heard the rail-splitter's clarion
call: "This nation cannot long endure, .h alf sla.v e, half free." Even free
men slaved from dawn until dusk for a pittance and little children were
still broken upon the wheel of toil. These were destined to pass away and
in the century of change our brother played his part guided by the cardinal
virtues of temperance, fortitude, prudence and justice,, firm in faith and
hope, with charity for all mankind.
Yes, James has walked into the sunset, but we see a wilderness richly
cultivated, a nation grown greater and the breaking of better day.

a

Young Jim is gone too. He was the youngest of our mystic tie. His
days scarcely made a score of years and there is much tragedy in his tory.
He never knew his father or his own son, for his dad fell in that charge
at Chateau-Thierry and Jim at St. Lo.
Jim had · wanted to be. an architect, an operative mason building useful
monuments of stone, but events plucked him from academic halls and cast
him upon a Normandy beachhead to throw· grenades at the monuments
of antiquity, and other men. He · had barely had time to wed that goldenhaired girl with whom he had strolled the campus lanes, but their love was
great though time was short. He was in England when the letter came
that now these two were three and there was the promise of a pictur.~ as
soon as Nature had smoothed out those funny little wrinkles.
Jim had heard all the speeches; he knew about all the new freedoms;
but out there those guns on yonder shore spoke for "keeps" and Jim
could not help asking himself many questions. What cared he for men
who talked about a new, brave world, but did not build it? Talk of peace
was fine, but it must be made manifest. Who dares to criticize if he fell
'asleep with the fervent prayer that his son would never learn the awful
truths of war?
Many of the questions Jim asked were still unanswered when he entered that fiery cauldron across the choppy Channel and there was no time
for answers in the weary days and sleepless nights that followed. Through
the hedgerows and across fie1ds churned by manmade storms he charged
and though he saw the gates of St. Lo, he reached them not.
As his sands of time swiftly ran out~ he thought not of the terrible
pain, but of home, family and what might have been. It was a Chaplain
who gently raised his head and tenderly wiped his anguished brow.
Strange, but Jim's last words were: "Parson, I never belonged to your
church.''

REPORT OF BOARD OF CONTROL

While this represents a decrease of 44 per cent in applications and 34
per cent in jobs filled compared to the previous year, it is an indication of
the high degree of employment prevailing today. All employment in war
plants is necessarily handled through the U. S. Employment Service, which
condition has reduced materially the m.,imber of applicants and the opportunity
for placements of applicants in such industries.
The total expense involved in operating the seven . offices was $31~500, 45
per cent of which, or $14,100, was appropriated by Grand Lodge. The amount
of fees saved applicants was over $200,000. Due to the decrease in the number
of placements the average cost per job filled increased from $3.97 in 1943
to $4.28.
,
H owever many services which are not reflected in statistics were rendered
by the sever~! offices to families of our brethren in the armed forces, including
many housing placements, counseling with families, etc.
All in all in addition to performing the usual function of helping to place
Masons and ~heir dependents in employment, the Masonic Employment Service
has made a very definite ,contribution to the war effort in many ..yays, and
thereby is continuing to render a real Masonic service where it is ,most needed.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California.:
The following is intended to give a brief synopsis of the work of the
Boards of Relief and Employment Services as supervised by the Board of
Control.
·
Before doing so, the board desires to express its appreciation of. the. courtesy, cOOperation and assistance given by the Grand Master, the Grand Secretary and his assistants.
Boards of Relief
It is felt that the very high standard of efficiency continues to be shown
by our Boards Qf Relief in handling their many problems: Commendations
of their personnel for excellent service is but a just tribute.,
It is felt that all justified relief has been freely extended in accordance
with the policy of Grand Lodge.
The Board of Control and the Boards of Relief and Employment Services
continue to work in closest cooperation for betterment of rou't ine and service.
War Service By Boards of Relief
Boards of Relief are rendering very fine Masonic brotherly services to
military brothers and thei,r families such as
Locating for their distant parents or other relatives, wounded or other
men in the U. S. military service and giving a personal touch to the information desired.
Locating homes for families of those in armed services.
Visiting sick and wounded in hospitals to cheer them up.·
Transporting where necessary .members of families to embarkation points,
and rendering other helpful services.
No' General Reimbursements
The board calls attention to the fact that for the second ·consecutive year
there are no reimbursements to be made by the Grand Lodge to any Board
of Relief in this jurisdiction for moneys that may have been advanced during
the entire fiscal year.
This evidences again the extreme care and thoroughness of our Boards of
Relief in the advancement of moneys.
Meetings
Conferences of the members of the Board of Control are held when necessary throughout the year by mail.
A meeting of the Board of Control was held on May 21st in Oakland.
A joint meeting of the Board of Control, and managers of Boards of
Relief and Employment Services was ·held today for consideration of immediate
and post-war problems.
The Board of Control is keeping pace with changing conditions so as to
be prepared to move quickly with Boards of Relief and Employment Services
in the endeavor to meet all early or post-war contingencie_s.
Employment Service
During the fiscal year ended July 31, 1944, our . seven employment offices
placed 8,586 Masonic applicants in employment, 7,003 or 81 per cent being in
permanent jobs. These placements represent 72 per cent of the applications
received.

work the·y are doing under most difficult conditions.

be instructed to write a special letter of congratulations and encouragement.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON POLICY
AND GENERAL PURPOSES
Masonic Clubhouse at Berkeley Emblem
A proposal has been made of a design for a badge or pin to be worn by
the students at the University of California making use of the Masonic Clubhouse which takes the Jorm of a square and compass 'enclosing a representation of the Campanile at the university, and having on it the letters U. C.
The proposed design so closely resembles the badge of a Master Mason
that your committee is of the ,opinion that the same should be modified so
as not to simulate a Masonic emblem. Your committee therefore recommends

189

that a change be made in the design and that the Grand Master shall have
the right to approve an acceptable de~ign with power to cause the same to
be adopted and used:

Adopted.
Committee on Lodge Financing
To the Most Wo1·shipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes respectfully and fraternally reports as follows :
A. resolution was presented proposing that Section 78a of the Constitution
and Ordinances of the Grand Lodge of California be amended to read as
follows : "There shall be :i. committee consisting of 5 members on Lodge
Financing, which shall be appointed annually by the Grand Master; the Chairman and any 2 of the committeemen shall have power to act."
The ordinance now in force provides for a committee consisting of the
Grand Treasurer who shall be Chairman, and the Chairman of the Committee
on Finance, and 3 other committeemen. It appears that the work of this
committee imposes an undue burden on the Grand Treasurer, who has many
functions under our law to perform and therefore should be relieved of the
duties in connection with the Committee on · Lodge Financing. Instead of a
committee having ex-officio members it would be proper to have a committee
of 5 members selected by the Grand Master to do this work and your
committee therefore recommends that the amendment to Section 78a of the
Constitution and Ordinances be adopted and the subject matter referred to
the Committee on Jurisprudence for the preparation of suitable legislation.

Adopted and referred to the Committee on Jurisprµdence.
Certification of Secretary
A resolution has been presented proposing that section 187a .of the Constitution and Ordinances be repealed. This section has to do with the certification
by the Inspector of the district with the Secretary-elect as proficient in those
portions of the Constitution and Ordinances relating to the duties of the
Secretary of the Lodge and to the government of the Lodge.
The passage of this law in 1943 has resulted in the examination and qualification of most, if not all of the secretaries in California, but has also resulted
in dissatisfaction in many quarters not only because of the examination but
also because of the implications in the law. It appears to your committee
that the Grand Secretary in his contact with the secretaries is able to make
such suggestions and corrections as seem to be needed, and that he is succeeding
in securing uniform practices and greater efficiency in the offices of the secretaries of the Lodges in this jurisdiction. It is the ovinion of your committee
that the resolution should be adopted and therefore the committee recommends
that section 187a of the Constitution and Ordinances be repealed.
The Jurisprudence Committee approves the form of the legislation.

Adopted by five-six vote.
Constitution Month Observance
The Constitution Month Observance Committee rendered a report to Grand
Lodge which was referred to this committee and the contents thereof are
approved by this committ~, which recommends that the committee be continued
for the ensuing Masonic year.

Adopted.

Method of Ritualistic Instruction
Brother Lester R. Starr of Illinoistown Lodge No. 51 proposes a resolution
to provide that Grand Lodge go back to the policy of full-time Grand Lecturer
who shall visit each Masonic district at least once a year or more often when
possible. Your committee is of the opinion that the present system of lecturing
is meeting with general approval, has been tested by time, and should not be
changed by the Grand Lodge, and therefore, recommends that the resolution
be not adopted ..

Adopted.

Physical Qualifications
A resolution has been proposed to amend Section 208 of the Constitution
and Ordinances of the Grand Lodge of · California by substituting in that
section the word "ostensibly" · instead of the ,word "substantially" so that the
last clause of said section shall read as follows : "and physically able to conform ostensibly to what the several degrees respectively require of him."
For many years Grand Masters and the. Grand Lodge l)ave struggled with
interpretations of Section 208 and a fair degree of certainty attaches to said
section as it now stands. In the . opinjon of your cqmmittee the word "ostensibly" for· the word "substantially" would open the way for future doubts
and diffisulties of inte.rpretation. Your committee is of the opinion that the
section would not be improved by. the proposed amendment, and that the interests of . the craft would be as well. served by the rule contained in the present
Ordinance as it would be by the proposed amendment, and for that reason
recommends that the amendment be not adopted.

Adopted.
Form of Application
Your committee approve; the •Comments of the Grand Master in his annual
message relative to changes in the forms of application for degrees and also
approves his suggestion that the matter be deferred until the next annual
communication, and in the meantime that the problem be subjected to careful
study by a committee appointed by the incoming Grand Master.

Adopted.
Funeral Service

A resolution lias been presented by a score of brethren ·providing that
before receiving Certificates of Proficiency Masters-elect must qualify or have
a substitute qualified to conduct the funeral service.
At the annual communication of this Grand Lodge in 1943, the Grand
Lecturer made a report relative to the funeral services and indicated that the
Inspectors should ascertain that the Master-elect was sufficiently familiar with
the funeral service ,to render the same effectively. We think no legislation
or other action is required, but that the Grand Lecturer, the Assistant Grand
Lecturers, and the Inspectors have the right as well as the duty to see that
Masters-elect are sufficiently familiar with the funeral ceremony to render
the same c~editably and impressively. \Ve therefore{ecommend that no action
on the subJect matter be taken at this time.

Adopted.

PROCEEDINGS OF .THE

does not recognize, approve, or sponsor any other organization, no matter how
popular or meritorious the same may be, and that it should not assume the
right to clarify or . define any relationship with any other organization. Your
committee is cognizant of the excellent work and influence of the Order of
De Molay which is composed of non-Masoqs, and casts no adverse reflection
upon it, as it does not cast reflections on organizations that are related t?

Grand Lodge, nor subject to its control or direction. For these reason5 your

has in its membership probably some one who is quite familiar with taxes
and may even be a tax expert; and it would be a very prudent thing if each
one of you would check your 'tax status, determined upon your own problems.
You have been advised by your tax committee concerning your unemployment,
social security tax, and we also sent out a report that you would not have
to make a return to the Internal Revenue Department as to your financial
set-up which is required of many organizations that are exempted under Section 101 of the · Revenue Act but fraternal societies are specially exempted
from making that report. You received that from your Grand Secretary's·
office. During the past year the Tax Committee has had under its consideration the problem that was presented to Grand Lodge last year. That was the
demand made by the State Unemployment Tax Commission that there be
counted as employees of Grand Lodge all of the Employment Bureau employees,
all of the clerical help of the Endowment Board and various others, including
the chairman of the Correspondence Committee, who was given his expenses
of $500.00.
·
Now we have cleared that up in part; we have got the ruling from the
Federal Internal Revenue Department, and it is our contention that we do
not come under the state act, but based upon the rulings of the Federal Internal
Revenue Department, we probably have for some years in the past been under /
the act, in which event there may be some assessment for back taxes with
penalties. Under the current year, it is very doubtful if we are under the
act, because there has been a change in the method of doing ·business in the
Grand Lodge agencies. It now all goes through the secretary's office, and if
we do m;1t have more than eight employees we are not under the Federal
act; and if we are not under the Federal act then we are not under the state
act. Fraternal societies are given that special exemption.
We have a considerable task ahead of us this coming year, because that
will have to be taken up with the State Department which may be in accord
with the Federal ruling and it may not be. Of course, if there is any tax
to be paid we will have to pay it. We may then file a suit to collect for it,
but so far there has been no levy of any tax and so far we have not been
called upon to pay tax on the Employment Boards which carried the heavy
salary on which there has heretofore never been any tax paid, and of course
they are obviously solely charities and would not be taxed.
The same sort of demand was made upon the Masonic Homes, and if that
tax would have been effective it would have cost probably $50,000.00 for back
taxes; but the homes have been fortunate in getting a ruling that they are
strictly charitable institutions and have no tax against them.
Taxes are something that have come to live with us, and I think that
all of the larger Lodges should check their tax status, because you may find
that you have been slipping up on something and in addition to the tax you
will have penalties assessed .to you.

Children's . Home
The Most Worshipful Grand Master in his message referred to the fact
that there was unused capacity in the Masonic Children's Home at the present
time and suggested that it might be well to relax our entrance requirements
at the time being so that a greater use of our facilities could be made.
It is the opinion of your committee that the present condition at the Home
i~ of temporary character and that in the near future all its facilities will be
required to carry on the work in this jurisdiction for which the Homes were
built and are operated. The proposal opens up a· number of questions of feasibility and finance which require a longer study than has yet been made of the
subject, and therefore your committee ' recommends that no change be made
in the present requirements for entrance into the Homes.

Adopted.

Duties of Grand Treasurer.
Sec. 41. It shall be the duty of the Grand Treasurer:
1st. To receive all moneys belonging to Grand Lodge from the Grand
Secretary, receipt therefor, keep proper books of account thereof and,
immediately upon the receipt of said moneys, to deposit the same ~o the

with the approval of the Grand Master. Funds on deposit shall be withdrawn by the Grand Treasurer, or in case of his inability oi: unavailability
by the Grand Master or Deputy Grand Master and the Grand Secretary.
2nd. To take charge of all other property of Grand Lodge, except as
provided in Section 44 and 79 of the Ordinances, and keep an accurate
account thereof; bonds and other securities shall be deposited with a
bank or trust company or in safe deposit vaults, selected as provided in

anyone of the foregoing Grand officers and the Grand Secretary.
3rd. To pay all bills, claims or demands and make transfers of funds
under such regulations as may be provided by Grand Lodge.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON FINANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the
State of California:
. Your Committee on Finance submits the following report :

Audit of Accounts
Following previous established policy of having the accounts audited, this
committee has employed Brother Walter Parker (formerly associated with
Ruckstell, Burrows and Webb, our former certified public accountants, now
dissolved) to audit the accounting records of the Grand Treasurer, Grand
Secretary, Ma~onic Homes and the Endowment Fund.
Brother Parker's certified reports have had the study and consideration of
your co:nmittee. . The· audit finds all receipts and expenditures have been
properly recorded. A copy has been filed with the Grand Secretary. The
report of the auditor will be printed in the annual proceedings.
The cost of the certified audit seems reasonable and entirely consistent
with charges previously made for the volume of work entailed. The cost
of the audit was, to Grand Lodge $150.00 and to the Masonic Homes $600.00.
Report of Grand Treasurer
For a number of years this committee has called to the attention of Grand
Lodge the large responsibility which rests upon this Grand Lodge officer in

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

properly caring for the many financial transactions which now devolve upon
him. The magnitude of this responsibility is amply demonstrated by the report
of this official for the year. The report clearly indicates the study which has
been required and the multifold transactions which have been handled.
It is worthy of more than special mention that the sale of a part of the
securities in the Endowment Fund has brought a net increase to that fund
o.f $64,752.83. It is also worthy of note that, since the close of the Grand
Lodge y~ar on July 31st, there have been sales of bonds and preferred stocks,
owned by Grand Lodge and which have resulted in a net profit of $6,773.58.
These bonds and stocks were, under regulations adopted last year governing
investments of Grand Lodge funds, no longer eligible securities.
While these profits are most commendable and. pleasingly acceptable and
yet, these transactions reveal a far greater benefit to Grand Lodge than the
actual profit and that is, the great care, sound judgment and hours of study
which this grand officer has given to the handling of these sales and reinvestment of funds, as well as in all the other manifold transactions of his office.
The Grand Treasurer is entitled to the profound thanks of Grand Lodge.
It is also to be noted and to be commended, that the Grand Treasurer has
made a fuller investment than heretofore of all the surplus funds in the
various accounts of Grand Lodge. This brings additional revenue to Grand
Lodge.
Your Committee on Finance is in hearty accord with the fullest possible
investment of all surplus funds in war bonds.
. The report of the auditor shows that all transactions of this officer are
in accord with regulations and that all records are in perfect shape.

Portraits of Preceding Grand Masters
It has been the thought of this committee for a number of years that our
gallery of portraits of those who have presided over the destinies of Masonry
in this jurisdiction should be complete. We are sure that all who were familiar
with our gallery of some :;ears ago will admit that its appearance has been
materially improved in the last few years. It is again the thought of this
committee that this improvement should be continued and that the portraits
of those Past Grand Masters which are not yet in the gallery ,should be
included.
To the gallery this year ·has been added the portrait of Past Grand Master
Wilson. The attention of Grand Lodge is called to its excellence.
The portraits of Past Grand Masters Warren, Smith and Wood are still
missing. This committee is sure that the Masons of this jurisdiction will want
the ·portraits of these three illustrious Masons included in the gallery. Your
committee, therefore, repeats the request heretofore made, that these three
Most Worshipful Brothers have their portraits painted, the bill for each to
be in an amount not to exceed $300.00 and when presented to the Grand
Secretary to be paid by him out of Grand Lodge funds and the portraits to
be hung in the gallery of our Past Grand Masters.
Grand Lodge will note that the increase recommended for the portrait of
the Grand Master is also made for these three Past Grand Masters.
There is also to be noted a change in the portraits of Past Grand Masters
in that there are new portraits of both Past Grand Masters Burke and Fischer,
each having been repainted at personal expense. The portraits are an improvement upon those previously in the gallery and portray a much better
likeness of each.

Reimbursement of Expenses of Inspectors
For a number of years Grand Lodge has reimbursed the District Inspectors
for expenses paid out in the performance of their duties by direct appropriation
from Grand Lodge funds. It is the intent that the Inspectors should have
returned to them all expenses incurred in the performance of their duties
under such rules as may be adopted by the Grand Lecturer and approved by
the Grand Master. This committee recommends the continuance of this policy.
It must be noted that were the Inspectors to request the return of the
expenses to which they are justly . entitled, the expenditure would amount to
approximately $4,000. For the past year only $823.93 has been paid out,
or in .other words, this body of Masonic workers has made a direct contribution to Grand Lodge in excess of $3,000 and this, in addition to the many
hours given to the advancement of the fraternity. For all of which this worthy
body of Masonic workers is entitled to the profound thanks of the Masons
in this jurisdiction.
The Grand Lecturer has suggested the budgeting of $1,600 for the purpose
of caring for these expenses and this committee is reconunending the appropriation of such an amount. This recommendation is made however, with the
understanding that should requests for return of expenses be made by the
Inspectors and in accordance with the regulations established by the Grand
Lecturer, the full amount of such requests are to be paid regardless of the
<\mount which is appropriated for that purpose. Your committee therefore
offers the following resolution and recommends its adoption :
RESOLVED, That the sum of $1,600.00 be appropriated 'from the funds of
Grand Lodge for the purpose of defraying the expenses of Inspectors in
performing their official duties, such repayment to be made upon bills duly
presented to the Grand Secretary, which said bills should first be approved by
the Grand Lecturer.

Sotoyome Lodge No. 123 ( Situate at Healdsburg )
A number of years ago this Lodge agreed to pay the owner of the property,
in which its Lodge room was situated, a monthly sum during the life of the
owner and his wife and upon the decease of both the property was to belong
to the Lodge. This arrangement became so burdensome to the Lodge that
in 1943 appeal was made to Grand Master Wood for assistance.
The Grand Master ordered the payment to the surviving widow from
Grand Lodge . fun~s of the amount necessary to maintain in good standing
the agreement between the Lodge and Mr. Bush (the original owner of the
property), with the understanding that the Lodge was to return $50.00 monthly
until the full sum advanceo by Grand Lodge had been returned.
This committee last year approved the action of the Grand Master and
recommended that the same arrangement be continued for the coming year.
There has now been paitl out by Grand Lodge $1,650.00, of which $500.00
has been repaid by the Lodge, leaving a balance due from the Lodge to Grand
Lodge of $1,150.00.
Mrs. Bush, the surv1vmg spouse, is still alive and therefore, if the Lodge
is to finally acquire its home and the good name of Masonry be sustained
it is necessary to continue the monthly payment to Mrs. Bush of $150.00. Th~
Lodge is still not in financial position to pay more than $50.00. It is understood that the Lodge is to eventually return. all funds to Grand Lodge and
to pay interest on all monies advanced at the rate of 3% per annum.
This committee, therefore, offers t)le following resolution and recommends
its adoption :
RESOLVED, That· there be paid from the funds of Grand Ledge monthly to
Sotoyome Lodge No. 123, a sam not to exceed $150.00, during the lifetime
of Mrs. Bush, with the understanding that such sum shall be used to satisfy
its obligation to Mrs. Bush and that all sums advanced, including the amount
heretofore paid, shall be considered as a loan t 0 Sotoyome Lodge and be
repaid by such Lodge in a sum of not less than $50.00 per month, until the
full amount advanced shall have been repaid, together with interest thereon
at the rate of 3 per cent per annum.

Grand Lodge Reserves
There has been referred to your Committee on Finance that portion of
the message of the Grand Master dealing with the finances of Grand Lodge
and which has been given the careful and thoughtful consideration of the
committee. ·
It appears to your committee that, in order for the members of Grand
Lodge to obtain a complete understanding, a careful review of the finances
of Grand Lodge should be made and that such review must include mention
of the financial condition of the homes.
It should also be borne in mind that in using the term "reserves " it
includes not only such sums as may be set aside as reserves, but als; accumulated surplus; that the surplus now on hand has been accumulated over
a long series of years and that the main source of revenue of Grand Lodge
is the payment made by the constituent Lodges through per capita levy.
It also should -be remembered that Grand Lodge has an investment in the
capital stock of the Masonic Temple Association of California, of $339,850.00,
but tha~ such investment, due to lack of liquidity, must be excluded from any
calculation of reserves and that only cash in the bank and investments in
securities of easy convertibility are included in the c~lculations.
· At the time of the clO!.e of last Grand Lodge year the surplus in the
treasury amounted to $484,980.50, of which amount $40,371.85 is cash in the

211

bank and $244,608.69 in liquid securities. Since the close of the year securities
have been sold at a price above that at which they were being carried and
which have netted an addition to the surplus of $6,773.58. To this should
be added the amount received since the close of the Grand Lodge year through
the twenty cents additional per capita levy made last year to replace monies
appropriated from the surplus then on hand, the amount received being
$27,170.60 and which makes the surplus at this time $318,924.72.
The Auditor's report discloses that the homes had total surplus on hand
of $529,336.24, which sum includes the Patton reserve and the reserve for
rehabilitation after the war. Of this amount there has been accrued in the
year just closing $268,459.18. It therefore can be seen that it is reasonable
to expect that within two and one-half years the homes will have a surplus
of one million dollars and that if conditions after this war parallel those of
the first World War, a total surplus of two million dollars is well within
a possibility and therefore, the need of planning an additional surplus for the
homes does not exist.
Reserves are comforting to have and also must be carefully guarded because
the temptation to spend is always greater when the money is available.
It is therefore thli conclusion of your Committee on Finance that, while
there sh0uld be an increase in the surplus of Grand Lodge and yet, the need
to place an additional burden on the Lodges for that purpose is not necessary,

•

Grand Lodge Per Capita
The constitution provides for the levying of a per capita of fifty (50c)
cents, to pay for the expenses of Grand Lodge and its various activities. In.
addition to the sum provided for by this per capita levy, there is additional
revenue accruing to Grand Lodge from degrees conferred and income on
investments and from some other sources of approximately $49,000.00.
There is also some other revenue derived from the sale of supplies and
from surety bonds coverin:I Lodge officers. This revenue, however, cannot
be taken into consideration in the budget, because it is offset by corresponding
items of disbursements, which are also eliminated from the budget. It also
should be borne in mind that there are always expenses which cannot be
estimated-this is particularly true this year due to war conditions and the
probability that further emergencies will arise.
.
Despite the uncertain conditions under which Grand Lodge operated this
past year the budget which was set up a year ago has been as closely adhered
to as co:iditions would permit. The year has ended with a material surplus
of income over expenses. This surplus is being added to the general reserve
of Grand Lodge. It should be borne in mind th11t $271170.60 of the surplus
this year has accrued due to the replacement of surplus of previous years
expended because of the need last year to return to the War Relief Fund
and to create the Grand Master's Emergency War .Fund.
This committee has again prepared a budget which will be submitted immediately following this portion of the committee's report. The estimated
income. and expenses for the coming year are set forth in the budget. The
n;oney is already on hand to care for all appropriations now being made
and the expenses to be incurred for the operation of the activities of Masonry
in this jurisdiction.
The per capita levy which is now being made is for the purpose of raising
the funds for the next fiscal year's operation.
It must be recognized that imponderable conditions may arise and there
may _be expenses which cannot now be foreseen and the amounts budgeted
are only estimates, but are as accurate as can be determined at the present
time.

There is a constitutional provision for the levying of a per capita of fifty
(SOc) cents for the maintenance of the homes and which, of course, is mandatory.
The total per capita levy of a year ago was $1.7S. In this were included
two special levies of twenty (20c) cents each, one for homes maintenance
and one to replace. appropriations from accumulated reserve, both of which are
unnecessary this year.
It is the opinion of your Committee on Finance that the reserve of Grand
Lodge is of a satisfactory size and the need to assess the Lodges for any
material increase does not now exist. In establishing the additional per capita
levy of twenty-five (2Sc) cents for this year your committee has calculated
only the needs of Grand Lodge· and a margin for a safe estimate. This will
make the total levy as follows :

George Washington Masonic National Memorial
The Grand Lodge has referred to this committee the ·report of the
Special Committee appointed by him to study and report on the George
Washington Masonic National Memorial.
The Grand Master is to be commended for having decided to bring
thi~ situation to Grand Lodge in this manner and for the able personnel he
has placed on the committee. The committee is also to be commended
for the complete report which it has rendered.
Your Committee on Finance is in agreement with 1:he findings of the
committee on the need of completing the Memorial and also, th~t this
Jurisdiction should make further co.n tributions towar~ the completion of
the enterprise.
·
. .
This committee would be in accord with Grand "Lodge go1hg even
farther than suggested by this Special Committee and express a willingness to contribute its share toward the completion and furnishing and also
the ·raising of an endowment fund, the income from which was to care
for maintenance, but upon the following conditions:

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA •

That p·lans and specifications be prepared and adopted for the completion and furnishing of the Memorial and thus assuring no further additions
to the Memorial.
That estimates be had from experienced and practical sources of the
cost of completion and furnishing.
That an estimate be made of the cost of maintenance, which estimate
shall include obsolescence and depreciation and overhead costs of the
association.
That it be determined as to the amount of an endowment which will
be required to provide sufficient revenue to care for such expenses of
maintenance and overhead costs and obsolescl!nce and depreciation.
That sufficient of the other Jurisdictions agree to raise their share of
the total sum required to finish the Memorial and to furnish · and endow it,
so that all may have assurance that the .Memorial will be completed and
will be adequately maintained.
Until such assurances can be had your Committee on Finance is unwilling to recommend any appropriation from the funds of Grand Lodge
as a further contribution to the association.
Your committee points out that to ma)<e the contribution as recommended by this Special Committee will still ieave the Memorial incomplete
and without adequate assurances that the money will ever be forthcoming
for its completion and therefore, the present embarrassing situation · will
continu~
·
This committee feels constrained to express disapproval of the source
of appropriation recommended by the Special Committee selected to .report
on the George Washington Memorial, which recommendation is, that the
appropriation be made from the General Funds of Grand Lodge and that
no assessment be levied against the Lodges, which means that the funds
will come from the Reserve of Grand Lodge and no levy made to· replace.
This is contrary to the long established policy qf Grand Lodge and
your Committee on Finance,· which has always maintained that Grand
Lodge Reserves are for emergency purposes and to be used to . relieve
distress in the Lodges and among the Brothers. The suggested appi:opriation can neither be considered as an emergency, nor as relief. · This committee, therefore, is of the opinion that when, as, and if any cont'r ibution
be authorized to the Memorial Association .,it should be raised by an . additional per capita levy and only after the above outlined requirements are
met.
Respectfully and fraternally submitted,

Communication, thus setting aside the Constitution. It had almost unanim6µs approval but there was some disapproval, and before we close the
business of the annual communication I just want to point out to you
that the Grand Master next year will be faced with the same problem and
possibly that it may be necessary to curtail even to a greater extent the
activities of Grand Lodge, and the Grand Master may be faced with the
necessit:y of setting aside the Constitution as I have. I think that the
success we have had at this session has justified my actions. I am not
asking any action. I am just advising you that should the same conditions
prevail next year that prevail now I am sure the Grand Master next year
will feel that it is his duty to do as I have done, and possibly more.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRA,ND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

GRAND LODGE AUDIT

The Grand Lodge ordinances which prescribe the · methods of disbursing
Grand Lodge funds do not authorize the payment of bills and claims under
this system. However, the new system permits practically all the clerical
work to be done in the office of the Grand Secretary instead of in the office
of the Grand Treasurer as would be necessary under the present ordinances.

Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California,
San Francisco, California.
Gentlemen:

September 25, 1944.

We have audited the accounts and records of the Grand Lodge, F. & A. M.
of California for_the fiscal year ended July 31, 1944, and present the following
statements :
Grand Lodge Funds
Exhibit A: Statement of all Grand Lodge cash received and disbursed by
the Grand Secretary and Gra?d Treasurer, August 1, 1943, to .July 31, 1944.
Grand Secretary's Accounts
Exhibit B: Resume of cash received and disbursed, August 1 1943 to July
31, 1944.
,
,
Exhibit C: Statement of cash receipts and disbursements for War Relief
and Philippine Dues Funds, August 1, 1943, to July 31, 1944.
Schedule 1 : Statement of Grand Lod~e per capita dues collected from 1943
annual dues.
Schedule 2: Statement of Masonic Homes per capita dues and $25.00 contributions collected during the year 1943-44.
Schedule 3: Analysis of War Program expenses for the fiscal year ended
July 31, 1944.
Grand Treasurer's Accounts
Exhibit D : Statement of cash receipts and disbursements, August 1, 1943,
to July 31, 1944.
•
Exhibit E: Statement of assets and capital account as at July 31, 1944.
Exhibit F: List of investments as at July 31, 1944.
Comments
Cash:
As shown in the capital account of Exhibit F, the revenue from per capita
dues and other sources exceeded the total of the expense and appropriations
by $5,448.13.
All per capita dues,' as reported on the 1943 annual returns from constituent Lodges, have been paid in full. Our Schedules 1 and 2 show proof of the
revenue due from the Lodges in accordance with their 1943 returns and the
$25.00 Homes Contribution reports for the first three quarters of the fiscal
year 1943-44. The total revenue due, as shown, agrees with the total cash
received from the Lodges by the Grand Secretary.
Cash receipts were accounted for and traced to the proper depositaries.
Disbursements were made by checks and supported by vouchers. The receipts
are deposited in savings and commercial accounts of various banks and are
subject to withdrawal on the signature of the Grand Treasurer only. All bank
balances were verified by correspondence with the depositaries.
The Grand Treasurer has opened a new commercial account for the account ·of the Grand Secretary with an initial. deposit of $5,000.00. From this
account, called "Grand Lodge Operating Fund," the Grand Secretary pays all
bills and claims against Grand Lodge. An accounting is made to the Grand
Treasurer for all monies disbursed, who, in turn, reimburses the Grand Secretary for the actual disbursements. Under this system, the account should
never have a . balance over $5,000.00.

221

Accounts Receivable:
Certain payments were made to the San Francisco Board 6f Relief and
to Sotoyome Lod$e No. 123 as authorized at the last communication of Grand
Lodge. The payments are carried as an asset of Grand Lodge since reimbuIJsement is to be made at some future time. The loan of $2,500.00 to Carpinteria
Lodge No. 444 was paid in full during the year.
·
Securities:
Certified. lists of the stocks and bonds were received from the Anglo California National Bank which holds the securities for safe-keeping. Securities
as recorded in the books of account were verified to these lists.
Committee on Acco1tnts:
The Committee on Accounts, at their monthly meetings, are not given · all
bills, claims and demands against Grand Lodge as called for under Section 72.
Payments for office rent, salaries, relief and taxes, which are usually made
before the Committee meets, are not included with the bills presented to it.
Also many of the claims and bills are paid prior to the approval of the Committee, which is contrary to the procedure prescribed in the aforementioned
section.
For the past year and a half, an effective system of control has been ·in
effect, which is used in conjunction with the "Grand Lodge Operati.n g Fund"
of $5,000.00, pending the adoption o.f corrective legislation. We have been
informed that the necessary legislation has been prepared for introduction at
the coming communication of Grand Lodge and we would recommend that it
be given serious consideration.
Certificatc:
We certify that, in our opinion, the attached statements set forth the financial condition of the Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California as at July 31,
1944, and the result of its operations for the fiscal year 1943-44.
Respectfully submitted,
WALTER A. PARKER, Certified Public Accountant.

Comments
Cash:
The bank balances were verified ·by correspondence with the depositaries.
The cash is carried in savings accounts at the Anglo California National Bank
and is subject to withdrawal on the signature of the Grand Trea,5urer only.
All interest coupons and checks due were received and accounted for. The
endowment fund income earned during the fiscal year and transferred to the
Masonic Homes General Fund amounted to $SS,72S191.
Secut"ities:
The securities donated and purchased in prior years and still on hand are
listed on Schedule 1. The securities donated and purchased during the current year are listed on Schedule 2. Securities· sold and called during the current
year are listed on Schedule 3. These sales were made at a net profit of
$64,226.81.
Over a period of years the Endowment Fund has accumulated, through
donations and bequests, a number of securities of doubtful value and others
that are of no value. In order to keep the fund on a con,ser.va~ive basis, . tqe
doubtful value securities have been reduced to a nominal valhe of $1.00. The
worthless securities were written off the books. A list of "these securities are
shown on Schedule 4.
· ·'
" Bonds purchased are recorded at cost.' As many bonds carry' a high 'pr~
mium, an amortization Schedule has been provided to reduce to a minimum
any loss to the Endowment Fund when the bonds are .,..r~deemed.,
Certified lists of the stocks and bonds were ..received from the Anglo
California National Bank which holds the securities ..as. an agent· ~f Grand
Lodge, The securities as recorded in the books of account were checked to
these lists. Those not listed by the bank were found on hand at the o'f1'ce. of
the Grand Secretary and -were personally inspected by us.

Comments
Cash:
All recorded receipts were properly accounted for and deposited in the
banks. All interest coupons and checks due were received and accounted for.
Disbursements were made by checks and supported by proper v9uchers. Bank
balances were verified by correspondence with the depositaries.
The 1943 annual returns from the Lodges were audited and the amount
due to the Homes thereon, plus the $25.00 contributions during the first three
quarters of the current year agreed with the amount turned over to the Homes
by the Grand Secretary.

Securities, Real Estate, Etc.:
During the year $186,856.25 was invested in U.S.A. Treasury and Savings
Bonds, as shown on Schedule B-1. All other securities, etc., listed on this
schedule were received by donation. The book value rep.resents the market
value at the time of donation. . A nominal value of $1.00 is used for purpose·
of record when the actual value is unknown."
Life insurance policies are recorded at the amount recoverable at the death
of the insured, if determinable, otherwise at a nominal value of $1.00.
Notes and contracts receivable are listed at the unpaid balance as at July

31. 1944. Interest was received on all the ·notes and contracts except one,
the David E . and M. Frances Groo note for $1,000.00. This is a note donated
to the Homes a number of years ago and no payments of principal or interest
has been received.
The older real estate is recorded at the assessed value the time it was
donated. That which was received during the past several years has been
'
recorded on the books at a nominal value of $1.00.
The stocks, bonds· and notes that are held by the Anglo California National ·
Bank were verified by certification from the bank, The notes, life insurance
policies, and stocks held at the office of the Grand Secretary were examined.
All were accounted for except one Prudential Life Insurance Policy. T he
Grand Secretary's file on this policy contains an assignment of the. polity
together with a letter stating the original policy is held by the insured's divorced wife.

243

Other F1mds:
The Masonic Homes have numerous separate funds which have been created for definite or special purposes. Full details of these funds are shown
on the attached Schedules B-2 to B-12 inclusive. Two new funds were created
during the current year. The Summer Camp Fund °( Schedule B-4) was
created from the proceeds of the sale of Camp Tucker which has been set
aside to purchase a new camp. The Post-war Reserve Fund (Schedule B-5 )
was authorized at the 1943 communication of Grand Lodge for post-war
rehabilitation of the buildings.
Payments. due from the annuity funds in accordance with the contracts
and agreements were made from the Homes General Fund. Reimbursements
were later made to the General Fund from the various annuity funds.
All interest due on the securities of these funds were received and deposited in the proper bank accounts. All bank balances and securities of these
funds were verified by correspondence with the depositaries.

Contributions Received After July 31, 1944
This being the first year that tne "Contribution Year" of the Endowment Board was made to coincide with. the "fiscal year" of Grand Lodge, •
it was inevitable that many Lodges would continue to send in contributions after July 31. In order that credit may be given and acknowledgment of splendid work may be made, there is published here a list of
such contributions received up to and including September 25. These
contributions are a fine "nest egg" for the fiscal year August 1, 1944July 31, 1945.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
CORRESPONDENCE
To the Most Worshipfitl Gra11d L odge of California:
Your Correspondence Committee for this year reports the review of
46 grand jurisdictions. All the committee members, as in the past several
years, have participated in selecting items which they considered outstanding. These extracts were then compiled into a topical, as distinguished from an individual form. We have omitted much detail, such
as the names of the officers and the routine statistics. Also, we have
refrained from intruding into " other people's business." Our personal
viewpoints are reserved for the activities of our own Grand Lodge.
Generally speaking, the craft is now post-war minded. Hence, it is
appropriate to say a few words as to the consensus of our brethren which
seems to exist in this regard. Your chairman is of this belief perhaps because he is writing this foreword as he is flying to an overseas assignment.
The importance of such emphasis is apparen't also from these remarks
which were recently made by the Secretary of State at a press conference : "I wish I could burn this into your minds and memories for the
next 50 years at least. The human race at this hour, this day, this week,
this year is confronted by the gravest crisis in its experience. And we
who are here on the scene of action have the responsibility of saying
which way it is. going."
Leading Masons have had the foresight to see the approachfog turbulence of the post~war era. They have expressed a belief that we of
the craft would cheerfully assume a part in saying which way civilization
is going. We, whose Masonic forebears brought this nation into being,
may well be in the forefront of the thinking' which will .decide that
question and do our part to shape that thinking so our way of life will
be the one to endure.
·
Parado:is:ically, when there is now so much need for clear, constructive
thinking; the quest for rational guidance is all the more difficult. The
impulse of events leads to emotions, discolorations, fantasy and suspicions.
External verities are hard to find and harder yet to follow when found.
Thus, the times call for deep analysis, an understanding of our constitution;' our state, our ills and our society.
A basis or norm is necessary for this evaluation. The reconstruction
program must match the concepts w!4ich were in the minds of free men
when our country was envisaged. A good physician must know health
to know sickness.
H ence, Masons may consider these ancient but pertinent · words as
a rule of guidance: "He who would duly inquire about the best' form of
the state must first determine the most eligible life." Masonieally speaking, the most eligible life is Masonry in action. It is ingrained and ingrafted into the breast of every true lover of the craft. Let us, therefore,
in concert with our brethren throughout the world, point our thinking,
clearly and certainly, toward a preservation of those principles.

Respectfully submitted,
HENRY C. CLAUSEN,
OSCAR C. OLSON, .
FREDERICK 0. EATON,
CHARLES S. PIODA,
