CANDIDATES
Touching on the question of jurisdiction ·over same, instilling Masonic
education with the degrees, objections and courtesy degrees.
Quebec, 1943 (Committee Report):
Prior to a candidate signing the usual application form, he should be
requested to complete a questionnaire upon which is printed a concise
statement of the aims and purposes of Fre~masonry and the duties and
moral obligations which membership imposes, and from the answ~rs given
to the que~tions thereon, relative to his reasons for wishing to become a
Mason? The benefits he expects to . receive, etc.? The Committee could
more accurately judge his qualifications and the possibilities of his mem- .
bership being an asset to the Lodge.
It is 'too much to expect that without guidance any ma!). can take his
proper place in his Lodge and work with credit to himself and honor to
the fraternity. He has the right to expect that the Lodge shall give him
much of the information he needs. It is because so many brethren never
receive this information, and are permitted to come-and perhaps to goundirected and uninstructed, that they cease attending Lodge.
We, therefore, believe that after each degree a candidate should be
carefully and fully instructed by a skilled P.M. or members of a Committee appointed by the W.M. for this particular task who would explain
to him the meaning of the degree he has recently received. We are fully
aware that' this .is covered by the lectures and charges, etc., but we believe
a more C01P-plete understanding may be obtained in this manner and the
candidate better qualified for his subsequent degree and finally that his
knowledge of the degrees and their teachings will be sufficient so that he
will voluntarily make advancement in Masonic knowledge.
Victoria, 1943 (Grand Master):
May I refer briefly to one of the responsibilities of a Grand Master
which is little known, but which takes up a good deal of time, and in
some cases involves much thought and consideration. I refer to the cases,
which are much more frequent than most people imagine, where objections are raised by individual Freemasons to the initiation of particular
candidates. Each of these cases has to be considered carefully, and a
just decision, so far as that is possible, has to be made. To one not
unaccustomed to making decisions upon evidence, this. task is one of .
peculiar difficulty having regard to the fact that the ordinary rules are
observed. As you know, the objections are made under the cover of
secrecy, and are regarded as strictly confidential. Not only can they not
be disclosed to the candidate, who thus has no real opportunity of testing
or refuting them; but they cannot even be communicated to his proposer
and seconder, nor to the members of the Lodge. It has been my practice,
as well I think as that of my predecessors, to give the benefit of any
doubt not to the candidate, who is in the position of the accused, but to
the craft to which he seeks admission. The result must necessarily be
unsatisfactory in some cases · when judged by ordinary standards as they
prevail in our courts of law; but that is inevitable under the circumstances.
In mentioning this, I desire to emphasize something which is not always
understood and which is important, namely, .that the staying of a candidate by the Grand Master casts no reflection whatever upon his proposer
or seconder, or upon the members of the Lodge which may have elected
to accept him, Experience of human nature shows that there are men

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

who, in certain circles, bear the highe.s t reputation, and yet ~hose unworthiness to be admitted to our order may be well known to others.
May I · take this opportunity of expressing again the necessity for the
strictest caution and care in the selection of candidates for this great
fraternity, whose strength will depend upon the character of its individual ·
members.

I, think the Grand Secretaries are particularly benefited as they have
to communicate frequently on various inter-Grand Lodge matters that
arise.
The conference takes the form, mostly, of a round table discussion
of interesting subjects. Many topics were dealt with and as an illustration
of their importance and value, I cite the following :- ·

360

Victoria, 1943 (Board of General Purposes):
Consequent on the admission of American soldiers as c~ndidates or
joining members in Victorian Lodges, the board has examined the position
from the point of view both of the soldiers concerned and of the effect
of such admissions upon our rraternal relations with the American Grand
Lodges.
•
Almost every Grand Lodge in the United States of America jealously
insists upon a strict observance of the purely American doctrine of "exclusive territorial jurisdiction" over all Masonic potentials resident within
its boundaries and would resent the acceptance as a candidate by another
Grand Lodge of a person resident within its own territory, regarding it
as an innsion of its jurisdiction, and a decidedly unfrafernal action. It
might even decline to recognize the candidate, unless previously it had
given the other Grand Lodge a "waiver" for that particular case. Sc)me
Grand Loi:lges hold that, constitutionally, ' they cannot give a waiver,
whilst many forbid dual membership.
In the interests of such candidates, who, on their return home; might
find recognition withheld, or be tegarded as clandestine, and of the
maintenance of the excellent fraternal relatio.ns now existing, the bo'a rd
expressed its earnest hope that, prior to the admission of any American
citizen, either as a candidate or as a joining member to any L6dge,:
there shall be a previous communication by the Lodge of all the circum~
stances to the Grand Secretary, so that, unless already given, a waiver of
jurisdiction or other satisfactory consent may be obtained from the grand
jurisdiction located at ·the place of legal residence of such candidate or
joining member.

CONFERENCE OF GRAND MASTERS
Pertinent comments, pro and con, relative thereto, with a copy of the.
agei;ida before the body for your own consideration.
British Columbia, 1943 (Grand Master):
This year the annual conference of the principal Grand Lodge officers
of the four western Canadian jurisdictions was again held at Banff. All
four Grand Masters were present, accompanied by the principal officers
of their Grand Lodges.
·
I found Bro. S. H. Fahrni, Grand Master of Manitoba; Bro. D. Fraser,
Grand Master of Saskatchewan, and Bro. F. P. Galbraith, Grand Master
of Alberta, to be outstanding Freemasons, and am confident that they
are giving splendid leadership to the craft in their respective jurisdictions.
I was privileged in this manner to obtain a closer acquaintance with them,
and trust that the friendships made and cemented at the conference will
long continue.
Freemasons of the four western provinces have much in common,
similar problems and difficulties confront them, and they strive for a
realization of the same ideals. It is therefore most desirable that we
should, (rom time to time, discuss these things with one another

The Problem of the Indifferent Member.
The Practical Appeal of Masonic E.ducation.
Freemasonry and Adult Education.
Masonic War Relief Funds ..
The Appeal of the Craft to Youth.

361

"'

.

These subjects indicate the general scope of the meetings and the
values to be obtained from them. A full record of the paper11 given and
discussions held was kept, and a copy was sent to each of those attending
the conference, and. the information contained in them is available for ·
dissemination to our brethren.
I hope this conference will be regularly held hereafter · and that .our
principal officers will attend and consider it one of the most useful of
their yearly activities. Our good brethren of Alberta insisted on acting
as hosts. to the conference, and we much appreciate the splendid hospitality ·accorded us.
Connecticut, 1944 (Grand Master):
For the first time in its history, each of the forty-nine grand jurisdictions was represented. M. W. Carl H. Claudy, Grand Master of Masons
in the District of Columbia, welcomed the visitors to the capital city.
Later, as executive secretary of the Masonic Service .Association Brother
Claudy spoke on "Freemasonry's Obligation to those who are Defending
Alike the Principles of Democracy and the Principles of Freemasonry,"
and from his closing words I quote: "Some day this war will be over.
Some day there will return to this nation. many millions of young men
who will examine all human institutions in the light of what they have
seen and endured in the hell of war. None can escape it; church, school,
government, labor, business-all wiU have to stand clear~eyed scrutiny.
'Is that worth while?' they will ask. 'What have you done to prove that
you ·have a right in this new world we have made?' Like all the rest,
Freemasonry will stand and be looked at, and we will have to answer.
What will we answer? Cain's answer-'Am I my brother's keep~r?'-will
not satisfy. Hardly can we say: 'It was a fifty-cent war, so we-at least
some of us-spent fifty cents ' a year on you.' It is not yet too late to
provide so .that those who return will not look at us with hard eyes and
ask hard questions. 'rhey may come back to our Lodges saying: 'You
followed us with our Masonry. You gave us hospitality. You offered
us sympathy and understanding. You brought us brotherhood and fellowship and comfort. You spared not your pocketbooks in so doing. You
did not say: 'Am I my brother's keeper?'"
The 'answer of the future is still in our hands. If we are to discharge
our Masonry obligation to our brethren and their sons and buddies in the
armed forces, we must end the muddled thinking that this is a fifty-cent
job and .g ive a decent sum, every one of ·us, to make the goodly Masonic
work sweet and dear where it is now performed, available to every Mason
in the service. Until we so do, we cannot boast "I am my brother's
keeper."

Louisiana, 1944 (Grand Master):
I attended the Annual . Conference of the Grand Masters in Washington
on February 23 and 24, 1943. I regret to say I am not much impressed
with the Grand Masters' Conference. It could be made to be of great
benefit to the Masonic fraternity if the Grand Masters were brought
together and knew each other. Unfortunately, the spirit of comrad'eship
does not enter into these meetings and most of the Grand Masters do
not meet each other. It would make a wonderful working force if the
brethren of these conferences would practically live together for two days
and get to know one another and thus be able to understand each other
better.· There was some improvement last year in that the Grand Masters'
Conference was more of a Grand Masters' Conference, as nearly all of
the speakers were Grand Masters in office and there was. qui.te an amount
of participation in discussions by the presiding Grand Masters.
I was unfortunately unable to attend the Grand Secretaries' Conference because it was executive. I believe this is a mistake. However, we
cannot dictate to the Grand Secretaries' Conference what it should do.

COURTESY DEGREES
There never has been and probably never again will there be so many
courtesy degrees conferred as has been the experience of all United States
and most foreign jurisdictions.
South Australia, 1943 (Proceedings):
The arrival in Australia at the beginning of the year of a number of
soldiers in the American armed forces prompted the thought of communicating with the forty-nine grand jurisdictions in the United States
with which this Grand Lodge is in fraternal relationship.
A cordial welcome was extended to any of their brethren who may
be among the troops, inviting them to attend, if in good standing, Lodge
meetings in the town in or near which .they may ' be located. Although
it was clearly too late to pass on the invitation to the brethren who had
already left their shores, the replies from the Grand Lodges showed tha't
they were sincerely appreciative of our offer to extend the usual courtesies
of Masonic fellowship to those who may make themselves known to our
Lodges.
It is pleasing to record that the opportunity was afforded of renderirig
a real service to three brethren of the Grand Lodge of Wisconsin by
making arrangements on receipt of a request by beam wireless fr()m · thdr
Grand Master to enable them to take, in our jurisdiction, another step
towards the completion of their degrees.

Queensland, 1943 (Proceedings):
The Grand Secretary read the following letter from the United Grand
Lodge of England, dated 3rd December 1942:"Dear Sir and R.W. Brother,
Initiation of Candidates on Behalf of Other Jurisdictions.
' "'For some time past we have had under consideration the question
of the initiation of candidates who had been elected by Lodges of other
Jurisdictions, but had been transferred overseas before the first degree
could be conferred upon them. Under our Constitutions, only the second
and third degrees can be conferred as a courtesy, but it was felt that
candidates should not be under any har,dship through the calls upon them
by their countries during the present war.
"At the meeting of Grand Lodge on 2nd becember · 1942, therefore, it
was unanimously decided that, during the continuance of the war the
courtesy should be extended to all three degrees, and I am pleased to
inform you that, in future during that period, I shall be very glad to
arrange for such ceremonies to be performed ·in Lodges under the English
Jurisdiction, on receipt, of an application certified by yourself on behalf
of any of your Lodges. The ceremony will, of course, be performed
according to our ritual, b.ut a suitable explanation will be made to the
candidate."
Our Grand Lodge office has had several requests to initiate, pass and
raise candidates who had been balloted for and accepted in Lodges responsible to other jurisdictions, but who, owing to the exigencies of war, had
been removed to another area. We had a case in the North where the
son of a very esteemed Past Master was duly accepted for initiation into
his father's Lodge, but before the ceremony could be performed he was
sent to Canada. It wa'.s . not possible to have him. initiated in Canada
under the constitutions tnen prevailing. We have had requests to initiate
candidates from the southern States and a few-,very few so far-from
the United States of America. As the letter from the Grand Lodge of
England indicates, the proposal set out in this clause is deemed to be
only fair to the candidates who are serving their country, and this privilege should be extended to them.
It was thought that in the case of candidates in the forces of the
United States of America, who have come a considerable distance and
who may have been here for some months, it would be wise to. ascertain
from responsible authorities of .the army here information as t~ whether
those candidates for admission to . the order have, since their arrival in
this country, comported themselves in a proper and acceptable manner.

Today's youth is tomorrow's Mason I Most of the jurisdictions are
agreed that "something should be done about it."
Mississippi, 1943 (Past Grand Master):
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Members of the Grand Lodg!; of
the State of Mississippi: It is an honor to lead a million and a half boys
-American boys-because they are your sons and mine. There is one
thing that you fellows need never be afraid of, that we are going to allow
any Mussolini, or Hitler or Hirohito to be Grand Master of the Grand
Lodge of the State of Mississippi, or any other Grand Lodge in the United
States. Don't be afraid of that. But one thing you must be afraid of,
and that is this: That the very boys of the DeMolays today are going to

365

become the Masons of tomorrow and the Grand Masters of the Grand
L6dges of the United States of America tomorrow. Listen fellows! I
have noticed· one thing that is absent on this occasion, and that is the
• absence of youth. You may say, "Oh! yes, I am not an old. man." No,
you · may not be; but you can't be a Mason as long hereafter as you have
been; and the fellows that will follow you are the boys of today, your
sons ·and mine.
Do you ever stop tci think about Masonry? I want to ask you a few
questions and let you answer them. What does our existence as Masons
necessitate? What are we 'here for? What can we do? What are we
doing? What part are we playing in this crisis? What about foreign
espionage? Can we do anything about it as Masons, and what? Now
is the time, and here in the United States is the place. The world is
completely changed,..and so must our code. We are the .strongest secret
order in existence, and we can and should do something for our country.
What is that going to be?
·
I can tell you what it can be. You, as Masons in Mississippi, can
recognize and foster the organization which I have the honor to be the
head of. I had· an occasion a short time ago to write a letter to the Grand
Master of one of our northwestern states. If you will pardon me for
one minute,' .J am going to read a portion of that communication t'O him,
because he :·was opposed to, and his Grand Lodge went on record as
opposed to youthful organization of the DeMolays, in fact, to any organization of the youth; and I stated to him:
"If I were Grand Master again, I would direct the attention of the
Brethren to the East-to the rising rather than to the setting sons. With
my hindsight ~hich is so much better than my foresight, I now see
that you can't kill quack grass with a mower-you have to get a field
cultivator.
·
"Masonry will thrive and flourish like the 'green bay tree' when you
get down to the roots and not until then. Times have changed. When
you and I were boys we formed our conception of morals at our mother's
knee and sometimes over her knee if we had the right kind of mothers.
The Thursday afternoon bridge club hadn't yet replaced the Thursday
night prayer meeting, and the public schools were teaching reading,
writing and arithmetic instead of problems in democracy and social
science, with sometimes a slight slant to the left.

"Father and son worked 'together. Together we ploughed for corn in
the spring. Together we planted the corn; together we hoed the corn;
together we harvested the corn, and together we hauled it to the millalways together. We didn't need ' annual 'Father and Son Banquets' so
we could be introduced to our fathers. At our house we held 'Father
and Son Banquets' three times a day.
"The institution of family worship still existed-everybody said. grace
three times a day and went to church on Sunday. The juvenile court
was in the woodshed. Dad was prosecutor, judge and jury, and, having
pronounced .sentence, executed it with a b!!d slat. Second offenses were·
rare.
"We weren't troubled much with 'isms' in our day. We were all pretty
busy trying to get something to eat three times a day, clothes to wear,."
a little set aside for a rainy day and something to apply on the mortgage
that lay heavily on the roof. That mortgage ate away at the family
savings night and day. If 'you lay real still at · night in bed you could
hear it gnaw.

"A boy's wages were his dad's until he was twenty-one, and he usually
worked at home until then. Unless he worked out a little, he had no
money of his own. The . automobile hadn't been invented. Many men
· had never traveled farther than the next c.o unty. There were no movies, ,

halls or night clubs, and right and wrong were not so gradually shaded

woman who painted, wore short skirts and a low neck was advertising
the most ancient of professions. Everybody knew everybody else's business and whereabouts, and the paths of virtue were simpler than those
of vice.
"Times have changed. We have become so successful that we have

lights are so close they have blotted out the eternal stars. We have
debunked the old time religion and the old time Fourth of July oration
and legalized the promotion of minor vice among youth after removing

New Jersey, 1943 (Grand Master):
A program to help Masonry must include one of helpfulness in the
wider field of public welfare, specifically interesting our own sons and
the young men of our communities in the w,ay of fraternal living. This
can be done best through the Order of DeMolay. This fraternity was
founded by members of our Institution 25 years ago. Today it is carried
on exclusively by adult Masonic leaders.
·
More than a million youQ.g men have been inducted into approximately one thousand chapters of the Order, leaving its ranks at the age
of 21 with a new conception of the virtues of parental love, patriotism,
courtesy, reverence, cleanness, comradeship and fidelity. A large percentage of these former DeMolays are members not only of Masonic lodges
throughout the country, but many are members of this and· other Grand
Lpdges. Some already are Grand ·Masters. Masonry benefits from
having this generous supply of trained youth.
The future of Freemasonry lies more in our young men than in ourselves. Ours is the duty to maintain Masonic ideals at their best, and
to transmit. them unimpaired to those who will carry on in later years.
Ours is the privilege .of helping young men to understand these virtues,
showing them how these ideals may be applied to the complicated situations of everyday life.

Tennessee, 1944 (Grand Master):
On February 26, 1943, I was privileged to attend an initiation in the
Order of DeMolay. The contribution of an organization such as this, is
immeasurable in its good effects upon our youth. It fills a need today
that no other organization can fill.
Persons who are concerned over the youth problem have been aghast
at a statement of J. Edgar Hoover, I quote:
"Crime figures last ·year were truly alarming.
"Something has happened to our moral fibres when the 'nation's
youths under voting age accounted for 15 per cent of all murders,
35 per cent of. all robberies, 58 per cent of all car thefts and 50 per
cent of all burglaries. Arrests of girls under 20 for offenses against
common decency increased 76 per cent. Now is the time to start a
counter-offensive to keep the home front clea'n, wholesome and· strong."
What better answer to this problem can Masons make than to support
youth in its high idealism of the Order of DeMolay?

Montana, 1943 (Committee Report):
Your Committee on Publi'c Schools Week fraternally report as follows:
The Grand Master issued his proclamation in due time relative to
observing Public Schools Week in all Lodges of this jurisdiction. Many
of our Lodges carried out the suggestions therein contained and held
meetings with "Our Public Schools" as the theme. Reports of these
meetings were sent to the chairman of the committee and were read and
filed. Some Lodges h~ld open meetings and reported good attendance.
All reports stressed the value of having such meetings.
At no time in history has it been more emphatically brought to the
minds of men that public schools are the foundation of democratic government. A nation can be changed either for good or bad by the teaching
of the youth. When public schools are rightly used the country's welfare
is better assured. We must support our schools as public schools. ·Then·
is no need to stress the importance of the public schools when dealing
with Masons. We do need, however, to have a plan of action that provides opportunity for making clear our own stand and at the same time
furnishes ways· and means to become better acquainted with our ·s chools
.and their work.
We therefore recommend that such a committee be continued and
that the Grand Master issue a proclamation to all Lodges setti~g· fQ,rth.
his plans for the Lodges of Montana during the coming year.

meetings, and suggested immediate and co-ordinated activities along practical lines. The response of the brethren was enthusiastic. Accordingly

contribution to the rehabilitation of those who are giving themselves so

launched a Post-War Masonic Scholarship Scheme. It is essentially local
in its incidence as to finance, administration and benefits and, as such,
should appeal, not only in its wider implications, but in its actual working
out. We commend it to the enthusiastic support of the brethren and
trust that our succ·e ssor may have the joy of seeing it richly endowed.
Out of this war and to be solved as a pre-requisite to a just and lasting
peace emerge problems of reconstruction for the creation of a post war
economy that will guarantee to all peoples everywhere the freedoms for
which we contend. "The blueprints must be drawn and the foundations
laid now." We look for. national and international policies to be defined
by our governments but in so doing they need guidance and advice and
having formulated those plans will require the co-operation and support·
of individuals and organizations to perform community duties which no
government can do alone.

strange idea has become fixed in the minds of many Masons, and is
embodied in the regulations of some Grand Lodges, that the funds of a
Lodge can only be used for "Masonic" purposes. Brother. Freeman, and
his Grand Lodge, uphold the ancient freedom of the Lodge . to .do what

The financial structure of the Grand Lodge was the subject of a

odd, this is evidently a matter for serious consideration and constant
care. But it does not appear that any serious defects have appeared in
this structure, it is only that our Virginian brethren are prudently ensurin_g that nothing shall go wrong with it.

I strongly recommend, therefore, that no general rem1ss10n of dues
be voted or granted, but that every consideration be given to meritorious
cases of individual members, whether within or without the armed forces,
and that no · suspension for nonpayment of dues be voted until after a
full and careful investigation has disclosed the actual status of the delinquent brother.

The question of the use of Lodge funds came up again in connection

Massachusetts, 1942 (Grand Master):
It has · come · to my attention that a number of Lodges have voted
to remit the dues of all members in the armed forces. From numerous
inquiries I have received concerning the attitude of the Grand Lodge
relative thereto, I am convinced that a considerable number of other
Lodges contemplate similar action.
First, may I point out that it is peculiarly within the province of each
individual Lodge to determine both the amount of its annual dues and
the circumstances under which a member may be exempted from payment thereof.
·
Next, may I point out that remission of dues should not be granted
merely because the Lodge is perhaps momentarily in excellent · firianeial
condition, nor should remission of dues be denied because a Lodge is
in poor financial condition. The determining factor is and should continue to be the circumstances and need of the individual member. Remission "of dues should never be merely a reward for meritorio4s conduct.
Active war service alone, in and of itself, affords no ample justification
for any general policy. Where induction in service ·has ~ffected not at
~ an or only to an inconsequential degree the financial status of a member,
'there would seem to be no sound reason to- remit dues.

Connecticut, 1944 (Grand Master):
From my own · observation and the reports of the district deputies,
the ritualistic work has been of high standard. Certain irregularities I
wish to call to your attention. Numerous reports have been received
indicating that unnecessary 'roughness has been evident in the e~empli­
fication of the second section of the Master Mason degree. These reports
seemed at first to be unfounded, but investigation revealed them to be
true. This practice is not only contrary to good Masonic procedure, but
it detracts from the solemnity of the degree by putting it on a par with
a hazing party. The symbolism of this degree has a definite purpose
which should be uppermost in the mind of every actor in the great drama,
lest it be defeated. Freemasonry viewed in the aggregate, is an elaborate
allegory of human life. The three degrees collectively symbolize man's
existence ' both here and in the hereafter. The Lodge is emblematical
of' the' world:' Initiation of birth; Entered Apprentice of youth; Fellowcraft of ma·nhood; and the Master Mason of old age, death, the resurrection, and e'rerlasting life.

Kansas, 1944 (Grand Master):
Modern historians seem inclined to treat history not as bare statement
of facts, but as events which have happened because of tl\e influences

381

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

whith have been at work behind the scenes. They treat of trends and
not of battles. They emphasize the background of certain movements
and mention the battle only as the culminating day of final decision, on
the one hand, or the part which that battle plays in some event which
may take place long after the grass . has blanketed the resting place of
the dead. In a similar manner we should like to consider for a moment
our situation with regard to Freemasonry.
We say that we are an ancient and honorable society. We know
that for many centuries our order existed as an operative guild but we·
are not primarily concerned with operative art. We labor as Speculative
Masons and as such we are drawn to England in the early Eighteenth
Century when Freemasonry as a speculative science came into being.
This was indeed a proper setting for a science concerned with Individual
endeavor.
·
One of our historical writers says: "The history of no other people
affords such an illustration of a steadily prdgressive national development
from seed to blossom, compelled by one persistent force. Freedom in
England has unfolded like a plant from a life within; one leaf afte1
another freeing itself from the detaining force. Only a few more remain
and we shall behold the flower of fourteen centuries in which the most
practical nation in the world has steadily pursued an ideal-the ideal of
individual freedom subordinated only to the good of the whole!"
Speculative Masonry is concerned with this freedom of the individual.
It came into being during that period in England when this struggle was
at its height. It immediately found
fertile soil in colonial America and
was adopted by the leading men of that dzy and time. It appealed to
the common man for by its precepts he was taught that all men are
created equal and have the right of equal opportunity.
We improve in Masonry as individuals but we also have a duty to
our neighbors. That duty, however, is largely exercised as individuals,
for as we improve in Masonic intercourse, we communicate our improvement in mind and in spirit, unselfishly to our fellows. Thus, through a
succession of effort as individuals and through our individual associations
do we bring that which we are taught to all affairs of our society, our
church, our community, our state and our nation.
The immortal Washington brought to the early formation of our government the principles of democracy, a devoutness of spirit and a religious
determination that right should prevail. Other Masons of our early history made .similar contributions. I have no doubt · whatever but that the
principles of right and justice inculcated in his Masonic association had
much to do with guiding the mind that moved the pen of Chief Justice
John Marshall.
.
.
I believe that Masonic influence, not collective but exemplified through.
the i~dividual, was the guiding· influence in shaping much ·o'f the pattern
of ·this government, for many of tho~\! active in governmental affairs
were Masons. This, in itself, would not prove ·anything, but the close
resemblance of the principles which were written into our Great Charter
and the principles that are taught in our Lodge coupled with the fact
that so many of the men of affairs of that day were Masons, indicates to
me that truly Masonic ideas permeated the minds and actions of the
individuals who wrought in the governmental quarries of that time.
As Masons we can be justly proud of the her.itage which they have
left. Although our brethren were in a majority, they did not. decree that
only Masons could hold office, nor did they undertake any effort to perpetuate themselves in office. They ask'ed nothing for themselves, whether

it was religious ft eedom, economic advantage or political prestige, which
they were unwilling to grant to their fellows. They fully recognized the
right of free men to be free, and that improvement in society should
come about through the peaceful processes of individual education and
individual endeavor.

Louisjana, 1944 (Grand Master):
Our forefathers made a noble experiment over one hundred and fifty
years ago. It has succeeded and from it has come the. greatest government on the face of the earth. It is the greatest because it is based on
equality. We now admit that all the world is one 'great brotherhood
and we are our brother's keeper just as much as ·Cain was when the
Great Architect of the Universe . so informed him. Brethren, we have
had a great advantage. We should share it with the rest of the world.
It is only by going into the world and calling the attention of the European people, both small and large, to the advantages of the form of
government which we have that we can succeed in convincing them that
all men are created equal and come of the same stock, a lesson which is
taught to us by the level.
We as Masons are believers in education. The more education we
have the firmer our democratic institutions become. We must support
our country to the limit. We must do it in the war. We are under a
great duty in supporting it for a just peace, a people's peace, one which
is going to recognize that all men are created equal and which is going
to grant to all men freedom of speech, freedom of press and freedom of.
worship. We should not seek vengeance because Masonry teaches love.
With love, however, there must be respect. We should love our enemies
that we may teach them the great principles of Masonry, the Fatherhood
of God and the Brotherhood of Man. We hope the great leaders of our
country and our allies, after they shall have obtained peace, will attempt
to eradicate from the minds of all men all thoughts of hate and that
through proper education those who are our enemies will realize that the
advancement of mankind can only continue through ways of peace and
not through ways of war. I sincerely trust in our country all persecution
will be downed as quickly as it raises its head. We in our Lodges are
taught that we do not exact any religious or political belief from a man,
but require that he believe in a Supreme Being. We must protect every
man who may be persecuted on account of his religious or political belief
and grant to him the rights which we claim as ours. We should be
particularly careful in our Lodges not to inject any dogmatic teachings
but continue meeting on the common level of brotherhood.

in official positions in those bodies, which predicate their membership
on membership in a subordinate Lodge, and which are recognized by
this Grand Lodge, are officially received as brethren among us, and it
seems to us that all the desires that can emanate from the heart of any
Mason should be fully gratified and satisfied in these recognized bodies.
Masonry cannot tolerate every whim and fancy of its members to form
such organizations in order that they may receive additional honors, or
have unusual designations or titles affixed to their names. It is to. be
~nderstood that during the time that this present Grand Master holds
official position, he will not look with favor upon the organization or
constitution of any such bodies, unless permission is granted by this
Grand Lodge.
Masonry has many projects within its active organization in order
that all its members may expend every ounce of surplus energy which
they have to devote in the further solidifying and advancement of our
great brotherhood.
West Australia, 1943 (Grand Master):
Our enemies speak of a new order and a planned economy, a new
order which we believe to be destructive of all that is good in human
life and of hope for life here.after. We too speak of a new order after
the war and we hope that the spirit of service and brotherhood, brought
about in our own Empire by the war itself, will continue as the spirit
of a new life in the world that will evolve when the war is ended. Many
suggestions have already been put forward embracing improvements in
our political, economic, and social system. We talk of the necessity to
provide the means of subsis~ence and some of the cultural pleasures of
life for every man, and we envisage a new society that shall be almost
ideal for everyone. With the best intentions in the world much water
will flow . under the bridge before that is achieved, but every step towards
it will mean an improvement. We have all read the Atlantic Charter,
which endeavors to put into words what we know is needed. All the
principles underlying that document were enunciated the best part of a
century ago by a great American President and if, after the war, we
can live up to that declaration we can look beyond the present gloom
to a happiness which will be assured to those who come after us. With

and for the people, shall not perish from the earth.

the right, as God gives us to see the right, let us strive on to finish the

lasting' peace among ourselves and with all nations."

Louisiana, 1944 (Proceedings):
From oration by Most Worshipful Brother Luther A. Smith, Past
Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Mississippi.
We are awed by the venerable grandeur of Freemasonry when we
view it in its historical perspective across the countless centuries as it
breaks through the mists of antiquity.
Like some tall cliff that lifts its awful form.
Midway from the vale and rising, leaves the storm;
While around its breast the rolling clouds are spread,
Eternal Sunshine settles on its head!
But let us examine in detail this majestic institution and see what
is its nature. The first observation is that it is firmly embedded in the
earth. Freemasonry's feet are in the soil where men live and work and
love and play and look up at the stars. It grew up among the people.
It is unique in that it never claimed any miraculous origin. Its system
of philosophy, its teachings and dogmas were not handed down by means
of some sunburst of ·divine revelation, but are the product of the experiences of craftsmen over many centuries of associating together in building
and adorning temp-les and other structures over Europe.
They were strong, sturdy men, skilled and intelligent artisans who
came up through years of apprenticeship and who took a robust joy in
their work. Life was meaningful to them. They viewed the world as
a vast workshop, a mighty building enterprise with the Grand Architect
of the Universe as the Superintendent who worked according to plans
and specifications. They in turn placed designs on the trestle board of
their lives and worked with intelligence and precision. They loved the
world. To them it was no vale of tears, but a place of opportunity and
responsibility. It was their home and they concentrated their energies
upon making it a fit place in which to live. They did not torture themselves with theological and metaphysical speculations. They frankly
recognized that there were many problems beyond human understanding.
Therefore they did not waste time to argue about them. Beyond a
belief and firm faith in God and the immortality of the soul, they had
no creed. They did ordain certain "tenets." The principal ones were
brotherly love, relief and truth-about the value and validity of which
there could be no debate or difference of opinion. They were self-evident
truths-not. something that ought to be, but are; and they professed no
belief in them, but acted upon them-put them into practice.

*

*

Standing before the pyramids of Egypt, Napoleon Bonaparte sought
to inspire his troops to victory by pointing to those ancient monuments
and exclaiming: "Soldiers of France, forty centuries look down upon you!"
He was urged on by personal ambition and lust of empire. But Brother
Masons, I humbly say to you that six thousand years of humanity's
struggles in blood and sweat and tears for liberty, equality, and fraternity
look down upon us and our way of life as the only sure foundation for
the realization of their hopes.
May the Great Architect of the Universe inspire and aid the true
lovers of mankind to ~stablish a just peace based upon the Fatherhood

Nebraska, 1942 (From Oration):
America is engaged in a life-and-death struggle with implacable foes.
The powers combined against her and her allies have been actuated for
many generations by a lust. for. the domination_of. the .woi;ld. Great,. if
war-like, .peoples, credited with no little advancement in the arts of civilization, pursue the fanatical ideal of a periodic rejuvenation of mankind
through reversion to barbarism, in the belief that they are the chosen
instruments of destiny through which it is to be accomplished.
Is it not an evidence of a moral conscience in the universe, of an
inextinguishable moral goodness that will not be entirely denied, that
even a wicked and depraved aggression must assert some pretended
justification by the claim that some ultimate good is the object of the
evil act?
In this clash of fundamental concepts, there can be no room for compromise. Compromise presupposes an area, however limited, of community of interest, of agreement in principle ; some common ground,
however small, on which both contenders may stand.
Is there any conceivable community of interest, any possible agreement in principle between the democratic affirmation and the totalitarian
negation that these are irreducible conditions of human life upon this
planet on terms which make living desirable: that all men have rights
which others are in coinmon decency bound to respect a nd that among
them is the right to be free, not slave, in their minds, their spirits, their
persons; ·that peace is to be preferred to war, kindness to cruelty, mutual
respect to class or race hatred, friendly intercourse among the peoples
of the world to conquest and pillage by those who, for the time, are
better able to command the forces of violence and destruction?
That affirmation and that negation have no common denominator. If
one is to prevail, the other must be destroyed.
Whether this war continues for two years or, with intel'ludes of temporary cessation of hostilities, for a hundred years, it cannot end until
one or the other of these ideals becomes the dominant actuality in the
life of huclankind.
"The people," said Edmund Burke, " never give up their libertie11
but under some delusion." The people act under a delusion only when
enlightened leadership is lacking.
America has become an arsenal of Democracy; let Masonry be a citadel
of Faith.

Now, my brethren, I am going to try to show you where Masonry,
Masonic law, Masonic teachings, and Masonic principles can be used to
insure a permanent peace when this terrible conflict is over. And it
will be over, and the United Nations will win this war and the ensuing
peace.
Be he prince or potentate, president or prime minister, no man should
be allowed to take the reins of government of a free people unless he
has proven himself to be qualified. Let him have the qualifications of a
Grand Master of a Masonic jurisdiction, elevated by his people on the
basis of the good he has done and tried to do in this world, not promises
of a master race and an invincible military machine.· A leader of that
calibre could eliminate power politics which indirectly cause all wars.
Whether the law-making body is known as Congress, Parliament or
Chamber of Deputies, let each member have the qualifications needed
by a Master of a Masonic Lodge. If this could be done, we would have
no i'ear of laws oeing enacted for chosen cliques or groups who are
able to put money in.t o the pock!!ts of the lawmakers, or statutes fayoring
either capital or labor, black or white, rich or poor, Catholic, Jew or
Protestant. We, ~s Masons in our Lodg~ rooms, are not measured by
our financial statu s or the church to which we choose to belong, or
whether we are .e mployers or employees. Therefore, those elect<;d . to
make the laws which govern a free people could do much toward assuring
a permanent peace if our own simple Masonic .creed were adhered to in
the legislative halls of free countries.
Brethren, this definitely does not mean that we . should consider only
Masons to govern this world (although it wouldn't be a bad idea). We
all know that there have been and always will be members of our organization who have. become members and retain their membership purely
for persona[ r.easons and · have no desire to better anyone but thenl!;elves.'
Also there are those, whom we call the profane,, 'Yho have never had the
opportunity to ally themselves with us who would measure up fully to
the qualifications of our fraternity. That is why I. have mentioned .the
word " qualifications" several times. Think of this word the next time
you elect a man. This could be done right at home In our .own muni~ipal
elections, carried on through our county, state, and nat10nal elect10ns.
Those who have been chosen by ballot to represent the people can use
the same idea (Is he qualified?) in making their ap_poihtments. Masters
and Wardens of Masonic Lodges, before appointing their officers, look
for men who are qualified to do the job. I know of several instanc~s
where a Master has turned down a personal friend because he did not
think the man was qualified. If only our leaders had done that, millions
of dollars and many hardships and heartaches could have been averted
in this present conflict.
Now, brethren, you may wonder how a permanent · peace 'w ill be
achieved. If a peace could be made which embodied ' Masonic principles,
it would be a permanent peace.
The Constitution. of the United States of America provides that the
Senate shall ratify peace treaties. Our Senate is composed of a large
numb er of Masons. There are Masons in every country of the world.
Masonry could be a guide in the forthcoming plans, and our members
the builders. When the light of Masonry shines again in the suppressed
countries, those brothers will also be able to aid in promulgating a lasting
and stable world.
·
I do not say that we must dictate to the other nations how their
countries should be run any more than the Grand Lodge of Nevada can

dictate to the Grand Lodges of California and Utah how to run their
jurisdictions. But we do have underlying basic principles embracing the
Golden Rule. We have certain moral standards which prohibit us from ·
disagreeing to such an extent that the sword is needed to settle our
differences. Those principles and standards could not help but lead
toward the tight path in government as in fraternalism. Proper education
in all civilized nations embracing Masonic truths can succeed, whether it
takes ten years or a hundred years. We could instill enough of .our
teachings and beliefs (without converting the world to Masonry) tO'
forever assure the Four Freedoms.
In closing, I am going to trespass into the field of the Grand Chaplain.
There is no room for atheism iO" this world. Everything good and true
and pure can be traced directly to the Supreme Architect. Let us not,
when this conflict is over, forget God. We have been too lax in thanking
.God for what we have and have had. We had begun to take our blessings
for granted when suddenly the world was turned upside-down. Then we
began asking God for help. We 'began asking God why this conflict
had been forced upon us. Sometimes I think God visits these things
upon us to teach us that after all He is the One to whom we should pay
homage, not the dollar or good business or a high office. Let us remember
to thank God every day for what we have, no matter how little, and
we will go a long wa;v toward peace, contentment, and security.

T exas, 1943 ( F rom Oration ):
During these days when this cruel and unprecedented world conflict
attracts most of our attention and thought, many of us are prone to think
of the lives needlessly lost, the unnecessary cruelty displayed, the property
destroyed, and the attendant suffering as a direct result thereof. We are

is now sweeping this world? What of this class consciousness which is

things well known to us are destructive of all those things which we must
preserve, if we are to keep the sort of nation which our forefathers
dreamed of establishing and our fellow citizens and brother Masons are
today fighting to preserve.

that we stand united and unalterably opposed to those things that would
array citizen against citizen and nation against nation. Let us take the
lead in demonstrating at every opportnuity that the Brotherhood of Man
and the Fatherhood of God are real and vital, and offer to suffering
humanity a way out of darkness and destruction. As Master Masons
and as those ·who have been brought to Light, may we do all within our
power to assist in returning to this world "Peace on earth and good will
toward men." This should be our immediate goal.

As regards the future of Freemasonry, it is impossible, at least
for outsiders, to say much. The celebration of the brotherhood

Colorado, 1943 (Committee Report):
During the year we have administered relief to 39 beneficiaries and
in so doing have expended $8,748.00. This is the lowest number of beneficiaries we have had on our books since 1927. The decrease seems to

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

be due in some measure to old age pensions and to the ability of older
people to find employment under the present existing conditions.
In 1903 the then Board of- Trustees reported to the Grand Lodge
that they had expended $75.00 in relief during the year. Forty years
later your present Board reports that during the last year they have
expended $8,748.00 in relief, and a perusal of the records of the Board
of Trustees will show that in 1936 the maximum amount for relief was
expended, in the amount of $20,034.25, and that during the forty years
there has been expended by this fund $274,079.52 to 349 beneficiaries. ·
The revenues from the fund during the period of depression from
1930 on were not sufficient to take care of the applications for relief
and the Grand Lodge appropriated, during the period from 1930 to 1937,
$19,100.00 so that the Trustees would not have to curtail the benefits
sought by .any applicants approved by the Trustees and all such applicants
were taken care of. Realizing that if unexpected demands should be
made on the fund in the future, the Grand Lodge ought. not to be called
upon to again deplete its treasury in a similar way, the board thought
the fund should provide its own reserves. A plan, therefore, was inaugurated to take a certain percentage. of all earnings from invested capital
and apply it to a reserve for em~rgencies. This reserve now amounts
to $22,610.90. It is not probable, in the opinion of the Truste~s. that
this reserve will be adequate to take care of the demands upon our fund
during the post war period. It is hard to make an estimate of . what
would be required. The experience after World War I may throw some
light upon it.
The Colorado Soldier Masons War Relief fund was functioning at
the time and took care of all applications for relief of Masons who had
been in the armed forces, but there were many applications for relief
from Masons and their families who had not been in the war, but who
were adversely affected by the change from a wartime economy to a
peactime economy.
To illustrate this, in 1920 your Board rendered aid to 19 beneficiaries
in the amount of $3,217.50. In 1930 your Board rendered aid to 56
beneficiaries in the amount of $11,379.74. The number of cases had
increased approximately three times and the amount of relief necessary
had increased about three and one-half times.
The losses that have been sustained during the 42 years of the operation of the fund have actually been very slight. The reserve against
losses which we have set up on our books will be adequate to take care
of them and keep these funds intact.

Louisiana, 1944 (Grand ·Master):
Our Relief L odge is a unique organization in that it is composed of
the Masters, Wardens and Past Masters of New Orleans Lodges. For
this reason it has been contended it is a New Orleans institution, but
in my humble opinion it is a Grand Lodge matter, because most of its
work is done for the relief of brethren hailing from other Grand Lodges
of the United States. Men who come to New Orleans and suffer either
from sickness or are summoned to their last reward require attention.
You no doubt will find it most interesting to listen to the report which
will be made by W. Bro. Louis Walsdorf, Master of this Lodge. It
merits your attention because you will find here Masons doing work
which is indeed truly Masonic. The Grand Lodge should continue to
contribute towards the maintenance of this Lodge and should not for a
moment hesitate to make an appropriation to assist it in its gooi:I work.

Brother Bricker, Governor of Ohio, ' Welcomes Grand .Lodge (Proceedings, 1943).
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
I am grateful that I could come here this morning with a word of welcome
to this body that spreads over the State of Ohio, this most powerful
force of right and righteousness outside of the Christian church that
could b~ found in the domain of this great State. And our power is
linked inseparably with that of the· church. I do indeed appreciate the
opportunity of welcoming you here. I wish you not only a successful
meeting-7,and I know it will be' that-but wish for you a pleasant sojourn
in the capital city of your State. I know that Ohio will be much better
for this m.eeting.
Around the world there is disturbed thinking. Men have been broken
from their moorings. Nations th at have heretofore been free have been
destroyed. Autocracy and brutal might have taken the place of selfgovernment. Today we live in the midst of all of the things that the
human· soul can want for its enjoyment, its comfort, and its convenience,
and yet there is hardship and suffering and woe around the world.
Man has tried to live by his power and might and reason .alone and
has forgotten Almighty God, and as a result his course has been disturbed, his thinking confused, his rights and liberties destroyed. And,
as we see the end of the war coming, when the forces of righteousness
must ultimately prevail, yet there is going to be a period when leadership,
strong leadership and consecrated guidance will be needed around the
world. The 'war has held together many peoples of the world wl;lich
now are threatened with radicalism, with an internal disruption, weakened g 0 vernments, disloyalty, distrust, and we may even see a recurrence
of corruption in high places, such as occurred after the last war. There
may be internal revolutions in many of the nations of the world. And
if there are," we know not what course they may take.
So 'as we come down to the day of victory there .is need for an Order
such as this rp9re than ever before in the history of the world, that there
might be. guid;i.nce to men's thinking, that there might be an appreciation
of the full meaning of free government, that there might be a realization
that in ourselves alone we cannot live righteously, but there must be a
dependence and a faith and a belief in Almighty God.
. This order is challenged as it has not been challenged in the one
hundred and seventy years of its history to keep th is segment of our
national life going in the right direction.
Today let us not forget that•we have a responsibility in the midst of
war fo•' protect our thinking and our services beyond the day of war.
There has been too ·:much reliance upon government itself in the last
fifty years, even in this country. There has been a sweeping of abso-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNI;\

lutism around the world that has caught us in its backwash. There has
been a feeling of dependency on the government. There has been a
dependency by the local community on the government higher up. And
there has been a tendency for people to say,· "Well, the government will
take care of that." The time has come for the average citizen to say :
"This is my government. I will give my services to it." Let us ask
ourselves the question, "What can I do for my government?" instead
of what the government can do for me; and then we are on the road
to the redemption-to free government.
.
Oh, that Masons everywhere would ask ourselves what we can do
for this land of the free, that it may be strengthened. Instead of asking
the question, "What will the government do in any given situation?"
let us ask the question, "What will we do as citizens of this government?"
Tomorrow must be implemented the strength and power of every
local organization, every nonpolitical organization, every nongovernmental
movement, that it might serve its purpose in every community. We
saw here a while ago in this state, and this has no political significance,
an attempt on the part of government to bring together all of the youth
organizations under a single authority. I want to say the more organizations we can have in this country, independently wotking with the boys
and girls, to build them up and · make them a better community, the
better off America is going to· be. So that we ought to have an . effort
on the part of every group to · help in every community to builcf more
strongly the foundation of this· government of ours.
And then · a last •word that every Mason ought to speak. Let us
remember that each one of us has lifted the heart and bowed the knee in
humble adoration of the Almighty. Any nation that forgets God is on
the road to ruin and destruction. And that nation which remembers
that there is a Divine Providence, that has the will to follow Divine
. guidance, will ultimately survive and lead the world into the dawn of a
new day of peace and good will among men.

We must conclude, therefore, that the faith of the Masonic signers
dominated the assembly, and their principles became a permanent inspiration to all of the members of the assembly.
These are tangible results of Masonic faith in the indiv\ltual, upholding
Freemasonry to the world as the highest development .of nl>ral philosophy
as applied to a design for · living.
,
Other early exponents of Masonic faith and principles, in the history
of our country were: Samuel Adams, Patrick Henry, he who gave utterance to that truly Masonic expression, "Give me liberty or give me
death"; John Paul Jones, Robert Morris, the financier of the Revolution;
Paul Revere, whose famous ride is legendary; John Marshall, Ethan
Allen, Anthony Wayne, Nathan Hale, he who said, "My only regret is
that I have but one life to give for my country"; Israel Putnam, Andrew
Jackson, and many others too numerous to mention her~
No less than twelve of the presidents of our country llli.ve been FreemasoRs, as have thirteen of our vice-presidents, and the governors of
some thirty-six of the forty-_eight states at the present time are members
of the Fraternity. In addititon, some fifty-five of the members of the
United States Senate are Freemasons, and more than two hundred and
sixty-two representatives are also members of the craft. Contemporary
men of prominence who are Masons are : Douglas MacArthur, Winston
Churchill, Generals Pershing, Summerall, Marshall, Arnold and Doolittle;
Admiral King, Rear Admiral Shl!rman, and others of a long list.
I now call your attention to a different type of manifestation of
Masonic faith or strength of but recent occurrence, of which I trust all
of you have heard, but possibly not in the same light as we shall consider
it now.
I refer to the great example of faith and Masonic belief presented in
the recent experience of our brother, Captain Eddie Rickenbacker, whose
so-called miraculous escape from death with his companions in the South
Pacific war zone was related in the newspapers a few months ago.
You may remember that Brother Rickenbacker, while flying southwest
from Hawaii on an inspection tour of our Pacific island bases, was, with
his eight companions, forced down at sea when their fuel supply became
exhausted. -They managed to get into three small rubber boats or rafts,
with no water supply and but four oranges as food, being unable to
get their emergency supplies from their plane in the confusion of their
crash landing. These boats were so small that they were compelled to
rest in them with th·e ir bodies overlapping, and Captain Rickenbacker
says that after some days at sea, all were suffering terribly from a lack
of food and water, the torments of tropical sunburn by day, and of chill
winds by night, and they were steadily growing weaker. He relates that
he led his companions in prayer services morning and evening, and, at
these times, each one, when able, would read passages from a testament
that one of the men carried.

The address of the King is so touching· that we quote it in full:
Most Worshipful Grand Master, at tll.e installati.on of your
predecessor, the Duke of Kent, it fell to yoµ to address him upon
the duties of the office he had undertaken. So little time has
elapsed since then that it might appear unnecessary to repeat
them today. Moreover, your own Masonic experience is such
that they must be better known to you than to any of your
brethren. But it is right that the time immemorial practice
should be preserved. The short period of Grand Mastership bf
the Duke of Kent, following as it did the lengthy ones of King
Edward VII and the Duke of Connaught, was overshadowed by
the world war in which we are still engaged. It is not to be •
expected, therefore,· that the progress of M·asonry during his term
of office can be measured by the increase in the number of Lodges
compared with previous Grand Masterships. But those short
years have shown what is more imp_ortant: we have seen how
the . brethren have looked to Masonry to provide the moral
support and fraternal association which is at all times, and particularly in times of stress, so necessary. I have been most interested to hear how difficulties have been overcome by brethren
in certain areas in their determination to continue their Masonic
privileges.
In spite of claims in other directions, the craft has not failed
in its duty towards those who are in need, and has continued to
meet its obligations in tpis respect.
We cannot expect that our difficulties of the past few years
will cease with the ending of the war. There will be further
problems which will have to be solved. Many of our Lodges are
situated in countries at present in enemy occupation. They will
have to be reestablished. Their members will be most anxious
to renew their activities, but they may need guidance, and, in
some cases, perhaps, a helping hand. There are also countries
where the Freemasonry which we have recognized as regular has
been dissolved, or has ceased to operate. This is a sad phase in
the history of those constitutions, and, when circumstances allow,
I have no doubt that the Mother Grand Lodge of the world will
gladly offer its help to restore the craft, which will be strengthened by the adversity through which it has passed.
You will appreciate, Most Worshipful Grand Master, that you
enter upon the duties of your office at the beginning of perhaps
the most critical period in the history of the craft. English Freemasonry has behind it the experience of nearly two and a half
centuries of steadfast adherence to fundamental principles, and I
believe that a determination to maintain the values which have
been the rock upon which the Masonic structure has stood firm
against the storms of the past is the only policy which can be
pursued in the future. I have every confidence in your will and
ability to undertake the great responsibilities which are attached
to your office. I wish to express to you my sincere good wishes,
and I shall follow with interest all that you cio in the performance
of your duties.

Mason Leads First West to East Arctic Passage (Grand Master, British
Columbia, 1943).
In the fall of the year 1942, a crew of eight men under the leadership
of Brother Sergeant Henry A. Larsen in the Canadian Government boat
the "St. Roch," completed the first west-to-east voyage made by man
from the Pacific to the Atlantic ocean by way of the northern shores of
the Dominion.
·
Theirs was a tale of hardship and heroism-a twentieth century saga.
They endured hardships and privations, but all that they 'did was not for
fame or glory, but in the discharge of a plain line of duty. With resourcefulness and endurance, with skill and courage, they brought their · long
adventure, which lasted for the better part of two years, to a successful
completion. Their accomplishments take rank with those of the great
explorers of the past. If the world were not so engrossed in a world
war now raging, this adventure would have been everywhere acclaimed
with universal praise. Newspapers would have regarded it as front page
news, and competed with each other in . publishing details of the story;
magazines would have made it the basis of special articles; scientific
societies would have recorded the related historical data, and been eager
to award them recognition and honors. These things may come to our
brother and his men in due ' course with the return of peace. I regard
· it · as but just, however, that even in the midst of a struggle that will
decide the fate of civilization, they should know that what they have
dc;me is regarded with pride and admiration by those aware of the facts.
As citizens of the Dominion we are proud to associate ourselves
with a tribute of deserved admiration. But as Grand Master, I felt I
think a justifiable and natural pride that what Brother Larsen has done
was done by a Freemason, and, moreover, by a brother of my own Lodge,
for he was initiated. passed and raised in Mount Newton Lodge No. 89.
I therefore as Grand Master caused a letter to be written to him, had
it countersigned by the Grand Secretary, and sealed with the official
seal of Grand Lodge, in testimony of the esteem and honor in which
he and what he has done is held by the craft.

Mexican Grand Lodge Problem (Louisiana Correspondence Committee,
1944).
One of the most serious problems of Mexican Masonry arises from
the fact that- the York Grand Lodge, consisting of Lodges made up of
American and English-speaking members residing in Mexico, the constituent Lodges of which are located in various states of the M exican
Republic, constitutes. a challenge to the jurisdiction of the states within
which they are located. Due to· the fact that the York Grand Lodge
was largely made up of an English-speaking membership, most Grand
Jurisdictions in the United States have recognized the York Grand Lodge
and ate withholding recognition of other Grand Lodges ' of the several
states of the Mexican Republic, the consistent idea being that if the
York Grand Lodge is recognized, it would be improper to recogmze
other Grand L odges disputing its jurisdiction. However, there are several instances in Masonic history where two or more Grand Lodges
recognized each other and consented to a concurrent jurisdiction, in which
case these Grand Lodges have been accepted and recognized by the
other Grand L o dges of the world. In Mexico, there appears to be a
tacit consent, if not an official recognition, of the severa l Grand Lodges
of M exico, to the existence of the York Grand Lodge and at this time
there appears to be no serious conflict between the York Grand Lodge
and the other regular Grand Lodges of the several States of the M exican
Republic. I am not informed as to the attitude of the Mexican-speaking
Grand Lodges, to the visitation and the holding of Masonic communication with the members of the York Grand Lodge. However, the York
Grand Lodge has gone on record, at its meeting in April, 1943, at which
time it voted to extend fraternal recognition to "members in good standing of the respective constituent Lodges under the jurisdiction of the
regular State Grand L odges o~ the Republic of M exico."

Scottish Rite Authority Used in Louisiana (Correspondence Committee,
1944).
Another error which some of the Grand Jurisdictions have fallen into
is with respect to the Lodges in New Orleans that . put on the work in
accordance with the Scottish Rite Ritual. Brother Wallace R. Chavez,

the State of Louisiana. The Grand Lodge of Louisiana has, ·by agreement, consented to the use of the Scottish Rite Ritual by these Lodges.

to qave any jurisdiction or authority over the conferring of the first three
ciegrees in Masonry.
Warning Against Carrying Masonic Emblems or Identification in War
Zone (Rhode Island Proceedings, 1943).
Information reaches us from .t hree sources, one of ,which
am not
permitted to identify, which I pass on to you for what action, if any,
you in your wisdom may desire to take.
A letter from R. W. Robert Tate, Grand Secretary in Saskatchewan,
states, in part: "We are advised, unofficially, through high ·r anking officers
in his majesty's Canadian forces, that we should take every possible
precaution to prevent any members of the Masonic order serving in his
majesty's forces carrying anything on their persons that would identify
them as Masons. We were told that every possible precaution was taken
to prevent them so doing prior to taking part in any activity when there·
rriight be a possibility of their being taken prisoner. However, it is only
human nature that occasionally a brother might carry something on him
that had been overlooked and that would identify him as a Mason. We
therefore have been asking our Lodges not only to refrain from issuing
any' hon-destructible type of identification but also to continually warn
their members fo deposit any papers or items that would ide.n tify them
as Masons with some member of the craft in England, or if they were
serving on the high seas, with some member of the craft at the home
port, and to only obtain possession of this material when it was to be
used for the purpose of Masonic association. · We have definite information to the effect that we cannot too strongly impress the necessity of
our brethren being extraordinarily cautious in this matter. We have no
official instructions from the War Depanment but the advice which we
received possibly was even stronger than had it come from that source.
"Even a letter written by a Lodge committee might have disastrous
results and it has been suggested. in this jurisdiction that letterheads used
for correspondence with Masons or sons of Masons serving in the armed
forces; have a warning printed thereon to the effect that the letter is to
be de~troyed immediately after its receipt."

West Australia Grand Lodge Celebrates Century of Existence (West
Australia, Grand Master, 1943).
A century after thf establishment of Freemasonry in this state Grand
Lodge meets in special communication to mark t hat even t. We have
now passed the hundredth milestone in our career, every step of which
has been characterized by the fundamental principles of Freemasonry to
uplift the moral and ethical standards of all those who have come within
our sphere.
,
Amid all the chang~s of human life and human affairs, an institution,
which has maintained an ·unvaryingly high standard for so long a period,
may well congratulate itself as it celebrates with appropriate ceremony
an event which is not only of great local importance, and which speaks
in no uncertain tone of the substantial nature of its fou ndations, but
also offers undisputed testimony to the value of its principles and the
wisdom and foresight of its ancient brethren.

whose purpose shall be to arouse an interest in Freemasonry.

A subject that presents much food for thought. Three states, Iowa,

Iowa, 1943 '(Proceedings):
The three largest, most complete, and important Masonic Libraries
in America are the Grand Lodge Library of Iowa located at Cedar Rapids
and the Grand Lodge Libraries of Pennsylvania and Massachusetts. The
Grand Lodge Library of Iowa has a separate building devoted entirely
to its use and containing an immense number of books and collections
of manuscripts and writings, many of which are exceedingly rare. They
are all ardent collectors of Masonic literature and related ·material. The
Grand· Lodge Library of Iowa is foremost in this field, a place it well
deserves and no doubt through the years will continue to hold by real
merit.
Pennsylvania, 1943 (Committee Report) :
It is interesting to know it had been the desire of the brethren since
the latter part of the 18th century that the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania
should possess a Masonic library that would reflect credit . upon the
fraternity. This aspiration was first brought to the attention of the Grand
Lodge officers as early as March 26, 1787, and subsequently on October
7, 1816, and March 17, 1817. It was not until June 7, 1871, that a resolution was passed in Grand Lodge authorizing the establishment of a
library. On June 7th of this year the library reached the age of seventytwo years of its existence. During these passing years much thought and
labor have been given to this special department, and every effort is
being made by the present Committee on Library to continue the good
work of their predecessors in making the library and museum more
helpful to the members of the craft.
The very great difficulties to be ~ncountered in maintaining a special
Masonic Library, will at once be apparent to anyone familiar with the
necessary qualifications. The collecting of preferable books for a library
of this nature is quite different from securing literature for a public
library, and care must be taken in the purchasing of proper publications
and material interesting to the members of the fraternity.
Books are the truest and most ·silent companions, and we find that
Masonic writings have been invaluable to the Masonic student. Many
authors can be now found in the field of Masonic literature, and it will
be surprising to the Master Mason to learn of the vast number of books
.a nd pamphlets that have been written on Freemasonry which are available
in the library of this Grand Lodge.
The origin of Freemasonry is one of the most interesfing· subjects
to which the Masonic student can apply his time and talent. The cloudy
mists of antiquity may no longer remain; for within the past· few ·years
there has been discovered a way to decipher and read the ancient writings
on the walls of the old ruined temples and cities, thereby unlocking the
ancient myste~ies of the past and r evealing the otigin of our signs,
symbols and rituals. ·
A beginner should first of all read the " Declaration of Principles" of
Freemasonry adopted by the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania. Lodge
histories are also a feature of present-day Masonry, and beyond a doubt
the most attractive and interesting form of publication in connection with
the craft. Ther.e are in Pennsylvania many Lodges that have existed for

Arizona, 1944 (Grand Master):
We all know that following the first world war, the experience of the
craft in general, throughout the United States, as well as in other parts
of the world, was disastrous. We lost a tremendous number of members;
interest in Masonry fell to a low point; and it was the · dedication and
perseverance of the grand leaders of Masonry, as well as a fortunate
recovery from economic and other conditions, which has again permitted
the craft to take a high position in the annals of its history.
It is trite to say that we are passing through an experience which
tries the souls of men; we all know it; we can all perceive that the period
immediately following this war, which, happily, the forces of freedom
are winning, may again be a time of trial and of loss for Masonry.
What are we, as Masons, going to do about it?
That is a question to. which I have given much thought, and which is
a matter of deep concern to us, as well as to many others of our Masonic
brethren. It seems certain that we cannot face the immediate future
with any hope of credit to ourselves if we sit with folded hands and
wait for the storm to break.
"
What, then, can we do?
In the first place it seems to me that we should satisfy ourselves as to
what Masonry is-and Blue Lodge Masonry in particular. Proud as we
are of them, fortunate as the craft has been to have them, helpless as it
would have been without them~ur Masonic leaders do not constitute
all the craft. Masonry is composed of little fellows, the man in the
street, the ordinary citizen ; its life and vigor come, ii at all, from the
fact that it is, and it ought to be, ·a sort of cross-section of our life. It
ought to take in the workman, the clerk, the small employer, the farmer,
the fellow that works with his hands; it ought to emphasize the common
touch. If it does not, if it loses this concept of what Masonry is, it is
on the downward path from which it will not rise again. Therefore the
material, of which Masonry as a living force is to be sustained, is from
the ordinary walks of life, from the little places, from groups that seldom,
if ever, get into the news; that only on rare occasions gets into the
spotlight.
