The n~t question is: What . is Masonry for?-and I mean Blue Lodge
Masonry, the foundation upon which all the rest is based and upon which,
only, it may g~ow.
Masonry in my humble opinion, is not an organization created and
sustained to' support a "line" of officers in the Blue Lodge, or a "line" of
officers in the Grand Lodge. No, the principal purpose and object of
Masonry is to make men better; to take the material we can get hold of,
a'r)d improve it; to leave the world a little better because Masons have
lived and worked and strived in it-and the principal target of such efforts
and such activities is men-men individually-men in groups--ordinary
men-men we can find out on the highways and byways. Only so can
Masonry justify itself, justify its structure, its history, its traditions, its
ritual its lodge meetings-'-all, every bit of it, is of importance and value
only ~o the extent that it contributes to the purpose and objeCt of making
better men, and making men better.
Loufsiana, 1944 (Correspondence Committee):
. M. W. Bro. Winthrop Buck, Connecticut reviewer, wants to know
if our District Lodges are something new. It may be of interest to this
Grand Lodge to know that our action with reference to District Lodges
is somewhat of a departure from Masonic practice when reviewed by
brethren in our sister juri~dlctions. It is not generally known that our
District Lodges are a sort of development from district meetings, under
the direction of the District Deputy Grand Master. This Grand Lodge
has gone so far as to authorize these district meetings to use the name
of District Lodges and to elect officers but these district meetings have
no further function than to conduct and supervise Masonic educational
instruction. They do not hold a charter nor do they have the power
to confer degrees or to elect anyone to membership therein. In most
parts of the state, we still continue to have district meetings and very
few of the Masonic districts have organized themselves into District
Lodges.
I note from the proc,eedings of several of our sister jurisdictions, that
they seriously question the practice in Louisiana during recent years, of
our Grand Masters in delivering radio addresses. Some jurisdictions
seem to think that this· is a departure from 'the established Masonic
customs. We of Louisiana are rather broad and progressive in our
attitude and in view of the fact that radio is something very recent in
human history', there was no opportunity for our ancient brethren to use
the radio in communicating with the craft. It has long been the ,practice
in many jurisdictions for Grand Masters or other Masonic officials to
deliver public addresses and since the address is public, there is no reason
why it should not be carried on the radio as well as in the public press,
as has oft.en been the case.

Freemasons may well ask, "What is to be the future of the craft?"
Everything advances, improves, broadens and Freemasonry must keep
step with the march of mankind or fall by the wayside. Masonry .must
adapt itself to the demands of the age in order to be effective .in the
fulfillment of the great purpose for which it exists and which alone can
justify its existence. If, therefore, · our young men are to serve Freemasonry, and. make it effective for its high and noble end, they must be
taught what Freemasonry is, whence it came, what it brought to us from
the remote past, and what it is trying to accomplish so we can apply its

the selection of candidates will, at least to considerable extent, elimin~te
the opportunist, the vain and selfish hyp9crite, it requires an effective
program of Freemasonry education to arouse interest among the brethr~n
in order to overcome that inerti9 and apathy which paralyzes Masomc
thought and action.
.
The future of Freemasonry lies in the bringing of the wisdom of the
past to the service of the present,. in' teaching the truth ':"hich ma~es
men free "with malice ·toward none, with charity for all." Thus .showmg
in the quality of our private lives and by public service what Freemasonry
means, and if rightly understood, the kind of citizens it produces.
. In short, we must form Freemasonry into a body of men initiate~,
obligated and trained to make liberty, justice and brotherly love prev~1l,
to attain the truth, and to serve our fellows, our cou_ntry and mankmd
in the noblest destiny of man.

Washington, 1943 (Committee Report):
For a long period it has been apparent that too many men make
application to receive the degrees of Masonry, appear in ·the ' Lodge a
minimum number of times to take three degrees, pin emblems on the

407

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

left lapel of their coats, and go forth into the world as Masons, but
thereafter darken the doors of the Lodge seldom or never.
The fault does not lie entirely with the candidates. It has long been
recognized that there should be some plan for their education as they
take the degrees, so, that insofar as the capacity of the Lodge itself
permits, when a candidate has finished with his third degree he wilt be
a Mason in reality rather than one in name only.
With that end in view the Grand Master appointed this committee to
lay a plan for education of candidates in this jurisdiction. Your committee has prepared a series of four short lectures, none of which is planned
to be delivered within the Lodge room. The first is to be delivered to
the candidate after his election but before he receives his first degree,
the second after the first degree but before he starts to learn the posting
lecture, the third after the second degree and the fourth after the Master
Mason degree.
These lectures are completed except for a bit of editing. At a ·very
early date they will be in the hands of the printer and copies wili be
mailed to the Masters of the various Lodges just as soon as possible.
Your ·committee is asking for the cooperation of the District Deputy
Grand Masters, and for the help of the Worshipful Masters and Wardens
to establish these lectures as a part of the Masonic program of this jurisdiction. They have been careftilly compiled, they have been just as carefully checked and passed upon by Grand Lodge officers and others, and
it is the belief of the committee that they are a step in the right direction.
At the same time the committee knows that they are not perfect and that
constructive criticism can make them more practical. We are asking that
you take them, conscientiously try them out, and then later in the year
write us a letter ,and tell us how they work in actual use; what you deem
to be their strong points and their weaknesses. Then this committee,
which really wishes to see the matter through and do a good job, can
ultimately have something for you quite worth while.

influence be felt both in their own community and in the country at
large. · Thus . will they truly help Masonry to fulfil its high destiny in
the advance of civilization.
I have been astonished at the deplorable ignorance displayed on the

of the constituent Lodges, in particular, and the line of District Deputy

· The tendency becoming annually more evident of Lodges to seek

subjects to the enlightenment of their brethren. The desire of many
Masters of Constituent Lodges to fill practically the entire refreshment
hour with speeches and so limit the friendly social intercourse which
knits the brethren together defeats one of the main purposes of our order.

Quebec, 1943 (Grand Master):
There have been repeated suggestions during the past few years that
the Masonic order should widen its scope and take a larger place in
public affairs. It has been pointed out that the excellent work done by
service clubs and other organizations places them in an enviable position
to attract members by the public knowledge of the work done by them.
I can see no advantage in our order entering into this field which is
sufficiently well covered even if it were desirable, which I do not consider it is.
It must be recognized that the Masonic order is in the last analysis
a philosophy of life and likely to appeal to the few rather than to the
many. Its contribution to the field of ' public service must necessarily
· be indirect rather than direct. Members of the order, as individuals,
take a foremost place in positions of state, church and these institutions
organized for the alleviation of suffering or the improvement of the status
of humanity. The active efforts put forward by members of the craft
in these directions carries with it an influence very much out of proportion
to the number contributing.
There has been the feeling in certain quarters ,that the Masonic order
is getting out of date. The principles upon which the order rests are
eternal and .will never be out of date. As the members of the order
become more conscious of the extent of their responsibility to carry out
to the fullest extent the principles and teachings of the order, will their

Colorado, 1943 (Grand Master):
Much discussion has been given to this subject and there is a wide
variation of opinion as to amount and type of service which should be
rendered to our brethren in the armed forces. Many of our members
have given serious thought to the question of our obligation to these
brethren at present and in the post-war period. Our service should be
designed, to meet the need in our particular jurisdiction. Thus far,
Masonic service in Colorado has been administered without special organization or special funds through the office of the Grand Secretary and the
· individual Lodges; and through this means, many of our brethren have
received comfort and ~ssi1tance. It has seemed . to m~ that there is a
growing need and deinand for an organize\!, independently financed
service. Realizing that the Denver Masonic Officers Association had
made some study of the .situation, I submitted to that association a request
for a survey and recommendation. On July 16, last, I received a report
of their activities with a definite suggestion that organized service be
undertaken and a plan of organization. Upon my return from a trip to
the Western Slope the latter part of July, I arranged for a conference
on August 12, at which I was fortunate to have the presence of Deputy
Grand Master Herschel Horn. As a result of such conference, it was
decided to undertake organized service. Accordingly, I appointed a
Masonic Service Committee consisting of Brother Lester L. Barton of
Denver, Brother H. Elwyn Davis of Pueblo, Brother Frank R. Foster
of Colorado Springs and Brother Jerry E. Lawton of Denver. On September 3, I prepared and forwarded a letter to all of the Lodges in
Colorado directing that they notify the brethren of their respective Lodges
of the plan and requested a voluntary contribution of one dollar per
member to be paid into the constituent Lodges and 1?,Y them forwarded
to the Grand Secretary. I made the call for the cre'ation of a fund for
service to our brethren in the armed forces and to any brancli thereoi,
and to their dependents, during and after the present World War, to be
administered by the Grand Master through such committees as he might
appoint and as directed by the Grand Lodge in regular communication.
Further, that any balance of such fund thus created might be diverted

New Hampshire, 1942 (Correspondence Committee):
In my mental peregrination among the Grand Lodges of the United
States and Canada, I have found much to encourage a more optimistic
view of the condition of the craft. Sixteen Grand Lodges in the United
States report a gain in membership, all others, with few exceptions, report
smaller losses than i:n any previous year since 1929, and· Grand Masters,
without exception, fake pride in reporting an increased interest in things
Masonic among the craft. In their annual messages many of these same
Grand Masters expre~s fears that we may have too great an influx of
candidates; or .that our so-called mistakes of a couple of decades ago may
be repeated. Few seem to take into consideration the fact that financial
conditions a:re not the same as in those well remembered hectic days,
and that money is "burning holes" in no pockets today. It would seem
to the writer that it's about time to cease blaming "undesirable material"
for the heavy losses in membership we have experienced, and to place
the blame where it belongs : squarely on our own shoulders. In our
opinion, 90 per cent of that material was good; but, we failed to mold
it into a finished product. We made them Masons in name and then
overnight we sent them out in the armed forces of our coulit;y,_wit.hout
any effort on our part to finish the job we had started, or· to provide
Masonic contacts for them, either at home or abroad. Oh .I know, we
tried to do things in a big way, and because we met with lamentable
failure, we forgot to do the little things we might have done. We could
at least have k~pt contact with them by letter.; .or, through correspondence, we might have arranged Masonic contacts for them with Lodges
near their stations; then too, we might have urged them to attend communications of their Lodges after they got home. Did we do any of
these things? Let conscience dictate the answer. All this is 'just leading
up to the all absorbing Masonic topic of the year: "Masonic ·Service to
our Brethren in the Armed Forces." Must we doubt the truth of the
old adage: "Experience is the best teacher?" We ascribed our failure
to participate in war service during World War I to the· fact that we
lacked a central agency. Right! Now, we have such an agency with
machinery nicely attuned to the needs of the occasion; with every facility
for smooth and effective operation. Added to this we have the opportunity to show to the world, that although we are of many jurisdictions,
we are as one in this great and vitally necessary service to those . of our
brethren who are in the armed forces, and to the sons of those at home.
Can it be that some of us feel that in pooling. our resources and our
endeavors we may be surrendering just a little bit of our precious sovereigqty? Or, do we think that we can do more effective work alone?
We· grope for the answer. In all the reasons given for noncooperation,
we have heard none, that to our mind, is truly valid. Of one thing we
are assured, however, and we rejoice in the assurance: no matter how
much we differ in how to do it, we are united in the firm conviction
that . it ~ust be done. All Grand Lodges, without exception, are tackling
the Job m some manner, not only in the matter of service to the personnel

Oregon, 1943 (Correspondence Committee):
In preparing and presenting this, a review of the actlv1t1es of some
sixty odd jurisdictions, an effort has been made to include ther.ei.n. such
items that we felt would be of interest ·to those who read, and to bring
to them a comprehensive idea of the manner in which our· brethre~ have
met and are meeting the problems that have been common to the craft
in all jurisdictions during the year.
The exigencies of these war-plagued days have called for the exercise
of much thought and effort along with the expenditure o·f funds by the
craft in an e~ort to measure up to what they deemed their responsibility
and likewise their contribution to further and hasten the day through
allied victory, that brought a return of an appreciation of human worth,
the sanctity of human life, and world peace.
Personally, this writer feels that Masonry has failed to measure up
to its responsibility in its war efforts. Not that there has been a dearth
of effort or lack of desire to be of service, nor an understanding of the
need of such service. Rather it has been the lack of a plan of action in
which all were agreed by which this singleness of purpose could be put
into effect and operation:
We contend, and our perception; we admit, is brought about by a
liberal use of hindsight rather than by reason of our being an oracle, that
a real, effective all-embracing ·service could have and would have been
offered by Masonry had a plan of action been adopted wherein, first,
all service within the boundaries of a juris.dictiori would have been the
responsibility both as to finances and personal service, of that jurisdiction;
second, that all jurisdictions would have been contributing members of
the Masonic Service Association so far as pertained to war service, and,
third, that all war activities of the Masonic Service Association would
have been confined to our armed forces in their over-seas operation.

,_ service centers, one in Bristol and the other in Providence, in addition to
assistance rendered the men at various forts and camps throughout the
state.
Tlje opportunity for work at Bristol was first learned from an item
in the newspaper. I made several trips to Bristol and arranged to have
the club rooms in the temple opened for the use of the men in the service.
A large sign was erected on the front ol the building.
The Providence center was opened about three months ago. This
center has already been visited by about 500 service· men, representing
46 states, and has been another fine addition to our work in this state.
The center at Newport is progressing very nicely and doing fine work.
This center is sponsored by the Masonic Service Association of the United
States, except for the rent of the building, which is paid by our Grand
Lodge.

PATRIOTISM
And Freemasonry is patriotic-very much so. But it is not a political
party in any sense of the term. However, loyalty to one's country and
its institutions has always been practiced by Masons. And this is especially true of American Freemasonry.
Connecticut, 1944 (Grand Master):
At the request of the War Bond Finance Committee of Conneeticµt,
that the Masonic fraternity take an active part. in the Third War Bond
campaign, a committee was appointed to stimulate among our brethren
and Lodges, the purchase and sale of bonds and to concretely establish
the fact that Freemasonry is standing squarely behind our government
in the prosecution of the war. A letter setting forth our plans was prepared by the committee and mailed to each member of the constituent
Lodges. At the end of the three weeks' drive, which lasted from September 9 to September 30, the amount of $7,715,353.00 had been
subscribed.
Kansas, 1944 (Grand Orator):
And, lastly, Freemasonry is patriotic-very much so. But it is not
a political party in any sense of the term. It takes no part, as a Lodge,
in partisan politics. Masons belong to and support whatever parties
they prefer. However, loyalty to one's country and its institutions has
always been practiced by Masons. And this is especially true of American
Freemasonry.

From the introduction of Freemasonry into the American Colonies in
1723 to the present, Masons have been out in front in every war, in every
effort and in every sacrifice to liberate the colonies, in the first place,
then to set up a "pattern of government which the nations of the world
may copy," and finally to maintain that liberty for which our forefathers
of colopial days suffered and died. And Freemasonry will ever stand
for, fight for and defend the American way of life.
.
But first let us note the activities of Masons in the Revolutionary
War.
Some of the leaders in the movement that led up to that. war were
active Masons, such as Paul Revere, Robert Newton, who h"ung the
signal lanter11 from the old North Church; William Dawes, who gave
the alarm to Roxbury, as Revere did to Charleston; Patrick Henry,
· whose eloquence set the Virginia House of Burgesses on· fire" for liberty;
Samuel Adams, Josiah Quincy, Joseph Warren, who assisted in laying
the plans for the revolution, were all Masons. The Boston Tea Party
was planned and carried out by Masons. These men were members of
St. Andrew's Lodge. Paul Revere was in charge of a small patrol of
colonial soldiers who accompanied the "Indians" to the harbor, and who
stood guaFd while the "Indians" dumped the tea in the harbor. The
ride made famous by Longfellow, now so well known, was neith.er his
greatest ride nor the most important, for it failed. But he made many
other rides, sometime.s for days and nights, in all sorts of weather and
in constant danger, to carry secret and military messages between Boston,
New York and Philadelphia; in fact, he was the man to whom all of the
leaders looke\:i to carry the confidential messages. He was a silver-and- .
gold-smith of note. The very night of the tea party Paul "Revere was
Junior Warden of his Lodge. The Declaration of Independence, 's o tradition says, was written, originally, on a lambskin apron and was signed
on a Masonic altar, by a Congressional representative, John Hancock, a
Mason. Fifty of the fifty-six signers of the Declaration of Independence
were Masons. A convention of great purposefulness assembled at Charlotte, North Carolina, in May, 1775, and prepared the so-called Mecklenburg· Declaration of Independence. This was of Masonic origin. Of
the fifty-five men who sat in the Constitutional Convention, fifty were
Masons. Before the Revolutionary . War was half over, ten military
Lodges had been organized under command of Washington. Night after
night, when Washington and the Continental Army were in dire straits,
the word was sent down the line: "No one on duty tonight but Masons!"
Of the twenty-nine major · generals under Washington, twenty were
Masons. Of the sixty brigadier generals fifty-nine were Masons. When
Washington was elected President of these newly organized United
States of America, he called all of the thirteen governors bf the states
together, and there sat about that table just kmrteen '.M:asons, Washing~
ton and the governors-all Masons. The cornerstone of the new National
Capitol Building was laid with Masonic rites by Washington, as the
acting Grand Master. John Marshall, Alexander Hamilton and James
Madison were all Masons.
This has been the spirit of Masons from that time to the present.
In war and in peace, Masons have b.een the leaders in every constructive
movement to advance the United States to its pre~ent place of power
in the world:
Presidents, governors, members of ·the U . S. Supreme
Court and the Congress have been Masons far beyond the percentage
of members in this country. William Clark and Meriwether Lewis, both
Masons, opened the trail into the Northwest in 1804. Commodore Stephen
Decatur, Jr.,, "Hero of Tripoli," and Commodore Edward Preble, who

distinguished himself in the same campaign,_ were Masons. In the war
of 1812, Masons again were the leaders. Maior General Andrew Jackson,
tater President of the United States; Commodore Lawre~c~ Kearney,
Major. Gene~al Montfort Stokes and Brigadier General Wilham Henry.
Winder were Masons. No greater names than thes_e are to be f?und
among the patriots of the United States. But more: m t he war of mdependence of Texas from Mexico, General S~muel H_ouston, a Mason,
led in this successful war. Later, in war with Mex1c~, ~asons were
leaders. Major General Winfield Scott Hancock, Brigadier Gen~ral
Archibald Yell, Major General John Anthony Quitman and Rear Admiral
John Drake Sloat, Commodore Matthew C. Perry, who opened Japan
to world trade, all were Masons.
· During the Civil War such Masonic names as James A. Ga~field, later
President of the United States; David G. Farragut, first admiral of the
u. S. Navy; Major General John A. Logan; Lieutenant ~eneral Nelson
A. Miles, General Grant's chief of staff, and later Gr~nt s Secretary of
War, Brigadier General John A. Rawlins. On the s1d~ ?f the South
such names as General George Pickett, General Albert Pike, one time
Grand Commander of the Supreme Council, A. & A. S .. R., Southern
Jurisdiction, U. S . A., and General Joseph Wheeler.
In the Spanish-American War such names as. Colonel Theodore
Roosevelt, later President of the United States; . Maior General Leonard
Wood, Rear Admiral Winfield Scott Schley, Maior General Art~ur MacArthur, father of General Douglas MacArthur, appear on Masomc Lodge
rolls.
The discoyerer of the North Pole, Rear Admiral Robert E. Peary,
was a Mason, as was Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd, w hose work in
and near the South Pole is well known.
In the first world war we have such men as General John. J. Pershing,
Rear Admiral Henry T. Mayo, Major General John A. L~ieune of ~he
Marines and .General Charles P. Summerall of the Masomc Fraternity.
Leaders fo the second world war include General Dougl~s MacArthur,
Gener<)! George· C. Marshall, U. S. Chief of Staff; Admiral Ernest J.
King, Chief of Naval Operations, and Lieutenant General Ben Lear,
to name just a few.
And what do we say about the great host of men in t he service' of
their country below the rank of general and admiral? Masons are scattered throughout the many commands fighting on scores of fronts and
brin&'ing honor and glory to the already glorious United States.

South Dakota, 1943 (Grand Master):
In the midst of the grim realities of a world conflict, the like of which
has never before been perpetrated on ~ankind, Masonry faces its greates·t
crisis., The conflict is a total warfare between the forces supporting the
ideals of government by and for free men, and those forces founded upon
the false premise of government by destructive force and aggression.
Builded on two basic tenets: The Fatherhood of God, and the Brotherhood of Man, Masonry is alert to, and will accept, its obligations to aid
in the defense of truth, justice and liberty. Not a militant organization,
but with its very existence endangered, Masonry will ever respond to
the call of our government to preserve and defend that government, and
the democratic way of life that is our heritage, through the hardship and
sacrifice oi those who have gone this way before us.
History has recorded the activities of Masonry during the entire life
of our country, molding its form of government, and, in every crisis,
ready to make any sacrifice to keep secure, for ourselves arid our posterity,
the religious freedom and civil liberties guaranteed by our constitution.
Our duty is clear. Our first concern is to aid, in every possible way, in
the prosecution of this war to a successful conclusion.
Victoria, 1943 (Grand Master):
Towards the end of last year, the British Prime Minister, whose utterances have so inspired us all, said that he believed that we had then
reached the end of the beginning. It would be the highest folly for us
to imagine that, even after the encouraging achievements of the last few
months, we are witnessing the beginning of the end. That time will
come; but, brethren, the wisest of us know not how soon; and in the
meantime we must accept the assurances of our leaders, both here and
overseas, that a long and bloody struggle still confronts us. We may
justly take heart from the successes which have been won, we must be
grateful to those who have been responsible for them, and espei;ially
grateful to those who had stood, and still stand, between our land and
our enemies; but we must not be found wanting in the discharge of our
own duties;· we must fight and work and lend and give as we have never
done before; and we must never relax until the foe has been vanquished,
the battle won, and the blessings of peace and honor and decency restored
to the whole world.

To modify or not to modify one of our landmarks is a question that
has agitated nearly every jurisdiction in the United States the past year.

Louisiana, 1944 (Proceedings):
Whereas, Recommendation No. 6 of the Grand Lodge Proceedings
of 1943 was referred to the Committee on Masonic Law and Jurisprudence
for study and suggested action ; and
Whereas, the subject of physical requirements for candidates has been
given serious study by the committee throughout the year; and
Whereas, it seems wise to reconsider our traditional attitude on the
doctrine of physical perfection;
Therefore; Be It Resolved, That physical qualifications for the degrees
in the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge be and the same are hereby defined
as to require only that the candidate be able in a reasonable manner
by the use of natural or artificial members to give all the signs, grips,
and steps; be of sound mind; and self-supporting so as not to become a
financial burden on the fraternity.
Be It Further Resolved that all edicts and general regu lations in conflict herewith are hereby repealed.
Be It Further Resolved that th e constituent Lodges shall have the
responsibility of determining that app licants meet these physical qualifications.
Be It Further Resolved th~t we reaffirm our declaration that the in-.
ward and not the outward qualifications are what we as Masons regard
as of permanent importance.
The resolution was adopted.
Ohio, 1943 (Grand Master):
· Perhaps there has never been any question which has so engrossed
the thought of Masonry throughout the years as the interpretation of the
rigid physical qualifications required of candidates. It does seem strang.:
that those qualifications, so essential in the days of operative Masonry,
should have been carried over in the transition to speculative Masonry.
Then we became active in the sphere ·of spiritual development, labor, and
thought, making use of the symbolisms operative Masonry suggested. It
may have been that such physical fitness was intended to symbolize that
the candidate must be possessed of that high character and integrity indis-

pensable for the development and utilization of our inherent moral and
spiritual virtues.
At this particular time, when the world is forced to face and use the
most inhuman and devastating inventions the world has ever known, in
order t.o preserve the .national supremacy of nations which stand for freedom, justice, an<;! liberty, which God ordained for all men, tl).e question
as to whether · M<isonry -may continue -to maintain its interpretation--of the
·requirement of the physical perfection of youth, has become an overwhelming consideration.
In the organization of its armed forces, our government is demanding
physical perfection in our youth, and must perforce expose it to dangers
and hazards so appalling that escape seems almost impossible. There
will be found among those youth thousands who would have sought
entrance within the portals of Masonry had they not been called to a
vicarious life for you and me. We surely dare not deny them a welcome
to our fellowship because they have been maimed in body in defense
of our country and the protection of Masonry.
In insisting on the physical perfection of youth as a requisite for
candidates for the degrees, we are not following the expressed declaration
of Masonry that "the internal and not external qualifications of a man are
what Masonry regards." Let us remember also that our Great Light
says, "Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh
on the heart."

to go out and fight, bleed and suffer to defend the principles and ideals
of Freemasonry, but because · you have lost a limb or , an ,eye or some
other part of your body you are not fit to take your place as one of
us?" Is it worthy of Freemasonry to deny to these men who shall hav.e
borne the burden of battle the warmth and fellowship they might have
as members of the craft? Is Freemasonry to penalize patriotism? I
hope not.

South Carolina, 1944 (Grand Master):
From the early days of Freemasonry to the present time many Grand
Lodges have adhered to what is known as the "Perfect Youth" theory.
The idea behind this theory was that in order to become a Mason a man
must be physically perfect to all outward appearances. It is easy for
us to understand the necessity for this when practically all men had to
earn their living by manual labor. As civilization advanced and many
means of earning a livelihood developed it became less and less necessary
for one to earn a livelihood by manual labor. And, too, as Masonry
became more and more a speculative art rather tha~ an operative art
there was less and less reason for adhering to the "Perfect Youth" theory.
We know that it is impossible to judge accurately as to the soundness
of one's physical body by outward appearance.
According to our present law it is very difficult to know where to
draw the line in trying to determine whether or not a person is physically
eligible. This is true of mariy cases presented to the Grand Master. It is
also true that many very questionable cases are never brought to the
attention of the Grand Master. Consequently Lodges have received candidates with very varying degrees of physical imperfections,
We are taught that a man is first prepared to be made a Mason in
his heart. In my opinion he is prepared there first, last and always.
If he is not prepared in his heart it makes little difference that he has
a perfect physical body. Masonry is a thing of the soul. Character
and character alone counts. It has' been a source of disappointment to
me that some of the most honorable and· upright men of my acquaintance
have been denied the privileges of Freemasonry, and that Freemasonry
has been deprived of their fine leadership simply bcause they had had
the .misfortune .to have lost a limb or suffered some other physical
defoi'mity. Already there are coming back into our midst fine young
men who ~ave suffered the loss of a limb or some physical deformity
in the defense of our country. There will no doubt be more. Is Free-

GILBERT C. DEFOREST
Grand Master 1944-1945

Gilbert C. DeForest, the 78th Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of
California was born in N ew Lancaster, Miami County, Kansas. In his
early youth he moved to Redding, California, where he still resides and
is the o":ner-manager of the Reddin.g Laundries; Inc.
He received his grade school education in the public schools of
Redding and attended the College of Commerce at Stockton, California in
1908-1909.
In 1911 he was united in marriage to Miss Meda V . Everhardt and
this marriage was blessed with the birth of two sons, Stanley and
Russell. Brother DeForest and his wife are the proud grandparents of
Russell's children, Gail, 50 years of age and Craig, 10 years.
" Gil." as he is affectionately known to his many friends was raised in
Reading Lodge No'. 254 on January 17, 1922; was appoirit ed Senior
Deacon in 1923; elected Junior Warden in 1924; Senior Warden in 1925
and served as Master in 1926.
·
In 1927 he was chosen by the Grand Master to be the Inspector of
the Sixth Masonic District in which capacity he served until August,
1936, when he w as appointed Assistant Grand Lecturer, which position
he occupied until his election as Junior Grand Warden in October, 1941.
He was elected Senior Grand Warden in 1942; Deputy Grand Master in
1943, and Grand Master in 1944.
During his year as Grand Master he had the distinction of installing
his eldest son, Stanley, as Master of his Lodge. Later, t he team of
DeForest and DeForest, one the Grand Master of Masons in California
and the other Worshipful Master of Reading Lodge No. 254, had the
further distinction and pleasure of conferring the degrees of Masonry
upon the younger son, Russell.
Brother DeForest is a member of the York Rite Bodies of Redding
and the Scottish Rite Bodies and the Shrine in Sacramento. At the
.meeting of the Supreme Council of the Thirty-third Degree, held in Washington, D. C., in October, 1945, he was elected to the rank and dignity
of Knight Commander of the Court of Honor.
His long service to Masonry is appreciated . by his brethren of California and it is their earnest wish that he may enjoy a long life of success
and happiness.

GILBERT C . DEFOREST

Proclamation
San Francisco, June 25, 1945.
To AU Members of Grand Lodge:
In January of this ye4r the Director of War Mobilization appealed for a
curtailment of all non-essential travel and particularly requested a cessation
of all group meetings, conventions, conferences, etc., that could not be
shown to be essential to the war effort.
It was immediately evident that compliance with this request would
make impossible the holding of a regular annual communication of Grand
Lodge, as provided for under our law and as ha.s customarily been held.
The Director of War Mobilization suggested a number of alternatives
all designed to take the place of such conferences and conventions. In '
our situation none of the alternatives would provide a method by which
we might have a legal communication of Grand Lodge.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

437

I have been giving very serious consideration to this entire problem and
have consulted with the Grand Lodge officers, and others whose counsel I
value, in an effort to determine what we should do in this situation.
The sirnple facts of the case are that we are at war, that we are in an
area which is likely to beco.me more and more the center of war activities
and where, as far as we can see, the situation in October is likely to be
worse rather than better. For almost four years we have cooperated to
the full extent of our ability in the war effort and have urged our Lodges
to do likewise. It is the duty of every Mason to C0mply with every reasonable request of our government in order that the war might be successfully
prosecuted. This is no time for the constituent Lodges, or for Grand
Lodge, to take any action that will in any wise change this established
practice.
After due consideration of all factors involved I have reached a conclusion and now,
Therefore, I, Gilbert C. DeForest, Grand Master of Masons
in California, do hereby declare and proclaim that there will be
no Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge convened on
October 8, 1945.
Plans are now being developed for the conduct of Grand Lodge affairs
during the coming year and when they are completed a full statement
concerning them wil) be made to all Lodges.
I direct that this Proclamation be read in full at the next stated meeting
following its receipt.
Fratern.a lly yours,
G. c. DEFOREST,
Grand Master.
Attest:
LLOYD E. WILSON,
Grand Secretary.
Proclamation
San Francisco, Sept. 4, 1945.
To All Members of Grand Lodge:
On June 25, 1945, I issued a Proclamation in which I directed the attention of all members of Grand Lodge to an appeal by the Director of
. War Mobilization for a cessation of all group meetings, conventions, conferences, etc., and in which I informed them that, complying with the request, there would be no annual communication of this Grand 'Lodge convened on October 8, 1945.
The Director of War Mobilization has now removed the restriction as
far as conventions within a State are concerned and there is no longer any
Governmental reason why we cannot hold a communication.
The hotel situation in San Francisco is, however, still critical and in
my opinion it would be inadvisable and inappropriate to attempt to hold our
customary five <lay session. It is, however, desirable to have a communication and it is entirely practical to have a one day session. I am, therefore,
declaring the Proclamation of June 25th null and void and I am issuing
this call for a one day annual communication.
The purpose of the communication will be to transact only the necessary business of Grand Lodge and to elect and install officers, except
Junior Grand Warden. No legislation will be enacted and no controversial
matters . will be acted upo~.

Lodge of .California will be convened in annual communication in the City of San Francisco on Friday October 12, 1945,

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Upon retiring as your Grand Master, which office you so kindly
entrusted to me for the past twelve months, I had hoped to be able to
report to you that I had visited a goodly number of t~e L:od~es and that
those visits had contributed something to the great institution of Free
Masonry. We!J, my brehren, such visits as I made were. certainly worth
while but the extreme difficulty of getting around over this state, together
with the sincere desire to co-operate with our Government in prosecuting
the war, prompted me to forego one of the greatest pleasures of the office
-that of meeting and visiting with you personally. However, 1. shall
always be grateful to the members of this Grand Lodge for making it
possible for me to serve this Grand Jurisdiction as its Grand· Master.
While this has been a year of many sorrows and much bloodshed, it
has also been a year of great rejoicing, for during this Masonic year we
have seen complete victory come to us and our allies in both the European
and Pacific wars. The dictators and similar rulers have been conquered
and we are now in the process. of assisting in establishing a civil and progressive form of government in those countries, which until now, have
been ruled by the hand of force and greed. It is my hope and the hope
of every Mason that our loved ones in the armed forces may soon return
to their homes feeling that the principles for which they fought and bled
shall guide the peace ·that will follow and that that peace shall be everlasting and eternal.
In February of this year there was issued fr.om Washingt?it'. D. C.,. a
directive prohibiting conventions or group meetings except within certain
limits as to the · number attending. As a result of this directive a very
serious problem confronted us relative to our annual communication in
October. Feeling entirely incapable of handling any such problem your
Grand Master held several meetings in San Francisco and Los Angeles
with brethren whose judgment he valued and it was the opinion of most
of those present that unless there was a m~dification of the direc!ive
within a reasonable time, no effort should be made to hold the commumca. tion. For several months no material change was made in the order and
as a consequence I caused to be issued on June 25th a proclamation callii:ig

439

off the annual communication. By September 1st the situation had cleared
to such an extent that the Government lifted all restrictions within the
state so I thought it proper to convene Grand Lodge in annual communication for one day only for the purpose of transacting only the necessary business. of Grand Lodge. On September 4th I issued a proclamation
decl~ring null and void the one of June 25th and proclaiming a one-day
session to be held on October 12th, at which no legislation would be
enacted and no controver~ial matters acted upoil and called attention to
the fact that we would elect and install officers, except Junior Grand
Warden. I did not deem it proper that a Junior Grand Warden be
elected unless all Lodges had a fair chance to be represented at the meeting and certainly the time was too short between the lifting of the order
and the date of our meeting for all the Lodges to make arrangements to
be represented.
·
John Downen
Because of continued ill health, Brother John Downen resigned as
superintendent of .our home for children at Covina. During the nearly
20 years of his service at the home many children have come under his
supervision, have been guided through their youthful years, have been
trained and educated under his direction and were fully equipped on leaving the home. to take their place in the world. In his work John was
materially assisted by Mrs. Downen who was a wonderful mother to all.
May they both live long and be very happy in their new home.

Bo.th of these illustrious brethren serv.ed the craft as Grand Mastet
many years ago but were active in Masonry until the end. We can all
join in the assurance that they are "happy in their father's house" and

Decisions
No. 1
A member requested his Lodg-e to become a co-signer on a note, securing a loan of $1,500. The Lodge voted to grant the request and asked if it
was legal for them to do so.
I held that a Lodge could' not legally become a co-signer on a note,
under the circumstances set forth.
No. 2
A Lodge has made a practice of taking a vote upon a member's request
to take out a Life Membership. A member of the Lodge contended that
when the proper amount was tendered to the Secretary no action was
required by the Lodge. I was asked if action by the Lodge was necessary
and if the Lodge could refuse to issue a Life Membership.
I held that no formal action by the Lodge is required and it could not
refuse to issue a Life Membership.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
I have the honor to present to you herewith my fourth annual report as
your Grand Secretary.
With the .excep.tio~ of two months all of my services as Grand Secretary
has been durmg a period of war with all of its problems and difficulties.
In previous reports I have indicated the manner in which the Grand Lodge
office has been affected by the war and the same general facts hold true
for the year just closed.

In spite of l.al:>or and other personnel problems we have been able to

co?d~ct the affairs of the Grand Lodge office in. a creditable manner, due

pnnc1pal1y to the loyalty and efficiency of our old time faithful employees.
. T~e work of our· Lodge se~retaries has been done efficiently and conscientiously and generally speakmg on a very high level. There have been
many changes, due to death, removal and other causes and the new secretaries
have taken hold in a most creditable manner.
War Program
There has been little change in the general pattern of the War Program
which has been conducted.
In the matter of courtesy degrees I reported last year that since the war
started we had received from other grand jurisdictions requests for a total
of 4,782 .courtesy degrees. This figure has now grown to 8,290. During the
same period we had requested a total of 1,739 and this has now grown to 2,603.

Philippine Islands
The Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands has been re-formed and is
again operating.
Immediately after the liberation of the Philippine Isla·nds we began
correspondence with the officers of that Grand Lodge for the purp~se of ful~y
acquainting them with what we had done in the matter of acceptmg dues m
trust. We indicated our willingness to continue to function in this respect as
long as they desired us to do so but also indicated our readiness to turn over
all records and funds to them when they were prepared to take over that
responsibility. We have recently received word from them stating that they
are prepared to take over this function and we have accordingly closed this
portion of our war program.
The individual case records of every man have been prepared and have
been shipPecl to Manila in the custody of Captain W. E. Williams, Master
of Cavite Lodge No. 2, who left San Francisco approximately September 15th.
These records represented- our contact and corn:spondence with 746 members.
A check approximating $18,800, representing the dues collected and the interest
earned on the investment of the principal in United States War Bonds, will
be forwarded to the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands. The expense
has been borne by the Grand Lodge of California. Thus ends one of the
most practical fraternal services rendered by any Grand Lodge to the distressed brethr'en of another grand jurisdiction and it writes another glodous
page in the history of the Grand Lodge of California in its relationship to
the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands.
·
The story of the relief campaign conducted by this Grand Lodge in behalf
of the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands will be related by the Grand
Master in his message.

Consolidation
Under date of January 10, 1945, Most Worshipful Gilbert C. DeForest,
Grand Master, approved the request for a consolidation of Inyo Lodge No.
221 and Waucoba J;.odge No. 413 into one Lodge, to be known as Inyo Lodge
No. 221, with its meeting place at the present place of Inyo Lodge No. 221.
Duplicate Charter
On July 15, 1945, the charter of Claiborne Lodge No. 185, Point Arena,
was destroyed in the fire which resulted in the loss of their Lodge hall.
Under date of July 26, 1945, the Grand Master approved the issuance of a
duplicate charter ·to this Lodge, the same being forwarded to them July
28; 1945.
Grand Lodge of Texas
The Grand Lodge of Texas, through its Grand Master Most Worshipful
Claud L. Austin, honored the Grand Lodge of California by inviting the
Grand Secretary to be its .guest and principal speaker at the 109th anniversary
communication held at Waco, December 6-7, 1944. ·
With the approval of the Most Worshipful Gilbert C. DeForest, Grand
Master, the Grand Secretary accepted the invitation and was received with
the hospitality for which Texas is famous.
George Washington National Masonic Association
As a director of the Memorial Association the Grand Secretary attended
the directors' meeting in Washington in February and as a member of the
Special Committee of Four to devise ways and means for the completion of
the Memorial and its Endowment, attended the meeting of that committee
in Chicago in May.
It is expected that the plan proposed by the committee will be presented
to the Executive Committee, and finally to the association, for action at its
next meeting.
Mountain Lodges
During his summer vacation the Grand Secretar~ visited a number of the
old mo~ntain Lodges, including Harmony Lodge No. 164, at Sierra City,
Mountam Shade Lodge No. 18, at Downieville, Gravel Range Lodge No. 59,
at Camptonville, Forest Lodge No. 66, at Alleghany and Forbestown Lodge
No. SO, at F.orbestown.
Stated meetings· were attended at most of these Lodges and in addition
a second degree was conferred at Forbestown and the lecture of the third
degree delivered at Camptonville.
These mountain Lodges have been carrying on in the face of extraordinary
difficulties and too much praise cannot be given them for the splendid work
which they have done arid .the personal effort and sacrifice which they ha~e
made in traveling long distances to keep these Lodges operating. The close
cooperation among the Lodges in the matter of attendance at their respective
meeting sets a fine example for other Lodges not working under such
difficulties.

Membership
In presenting membership figures for the year I have supplied figures
for the years 1931, 1941, 1942, 1943, 1944 and 1945. The year 1931 has be~n
selected for purposes of comparison becaus.e the peak of. our membership
growth was reached in that year with the total mem?ersh1~ of 142,422 and
the present membership of 150,368 represents the all-time high to date.
It is interesting to know that 40,386 degrees have been conferred upon
our own members in addition to ~ourtesy degrees conferred for o~her ~rand
jurisdictions. There has been a net gain of 11,630 members and m spite of
our increased membership there are fewer deaths reported by twelve; than
in the preceding year. It is also good to note that there .was 212 less suspensions for non-payment of dues.

Reference is made to that portion of the report of the Grand Treasurer

Southern Pacific, United States Savings and Treasury Bonds,_and Masonic
Temple Association of California capital stock were sold. The list of
securities sold was filed with that Annual Report, also the profit on the
transaction was reported.
The total funds available from the sale were: from bonds, principal
amount $78,328.34, accrued interest $855.43; from shares $77,830.21, or a
total of $157,013.98.

States 2% Treasury Bonds 52-54, dated June 26, 1944, principal amount

obtained at that time but it was deemed sound to hold because of conversion privileges, among other factors. On Decemb'e r 26, 1944, the

Municipal Securities and Sixth War Loan Transactions
It will be recalled that in my report to Grand Lodge at the Annual

Communication, 1944, I recommended that we make note of the fact that
the remaining municipals in all funds indicated a potential gross profit at
that time of approximately $76,805.46. In the latter part of November,
1944, I invited attention of members of the Committee on Investment of
Endowment Funds to the results of a review of the municipals in the
portfolios of the Endowment and Luckenbach funds made by the trust
department of Anglo California National Bank, a copy of which marked
Exhibit "C" was attached to the Interim Report referred to.
That review revealed that current market approximated $781,697.30 as
against recorded book value of $706,920.97 and a potential gross profit of
approximately $74,776.33.
I also invited attention that there were in the Patton, Flint Annuity
and Flint Trust funds municipals totaling at market $41,354.80 with recorded book va~ue of $39,383.67, indicating a potential gross profit of
$1,971.13. I also informed the Committe_e that there were additional
amounts in several funds available for investment.

to municipals reported in my 1944 report to Grand Lodge. Also there
were these other a:vaila,ble .facts. The Board of Retirement System of
the City and County of San Francisco. had currently sold municip~ls
approximating $6,763,000.00 at market. From the proceeds the Board mvested approximately $3,200,000.00 in United States 2~% Treasury
Bonds, 59-56, at market to yield approximately 2.19%. It was also reported that they would invest $1,750,000.00 fo the Sixth War Loan United
States 2%s; 52-54. There were other sales of municipals in substantial
amounts by ·life insurance companies. Also I had the advice and counsel
of the Trust Departments of both the Wells Fargo and Anglo Banks.

States Savings Bonds for the Scholarship Fund, that the funds realized

Amortization Accumulations
During the month of July the Grand Treasurer in an endeavor to reconcile the foregoing profits with office accounting, learned that amortization
accumulations were being released to the Trusteee of Masonic "Homes on
an established formula. One contingency related to sales of securities at
a profit.· In ~mch instances, amortization accruals have been released to
the Homes Trustees. It seems that· the formula resulted from a conference
between the. former Grand Treasurer, the President of the Homes Trustees, and at least some members of the Committee on Finances. So far it
seems there has never been any direct official action on the subject by
Grand Lodge. The practice has been reflected in the Auditor's reports.
It may be that approval of these reports would constitute approval by
Grand Lodge. However, as that practice could not be discerned without
competent analysis, it seems requisite that thete should be action by Grand
Lodge on the specific problem.
The Grand Treasurer questions the legality of allocation of amortization accumulations as indicated. Certainly the good faith or the intent of

457

the brethren concerned, whose devotion to the fraternity has been practically demonstrated by years of distinguished service, is not questioned
for a moment. In fact, it was probably with the desire to assure greater
income for · maintenance at a time, when it was more important than at
present, that the procedure was established. Also, it might have been
conceived that there was no difference between allocating the amortization
accumulations to the Endowment Fund or the Trustees-that the same
purpose was being serv:ed. The Grand Treasurer takes the position that
where capital of the EJdowment and Luckenbach, or any fund is used to
purchase bonds at a premium, amortization accruals which are essential
for the purpose of recovery of capital expenditure at or before maturity,
depending upon whether or not there is a specific call date, are a return
of capital and not income. Where a sale of securities being amortized is
made at a profit such accumulations should be released to the capital
account. It is probable that the adoption of the formula was urged with
the concept that the Trustees were entitled to payments received on redemption of coupons. Of course, when bonds were purchased at a
premium, it must have been done in contemplation of a net yield less
than the coupon, and that income less than the payments received in
settlement for coupons had been anticipated. The funds involved are
trust funds of which the income is payable to the Board of Trustees of
the Masonic Homes. The terms of the trusts must be meticulously observed. Every member of the fraternity and probably others have an interest in proper conservation and administration. That the subject is
important is emphasized by the fact that in excess of $30,000.00 has been
released to the Trustees as a result of the three major transactions herein
reported. While Grand Lodge has plenary powers they are not sufficient
to remove the armor which protects a trust. It is, therefore, the suggestion of the Grand Treasurer that the subject be referred to the Committee on Finances for recommendation to prevent erroneous practice which
might lead to embarrassment.
Maturity Problems
The attention of Grand Lodge is invited to the great proportion of its
investments which are now evidenced by the United States Government
securities. They are prime investments, of course, and under the circumstances there has been nothing better in the securities. market eligible
for purch.ase. Also, in making such investment, Grand Lodge has materially contributed to the war effort. Diversification is not important
at the moment but must not be disregarded. Appended hereto is a
schedule of Federal Securities as of July 31, 1945. Attention is invited
to the necessity of adjustments to more nearly uniform maturities and the
annual investment problems. Something in respect to greater uniformity
may be accomplished in relation to the Eighth or Victory Loan offerings.
It is opportune now to give some consideration to investment problems
in the uncertain period upon which we are entering. The requirement of
investment of Grand Lodge and other funds in federal and municipal
securities limits, and will continue to limit, the yield to low rates of interest during the time that those securities are marketable at par or
better. Yields on preferred stock have followed the returns on bonds
downward. The market price on common stocks has shown a steady
increase despite the actual termination of hostilities and impending conversion. It is anticipated by some authorities that there is sound basis
for higher prices of common shares, namely, greater returns from operations and consequent greater yields and equity values. It is contemplated·

459

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALI FORNIA

that this may continue for some years. If that be .the case, during such a
period consideration must be given to a possible ·. lower ·.market price of
securities with low fixed earnings of the type · in which the funds of
Grand Lodge are being invested. This, however, need not cause any apprehension. Federal Government securities after the first world war
dropped approximately twenty points but recovered in due course. However, there are sound investments in other types of securities producing
higher yields and this has been recognized by broadening of legal investments for trust funds by the so-called " prudent, man theory." Should
such investment policy be contemplated for the purposes of higher . yields
and diversification, excessive precautionary measures should be taken to
assure the guidance of exceptional investment counsel. Officials of Grand
Lodge having responsibilities in this respect should give due consideration
to the intricate problems involved.

as well preteeted as our own, able to keep out the imminent disaster.
If we, the people of the world, had sought first the Kingdom of God and
His righteousness, we would not be where we are now."
Many years ago a Grand Master made a profound utterance that "the
stern morality of Masonry is practical." I believe that the Masonic
fraternity can give the process of civilization of individuals a great impulse
as it · inspires real devotion to the ideals of the fraternity, nationally and
internationally. Therefore, am I willing to make by contribution to a
great institution having for its purpose the uplift of mankind to the end
that it may inspire greater interest, seriousness, and understanding on the
part of its members that they may, by precept and example, develop finer
individual characters everywhere.
Respectfully submitted,

Independent Accounting
The Grand Treasurer has been giving consideration ~o an appropriate
set-up for maintaining the accounts of the office. The atcountitig has
been temporarily done as a matter of expediency in the Grand Secretary's
office pending consideration of an acceptable plan. The accounting of the
Grand Secretary and that of the Grand Treasurer should be independent
as a check one upon the other. The Grand Secretary concurs in thi.s :
Owing to the simplicity of the required accounting, the employment of a
staff should be avoided if it can be done economically and as satisfactorily
otherwise. By virtue of the accounting respecting -securities and cash
under the control of the Grand Treasurer on the part of the custodian
under agency agreement, setting up the additional accounting to serve
the purpose would be simple and inexpensive. It is believed that this
service may be performed by the Trust Department of any bank, preferably the one acting for the Grand Treasurer and Grand Lodge under
agency agreement. In addition to the economy- of such procedure, at
negligible or no cost, the· Grand Treasmer would be afforded the advice
and counsel of the statistical and investment department with respect to
portfolios. It is my recommendation that the Gr-and Treasurer be auth0rized to arrange for such a system of accounting at a reasonable cost.
Grand Lodge has had the benefit of very efficient: services of accounting and cooperation of the Grand Se~retary, Past Grand Master Lloyd E.
Wilson, and the- Assistant Grand Secretary, Brother Henry Oliphant who
has been most willing and diligent in response to the many demands of
the Grand Treasurer.

Grand Treasurer

Conclusion
By reason of the fact that I have been somewh.a t active most of my
life in public affairs; the question has naturally been asked by those who
do not understand the civic responsibility of every competent person,
"What do you get out of it?" One very successful man insisted that I
must be obtaining monetary compensation. That type of individual would
not understand the satisfaction that flows from the perfor'm ance of such
unselfish service which is far greater compensation. So, too, one might
well inquire why have I assumed the additional responsibility requiring
expenditure of time and energy in. serving the Grand Lodge as Grand
Treasurer. The answer is rather simple. Two world wars have demonstrated that civilization is a slow process. Sometime ago Dr. Harry
Emerson Fosdick said, "Today, however, I ask you to look at the world
faced with catastrophe, stalked by hunger and pestilence, millions confronting partial or complete starvation, no national boundaries, even though

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON BY-LAWS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on By-Laws reports that during the past year eighty-one
Lodges submitted one or more amendments to their By-Laws for the Grand
Master's consideration. The majority of these amendments call for substantial
increases in fees and annual dues. This trend reflects the higher value being
placed on Masonic association, education and knowledge. They also indicate
much Masonic activity and attention to Lodge finances.
The Grand Secretary's report sets forth these amendments as follows :
Increasing fees: Gravel Range No. 59, to $50.00; Lexington No. 104, to
$100.00; Sotoyome No. 123, to $75.00; Excelsior No. 166, to $75.00; Downey
No. 22, to $75.00; San Mateo No. 226, to $100.00; Athens No. 228, to $50.00;

REPORT OF COM~ITTEE ON CLANDESTINE MASONRY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Clandestine Masonry begs leave to report as follows:
Because . of no .regular communication being held this year, there has
be_en no opport~mty for the Committee to confer upon the matters in
this rep~rt. . It is t~ke.n. from the current records of the Committee and
communications of md1v1dual members and filed at this time at the request
of the Grand Master.

.

465

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The activity of clandestinism during the past year has been .along
substantially the same lines and among the same races as prev1ou~ly
reported. The activity has been increased somewh.at by the financial
prosperity of the working classes. No new or definite developme.nt has
taken place excepting a small number of new lod~es and a revival of
some of those which had a11 but ~ssec\, out of existence.
One development during the year seems to have become definite and
apparent. With respect to the activity in the Sp.anish speaking peoi;ile,
especially in the Los Angeles area, an opportunity may be pr~sentmg
itself. Further study has disclosed a large number of representative me.n
resident here who desire to be regular Masons, yet because of their
handicaps in the English language they have not found it entirely pleasant.
to joi,n existing regular Lodges. Many of these men are apparent~y of
proper Masonic material and would seem to posses.s the proper quahfications. California probably has more of these Nationals than any other
foreign language group. There would seem therefore to be every re~so11
and circumstance to argtie for the establishment of a Lodge under California jurisdiction to confer work in the Spanish language. .'Such a Lodge
could be started from our own regular members who might desire to
take on this work. This would be the guarantee that it would start right
and would be careful in accepting new members.
This matter was suggested in the 1942 report of this Committee, but
until now no demand has existed for it. The subject was again alluded
to in the ' 1943 report. Now, however, there seems to be opening up. an
avenue by which a substantial portion of this branch of Clandestinism
JTiay be ultimately healed.
The subject requires special legislation before the movement could
be inaugurated. With no Grand Lodge session this year, it is impossible
to have action on the matter. A recommendation by the Committee upon
the subject may be "expected at the next session when more complete data
will be furnished and the necessary legislation and procedure outlined.
Because it became apparent early that it was probable no session
would be held this year, the Committee has spent no part of its appropriation for a survey made last year. The data would be too remote to
base recommendations on for next year'.s action. The survey will be
made through the Lodges during the coming year and reported upon at
the next communication.
Respectfully submitted,

has been evinced throughout the jurisdiction in the matter of this observance, and I have been informed by members of the Committee as well
as others in responsible authority that the observance of the natal day
of our Constitution throughout the month of September was a most successful one.
Unfortunately on account of the war effort much of the preliminary

Secretary with particularity concerning the observance ceremonies and
in each instance I was informed that fitting ceremonies were provided.
In almost every instance a speaker well versed in the history of the
Constitution was invited to make a suitable address and in many instances
the meetings were open to the public. Supporting numbers of a patriotic
nature in keeping with the solemnity of the occasion were given.

members of the Committee, and I wish to take this opportunity to express to each of them my sincere thanks for the eff9rts which they have
expended.
I particularly wish to commend Past Grand Master James T. Fraser
and committee member Alvin A. Horwege, both of whom did yeoman
work in acquainting the membership of their particular jurisdictions concerning the special obligation resting upon them for a fitting observance
of our Constitution Day effort.
I would also be remiss if I were not to make special mention concerning Honorable Goodwin J. Knight and Honorable William B. McKesson, Judges of the Superior Court of Los Angeles County. These
brethren, both of whom are eloquent speakers and well versed in the
lore of the · Constitution, gave unstintingly of their time in addressing
numerous subordinate Lodges throughout the jurisdiction.

which have had a tendency to provoke an avoidance of important tasks

Constitution Month has been most heartening, and the membership
throughout the jurisdicti~n is to be heartily commended .for their every
effort expended toward acquainting our fellow men with the many blessings conferred upon us through the medium of this immortal document.

year, and may I also express likewise my deep appreciation as well for
the interest and cooperation of our Grand Secretary, Lloyd Wilson, whose
prompt and ready response to my every demand played a most important
part in the success which has attended our efforts during the year which
has just terminated.

The purpose of the Board is to "study, devise, and carry out plans for
the securing of adequate endowment for the Masonic Homes of California."
To that end and in keeping with the policy of previous Boards, it has
been our aim to stimulate interest in our two Homes among the Lodges
and membership within our jurisdiction.
.Your Board is continuing along the line of a long range educatio_nal
program. It would be impossible for any of us to determine, particularly
with such unsettled conditions ahead, the amount of an endowment
necessary to properly maintain our Hoipes. We all look with pride to
these splendid institutions, and have in mind a program for their continued maintenance at the present high level, and your Board is earnestly
endeavoring to make it possible that every individual Mason in the jurisdiction be given the opportunity of participating in this long range constructive program.
The cooperative efforts of all concerned are showing definite results.
We have closed by far the best year of our existence, not only in the
amount of money received but more important, by the marked· increase
of individual contributions.
Our program of gifts and benefits is likewise yielding very satisfactory
returns. This is not only gratifying to those who have worked so long and
patiently, but should be a great stit:nulation for those just having the
opportunity to do their bit along this line.
The change in program in handling monies and certain business affairs
of the Board has, as was anticipated, worked much more smoothly and
with less expense during the past year. This is a great advantage for the
efficient operation of the Board's work. Likewise, the cooperation from
the Lodges and, particularly, the Masters and officers for the year, have
gained a better understanding and have cooperated to the fullest extent.
. One of the most productive activities of the Board was the completion
· of the "Manual of Information," which was distributed to all Lodges as
well as to Grand Lodge officers and committeemen. This small pamphlet
contains in a concentrated form the important essence of -information
sought by Lodges, their Endowment Committee, and \)thers who have so
generously given of their time and efforts. The next printing of this
pamphlet should contain more valuable information, and be of· greater
help and should have wider distribution.

for a new colored 16 mm .. Picture, telling the story of the Homes in a

We must not conclude this report without our deep appreciation to the

work. Our special thanks must go fo the Grand Master, who has labored
throughout the year under difficult circumstances in presenting the cause
of our Homes to the brethren. We are grateful for the Proclamation,
proclaiming the month of May as Masonic Homes Endowment month.
This brought our important work and its opportunity of service to the

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON LODGE FINANCING
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Lodge Financing submits herewith the report of
its activities for the year.
On many of the requests which have come to the Committee this year
it has not been possible to sit down with the officers and interested members of Lodges and personally discuss and examine their particular
problem. Due to war time restriction on traveling it has been necessary to
assemble pertinent information for the Committee's use through much
correspondence. In every case, the entire file, including application,
financial statements and all correspondence has been submitted to each
member of the Committee for his consideration and recommendation before responding to applicants. Whenever an application was received from
a Lodge, not too distant from the place of residence of one of the Committeemen, a personal call and interview was had with the officers and
certain members of the Lodge,.
The Committee has approached all Lodge problems with a desire to be
helpful, but not inconsistent with good business judgment, and the Lodges
have evinced their desire to be helpful and cooperate by being amenable
to suggestions from the Committee.
The war effort, with its attendant full employment as a consequence,
has caused many to seek admission to our fraternity. In keeping with
this condition Lodges have enjoyed increasing income and prosperity.
This has had a direct influence on many Lodges now renting quarters to
lay plans for eventually owning their own Lodge home. The Committee
has passed on a number of applications asking consent to the incorpora-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

tion of hall associations for the purpose of raising funds toward acquiring land and ultimately erecting buildings, in addition, numerous inquiries
have been received and answered bearing on the same subject. In giving
consent to applications for the formation of hall associations, and the
raising of money through ·the sale of stock or by contribution, such consent has been limited to such activity only, with the qualification, that no
land be purchased or contracts for building negotiated, until such contemplated action was :again submitted to the committee for review and
consent. It was the opinion of the committee, that no building construction should be commenced and consequently detract in the smallest degree from bringing victory in our present war with forces of aggression.
Following is a brief resume of the requests passed on by the Committee
pursuant to Sections 78 and 152 'of our Ordinances, a full and complete
file in each instance, after completion, has been forwarded to the Grand
Secretary's Office:

September 27, 1945.

MASONIC CLUBHOUSE AT BERKELEY
San Francisco, California
October 8, 1945

To the Most Worshipful Grand·Lodge of California:
Dear Brethren:
On behalf of the Trustees of the Masonic Club of the University of
California at Berkeley, I respectfully report that notwithstanding the
vicissitudes of war which have fallen heavily upon the University and
its student body, including the members of the Masonic Club, and of the
consequent difficulties in maintenance and operation of its Club House,
the past year has been a successful one.
There were 178 members in regular registration at the Masonic Club
during the fall and spring terms and 120 during the summer term last past.
In addition, the facilities of the Clubhouse have been used daily by
these and other students, a large percentage of whom have been in the
armed services.
I append letters from Mrs. Edna H. Morton, our faithful hostess, and
from Miss Barbara Cope, President of the student organization, during
the summer term, to which is attached a list of 42 special events held at
the Clubhouse in addition to the regular Thursday afternoon informal
dances. The dinner and reception to the Grand Master attended by 350
members was a particularly happy occasion. Much enthusiasm for the
organization is reported among its membership.
Necessarily during the war period our maintenance work has been
largely deferred. I do not know what it will cost to appropriately refurnish
and redecorate the property, but soon this must be done. I venture to
say that $8000 or $10,000 will be required for these purposes within the
next three years. This is in addition to the $8700 required for the ordinary
operation and maintenance of the property during the coming fiscal year.
$1250 of that sum has already been contracted covering urgent repairs to
the heating plant and of additions thereto and· for other replacements.
Unless we therefore draw upon our reserves we cannot get by on the
$7500 appropriation which we have received during each of the past four
years.
Nor, can we make plans for the extensive refurnishings above m1ontioned until we are in a position to finance them. We do not indulge in
deficit spending.
The Trustees are submitting their financial problems to the Finance
Committe61twith the recommendation that the annual budget be increased
to a total of $8700 for next year and that provision be made ·for all or for
a substantial part of the $8000 to $10,000 needed for the above mentioned
repairs and replacemerits a's soon as war conditions permit.

477

Judge Milton T. Farmer,
Seventh Floor, Balboa Bldg.,
593 Maret St.,
San Francisco, 5, California.
Dear Judge Farm-er:
We are at the close of a very pleasant and successful year. The Club
membership has maintained a high, co-operative standard considering ~he
small registration at the University. Everyone is expecting and preparing
for a very much larger attendance this coming year, due partially to the
returning service men and women, of which we, already, have quite a
few members.
We are submitting a complete resume of the past year's activities and
attendance. These activities have been very fine and well attended, but
I feel the daily use of the Club for study, lunch time, games, radio, and
just relaxation, where students meet in a fine environment, is most important. The fact that you have made these facilities possible for so many
years is, indeed, something of which to be very proud.
Sincerely and fraternally yours,
EDNA

H. MORTON, Hostess.
September 25th, 1945.

Masonic Grand. Lodge F. & A. M.,
San Francisco, California.
Gentlemen:
On behalf of the members of the Masonic Club of the University of
California I wish to express our deepest appreciation to you, the Grand
L9dge of California, for your support and maintenance of our Clubhouse.
We are truly grateful for our University home where we are able to meet
the sons, daughters and other close relatives of Masons.
Although the war has forced our membership to contract considerably,
we have carried on with reduced numbers but with no diminution in
enthusiasm. We are now awaiting the fall term anxiously, as it will be
our first peace time semester in almost four years. During these past
years the Club has been host to many service men far from home but
close to Masonry, and I want to express their thanks also for your support that makes our Club possible.
Enclosed herewith you will find a list of our events from October
30th, 1944 to October 20th, 1945. I sincerely hope they will give you much
satisfaction for making so many events possible by your maintenance of
our Club.
Thanking you again for all of us,
Sincerely yours,

Respectfully submitted,

BARBARA COPE.
