REPORT O F THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS OF MASONIC
CLUB U. C. L. A.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Board of Directors of Masonic Club U. C. L. A. presents the
following report for the year just closing:
Reference to our report rendered October 10, 1944, relates the facts
that our arrangement with the University of California at Los Angeles·
to use the Clubhouse as
Mess Hall for Army Cadets was terminated
April 30, 1944, and that we had entered into an agreement with the
Los Angeles Chapter of the American Red Cross to occupy the property
beginning June 1, 1944 to September 1, 194S at a monthly rent of $250.00.
This agreement also provided that it could be terminated by either party,
after September 1, 194S, upon sixty days' notice.
· At a meeting of the Board of Directors of Masonic Club U. C. L. A.
held September 6, 194S, a motion to serve notice upon the Red Cross to
vacate the property was unanimously adopted.
The civilian enrollment at the University is greatly increased and it
is expected that there will be several thousand service men on the campus
in the next few months. It is quite evident that we should be properly
prepared and well equipped to serve those with Masonic affiliation.
We call attention to the fact that we have foregone the use of this
property since April 1, 1943-a period of more than two years; and by
reason of the income from it, it has not been necessary for Grand Lodge
to appropriate a sum in excess of $1S,OOO.OO, as would have been required
under past normal operation. ·
'.
Our certified .public accountant will not have concluded his report for
the year ending September 30, 194S in time to be forwarded with this
report, but· all funds have been properly accounted for and all financial
obligations have been met.
In reopening the Clubhouse we are convinced in the light of past
experience and the anticipated use of the property that we will require
one additional person to be known as "Director of Activities" to perform
duties implied by the title.
The following budget unanimously adopted by the Board of Directors
at its meeting of September 6, 194S, and covering a full twelve months
of operation, reflects this additional expense and the budget is correspondingly increased over the last budget we submitted:

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

G. WRIGHT.

Dated: September 15, 1945.
Report of Committee on Masonic History

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee on Masonic History begs leave -to submit the following report, together with its recommendations.
The activities of this committee have been somewhat curtailed during
the past year on account of gasoline rationing, rendering it impossible for
its members to visit Lodges in outlying districts where new and source
material has become available. We have carried on extensive correspondence throughout the State and some satisfactory results have been attained.
We have, during the past year, furnished much data to Lodges to be
used at anniversary meetings and other historic; occasions. Practically all
of this was taken from our records now on file in the Grand Lodge offices;
a small part came from original research during the year.
We have also carried on an active correspondence with many Lodges
in other grand jurisdictions in response to their requests to assist them
in tracing the activities of some of their members in this State during the
fifties and the sixties.
·
·
We were pleased to render this service. While engaged in this work
we have· learned much of the lives of distinguished Masons in California
from other states, many of whom did not affiliate with us or visit any of
our Lodges, hence their presence and lives in this State had not before
come to our attention.
We desire to urge all Lodges to keep records of the war activities of
all members in the armed forces. These records should contain accounts
of all engagements in which they took part and if prisoners of war, a full
account thereof.
We are anxious to obtain the names and locations of all overseas Masonic
clubs whose rosters contain the names of California Masons. If possible,

obtain in written form stories of Masonic experiences of your members
while abroad and other human intere~t items connected with their overseas service.
Your committee is hopeful that it will soon have available a full and
comprehensive history of Brother Homer Lea, the military strategist who
played so important a part in the overthrow . of the Manchu Dynasty
and the establishment of the Republic of China under Sun Yet Sen, its
first President.
Several years ago, your committee reported some phases of his· history
from the American standpoint. Now we desire to supplement this with
his hi.story from the Chinese standpoint. A full account of his Chinese
activities may add much to his colorful career. We hope to have this
completed soon by those fully conversant with the actual facts by some
who were with him in China.
The members of your committee feel a great personal loss in the
passing of Miles McK. Anderson, a member of the committee and a past
Master of San Mateo Lodge No. 226.
Brother Anderson was a well informed and enthusiastic research
student and rendered outstanding assistance to the committee in clearing
up some vexatious questions which had troubled the committee for some
time past. We acknowledge our great indebtedness to him.
In the passing of W. A. Chalfant of Bishop on November 5, 1943,
California lost one of its most beloved newspaper editors and Masonry
lost one of its most faithful membe'rs. For 55 years he sat at the editorial
desk of the Inyo Register and without fear or favor interpreted local and
state wide events as he saw them, By his conscientious and fearless adherance to the truth and his. refusal to be swerved from a course he conceived to b_e right he won the admiration and respect of even rabid enemies.
He served as a member of this committee for many years and prepared for us the History of Masonry in Owen's Valley. He served his
Lodge, Winnedumah No. 287, as Secretary for 41 years. He wrote and
published four historical books which for depth of research and historical
accuracy stand alone in historical literature. These are:
The Story of Inyo
Outposts of Civilization
Death Valley, the Facts
Tales of the Pioneers
Brother Chalfant can be justly characterized as a fearless newspaper
editor, loyal Mason, faithful historian, capital story teller, and an upright
civic leader.
·
We recommend that the committee on Masonic History be continued
for the ensuing Masonic year, and that the sum of $100.00 be appropriated
and set aside for its use.
Respectfully submitted,
L)!':ON 0. WHITSELL,

Guy J. GIFFEN!

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC INFORMATION
September 10, 1945.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
War restrictions and war conditions greatly limited the work of the
Committee on Masonic Information during the past year. Shortage of
paper placed an arbitrary limit upon th,e number of quiz programs that
could be sent out so that instead of the. usual eight or ten programs, we
were limited to three. Then again, even if the usual number had been
prepared the vast amount of degree work made it difficult, if not impossible, for Masters to use these programs in the Lodges. But with the
return to more normal conditions, it is hoped that it will be possible to
prepare and send out the programs· during the coming year.
The publication of the long discussed and promised manual for the
use of coaches and others for the instruction of young Masons and new
members has been unavoidably delayed, but it is hoped that it may be
prepared and submitted to the Grand M.a.s ter during the coming year.
Considerable correspondence was had with Masters of Lodges and
members in all parts of the Grand Jurisdiction answering ,questions and
giving advice regarding Masonic books and other literature.
We are considering the possibility of circulating sets of books among
the Lodges to provide instructive readi~g for interested Brethren. The
plan will be tried out in a simple and inexpensive manner and enlarged
in accordance with our experience and the wishes of the Brethren.
At the last Communication of Grand Lodge an appropriation of $750
was made for the work of this committee of which $382.03 was disbursed
for printing, postage, stenographic work, and incidental expense. In view
of th.e proposed expanded program, we request an appropriation of $750
for the fiscal year 1945-1946.
Respectfully submitted,

The death list is well below the average year, the increase over the
past year being twelve.
The World War has brought men into a closer relationship and this
spirit of cooperation has brought men into the Lo<iges where· they may
perpetuate that ideal which the .world has long needed.
Our hope is that each has found his place where fraternity and happiness goes hand in hand.
Respectfully submitted,

Hospital Section
Our work in the hospitals has been along the same lines as last year.
.Transportation difficulties have again made it impossible to visit all of
the hospitals in the state, but contact with our representatives has been
maintained through correspondence by the chairman of this section.
The sudden termination of the war brought drastic changes in the
plans of these hospitals. Where they had planned to care for a large
number of casualties when, and if, Japan was invaded, the unexpected
surrender of the enemy has changed the entire picture. Estimates have
been ni~de that, had it been necessary to invade Japanese soil, our forces
would have suffered casualties to the extent of 100,000 to 300,000 men,
and had the war lasted twelve months longer that number would probably
have been increased to 500,000. Some hospitals are now showing a daily
decline in the number of patients admitted and it seems only a matter of
a short . timt; until they cease operating entirely.
Offers of assistance to our members in the hospitals have been made
repeatedly but due to the splendid care given the patients, there has been
little need for relief on our part. We are convinced that the hospital
program is covering everything we can consistently do and that there
will be no great relief problem from this source excepting in a few isolated
cases, which will be met as they present themselves.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON TAXATION
To the Most W orshipfill Grand Lodge of California:
The Special Committee on Taxation has continued to function during
the year 1945, without any change in membership. The committee has answered inquiries made to it by the constituent Lodges and by other
agencies of Grand Lodge. Several formal opinions have been rendered
as to tax liability.
The status of Grand Lodge in respect to the State Unemployment Reserves Tax, is still not finally determined. The Federal Commissioner
has made some tentative rulings, and we have discussed the matter at
length with the State Employment Commission, at Sacramento, with the
result that we are in apparent agreement on the principles and rules involved, but we have not yet been able to supply the State Department
with detailed figures of wages paid in the several years preceding 1945.
As soon as a complete report can be furnished to the State Department
showing the payroll since 1940, we expect to secure a formal ruling from
the Federal Commissioner, and then, in turn, secure an adjustment from
th~ State Commission, based on the Federal ruling.
. As the matter now stands, we anticipate that credits to be claimed
will probably about equalize any taxes unpaid.
Respectfully submitted,
R. P. WISECARVER,
WALTER REMY JOHNSON,

Committee.

REPORT OF WAR ACTIVITIES COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee on war activities submits the following report of its
work during the past year.
At the time of our last report the world was afiame with war. Germany
had not yet been invaded and the war with Japan gave every evidence of
lasting for at least two or three years longer. The war has ended but the
work of Masonry must continue as long as any of our brethren who wore
the uniform are in need of assistance.

Lodge Activities Section ·
The chairman of this section has continued to stimulate activities in
the Lodges situated close to military camps. As we have pointed out before, some of the largest camps have been established close to our smaller
Lodges. These Lodges are doing a splendid thing for the Masons in
• uniform by encouraging them to attend Lodge and making them feel
at home. We know that the entertainment of these brethren by the
smaller Lodges has, at times, been a financial burden. We commend
these Lodges for their truly Masonic spirit in not asking assistance from
the War Relief Fund to help defray this added expense, but feel that,
where service men are being entertained at expense to the Lodge, it is
only proper that help should be given the Lod~e from this fund.
The majority of the Lodges have a well rounded war activities program.
We believe that the letter writing carried on by these committees has
been well received by our brethren in the service as evidenced by the
many answers that have come before us.
We have continued to urge members to donate to the Red Cross, the
War Chest, the Blood Bank and other welfart; agencies in the war effort.
During the Seventh War Loan Drive we were asked to canvass the
membership of the Lodges to stimulate the sale of bonds, credit for the
amount to be given to the Mason\c Lodges of California. Your committee
felt that it ,was not possible to conduct such a campaign where the Lodge
would actually sell bonds to the raembers. No other method would give
the correct total of bonds purchased and certainly would not justify establi~hing a quota for California Masonry. To merely accept pledges from
the members would not mean that the bonds were actually purchased
and would probably result in an exaggerated statement of bond sales. A
letter was mailed to the Lodges, calling attention to the drive and asking
that the Lodges and the individual members buy bonds to the very limit
of their ability. From all indications this brought satisfactory results.
Last year this committee established a club room with writing tables,
rest room and showers at Palm Springs. At that time there were 200,000

486

PROCEEDINGS 0F THE

GRAND LODGE OF C~LIFORNIA

men stationed in that vicinity, with no recreational facilities available.
The club room was opened on a six months trial basis and proved so successful that it was continued for. another six months. The majority of the
men have now been transferred and, after serving its purpose the club
room has been closed.
At the start of this year it was brought to the attention of the committee that the Masonic Club at Riverside, instituted by the Lodges of that
city, would be forced to cease operations due to a lack of funds. This
club has been operated in a very caref\tl and efficient manner and is serving a large number of service men, stationed in and near that city. To
continue this worth while work, this committee appropriated the sum of
seventy-five dollars per month.

Another case which was handled by one of the Boards of Relief was
that of a brother who found himself in immediate need of financial assistance. I quote portions of his letter to that board.
"Enclosed please find the first payment on the two hundred dollar
loan that you so kindly extended to me . . . . What the money meant at
the time I saw you I find hard to tell, but I assure you that it. made a
great burden leave my mind . . . . This act taught me the greatest lesson
in Masonic charity I have yet seen. It is something that both my wife and
I will never forget."

Relief and Employment Section
The eight employment offices maintained by the fraternity troughout
the jurisdiction are prepared to care for Masonic Veterans and their. employment problems. To date, however, there. has been little activity in the
employment offices from this source. Apparently most of the discharged
veterans are returning to their old jobs. In certain areas, however, the
calls for special services and courtesies to service men and their families
has made .necessary a twenty-four hour service in the Boards of Relief
and Employment offices. Men and their families traveling, often temporarily out of funds, with no place to stay, or looking for Masonic
favors have placed a terrific burden upon the individual Secretary-Manager.
One of these brethren has, on numerous occasions, housed service men
and their families in his own home when other accommodations were not
available.
Every possible assistance has been extended to Masons in the service
through representatives of our fraternity in this jurisdiction. To. these
men this committee owes a vote of thanks. Their unselfish work has
proved to members of the craft from all jur.i sdictions that California
Masonry practices the lessons learned within the confines of the Lodge
room.
A member of one of ·our Lodges, stationed in the Pacific with the
Navy, made a request, through his Lodge for aid for his wife and
children,. The letter was forwarded to this committee, with the result
that an ill/-mediate investigation was made. His wife had become bed
ridden at the birth of their third child. The baby was born requiring
special medical attention,. Doctor's and specialist's bills .had accumulated
which the allotment funds were inadequate to meet.
Investigation showed that the wife and children were living with her
aged father. The Red Cross was providing daily care for the baby while
the aged father was trying to care for the other two children and the
mother. Medical bills amounted to more than three hundred dollars,
with little prosp~cts of their being paid~
·
The brother got a short leave and brought home his entire pay check.
Part of the outstanding bills were paid with this money, leaving an unpaid balance of $162.00. This amount was paid by the Secretary-Manager
of the Board of Relief and Employment Service, out of money deposited
to his account from the War Relief Fund.
At the present time, the. wife has recovered sufficiently to get around
the house and care for her family, and the baby is now fat and healthy.
No further financial assistance is need at this time.

487

Arrangements have been made by this committee with the Selective
Service Headquarters of the State of California; whereby all Masons in
the armed forces will be requested to report to their own or some other
Masonic Lodge in the jurisdiction, immediately after their discharge
from service. As all California •men will be discharged in their own State,
this will give Masonry a contact with all its returning members.
'
A letter was directed to the Masters of the several Lodges, advising
them of this fact and asking that they immediately appoint a committee
t-o meet with the returning veterans and help them to work out any
problems they may have. Many of these men will need counsel and advice. Others will be looking for new jobs. Doubtless some of them will
be in need of financial assistance. This need, if worthy, should be met
promptly and should the Lodge committee determine that it is occasioned
by the war, the War Relief Fund should be used.
A second letter was shipped to the Lodges in sufficient quantity for the
Secretary to mail one to each member who served in the armed forces
during World War II. This letter was to advise them pf the arrangements made with the Selective Service Headquarters and to urge them
to come to the Lodges with their problems.
Due to the cessation of hostilities, the returning veteran picture iii
California is changing rapidly. In May of this year there were approximately 196,000 World War II veterans in the State, while at the end of
July this number had increased to 247,000 with about 22,000 being discharged monthly. As a result of V-J day mobilization plans, it is expected·
that approximately 45,000 veterans per month wiU be added to the population of California. Many of these men are members of our fraternity.
Too many people look upon the veteran as being in a class by himself,
whereas he wishes to be treated as any other human being. He wants to
know where he can go for information . when he wants it, but he does not
want to be "adjusted." He has proven, by what he has gone through that
he is quite capable of adjusting himself. We must impress him with our
willingness and desire to help him and then wait for him to tell us what
he wants and needs. We feel that the set-up in California is such that
no need will go unheeded and that we are ready to do everything for our
returning member and his family that ~asonry can consistently do.
Respectfully submitted,
LESLIE

As to these very few discovered places where the ritualistic work is
not up to minimum . requirements, I report that the deficiencies are primarily due to the total absence of acceptable applications within rather extended periods of time; that special attention is being given to these

brethren in these districts assures the success of the plan and their appreciation of our special efforts in their behalf is intensely gratifying.
With travel restrictions now removed, wark work at an end, and with
the School of Instruction at Grand Lodge omitted this year, your Ritual
Committee has planned an even more aggressive program of instruction
for the ensuing year. At least four meetings of the Ritual Committee
will be held in accordance with the prewar program. Schools of Instruction fo'r Inspectors in each of the Divisions are planned to the end that
each Inspector will have reasonable access to at least two group Schools
of Instruction. Our present program calls for these schools, where possible, to be of two days' duration to the end that these group meetings
may cover all ritualistic work without undue pressure. lnspectots of the
s.everal Masonic Districts are also being requested to hold more than
the usual number of District Schools of Instruction for Lodge officers,
with notice of such meetings to the Assistant Grand Lecturers so that
they may have many personal opportunities to observe the actual proficiencies and to prevent any local errors from creeping into the work.
By this program we hope to offset any loss that may arise by reason of
the omission: of the 1945 Grand Lodge School of Instruction and to avoid
any sagging of the work due to the general let-down in all things which
is certain to follow the end of the war. Thus, we will come to Grand
Lodge in the year 1946 with our usual high standard of ritualistic proficiency maintained and an even greater number of our brethren perfect
,in their work.

The brethren of this jurisdiction have certainly made my work in
Masonry a real pleasure and their friendships are my reward.
Again, I thank you for the privilege of serving.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Within the moment of the past few weeks, peace and tranquility again
pervade the world. The storm clouds of world encompassing conflict have
been dispersed. Germany, but a short time ago, capitulated and the Third
Reich is now but a few pages in history. Japan, foreseeing her own
doom and destruction, sought a negotiated peace, but suddenly accepted
unconditional surrender as her only defense against the searing blast of
our newly created atomic bomb. Never in history have the days been
so crowded with momentous facts.
But a month ago it was still contemplated that, in keeping with the
times, no communication · of this Grand Lodge would be held in 1945,
yet, here, today, we stand in assembly thanking God fo'r the victory that
is ours and praying that this · peace so established by force, may through
justice and righteousness become everlasting. In the face of these facts
it is diffic~lt to turn our thoughts to the proper subjects of this report.
Through these years of conflict Masonry in many countries has almost
been destroyed. Many of onr own brethren have suffered beyond description, yet California Masonry as an organization, doing a grand job in every
department of Masonic endeavor, has prospered and grown-a greater and
better fraternity.
Those activities falling within the province of the Grand Lecturer have
been hampered, but not critically curbed. Travel limitations have curtailed
the visitations and work of the Inspectors and of the Assistant Grand
Lecturers, yet by their careful and thoughtful planning and with the aid of
the Lodge officers' coaches, the officers of every Lodge of this jurisdiction
have had ample access to accurate sources of ritualistic authority.
During the past year the intermediate changes in lodge officers have
been less than in the previous years. The pressure upon Past Masters to
help out in the workings of the several Lodges has been considerably
relieved. Now that the younger men are returning from the wars and the
others are returning from their civilian war work, we may look forward
with optimism and less worry about the availability of capable and willing
men to fill the Lodge· offices.
During this term the Ritual Committee has held but one, instead
of its usual four meetings. The Assistant Grand Lecturers, though encumbered in their endeavors; still have held a reasonable number of
Schools of Instruction for lns!)ectors in various parts of the State. Two
of these schools have been attended in person by the Grand Lecturer and
two schools in the other Divisions are presently scheduled within the ensuing month. The Grand Lecturer hopes also to be present at these assemblies.
In connection with other duties, your Grand Lecturer has had the
privilege of visiting many parts of the State of California and has found it
convenient to attend, and assist at, many Schools of Instruction held by the
Inspectors, some of these schools being in our extreme outlying districts.
On several of these trips he has been accompanied by the Assistant Grand
Lecturer having charge of the particular Division. · In this manner the
Grand Lecturer has been able to observe at first hand the character and
quality of ritualistic work being done, to meet a great many Lodge officers
to inquire into Lodge operations and otherwise observe the actual work~
ings of Masonry in a great many places in our State. Upon the basis of
these personal observations, I am more than pleased to report to the
Grand Lodge of California that with the exception of one or two very

Respectfully submitted,

COMMITTEE ON NECROLOGY
We are advised through the files of the Grand Secretary's office that
203 members of this Grand Lodge have been cut down by the all devouring scythe of time since we last met in Annual Communication. Their
names, the dates of their respective deaths and the names and numbers of
their Lodges are included in this report as follows:
As we take note of the passing of our brethren, we regret that we
cannot hereon trace their manifold contributions to Masonry and to the
communities in which they lived. In the words of Worshipful Brother
Ellsworth Meyer which follow this report will be found a eulogy for all.
But one short year ago these brethren worked by our side, gave us
the benefit of their counsel and the joy of their companionship. Since
then, the all wise Creator has dropped the sable curtain between us
shutting off from our further view, their friendly faces. Death has placed
the seal of eterni~y upon their brows and the beautiful has been made
permanent.
We write not thus in a spirit of mourning and sorrow, but rather to
scatter a few flowers on the pathway of memory and to renew our faith
in a blessed immortality.
Were they to whom we pay this tribute numbered among those whom
the world calls great? We do not need to know. It is sufficient for us
to know that they were inen of honor who strove to the limit of their
abilities to do well, that with which they were entrusted. They loved
their God, their homes and their country, and we loved them. They were
our brethren and companions .in life's fitful journey. We recognize in
them symbols of that great humanity of which each of us forms equally
a part: It is this idea of the brotherhood of man and the fatherhood of
God which is ·destined by the irresistible sweep of its power to destroy
in time, every vestige of tyranny on earth.
Whether this journey of life be long or short, may the memory of our
departed brethren continue to be an inspiration to us, and as th~ dawn
of peace breaks over the world, let us render thanks to our Great Creator
and say within our hearts:
·
"This is the springtime of opportunity to serve God and home and
country."
Respectfully submitted,
Ross K. ROPER,
GEORGE JEAN,

A PSALM
BY ELLSWORTH MEYER

"Tell me not, in mournful number.s,
Life is but an empty dream."
On this occasion fain we heed the admonition of Longfellow and, with
him, would declare:

Dust thou art, to dust returneth,
Was not spoken of the soul."
Such declaration is not born of wishful thinking, rather it wells up
from such inner depth that we are re;,tssured. We doubt not that our
brethren who have departed from the scenes of their earthly endeavors
have but traveled to some fairer land.
We pause to say: Farewell brethren.
The year last past wili be noted by our posterity because of many
events which occurred during it.
During the year .s everal brethren of the Masonic fraternity who had
enacted preeminent roles in the affairs of state and who were distinguished
by their scientific or other successes answered the final summons. We
cross the intangible lines of grand jurisdictions to pay tribute to them,
to acknowledge our debts of gratitude and to add our humble words to
those which will be spoken elsewhere. Truly 'it has been said:
"Lives of great men all remind us
We can make our lives sublime,
And, departing, leave behind us
Footprints on the sands of time.
Footprints, that perhaps another,
Sailing o'er life's solemn main,
A forlorn and shipwrecked brother,
Seeing, shall take heart again."
The past year will also be noted because it brought the end of two
concurrent wars, wars in which many of our brethren paid the last full
measure of their devotion to country. Grief at the passing of any friend
or brother is natural, but we should feel particularly our bereavement
at the taking of these men in the forenoon of their lives. Mere words
are no adequate eulogy to those who have purchased the preservation
of those ideals which make our country and our fraternity what they are.
Eternal remembrance and eternal vigilance coupled with high resolves,
these only are adequate.
As we recall the names of departed brethren who traveled the high
road of life, as we hear the roll of those who were in the armed forces
or who merely walked along the low road, we are reminded that the
most may be derived from life, not by the pursuit of selfish aims alone,
not by running to the rainbow's end for some fancied pot of gold, but
b;y striving for the higher good, by service to others who pass by this
way. Life is not made up of days and ye'ars only. It is going on foot
and out of our way for another. It is remembering the welfare of others.
It is stretching forth a helping hand. It is whispering good counsel. It
is seeing the worth of every brother.
In life we receive that for which our spirits ask; we find that for
which we truly seek and we enter in where we have knocked. The lives
. of our departed brethren charge us to be the captains of our souls.

EULOGY TO ARTHUR P. CRIM
BY OAKLEY K. MORTON
Established custom at each communication of Grand Lodt:e provides
for a Memorial Observance in charge of the Necrology Comm1!tee. D~r­
ing recent years this service was ably directed by Arthur P. C~1m, Chairman of that committee. Illness prevented performance of this duty by
him at the October 1944 Communication. On Thursday, January 11, 1945,
the Supreme Grand Master of the Universe c~lled him to higher .duties
in that temple not made with hands, eternal in the Heavens. I hke to
think there is a concourse of Brother Masons, invisible to those pq:sent,
who are interested and participating in our communications. This thought
enables us to feel their influence in our annual gatherings.
Arthur P . Crim was born July 28, 1871, at Kittanning Township,
Armstrong County, Pennsylvania. He received his education in the. public
schools of that county and· at Grove City College, Pennsylvania. He
located in Redlands, San Bernardino County, California, on November 5,
1902 and engaged in orange horticulture, in wbich occupation he was very
successful and acquired extensive interests. On September 3, 1902 he ·was
married to Emma· Heffelfinger, who survives him. He is also survived
by their three . sons: Brother Arthur P. Crim, Jr., Brother Clifford J.
Crim, and W. Roscoe Crim. It was his happy privilege to raise his two
sons as Master Masons. He was a kind and thoughtful father in a real
American home. In addition to his home and business responsibilities,
Arthur Crim maintained an active interest in the church life and public
schools of his community. To him they were fundamental for successful
civic development.
In Redlands Lodge No. 300, F. & A. M. on December 8, 1919 Arthur'
P. Crim was raised a Master Mason. He was elected Worshipful Master
of that Lodge for the year 1924 and during his term it became apparent
that he was one to whom added Masonic service could be well assigned.
In his acceptance sp.e ech he said, "As Master of your Lodge, I would not
dare face the problems of this year were it not that 'divine assistance is
vouchsafed us through -the medium of prayer.'" He subsequently joined
Redlands Chapter No. 77, Royal Arch Masons; Valley Council No. 27,
Royal and Select Masters; and in 1921 was knighted in Redlands Commandery No. 45, Knights Templar. He was Commander of this Commandery during the year 1925. He was made a 32nd Degree Mason in
Long Beach Consistory, September 11, 1926. For approximately fifteen
years he was president of the Gateway Scottish Rite Club of San Bernardino and Riverside counties. In October 1943 he was honored by election
as a Knight Commander of the Court of Honor of the 32nd Degree of
the A.ncient and Accepted Scottish Rite. In 1926 he was appointed Inspector of the 105th Masonic District, and in this capacity he rendered
outstanding service to the Lodge& of that district. Teaching the ritual,
advising and counseling with Lodge offl.cers, there was no journey or
conference too long for his time and patience. For · twelve years he served
continuously and was recalled for additional service to bridge over emergencies.
Whether Arthur Crim was teaching the ritual as a Masonic Inspector,
giving an order as a Commander of Knights Templar, presiding over a
meeting of Scottish Rite Masons in an observance ceremony, or as
chairman of the Necrology Committee of Grand Lodge guiding and
directing the Memorial Observance-Brother Arthur P. Crim was always
the same composed, calm, dignified, kind, and considerate individual. It

493

could be truly said of hi.m , "Wherever the kind man goes he brings into
being priceless things-golden sympathies, radiant faces, glowing and
grateful hearts." As a final tribute to our friend and brother1 we conclude by saying: He did not fear the Angel of Death because h e believed
in the immortality of the soul. In all his activities of life whether
domestic, social, business, religious, or fraternal, he was at ait times a
loyal, earnest, and conscientious man. He seemed to understand and
practice the spirit and truth of Masonry;. he was one of our most useful
citizens.
JOHN DOUGLASS MURPHEY, Grand Master 1913-1914
By ROBERT B. GAYLORD, Pa.St Grand Master
!"ast .Grand Master John Douglass Murphey was born in Mono County,
California, on July 7, 1863, and lived an always respected life for more
than eighty-two years.
He was raised to the Sublime Degree of Master Mason in Alta Lodge
No. 333, at Bridgeport on March 15, 1899. He became a member of no
other Masonic body.
·
He served as Master of Alta Lodge and thereafter was elected Grand
Master of Masons of California October 17, 1913, serving the usual term
of one year.
He was appointed a member of the Jurisprudence Committee of Grand
Lodge in 1914 and continued his membership by appointment of successive
Grand Masters for nearly thirty years.
He. was a member for some time of ~he Board of Directors of the
Masonic Club of the University of California at Berkeley and held the
office of President for several years.
He is survived by his widow, a daughter and three sons one of whom
followed his footsteps in the practice of the law.

ALBERT E. BOYNTON, Past Grand Master

Eulogy by CHARLES M. Wou..ENBERG, Past Grand Master
. May I quote from a newspaper published in the Sacramento Valley in
1912.

This is an appraisement by his neighbors of the man whose memory we
in sorrow are honoring today.
Albert Eugene Boynton was born at Oroville, California, October 9,
1875 the son of S. S. Boynton and Kate Boynton. He was ~raduated fr?m
the Union High School of his city in 1894. After graduation from High
School Albert S. Boynton studied ~o become a co1;1~t reporter and at the
age of 18 years passed his examination for such position.
I well recall his telling me one day in Tokio, Japan, a~ we. were on. th_e
way to visit Dr. Shearer, formerly a professor of the University of M1~h1gan . how he had decided ~eading · law in a law office and at the same time
ear~ing his living as a court reporter was not. going to. gi.ve him what. he
wanted, and how he had gone to the University of M1ch1gan, supporting

f

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

495

himself by his shorthand, and becoming, in his last year in college, secre~
tary of the Chief Justice of the State of Michigan.
On graduation he returned . to Oroville to practice his profession and
fought his way up to one of the commanding. practices in Northern California, and we find that fifteen months after his return from Ann Arbor
he was married to Miss Susie C. Davis at Afton in Glenn County.
Law and courtship, however, did not deter him from interest in his
community. He served as Chief of the Fire Department and was elected
to the first Board of Trustees of his city and while a member of the
Board carried on a campaign which resulted in cleaning up long standing
corruption that had been a disgrace to the city of Oroville.
In 1906 he became the Republican candidate for Senator from the 6th
Senatorial District and was elected by a large majority.
•
The sessions of 1907 and 1909 were the last of the old regfme. There
was a handful of men, not half a dozen in both houses, who. consecrated
themselves to fight the machine that had a grip on California. Senator
Boynton was the leader in the Senate. Those were days when it took
courage and backbone to be progressive. Boynton and the few associated
with him did not yield an irich; their position commanded respect and their
courage attention. The press began to give publicity to the fight between
the old arid the new elements in the legislature with the result that in the
election of 1910 the old political machine was wiped out of office and the
new element placed in power. Senator Boynton was nominated the second
time by all parties under the direct primary system. His election was
unanimous. He became the acknowledged leader in the legislature and
for the first time in the history of the state the two offices of President
Pro Tern of the Senate and floor leader of the majority were united in
him. He served in that capacity from 1911 to 1915. Only sixteen years
previously he was, for a session, messenger to one of the Senate committees.
Senator Boynton's name is attached to some of the most important
legislation ever enacted in California. He was author of the constitutional
amendment providing that criminal cases could not be reversed upon
technical errors in procedure unless there was a substantial miscarriage
of justice; the Workmen's Compensation Act; the Teacher's Pension
Bill;· the Net Container. Law providing that all packages must have plainly
printed on their labels the net amount of their contents; the Full Crew
Bill making it mandatory for railroads to employ a sufficient number of
men for the safe operation of trains; and the Non-Partisan Judiciary Act,
by which all judicial offices were taken out of the realm of party politics.
These are but a few of the scores of measures which he introduced during
his two terms in the State Senate. He took a prominent part in committee
and on the floor in securing the passage of the Women's Suffrage Consti~utional ·Amendment, Railroad Commission Bill, Local Option, Direct
Primary Act, the Blue Sky Law, the bill establishing the State Board
of Control, and it was through his efforts that the farm of the University
of California at Davis was financed to make it the powerful factor in the
agricultural and horticultural life in California it is.
·
He served two sessions in the State Senate, refusing to run for reelection in 1915.
It was in 1907 that he became associated with the W . P. Hammon interest. The office of this corporation being in San Francisco, he found it
necessary to establish a residence here and since 1907 his home was.
_here, although he maintained his voting residence in Oroville.

496

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

He never lost his interest in the affairs of his state and nation. We
find that he was for two years Chairman of the Republican State Central
:Committee, a Presidential elector in 1916, and a delegate to the Republican
National Convention in 1920.
He was chairman of the State Commission of Efficiency and Economy
and from 1920 to 1924 Chairman of the State Board of Prison Directors.
This position he resigned in 1924 when he accepted the position of
:Managing Director of the San Francisco Industrial Association, a position
which afforded him an opportunity to bring happier relations between
labor and employer. He held this position until his sudden illness in 1938.
That he was an active member of his home community of Oroville is
.shown by his fraternal activities. He not only was a. member of the
Native Sons, I. 0. 0. F ., Elks, and Masonic Lodge, but served as the
presiding officer of each.
·
He had membership in the Shrine, Eastern Star, Knights Templar, and
Scottish Rite Bodies and was honored by being chosen as Grand Commander of Knights Templar in 1924 and Grand Master of Masons in 1925
.and crowned a 33d Degree Mason in 1933. He was a member of the
.San Francisco, California and American Bar Association, President of
,the Commonwealth Club of California in 1918-1919, and a director of this
great civic organization until his death.
He had membership in the Sutter Club of Sacramento, the Pacific
1Union, Union League, University, Olympic and Rotary Clubs of San
Francisco. All this is of interest, but more important is the memory he
deaves in the hearts of those close to him and those who call him "Friend."
It was my fortune to know him since 1916 and to be intimately asso.ciated with the Boynton family since 1920. Hardly a week passed without
our being together, and in 1934 we made up a party of six and journeyed
to the Orient-Senator and Mrs. 'Boynton, daughter Jeanette, Karl Walbach, Mrs. Wollenberg and myself. These were three months where we
had an opportunity to know and value each other, three months without a
1discordant note, and we returned home cemented by close ties of friendship and understanding.
'
Albert Boynton comes from pioneer stock and in Oroville from 1900
. to 1907 and in the Senate of his State he helped to achieve reforms that
bettered the lot of the common man and made California a. better . place
. in which to live. ·
He leaves behind him a heritage for his wife and children that time
cannot dim, a heritage for their children's children that will be remembered from generation to generation with joy and gratitude for that which
he wrought.
I can 's ee the pleasure with which he watched the youngest of his
nine grandchildren, John, and the kindly care and affection given him by
his oldest grandson, Charles. I know of the sunshine these children
brought to him in this last year.
We need not grieve for Sue; she will have not only the consolation of
a devoted son, Robert, and daughters, Katherine, Elizabeth, and Jeanette,
but in her grandchildren renew her interest in life. The knowledge of
nearly 45 years of close companionship, mutual understanding, and a
smile overcoming all troubles will afford consolation for the years to come.
Yes, Susan, you and the children will miss Albert and his friends here
gathered will with you miss the most courteous, kindly and true friend.
God bless him and his, and keep his memory bright in the hearts of
all who loved him.

REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES OF THE MASONIC HOMES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Trustees of the Masonic Honies of California herewith present the
fifty-third annual report, for the year ending July 1, 1945, together with
the reports of the Superintendents of our Homes, and the financial reports
of the Secretary and Treasurer.
· The Board of Trustees met on October 12, 1944, after the adjournment
of Grand Lodge with the following members present:
Chas. Albert Adams (term expires 1945).
Charles M. Wollenberg (term expires 1946).
James B. Gist (term expires 1947).
Samuel E. Burke (term expires 1948).
Lawrence C. Kelley, Deputy Grand Master.
Arthur W. Brouillet, .Senior Grand Warden.
John R. Moore. Junior Grand Warden.
The election of Lawrence C. Kelley, Deputy Grand Master; Arthur W.
Brouillet, Senior Grand Warden; John R. Moore, Junior Grand Warden,
were formally reported to the Board.
The Board then organized for the ensuing year by electing the follow.:
ing officers:
Charles M. Wollenberg, President.

The passing year has seen the end of the war and we welcomed, like
all Americans, VE and VJ days. While we feel this calls for a report to
Grand Lodge on a peace time program, at the same time we feel it
fitting that we review the year just ended.
Our Home at Covina shows an all time low i~ the number of children
cared for. This is probably due to opportunities for employment, as well
as l).igh wages, enabling mothers to keep their children at home and care
for them without asking aid from the fraternity.
The number of aged residents at Decoto shows a slight increase, and
this again we can attribute to the high cost of living and to housing
difficulties. The rationing program and' the shortage of staple foods caused
some difficulties which were met cheerfully by our family, who realized
:that they must adjust themselves to wartime conditions. This was particularly true last summer when red points for institutions were cut. However, we are looking forward to a time when all commodities will be
plentiful and rationing will be a thing of the past.
The report of our Superintendent at Covina indicates that there were
169 boys and girls in the armed forces of our country. They ranged
in rank from colonels to privates. In this group there are 10 nurses,
WACS or Waves. We regret to report that twelve of our boys have
made the supreme sacrifice and their membership in the Home is now
indicated by a gold star.
Resignation of John M. Downen
For nearly twenty years our Home at Covina has been under the supervision of John M. Downen, who not only rendered outstanding service to
the fraternity by his management of our property, but more important,
was adviser, father and friend to five hundred or more children who entered the Home since 1927. He has seen them through Grammar and
High School and on their own out in the world. When you realize his
work, when you see these young men and women return to the Home
for his counsel and advice, as well as that of Mrs. Downen, who was a
mother to all, we know that he will be sorely missed.
Mr. Downen's resignation was prompted by the fact that during the
past year he suffered from ill health and requested his release when a,
suitable successor could be fotind.
We were fortunate in obtaining the services of Paul Granston Parry,
who seems particularly well qualified for this important post. Mr. Parry
at the time of his employment on September 15, 1945, was a teacher and
counsellor at the Menlo School and Junior College. He is a native of
Arizona and was born in 1903. He was married to Martha Louise Wild
in 1927 and has a daughter, age 11.
Education: Attended public schools of Tempe, Arizona; H. S. diploma,
Tempe Normal, 1924; Teaching Credential, Tempe Normal 1924· A. B.
San Jose State, California, 1931; Major Education; Minors: Engllsh and
Social Studies; A. M. Stanford University, 1932; Major, School Administration; Minors, Public Speaking and Sociology; Thesis, Counseling and
Guidance Survey; Credential, School Administration; Additional Graduate
work, Stanford 1941 and 1942.
Work Experience and Positions: (1922-1924) Farming and ranching
partnership with father, Salt River Valley, Arizona; (1924-1930) Teacher
dormit()ry supervisor and summer camp counselor, Menlo School fo;
Boys, Menlo Park, California; (1931-1932) Teacher, Part time Arts and
Workshop, Las Lomitas Public School, Atherton, California; (1932-194'1)

Finances
The Homes end the year with a very comfortable surplus. It should
be remembered, however, that war conditions have prevented the proper
maintenance of our properties and that expenditures have been made
only for emergencies. This means that the Trustees are confronted with
heavy expenditures for repairs, replacements and new · equipment and
that these must be completed at the earliest possible moment.
To indicate just a few of the necessities, reference 'is made to the
need for the replacement of plumbing, piping, steam and hot water pipes;
replacement of refrigeration units and dish washing machines; and the
need for painting throughout is evident on any inspection of the premises.
, We are confronted too with the necessity of some rebuilding and
some remodelling, due to the changing of fire regulations.
Funds are a;ailable to do all that is required but your Trustees feel
that the program should not be started until both men and material are
available to carry the work t.hrough to completion at a stabilized price.
We look back to the period right after the first world war when we
had to ask for additional funds to carry on the work of the Homes and so
it is with pleasure· that we now report that the surplus in our possession
will make it possible for us to do what needs to be done without asking
for additional appropriations.
•
Recommendation
We recommend that no additional per capita tax for the support of the
Homes be levied at this time.
Report of Superintendent-Decoto Home
September 13, 1945.
Brethren: It is again my duty and my privilege to submit to you,
this my Fifth Annual Report as Superintendent of the Masonic Home at
Decoto, for the period ending July 31, 1945.
All details in connection with the financial operations of the Home will
be found elsewhere in the report. I will, therefore, deal only with matters
concerning the Home which are not otherwise recorded.
Our fo44 report indicated that we had 277 members in the Home at
that time. During the year we have lost by death sixteen women, at an
average of 79.06 years and twenty-four men of an average age of 79.5
years.

GRAND LODGE QF CALIFORNIA

509

During this time eighteen women, of an average age of 75.61 and
twelve men, of an average of 72.1 years, were admitted. One woman and
four men were withdrawn by their Lodges.
The end of the year leaves us with 149 women and 113 men. Included
in this number are twelve married couples.
The average age groups are as follows: .
5 between so and 60 years,
38 between 60 and 70 years,
118 between 70 and 80 years ,
90 between 80 and 90 years,
11 between 90 and 100 years.
The average age for women is 76.86 and for men 77.24.
Approximately 19% of the members are being cared for in our hospital
department.
·
Miss Esther G. Payne, who has been superv1smg the work in the
hospital for the past 25 years, is still with us, directing the work in that
department, and is doing a marvelous job. Dr. W. L. McWhirter is still
directing the medical end, making his regular visits, and responds very
promptly to emergency calls.
'
·
Mrs. Virginia Lord, our Matron, who is in charge of the different departments of the Home, has been exerting every effort during the past
year to provide our family with activities which would add to their
pleasure.
Appropriate cards on their birthdays ;i,nd a birthday dinner once each
month tn honor of those whose birthday came during that month, has
contributed considerable toward that end.
The reconditioning of our movie machine has improved it to such an
extent that pictures which we show every Thursday night are now a
source of great pleasure to our members.
While our family greatly appreciate, and get considerable enjoyment
out of the above mentioned innovations, the $2.50 which the Trustees
present to them on the first of each month has done more to create an
atmosphere of contentment and happiness among the members than any
other policy established during the past year.
I believe it will be possible for us to take care Qf the repairs, alterations and improvements which I mentioned in my last report. I shall in
the near future submit a list which I feel should receive our attention.
All the recommendations made by the State Fire Warden have been
complied with, with the exception of those referred to the architect.
Most of our farm land is still leased to the Zwissig Bros. Dairy on a
cash basis. The returns from that portion used by the Home is as follows :

many of the Lodges have signified their intentions ·of bringing groups to

The East Bay Past Matrons Association never forget the Home, on
August 18th the Association made its annual visit and presented their
usual generous contribution of jams, jellies, etc., a complete list of which
is made in another part of our report. One of the largest groups that
has attended teese visitations in recent years was present at a luncheon
served in our banquet room preceding the reception, which was held in
our Auditorium in honor of the Grand Officers of the 0. E. S. Mrs. Tora
Schneider, President of the East Bay Past Matrons Association introduced Worthy Grand -Matron, Mrs. Lillian W. Podesta of San Francisco,
Worthy Grand Patron, Logan R. Cotton of Redondo Beach, Associate
Grand Matron, Isabella Hilditch of San Diego and Past Grand Matron
Willa Jane Hellwig of Alvarado, each making a very interesting address.
Mrs. Lenore Keesling, Grand Organist, presided at the piano, .and vocal
solos were rendered by Mrs. Helen Clevenger, President of the Matrons
Association, and Mrs. Virgina Meek Lord, our Matron. The program was
enjoyed very much by the visiting members as well as by the residents of
the Home.
Brother Don Berry headed the caravan of East Bay Masters and
Wardens, who made their annual pilgrimage to the Home August 26th.
This fine organization presented an excellent program in our Auditorium,
which was thoroughly enjoyed by our family. On completion of the
program the groups adjourned to the banquet room, where a barbecue
was served. Brother Berry introduced many of the dignitaries and very
interesting addresses were made by Past Grand Master, Brother Charles
Albert Adams, Senior Grand Warden, Brother Arthur W. Brouillet and
Past Grand Master, our very genial Grand Secretary, Brother Lloyd E.
Wilson.
Record of all other programs and visitations will be found elsewhere
in our report. However, I do believe special mention should be made of
the fact that the film distributing companies of San Francisco are still providing the residents of the Home each week with complete programs,
for which we are ever grateful. The companies contributing are R. K . 0.,
Columbia Pictures, United Artists, Warner Bros. and Twentieth Century
Fox.
Devotional services are conducted each Sunday afternoon by the following ministers, Rev. 0. D. Ironmonger, Rev. Thomas Harris, Rev. H.
Herrald, Rev. H. A. Farrah, Rev. A. W. Anderson, Rev. Robert W.
Pertle and Rev. Richard Norberg, all of Hayward, Rev. Edward Groves
and Rev. Evaul of Centerville. These fine reverend gentlemen bring very
interesting messages to our members each Sunday.
. Our members are kept well supplied with reading matter, which will
be found in a very orderly condition in our library. Many of the books,
magazines and periodicals are provided by friends and members of the
Fraternity.
On May· 19th most of our Trustees paid us a visit, those present were
Past Grand Master Charles M. Wollenberg, Past Grand Master Chas.
Albert Adams, Deputy Grand Master Lawrence C. Ke)ley, Senior Grand
Warden Arthur W. Brouillet, Junior Grand Warden John R. Moore and
Grand Secretary Lloyd E. Wilson.
·
Mrs. Lord and myself want to express grateful thanks to the members
of the Board of Trustees for their assistance in helping us solve the many
pro~lems with which we have been confronted during the past. years.

Report of Superintendent-Covina Home
September 13, 1945.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The close of the war period appropriately brings into review in a final
way the part played in the war effort by the Alumni of th e Covina Home.
T he total number of our former wards whom we know to have ser',:ed in
the Armed Forces in the war was 169. Twelve of these died in the course
of their service to their country. The number of commissioned officers
was 35, or 20%, (more than twice the percentage of commissioned officers
in the services generally.) It :would seem that we are justified in the •
conclusion that the degree of initiative and leadership shown by those
who were reared in the Home is an indication that their training proved
its value under stress of war.
We have been gratified by the many visits to the' Home of its former
boys and girls, more especially because of their attitude and their comments about their experiences when they lived here as children. From
their many sincere expressions, we believe that they look back upon their
years in the Home as happy and profitable years. In the attempt to
measure what has been done here for these children, it seems to us that
these expressions must be given weight. A factor worth mentioning also
in this connection is the success of former girls of the Home in the role
of wife and mother. Talking with them when they come to visit the
Home, oftentimes bringing with them their husbands and children, one is
impressed with the fact that they believe that their experience while
living at Covina did advance them in the art of being good homemakers.
Every child who comes into our care comes because of personal misfortune which has deprived him of the security and protection of a good
natural home. It is our business in each case to find out what has happened in the child's life before he came to us. While•an institutional home
cannot give the child personal love like that of a parent, yet oftentimes
it can do better than the parent in understanding and fulfilling the child's
needs.
During the past year the number of children in our care has been the
smallest during the last twenty years. While this has caused us some
concern, it has brought the opportunity to give more individual attention
to the requirements of each child for his best development. Children grow
and progress in proportion as their particular needs are discovered and
supplied.
This is my nineteenth, and last, annual report as Superint endent of the
Covina Home. For Mrs. Downen and me, to have lived and worked with
these children through these years has been a rich experience. In this
time we have seen more than 500 children leave the Home to make their
way in the world. In many cases the tie formed between them and us
while they lived here has proved to be a lasting one.
In leaving this work, because we no longer · have th e strength to
carry it on, we wish to voice our appreciation for the support, encouragement and cooperation which we have had from the Trustees of the Home;
also for the innumerable kind expressions that have come to us from
members of the Craft.
JOHN M. DOWNEN, S uperintendent.

Employment Service .
For the year ended July 31, 1945, the seven Masonic Employment
Service offices placed a total of 9,048 Masonic applicants in employment;
8369 (92%) in permanent jobs, and 679 (8%) in temporary jobs. 71% of
· the total applicants were placed in jobs. These figures reflect an increase
over the previous year of 7% in the number of applicants and 5% in the
number of placements.
Of the total expenditures of the seven offices amounting to . $32,248,
Grand Lodge contributed $14,200 ( 41 % ). The amount of fees saved applicants was in excess of $250,000. The cost per job increased 25% over
the 1944 figure of $4.78 to $5.97 for 1945.
While these figures reflect the statistical highlights, they do not begin
to tell the whole story. War conditions have very materially affected
operations of our Employment Service offices. There has been a relative
scarcity of people to fill the available jobs, with the result that comparatively few have sought the assistance of our Employment Service offices
in this respect. However, due to the location of great numbers of military
and naval personnel on the West Coast and consequent movement of
families following them, our offices have had many calls from Ma3ons
and their families for assistance in securing housing, transportation, visitations to hospitalized relatives, etc., and even financial assistance for those
temporarily out of funds.

"1922, p. 221, Resolution :
"Whereas, The Order of De Molay for boys; . composed of Master
Masons' sons, their chums and other young men between the ages of°
16 and 21, which is organized for the purposes of the inculcation and
practice of clean thinking, clean speaking, and clean living, to the building of clean patriotic young manhood as the best preparation· for the
citizenship which awaits its members and which must be clean and patriotic
if it is to be effective in perpetuating our national institutions; and
"Whereas, The members of the Order of De Molay are co~secrated to
the preservation of the three-fold boon of citizenship.:....Lreligious liberty,
symbolized by the Holy Bible, civil liberty, symbolized by the flag of
our country, and intellectual liberty, symbolized by the school books of
the American boy and girl; and
"Whereas, We believe this work of the Order of De Molay should be
encouraged and supported; and
"Whereas; There are at present in California fifty-three Chapters of
the Order with a membi;:rship of over 7,000; therefore be it
"Resolved, That the ·Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the
jurisdiction of California do hereby approve the ideals, aitns and purposes·
of the Order of De Molay; and be it further
"Resolved, That the members of the Fraternity are requested to lend'
their moral and personal support to any Chapter of the Order of De Molay
now organized in their city or community, or that may hereafter be
organized, as a method of carrying out the ideals embodied in teachings
of the' order."
The Order of De Molay has grown to the point where it is now the
third largest organization in the United States, being exceeded. only by
Masonry and the Boy Scout Organization.
The Grand Council of De Molay, which is the governing body of the
Order is composed of mature men who are representative citizens and
all of them are outstanding Masons.
Its work in California is supervised by several Deputies who have
been active in Masonry and De Molay for many years. Among them
are Jesse M. Whited, Past Grand Master of De Molay, a Past Master of
California Lodge No. 1, and for many years Chairman of the Grand
Lodge Committee on Correspondence; Alexander D. Potts, Past Master
of le Progress de l'Oceanie Lodge No. 371 of Honolulu, Inspector of
the 103rd Masonic District and for several years the Grand Stand'a rd
Bearer of this Grand Lodge; The Very Reverend Francis Eric Bloy,
Dean of St. Paul's Cathedral of Los Angeles; Judge Wm. R. McKay,
Judge of the. Superior Court of Los Angeles; and present Grand Junior.
Deacon of the Grand Council of De Molay; Louis S. Goldstein a member of Lincoln Lodge No. 470 of San Francisco; C. Mantele of Stockton;
M. S. Oldershaw of Bakersfield; and Frank N. Killam Past Master and
Treasurer of Washington Lodge No. 20 of Sacramento .

. REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON DE. MOLA y
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
At the 9Sth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of California
the following resolution was adopted.
·
··
"With the hope that this Grand Lodge may be able to make a valuable
contribution to 'the Youth Movement' through the Order of De Molay,
. "Be It Resolved: That the incoming Grand Master appoint a committee of five members whose duty it shall be:
. "First: To make a t?orough investigation of .the organization, principles, precepts and practices of the Order of De Molay and of its Chapters
in the State of California.
"Second: To clarify and define any relationship which may now exist
between the Order of De Molay and organized Masonry in California.
"Third : If deemed advisable to recommend such action by Grand Lodge
as will result in a more constructive attitude toward the Order of De
M~lay and which will assure for its Chapters the type of advisers of
which they are now admittedly in need."
Pursuant to that resolution the Most Worshipful Grand Master appointed a committee of seven members. ·
The report of that committee is presented herewith and cover~ all
phases of the question and represents the views of the edtire personnel.
Due to present conditions it was impossible for the committee to meet
and all work was carried on by correspondence. The several members of
the com~ittee, ~owever, h~ve made personal investigation in the territory
surrounding their community, and have had access to various sources of
information.
In addition a circular letter was sent to the Grand Lodges of the
United States soliciting their views, and requesting information concerning any legislation which they may have adopted.
The response was most gratifying a.nd all of their correspondence is
attached to this report and is made a part hereof.
·
The Grand Council of the Order of De Molay was also requested to
furnish certain information which is also attached herewith.
. We have also reviewed the proceedings of Grand Lodge from 1920 to
the present date, particularly references . to De Molay made by various
Grand Masters in their annual messages.
After careful analysis we feel that the sentiments and views expressed
in the resolution adopted by this Grand Lodge at its 1922 Communication
fully d~fines the purposes and aims' of De Molay, and today more than
ever brings home to us the need for a worthy· institution of this type.

545.

Relationship to Masonry
The Order of De Molay was conceived by Masons who saw a need
for a youth organization among the young men of America. Its ritual,
particularly the Initiatory Degree, was written by an inspired Mason
who put into writing some of the noblest sentiments ever expressed by
man.

547

PROCEEDINGS OF '!'HE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Shortly after its organization leading Masons who were interested
in young people brought De Molay to California and it was here that it
had a phenomenal growth. The need for such an institution was proven
by its rapid increase in membership. In the early days of organization
some overzealous Masons referred to them as Junior Masons, but this
was quickly suppressed by the De Molay leaders. In fact the De Molay
organization has never claimed any Masonic affiliation and in its ritual
makes several references to the fact that it is not such a body. .
However the aims and purposes of De Molay are Completely in line
with the philosophy of Masonry. It was conceived and nurtured by
Masons and in every jurisdiction its work has been so universally acclaimed that it has attracted more and more interested Masons to its
support.
In California our 1922 Resolution urged the membership of the Fraternity to give its moral and personal .support to De Molay.
At least five of our Past Grand Masters in their annual messages have
seen fit to comment favorably upon the work of De Molay, particularly
the "late M. W. Albert E. Boynton, who said:
"In 1922 this Grand Logge placed itself on record regarding the Or.der of De Molay, and again reaffirmed its po.s ition in 1924. In its inception, the organization was an experiment, but the numerical growth of
this wonderful movement and the results of its efforts among the young
men of our land has justified its existence and warranted the confidence
that we reposed in those who were inspired to found the Order and have
governed it to the present time.
"While it is not a Masonic organization, its importance in the future
of the Craft is one that we cannot overlook. I bespeak for the Order of
De Molay a continued interest by the Masons of this jurisdiction along
the lines embodied in the r.esolutions above referred to. Our future membership must come from the young man of today. If he is throughly conversant with the principles and teachings of the Masonic Fraternity, e.ven
though taught to him in an organization that is not Masonic but labors
under its 'shadow, just so far will our future strength and efficiency be
multiplied.
"There is a time in the life of every boy when some man or older boy
is taken as an ideal. · That exemplar may be a good one or an evil one,
but in the initial instance that is not considered. Only after years cano
determine whether his mind has turned in the proper direction. I believe
that every man and Mason should continually carry this idea and ask
himself the question : 'Am I the kind of man I would like to see my
own son or the young man of today become?' Individually and collectively,
Masonry owes a duty to the coming generation. An interest in an organization that has for its object the building of character and good citizenship is one that will produce splendid dividends."
We feel that Brother Boynton's words completely outline the relationship which exists between Masonry and De Molay. Further De
Molay is an institution conceived by Masons, directed J?y Masons, and
morally and spiritually supported by Masons. In turn, by this support
the members of De Molay and the world at large have come to look
upon the Order of De Molay as an institution allied with, if not affiliated
with Masonry.
'
For these reasons we feel that a definite relationship exists between
Masonry and De Molay and we cannot escape that fact.

Conclusion
World events of the past few years have definitely proven the need
for such an · organization as De Mo lay. The upheaval of war, the shifting
of population and the change in habits of the An;ierican family have
caused a serious condition in our National social structure. All over our
country authorities are making a serious effort to combat this situation.
All agree that a breakdown in the outlook of our young people will seriously undermine the future of our country. Further we have all seen.
the result of the regimentation of the youth of Europe by the Nazi Youth
Movement in Germany, by the Fascists in Italy and in Asia by the fanatic
Japanese militarists. Each group captured the fancy of their youth and
developed them to follow blindly the teachings which have brought the
world to misery and bloodshed and have created a group of ·young
people who know nothing but hate, racial and religious persecution.' It
is our duty as Americans to see that these conditions shall not plague
our country.
The need today is for an institution that will inculcate in the mind
of the American boy, love of country, respect for family, consideration
. for others, toleration of all religious creeds and above all a sound theory
of the American way of life .
Our Masonic ritual is full of references to our duty, as citizens, to
preserve and defend our country. We hold arfnual celebrations honoring
the Constitution of the United States. California Masonry has taken
the lead in support of the Public School System. We have even gone so
far as to establish and maintain Club Houses at our State University for
students of Masonic affiliations. Yet all of these efforts would be in vain
if our young people who take part in these activities were to fall under
the spell of subversive fofluences.
We have · a real obligation to our youth, particularly our boys of teen
age, who will be the citizens and leaders of tomorrow. Masonry cannot
afford to stay in the background and watch the world go by. We have a
real opportunity to serve our young men and our country by supporting
an institution such as De Molay. For that reason we feel that the program
which we are to offer should deserve and receive the unanimous support
of this Grand Lodge.
The correspondence with the Grand Lodges of the United States has
disclosed much interesting information.
·
The Grand Lodge of Miehigan has taken over the complete operation
and sponsorship of De Molay in that state. Other states permit Lodges
to directly sponsir Chapters, others allow De Molay Chapters to meet
in Masonic Temples but prohibit sponsorship. A negligible number prohibit any support of De Molay. By and large most Grand Jurisdictions
have approved De Molay and have commended it to its members to
foster and support.
• In analyzing these methods we have determined that De Molay in
California is more in need of advisors and direction rather than sponsorship. The Grand Council of De Molay has the means to charter Chapters
without direct sponsorship. The real need in California is for able and
willing advisors. Men who are capable of working and counseling with
young people.
·
If sponsorship was permitted we are afraid that enthusiastic Lodges
would sponsor Chapters and then after the novelty wore off would allow
them to drift. We feel that the De Molay leaders can handle matters
better if sponsorship were kep~ under their control. Further, sponsorship

would entail financial support and there is no reason why the Order of
De Molay cannot stand on its own feet. We do not feel that Masonry
should in any way become obligated to the financial support of any institution that is Non-Masonic in character.
We do however have a plan that we feel would solve the matter in
California. It is a plan of education and coordination rather than one
of sponsorship. Our plan would create a group of men who would act
as coordinators between De Molay 'and Masonry in our state. From time
to time they would be authorized to bring to our Lodges the message
and needs of De Molay, to enlist the aid of men who would be willing
to assist in the work and to keep a watchful eye on the activities of De
Molay. Finally they would report annually to Grand Lodge the progress
of that Order in California. Accordingly we recommend the following

Plan
The Grand Master shall appoint a committee of eight members who
shall constitute the Committee on De Molay.
It shall be their duty to, First: Coordinate the activities of De Molay
with the Constituent Lodges of this Grand Jurisdiction.
Second: That the Chairman shall assign to each member a specific
area for which he shall be .responsible subject to review by said chairman.
Third: From time to time, with the approval of the Grand Master,
present to the Lodges of the Jurisdiction information relating to the
progress, aims, purposes and needs of De Molay.
Fourth: To assist the Deputies of the Order of De Molay in securing
the services .of Masons to assist in the promotion of De Molay.
Fifth: To report annually to this Grand Lodge a resume of its activity
for the year.
We further recommend the appropriation of the sum of $500.00 to
cover preparation and mailing of information referred to in Section 3 of
the Committee duties.
It is the earnest hope of this Committee that this plan be adopted.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TWENTY-SIXTH ANNUAL
OBSERVANCE OF PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK

To the M. W. Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
One of the most interesting things in connection with the Twenty-sixth
Annual Observance of Public Schools Week was the large number of
reports from our lodges in which the Masters expressed wonderment and
surprise, as well as pride and pleasure, in its success in their communities.
It would appear that the announcement of the date of the opening of

How groundless were. these fears is evidenced by the fact that perhaps
never before were there so many of those "biggest and best-ever" reports
;eceived from our lodges. And strangely enough, much of the success;
1t would appear, was due to that interest in the Conference which it was
feared would spell failure to our observance.
There were many reports disclosing that the United Nations Conference had been very cleverly "tied in" with' the local observance. For
instance, in ·o ne city in which the observance extended over the entire
week, with day and evening events, it was ushered in with an outdoor
pageant on Sunday afternoon. This was presented by the pupils of one
of the Junior High Schools in a beautiful grove of trees, and was dedicated
to the forty-four nations participating in the United Nations Conference.
The motif was "Building World Security and Lasting Peace" and was
closed with a massed display of the flags of those forty-four nations.
It furnished fine publicity for the programs to be presented in the schools
the following week. In an editorial on Public Schools Week in a newspaper published in the city where the Conference was held it was mentioned as having been "prepared as one of the significant 'public events
preparatory to the opening of the United Nations Conference.'~ It was
not only good publicity, but in its development it showed the work of
the public schools in war as well as in peace. Incidentally the editorial
referred to ~as h~ade? ".Take A I,ook At Your Own Sch~ols" and was
concluded with this significant sentence: (after saying the people would
find the school systems worthy of their attention and interest) "And if
the~. find something about it they don't like, they will be in a better
position to know what ,they are talking about when they criticize it ."
This pageant was only one of many of a mo1·e or less similar nature
reported. Some of them were designed to display the costumes music
and dances of the nationals of the countries represented at the Co~ference
in San Francisco. Others were more ambiti.ous and took the form of
re-enactments of various historic events with students playing the parts
of famous participants-but all leading up to the United Nations Conference. Among the events re-enacted was the Yalta Conference.
