It was not, however, only through pageants and tableaux that the
interest in the United Nations Conference was made to serve the purpose
of our observance. There were innumerable programs obviously built
around the Conference. This was especially noticeable in the nature of
the subjects discussed by the student forums. Among these may be
mentioned "Problems In Building The Peace'', "Do We Need World
Organization For Peace", "Will The Bretton Woods Agreements Promote
Economic Security", and "What Is The Role of The School In Realizing
Peace." Many of these forums were publicized as being "dedicated to
the United Nations Conference"; and as was said in one of the reports
"contributed in a large degree to a better understanding of the aims and
aspirations toward which the delegates to the Conference are striving."
In thus capitalizing on the interest in the United Nations Conference
there was presented another illustration of what has been repeatedly
demonstrated in the past-that, generally speaking, the success of any
particular observance is proportionate to the intelligence, as well as to
the zeal and industry, with which the arrangements are made and carried
out. It is very largely a question of "The Man Behind The Gun." In
a comment c;m the observance in his community, one of the foremost
school men m the State, who frcm the very first has been intimately
associated with the observance of Public Schools Week, wrote: "We did
have a very fine experience in - - this year. We had many more present
at our meetings than we have had for a long while. The attendance in
the various schools varied directly with the activity of the principals and
~each~rs. It goes back to the old story that everything which happens
m this world happens around some personality. Oh, I suppose thunder
sto~ms and tidal waves a~e excep_
t ions, but the exceptions are very few."
Incidentally, there was this year in that city an increase in attendance of
5239 over last year's total of 13,584.

. That our latest observance was an undoubted success there can be no

in the' way we have done) is not so clear. ·In "A Review In Retrospect"

following paragraph:

Perhaps no better illustration could be found of what has just been
said than is furnished by two reports to which we purpose referring.
As is well known, it is not our practice in these reports to specifically
identify any particular observance. But in this instance the circumstances
seem to warrant a departure from our custom- to some extent at -least
and without mentioning nanies.
'
There are two small neighboring lodges which in years past have
combined in a joint observance. But no report had been received from
either of them since 1941. When the notices for the observance went out
this year, a letter was written each of these lodges calling attention to
the situation. We explained that with the knowledge we had of the difficulties under which they labored, we were disposed to make every allow•
ance; but attention was called to the fact that a report was expected from
every lodge even though no observance was held; and that if no observance was held, the reason should be given. We also expressed the hope
that they would make a special effort this year, and that either jointly,
or preferably separately, they would hold some sort of an observance · if
it were nothing more than a visit to the school in its district.
One of the lodges (the larger of the two, by the way) reported that
no observance was held; and the reason given was " lack of interest and
cooperation by school authorities."
The other lodge, a very little lodge, one of the smallest in the state
came through beautifully. It reported an observance of which ever;
Mason in that little lodge has a right to feel proud. Arrangements had
been made for the presentation of a playlet by the pupils of the little school
where there are only five pupils enrolled. And then before the date set

551

"This year, Public Schools Week seemed more successful than
ever before. We debated and studied as to whether this success
was because of the fact that limitations on transportation and the
general wartime restrictions turned the interest of the people to
the activities and relationship near home, or whether true extensions of interest and concern about school, about public education,
and the responsibility of the adult and parent actuated our
visitors. We have concluded that the latter was the reason for
this year's success. By success we mean greater attendance of
visitors; parents and citizens; keener cooperation from lodges,
churches, service organizations and parent-teacher associations;
and more radio time, publicity and announcements."
Incidentally, one of the things done this year in that community never
before done (and which undoubtedly materially contributed to the success)
was "the designation, by each school of a committee of men and women
from the district of the school whose duty it was to study, discuss, advise,
organize, promote and activate the program for the particular school
concerned. Many advantages, much service and localized effort resulted.
No school was overlooked and no school was duplicating pla11s."
While success in every community could not be accounted for in the
same way, there could be no explanation of the success of any observance,
anywhere, which did not take into account the publicity given the observance by newspapers and broadcasting stations, and the support received
from those organizations which each year' so willingly a nd wholeheartedly
cooperate with us.
Having in mind the space that was devoted to the United Nations
Conference and to war news, and also the restrictions on the use of newsprint and demands of advertisers in excess of obtainable allotments, the
new.s papers were exceptionally generous in the amount of publicity given
our observance. As a matter of fact, in more than one report mention
is made of the local observance having received more newspaper publicity
than ever before. In most instances this was largely the result of iudividual effort by the local committee on publicity.
A very interesting and effective form of the publicity we received were
the editorials and special articles, including the contributions of well known
columnists... Among these contributions was one .written by a newspaper

man with a nation wide reputation. It was an admirable analysis 'of the
modern school, and the opportunities it offers as contrasted with that of
a bygone day. We wish we might reproduce it here, in its entirety. That
of course is not practicable, but we cannot forebear making extended
excerpts.
This columnist begins by saying : "Public Schools Week makes me
realize w.hy my children are so much smarter than I am"; and then goes
on to explain the difference between the kind of education his children •
are receiving and the kind he received. He says: "There is no comparison
between the opportunity offered by modern mass production knowledge .
factories and those of the little red schoolhouse, yet many of us think the
latter served better in some ways." And what we now quote is something
on which · every parent, and every critic of our schools, may well ponder:
"However I think many of us credit the I. r. schoolhouse with virtues ·
really inspired by our homes. My first schooling was in a little red
schoolhouse with a chicsalient feature on each side and I don't credit it
with teachmg me much besides spelling. We had a spelling bee every
Friday afternoon and I was champ-because at home I was surrounded
by books and my father kept me supplied with library books he thought
I should read. He picked out books which would interest a boy and
also teach him something; and to this day I believe if more parents did
that we would have a far more intelligent average than we have, de.spite
all the schools offer.. Of course my dad didn't have to compete with
radio, and movies, and jalopies. Still we shouldn't blame the schools if we
don't do anything to cooperate with them at home. We're a great people to
think that if we pay for the best, we can wash oiir hands of all fi1rther responsibility." (Emphasis supplied.)

In connection with the publicity given the observance by the news•
papers, reference may be made to a type of advertising used in some
communities; because it is indicative of a community spirit which materially contributed to their success.
With the ·clippings attached to more than one report, 't here were the
advertisements of merchants of the community with the insertion ·of. one
or two lines referring to the observance of Public Schools Week; and
from two communities came "spreads" of a full page which had been paid
for by public spirited citizens-One of these to which our attention was
particularly called was a full page advertisement which was run as of
Saturday, April 21, 1945, as an announcement of Public Schools Week
setting out the various types of programs, window displays, etc. and which
was obtained through the cooperation of the merchants association of
that community. Incidentally, the arrangements for the observance there
were so complete, and made with such detail, that it is not strange that
they resulted in an unprecedented success.
An especially effective newspaper advertisement included with the clippings attached to one report was the reproduction of a map with the
location of all schools plainly shown.
The broaricasting stations were no less generous than· were the newspapers. And this applies to the big networks as well as to the so-called
"local stations." Arrangements for radio time for the presentation of
their programs are made by the local committees; but each year, when
our first notice goes out, our Committee writes an individual letter to the
manager of every listed station in the State informing him of the date
of the observance and saying that we would be appreciative of, and grateful for, his cooperation, and suggesting "spot announcements" at times
the station would find convenient. From three of the statidtls this year

came acknowledgment of the receipt of our letters and asking for further
information with respect to Public Schools Week. And, by the way, one

broadcast every day during the week a program presented by school
children. Many informative talks on our schools were broadcast, and round

In addition to the newspaper and radio publicity, attention was called
to · the school programs by school exhibits displayed in store windows
and "downtown" buildings. From the frequent mention made of them
in the reports, it would seem that this year there was an unusually large
number of what have been called "live exhibits." In some communities
they are described as "action exhibits." They show students in store
windows and other- public places engaged in the work carried on in the
schools. There are actual demonstrations of many of the cultural, vocational and home-rriaking activities of the schools, including clay modeling,
block printing, book binding, art, copper and leather work and home
economics.
Among other exhibits reported this year was an art exhibit which
occupied the street side of the entire main floor of .a large building, and
where high school girls could be seen actually engaged in making linoleum
blocks, using a potter's wheel, sketching, lettering, weaving and poster
painting.
Another exhibit showed girls working at sewing machines with placards
giving information of other classes iri hometraining. And there were
numerous exhibits of boys engaged in tasks showing what the schools are
doing in teaching wood, metal and electrical work.
All this was rendered possible of course through the donation of win~
dow or store space by merchants who were thus cooperating in the
observance of Public Schools Week.
The reference to poster painting suggests the mention here of several
contests in the preparation of posters to be used in publicizing the pro·grams to be given during the week, and for which prizes were given. A
set of the prize winning posters accompanying the report from one of the
lodges was a revelation of the ability displayed by youngsters in the
elementary grades.
As has been many times reported to Grand Lodge, the factor perhaps
most largely responsible for the growth and development of Public Schools
Week is the support received from forward looking school people.
·Each year the State Department of Public Education, the Association
of California Public School Superintendents and the California Teachers
Association call the attention of superintendents, principals and teachers
t~ the observance, and reminds them of the opportunity afforded through
this lay · movement to bring the work of the schools forcefully to the
attention of the people.
In a statement issued this year by the State Department, the Superintendent of Public Instruction called attention to a new project in California public schools entitled "A Study In World Friendship..:..designing a
symbol for. the United Nations"; and this was adopted as the theme for
several local observances.
Among other suggestions made in the statement ·issued by the State
Department was "to bring the activities of the schools to the people by·
arranging for downtown exhibits and by sending the pupils to all appro-

priate meetings and gatherings of adults to describe the work of the

This was just what was done. in many communities; and it was ma:de
possible through the fine cooperation we always receive from the service
clubs and from other organizations on which we have come to confidently
rely-including, of course, the American Legion and the Parent-Teacher

The service clubs were again very cooperative this year; and the cooperation was shown in various ways. The reports show that in many
communities at the regular noonday luncheon the program presented was
a "Public Schools Week program." In some instances there was a single
speaker on a topic connected with public education, with instrumental and
vocal numbers presented by school children. In others there were student
speakers participating in a round table discussion.
A variation of this form was the transferring of the luncheon from the
regular meeting place to the cafeteria of a public school, with a visit to
the various classrooms afterwards. On one such occasion reported, every
member of the service club was accompanied on his tour of inspection by
a student host, or hostess, especially assigned to him.
From one of the reports it appears that every service club in the community held a luncheon or dinner meeting in the cafeteria of a public high
school. And from another, that instead of separate visits by individual
organizations, all the service clubs in the community combined to hold
what was called a Joint Service Club luncheon in the cafeteria. of a public
school. It was such a success that it was decided to make it an annual
affair as one of the events of the observance of Public Schools Week.
Student baked hot biscuits served with honey by the cooking class
was an attraction featured at an "open house" in another community;
and the special exhibit features reported from other places included
"fashion shows," with gowns made by the girls, war work of various kinds
including demonstration in the chemistry and biology classes, and of course
shop work of all sorts. More often than not, what visitors to the schools
saw was the regular work of the cla·ss, with the students at their usual
tasks, and not "dressed up for company."
Whatever may have been the reason for the success we had instead
of the failure some feared, two Masters in their reports expressed opinions
we think extr.emely significant, and which we quote without comment:
One said: "There is always a good observance in
because
our lodge has always taken an active part in the promotion of Public

Here is what the other said: "
has not in the past had as good
a turn-out for this observance as they should. I do not believe that our
Masters have been devoting enough time and effort to this event. I
realize now that there were several things that I shquld have done early
enough to get the assistance of civic organizations. I notified all the
service clubs and the American Legion of the event and asked them to
assist; but as far as I know only the Kiwanis Club devoted their meeting

I will be able to give the Master many suggestions which I am sure will

to turn in a better and more complete report than I have."
. Another Master suggested that the lodges should be given early notice
so that the service clubs would have notice befpre their programs are
made up in February. It would seem that he had forgotten that our first

notice goes out early in January; and that it would be impracticable to
address the Masters earlier because they are not elected until December
and freque1Hly not installed until the following month.
The fact of the matter is that although we ask that the Masters get
in touch with the. school people· immediately after the receipt of our first
notice, this is not often done. Attached to the report of a very successful
observance were 'printed forms which had been sent by the local committee of arrangements to the principals and teachers to be ·by them
returned with their comments. One teacher wrote: "It would help a
great deal to have plans made at least a month ahead so we could know
how to plan." Now although the arrangements for this observance had
been otherwise made with great care and intelligence, the letters asking
cooperation (and copies of which were attached to the report) were dated
April 9th. ·
Although it would appear that most of the Masters do not begin their
preparations for the observance early enough, there are some lodges which
do not even wait for our first notice. From a few of these come requests
soon after the close of the Communication of Grand Lodge asking for the
date oi the ensuing observance.
·
A word here with respect to the time of our observance. Experience
showed that the fourth week in April is the time best suited for all the
school districts in the State. At an earlier date the weather is inclement
in some communities, and a later date brings tht observance too close to
the summer vacation. It became, therefore, tacitly understood that the
Observance of Public Schools Week would commence on the fourth
Monday in April ·of each year--unless the Easter vacation would make
that time inadvisable. When the Easter vacation would interfere, the
date is advanced two weeks. That will be the situation next year; and the
Twenty-Seventh Annual Observance will therefore begin on Monday,
April s, 1946.
Of course there were some lodges which did not report a successful
observance-some, in fact, from which no report of any sort was received,
although special letters had been written the Masters. But that has always been the case, and, unfortunately, probably always will .be.
Our Committee is not disposed to criticize any Master. That is not
within our province. We realize, too, that it would be too much to expect
that the Master of every one of our lodges would devote to this movement
the time and effort others so willingly give to make each one of our
annual observances better than those which have preceded it. We realize,
too, that among the Masters of all our lodges, there will likely be some
who do not sense the importance of our annual observance to both the
,public schools and to the Fraternity, and who will not be as zealous as
they should be in the discharge of their duties. Fortunately they' are few
in number, because as has been repeatedly pointed out in these reports,
it is the Masters of our lodges who are entitled to the Fraternity's share
of the credit for the success of our annual observance.
·
Some of the lodges must be excused for not sponsoring a successful
observance. No effort the Master could make would be of any avail. But
no Master can be excused for not making a report; and if no observance
was held, giving the reason. That is the express direction of the Grand
Master each year; and this year it was especially called to the attention
of the lodges from which no report had been received for three years
preceding.
It is from these reports that the details of the local observances are
obtained; and it is through them that contact with the lodges is i:naintained by our Committee representing Grand Lodge. From repo~ts of

successful observances come suggestions which are relayed to other lodges.
But paradoxical as it may seem, those elaborate reports of successful
observances we are always so pleased to receive are really .not so necessary as are the reports of observances which have not contributed to the
general success. The reason has been repeatedly explained but does not
seem to be even yet everywhere understood; and it is perhaps because the
first report of this Committee a Master ever sees is the one he receives.
at Grand Lodge when the information comes too late.
An entire report could be profitably made dealing only with this question of reports from tli.e lodges. Here we can only again repeat what
has been so often said in the reports of this Committee with respect to
·one phase of its work.
.
If a lodge reports an unsuccessful observance, that r-eport is carefully
analyzed; and if we find as we usually do, that the procedure recommended
as a result of experience has not been followed, we immediately write the
Master of the lodge while the matter is still fresh in his mind-not, as we
are careful to explain in criticism of anything done, or left undone, but
solely with the desire of being helpful and with the hope that any mistake
which possibly may have been made will be thereafter avoided. We always ask that our letter be handed to the one who will be in charge ot
the observance the following year. We feel warranted in saying that the
results justify a continuance of this procedure.
We wish it were prahicable to make appropriate acknowledgment of
our appreciation of the many complete and comprehensive reports received from lodges, and from committees representing joint observances,
including those from Master and Warden Associations which feature reports of this sort. Incidentally, even though a joint report is made the
questionnaire sent to the lodge should be returned to be filed with the
other reports from that lodge. Of course it will be sufficient to merely
refer to the joint report; but the comment of the Master would be
appreciated.
Each year there seem to be more Masters who are not content with
merely filling in answers in the blanks on the questionnaires sent them,
but who supplement these forms with letters giving detailed information
of the arrangements for the observance as well as of the programs
presented. With these reports are the newspaper clippings neatly pasted
on paper of the same size, making them readily accessible.
·
There was received this year one of these reports in an unusual form.
In the space on each page not covered by the clipping, the Master had
written a detailed description of the event covered by the newspaper report, with his reaction as to its value as a feature of the observance. That
the report was of a successful observance goes without saying; because
the care and intelligence with which the report was made is indicative of
that same care and intelligence with which the arrangements for the
observance were made.

might well envy.
Walter Bachrodt was not only the greatly respected and well beloved

has decided to serve notice upon the present tenants, the American Red

will mean the cessation of income, and with the resumption of the activities for which the Club was formed, the Board of Trustees requests a
renewal of an annual appropriation from Grand Lodge. ·
The Board of Trustees of the Clubhouse at B.erkeley reports that . it is
intending to make considerable repairs to the building, which have been
'long delayed and also to restore and replace certain furnishings, and
suggests that Grand Lodge appropriate a sum sufficient to cover the
cost of these anticipated repairs in addition to the regular annual appropriation.
Your Committee on Finance, therefore, offers the following resolution
and recommends its adoption:
Resolved, That Grand Lodge appropriate the sum of $7,277.54 for the
use of the Masonic Clubhouse at Los Angeles, and $7,500.00 for the
Masonic Clubhouse at Berkeley for the regular operating expenses and
to build up the reserve funds for depreciation.
Be It Further Resolved, That Grand Lodge· make available to the
Trustees of the Clubhouse at Berkeley a fund of $5,000.00 to be used for
needed repairs to the building and for the replacement of furnishings
and equipment, and a further sum of $1,000.00 to pay the cost of a new
furnace, now being installed.

Report of Committee on Social Security and Unemployment Tax
This committee has rendered a 'report indicating that progress has
been made this past year on the problems confronting Grand Lodge on
Social Security and Unemployment Tax with the Federal and State Governments.
While definite progress has been made and yet the final determination
of the taxes that may be assessed against Grand Lodge has not been
agreed upon. This has been due to circumstances beyond the control of the
committee.
\
As the Chairman of the committee has indicated to your Committee
on Finance that it is probable his committee may find it necessary to
incur some expenses for legal fees and for traveling, for this purpose it
is desirous that there be set up for his use the sum Of $1,500.00. The
Chairman also indicates that he considers the liability for taxes that may
be assessed will not exceed $5,000.00.
Your Committee ·on Finance is therefore budgeting for expenses, of
the committee $1,500.00 and for possible tax liability $5,000.00 and recommends that these sums be appropriated.

General Offices of Grand Lodge
The Grand Master has again called attention to the need of remodeling and rehabilitating the present quarters being made use of in conducting the business of the Grand Lodge. of California.
A similar recommendation was made by Grand Master Smith in 1942
and by Grand Master Morrison in 1944. ·
·
It is obvious that the present quarters are not properly arranged and
that the furnishings and equipment are inadequate and not of any general
design, all of wpich is not comporting with the dignity and appearance
of what the general offices of Grand Lodge should be. A modernly
equipped office will result in additional efficiency in handling the affairs
of Grand Lodge.
It should be realized that Grand Lodge is a permanent institution
an:d is having and will continue to have a material growth, that California
is coming more and more to have world significance and therefore, that
Grand Lodge should have not only adequate facilities, but a place in
which to transact its business in which every member of the jurisdiction
can have a genuine pride.
This means a general remodeling and rehabilitating of the general
offices so that they will be up-to-date and completely furnished offices.
This will require not only new furnishings and equipment, but also rearranging of the rooms.
This committee is in thorough accord with the suggestions that a
modern up-to-date office should now be provided. It is probable that the
time has not yet arrived when this work should be done. The committee
holds, however; that the money should be made available so that should
conditions warrant between now and the meeting of Grand Lodge a year

At the invitation of the Grand Master Brother Stafford
addressed Grand Lodge, and although due to failing strength
his address was all too brief, it was a fascinating story of his
experiences as a prisoner of the Japanese in the Philippine
Islands during World War Two.
Brother Stafford is affectionately known as "the Father of
Freemasonry" in the Philippine Islands and the brethren were
delighted to have this intimate touch with so distinguished a
Mason.

The newly-installed Grand Master then invested his predecessor with a Past Grand Master's lapel button, in which was
set a beautiful diamond.
The Chas. Albert Adams insignia was transferred from the
retiring to the incumbent Grand Master and the other chair
officers exchanged the Arthur S. Crites lapel pins.

retiring Grand Master with the apron of a Past Grand Master.

in her behalf.

all the Communications of the Grand Lodge, and, in his absence, to preside therein; · and, in the event of the death of the
Grand Master, or of his absence from the State, or his inability from any cause to {5erform the functions of his office, the
Deputy Grand Master shall succeed to and be charged with all
his powers and duties."

Having succeeded to the powers and duties of the Grand
Master, Brother Brouillet succeeds to the title of Grand
Master under Section 20 of the Constitution of the Grand
Lodge of California:
"Section 20. The Grand Master, during the interval between
the communication of the Grand Lodge, may exercise all its
executive powers, except the granting of charters. This power
and the title of Grand Master applies not only to him who has
been elected and installed as Grand Master, but to either of
the Grand Officers who shall have succeeded 'to the powers
and duties of the Grand Master."

It is, therefore, officially announced to the Craft that the

Grand Master of the Grahd Lodge of California is
MOST WORSHIPFUL
ARTHUR W. BROUILLET
It is further announced .that the R. W. John R. l\Joore,
elected Senior Grand Warden, October 12, 1945, is the
Senior Grand Warden of this Grand Lodge.
It is further announced that the offices of Deputy Grand
Master and ] unior Grand Warden are vacant.

All of which is by the order of the Most Worshipful
Grand Master, who directs that this pronouncement be read
at the stated meeting next following its receipt.
Fraternally yours,

Lodge.

LLOYD E. WrLSON, Grand Secretary.

November 1, 1945.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

GRAND LODGE AUDIT

We certify that, in our opinion, the attached statements set forth the financial condition of the Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California as at July 31,
1945, and the result of its operations for the fiscal year 1944-45.

September 24, 1945.
Grand LOOge, F. & A. M. of California,
San Francisco, California.
~j
Gentlemen:
We have audited the accounts and records of the Grand Lodge, F. & A. M.
of California for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1945, and submit the following
statements:
Grand Lodge Funds
Exhibit A:. St.atement of all Grand Lodge cash received arrd disbursed by
the Grand Secretary and Grand Treasurer, August 1, 1944, to July 31, 1945.
Grand Secretary's Accounts
Exhibit B: Resume of cash received and disbursed, August 1, 1944, to July
31, 1945.
Exhibit C: Statement of cash received and disbursed for Special FundsWar Relief, Philippine Dues and Philippine Relief Funds, August 1, 1944, to
July 31, 1945.
Schedule 1: Statement of Grand Lodge per capita dues collected from 1944
annual returns.
Schedule 2: Statement of Masonic Homes per c~ita dues and $25 contributions collected during the year 1944-45.
Schedule 3: Analysis of War Program expense for the fiscal year ended
July 31, 1945.
Grand Treasurer's Accounts
Exhibit D: Statement of cash receipts and disbursements, August 1, 1944,
to July 31, 1945.
Exhibit E: Statement of assets and liabilities, July 31, 1945.
Exhibit F: List of investments, July 31, 1945.
Comments
As shown in the capital account of Exhibit E, the revenue from per capita
dues and other sources exceeded the total expenses and appropriations by
$99,717.43. Net profit from sale of securities amounted to $14,800.75, making
a total increase of capital of $114,518.18.
All per capita dues, as reported on the 1944 annual returns from constituent
Lodges, have been paid in full. Our Schedules 1 and 2 show proof of the
revenue due from the Lodges in accordance with their 1944 returns and the
$25.00 Homes contributions reports for' the first three quarters of the fiscal ·
year 1944-45. The total revenue due, as shown, agrees with the total cash received from the Lodges by the Grand Secretary.
Cash receipts were accounted for and traced to the proper depositaries. Distributions were made by checks and supported by vouchers properly approved
by the Committee on Accounts. All bank balances were verified by correspondence with the depositaries. Certified lists of the securities were received
from the Anglo California National Bank which holds the securities for safekeeping. Securities as recorded on the books of account were checked to these
lists. All interest due thereon was receiv.ed and accounted for.

Respectfully submitted,
BURROWS, PARKER & COMPANY,

Certified Public Accountants.
WALTER A. p ARKER.

The bank balanees were verified by correspondence with the depositaries.

Decurities:
Securities donated and. purchased in prior years and still on hand are listed
on Schedule 1. Securities donated and purchased during the current year are
listed on Schedule 2. Securities sold or ·called during the current year are listed
on Schedule 3. Certain donated securities were found to be worthless, therefor
were written off; these securities are listed on Schedule 4. ! •
Donated securities are recorded at market value when received, or at $1.00
if the value is unknown. Bonds purchased are recorded at actmil cost. For. the
past several years, certain bonds were purchased at a high premium. To prevent any loss to _the Endowment Fund when the. bonds. are redeemed, an amortization schedule was set up to make an annual charge against the income from
these securities, thereby decreasing the income received by the Masonic Homes
for operating purposes. During the current · year most of these high premium
bonds were sold at . a much higher pn!mium than paid at the date of purchase,
thus the . Endowment Fund and the Luckenbach Fund realized · a: profit of
$138,210.78. From this profit the Masonic Homes was given $21,699.11 which
~epresented a return to it of the annual ·amortization charges made against
Homes income over the past several years on these bonds. This left the Endowment Fund a net profit of $111,585.78 and the Luckenbach Fund a net profit of

$4,925.89.

TRUSTEES OF MASONIC HOMES AUDIT
September 22, 1945.
Masonic Homes of California,
San Francisco, California.
Gentlemen:
We have audited the books and records of the Masonic Homes of California
for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1945, and submit the following statement·s :
Statements of Funds and Properties
Exhibit A: Statement of cash receipts and disbursements, August 1, -1944,
to July 31, 1945.
Exhibit B : Balance sheet, July 31, 1945.
Schedule B-1: Statement of securities owned, July 31, 1945.
Schedule B-2 : Statement of Entertainment Fund.
Schedule B-3 : Statement of Students' Loan and Scholarship Fund.
Schedule B-4: Sta',ement of Summer Camp Fund.
Schedule B-5: Statement of Post-War Reserve Fund.
Schedule B-6 : Statement of Charles L. Patton Fund.
Schedule B-7: Statement of C. N. Flint Trust Fund.
Schedule B-8: Statement of C. N. Flint Annuity Fund.
Schedule B-9 : Statement of C. N. Flint Annuity "Morgan" Fund.
Schedule B-10: Statement ·of George and Harriet Wadleigh Annuity Fund.
Schedule B-11: Statement of Harriet Wadleigh Endowment Annuity Fund.
Schedule B-12: Statement of Decoto Residents' Monthly Grant Fund,
..1 Decoto Residents' Deposits and Covina Residents' Trust Funds.
Statements of Revenue and Expense
Exhibit C : Statement o.f revenue and expense.
Exhibit D: Statement of direct operating expense, Decoto.
E xhibit E : Statement of direct operating expense, Covina.
Schedule D-1: Detailed operating expense-Decoto.
Schedule E-1: Detailed operating expense-Covina.
Comments
Cash:
All recorded receipts were properly accounted for and deposited in the
banks. All interest due on securities and notes was received and accounted for.

Securities, Real Estate, Etc.:
A detailed list of all seCPrities owned by the Masonic Homes is shown on
Schedule B-1. Government bonds were purchased from the general funds at a
cost of $436,516.25; the other bonds, stocks, etc., listed were received by donation. The book value of stocks and bonds reprrsents the market value at the
time of donation. When the actual value is unknown, a nominal value of $1.00
is used for purposes of record. Stocks of various companies, all of which had
been donated to the Homes and carried on the records at $119.08, were written
off as valueless.
Life insurance policies are recorded at the amount recoverable at the death
of the insured, if determinable, otherwise at a nominal value of $1.00. The
value of one policy was decreased by $918.17 in order to reflect its actual value
as reported by the company.
Notes and contracts receivable are listed at the unpaid balance as at July 31,
1945. Principal and interest payments were received on all notes and contracts.
These receivables represent sales of real estate donated to the Homes. One
note for $1,000.00 was written off as worthless, This note was dated 1928 and
was donated to the Homes by David D. Groo in 1933; no payments of principal
or interest were ever received.
The older real estate is recorded at the assessed value at the time it was
donated. That which was received during the past several years has been
recorded . at a nominal value of $1.00. Real estate carried on the books at a
value of $720.00, and on which no taxes have been paid for several years, were
written off the records.
The stocks, bonds, notes and certificates hat are held by the Anglo California
National Bank were verified by certification from the bank. The stock, notes
and life insurance policies held at the office of the Grand Secre:ary were
examined. All were accounted for except one Prudential Life Insurance policy.
The Grand Secretary's· file on this policy contains an assignment of the policy
to the Homes together with a letter stating that the original policy is held by
the insured's divorced wife.
Other Funds:
•
The Masonic Homes has numerous separate funds which have been created
for definite or special purposes. Full details of these funds are shown on the
attached statements, Schedules B-2 to B-12, inclusive. Payments due from the
annuity funds in accordance with the contracts and agreements were made.
All interest due on the securities of these funds were received and deposited
in the proper bank accounts. All bank balances were verified by correspondence
with the depositaries. T he securities were verified by certification from the
Anglo California National Bank which holds them for safekeeping.
Total F1mds of the H omes:

1945, follows: ·

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
FOREWORD
This past year, in a period which included the now historic V-E and V-J
Days, we have revi~wed 60 reports of our sister jurisdictions. As expressed
in these reports, the minds of our Brother Masons show mingled and v·aried
emotions : prayerful thoughts for the end of bitter fighting-solemn tribute to
those who sacrificed their lives-concern about our individual and Masonic
responsibilities in solving the post-war problems-hopes for the future.
As in the past, we have reviewed the proceedings of each jurisdiction
carefully and conscienti9usly, seeking and reporting the unusual or outstanding.
Naturally, a repetition of routine material handled in a routine mannJ common
to all jurisdictions, would be a waste of time, both for the reviewer and the
reader.
The year has been uniformly abundant so far as members and ~oney are
concerned, only one jurisdiction out of 49 showing a decrease in membership.
The aggregate 'net gain for the nat!on is 85,198 members. Another encouraging trend was the number of restorations to membership from among the
thousands who have been dropped from the rolls. Almost all the jurisdictions
have conferred courtesy degrees, some in less than the prescribed time. A
common worry is whether the war time initiates have been sufficiently impressed with the principles and Ancient Landmarks of Freemasonry.
There is a startling similarity or parallel in the matters tha~ were most
vehemently debated in practically all jurisdictions. These subjects were physical
qualifications, ancient landmarks and post-war policies. Because these subjects
were such universal topics and of such paramount interest, we have devoted the
greater portion o·f our report to a record of the action of the various Grand
Lodges pertaining tci them.
Your chairman has recently returned ~rom a 72,000 mile trip by air to
all the active theaters of operation. While in the Philippines, he had the
opportunity of talking with the Masonic leaders there soon after liberation
from the Japanese occupation. He also discussed the problems of Masonry in
the Orient with Supreme Commander Douglas MacArthur and some Masonic
members of his staff. The liberation under such leaders should result in an
up-surge of a strong spiritual force, around which democratic-minded people
may rally. Masonry may well become that rallying point.
The necessity for active assistance to our brethren in the Far East was
self-evident. Their Lodges were forced to disband, their leaders were killed
or imprisoned, and the members were persecuted. The present Ac:ing
Grand Master of the Philippine Grand Lodge, Brother Michael Goldenberg,
the Grand Secretary, Anthony Gonzales, and Past Grand Master S. W.
Rosenstock, showed your chairman the ruins of their Grand Lodge headquarters
in Manila, the Plaridel Temple. It was reduced to rubble. They also showed
him the pit at the Fort Santiago branch in Manila where the Japs took the
Deputy Grand Master of the Philippine Grand Lodge, Santos Guidos, and
beheaded him in full view of his three young children. When the youngest
gave a cry of anguish, the_Jap captain shot the child dead. This pit still had

697

human skulls and bones there. In fact, dogs would come at night and dig
them up. He saw where the Grand Master, John McFie was killed in Santo
Tomas Prison by shell fire as the Americans were approaching to liberate the
prisoners.
It made him proud to know that these · men sacrificed their liberty, their
lives and their fortunes rather than reveal Masonic secre:s to the Japanese invaders. The members started the process of reconstruction as soon as the Japs
left and, working from nothing, were well on the way to re-establishing
themselves, with the prospects of assistance from their Masonic brothers
elsewhere as an incentive.
While in London, he talked at length with the Grand Secretary of the Grand
Lodge of England, Brother Sidney White. He heard at first h~nd the problems
of recognizing the distinction between the regular and irregular Mason. It
seems that the Grand Lodge of England insists, with respect to foreign jurisdictions, that there be first an adherence to the traditional Masonic principles,
secondly, an emphasis of harmony with the national government of their
country, and third, that they be men of correct standing. He later saw the wisdom
of this policy in his travels throughout Europe where he interviewed brethren in
France, Italy, Germany, Denmark and elsewhere. Obviously, in some cases
our ~ervicemen have joined the wrong Lodges and corrective action will be
necessary. The Masonic authorities in countries such as Denmark had to desist from Masonic activities during enemy occupation. In fact, a day had
been set in Denmark for the arrest of all Masons and, as a result, many of
the Danish Masons had fled to Sweden. They hoped, however, to commence
work again on September 19, which is the birthday of the King, who is the
Grand Master.
His observations and our review of the proceedings of sister Grand Lodges
leads us to suggest the prime importance of adhering to the established principles of Free Masonry. This is a lesson which should be taught our wartime initiates. No war, nor condition, can alter the Ancient Landmarks. Our
Order should never become a political tool, no matter how a:tractive the object. We should never ask members to join and should never seek unseemly
publicity; but we should, of ' course, attempt to reclaim dropped or dimitted
rnemb.ers. We believe in God and the immortality of the soul, but we say:
"Leave pridish priests do battle with creeds,
That church is mine that does most godlike deeds."
Fraternally submitted,
HENRY C. CLAUSEN,
OSCAR

c. OLSON,

FREDERICK
CHARLES

o. EATON,

s. PIDDA,

HERBERT G. POLHILL,
PAUL

CONFERENCE OF GRAND MASTERS
On February 23rd and 24th the conference of the Grand Masters was
in session. N9twithstanding the general conditions affecting travel and
hotel accommodations which threatened to cause a cancellation, there were
present at that meeting forty-seven of the forty-nine Grand Masters of
the several jurisdictions of the United States and in addition, the Grand
Master of the Province of Alberta, Canada. The other two jurisdictions
were represented by their Deputy Grand Masters, in each case because of
the inability of t~e presiding Grand Master to attend. This was the largest
attendance in the long history of these conferences and is ample evidence
of the strength and of the interest in Freemasonry throughout our land.

De Molay and the Rainbow Girls: Many of our brethren devo~e much time

to be an organization of men, it ~s no longer Freemasonry.

. On topic lb Gran·d Master Henry Collins of South Carolina spoke in
part as follows:
What is Freemasonry prepared to do? Very little. We stress the universality of Freemasonry and yet we stand today divided, disunited to such an
extent that to pursue any common end is utterly impossible. This is particularly true in America. About the only thing we, here in the United States,
can agree upon is that we are each determined to pursue our own individual
course. Here we are, an organization nearly three million strong, dedicated
to the highest of principles, with a potential power and influence surpassing
perhaps any other organization in these United States. But what does it get
us? Little more than con fusion. We make a lot of noise, speaking with
forty-nine different voices, we complain: that others are listened to, we criticise·
other organizations because they have the courage to do the thing we are afraid
to do. I am not espousing the cause of a General Grand Lodge in the United
States. I am not by any means convinced that therein lies the ,answer, but I
am convinced that if Freemasonry is to speak with authority, if her voice is to
be heard and heeded, some way must be found to bring about a greater unity
among us. So long as she continues to speak with the uncertain sound of fortynine voices just so long will her voice go unheeded and ignored.
This is a time of crisis. But such times always present opportunities. for
those who have the faith and courage to face them with vision. It is my opinion that Freemasonry is faced with the greatest opportunity of her history.
A new world is in the making, a new day is dawning. Freemasonry may enter
and wield a tremendous influence for good if she has the courage and is willing
to pay the price. I believe that an obligation rests upon Freemasonry to have
a part in the shaping Of this new world. I think she has a message for this hour
and for the coming era. I do not favor Freemasonry becoming entangled in
partisan politics. But I am in favor of Freemasonry taking such action as is
necessary to insure that her voice is heard and that it is heeded in this hour.
. May we have the faith and the courage to chart new courses when it is clear
that new courses are necessary to cope with changed conditions. (Applause.)
By Benjamin L. Hadley, Grand Master of Grand Lodge of Maine:
Returns from a ques'.ionnaire directed to the forty-nine Grand Jurisdictions.
disclosed that thirty-nine permit election to all three degrees on one ballot,
while ten require a ballot for each degree. In the face of that approximately
eigh:y per cent unanimity it might seem that a discussion of the subject would be
purely academic, but as there are ten dissenters from complete unanimity, off
hand dismissal would be begging the question, and there is the remote possibility that even a brief discussion of the subject might win a convert to the one
ballot system which so preponderantly prevails.
On topic 6B Grand Master Albert A. Hughes, of Michigan, spoke in
·part as follows:
Briefly, the findings in our forty-nine Grand Jurisdictions in reference to
the eighteenth landmark interpretation as compiled by · Carl H. Claudy in 1937

•

Our Grand Lodge makes no exception in favor of Service men who have
been maimed in war, as the above specifications would cover this feature of
physical qualifications. A further confirmation of the above was · incorporated
in Michigan law in 1928 and the 1940 revised Law reads as follows:
:•It is the exclusive right of the Lodge to det~rmine whether a candidate has
the necessary physical qualifications to become a Mason. The Lodge, of course,
should decide honestly and conscientiously."
I am in complete harmo)1y with our Michigan Law and any further treatise
of this subject is based upon these premises, rather than upon ', he opposite view,
which should provoke greater comment from those who may differ:
Physical perfection business can be made to look ludicrous. We may bar a
man infinitely superior, morally, spiritually and mentally from the privilege of
Masonry because of maimed body. To deny admiss.ion to such is an act u.terly
at variance with the principles of Freemasonry as a speculat ive science. Let
us look more to perfect minds and character than to perfect bodies.
But the one dominating requisi'.e should be that a maimed brother who applies never will become a burden or charge upon the Lodge. Make sure that he
is and will remain self-sustaining.
John Marshall, one of the early Grand Masters of Virginia, said, "A good
man who is capable of supporting himself and family, as well as being in a
position to contribute if necessary, to the welfare of his fellowman, should
never be barred from Masonry because of some physical defect over which he
has no control.''
I ·believe that the contention that with the bars let down and maimed applicants or so-called cripples being received will increase the hazard of future· ·
charges or dependents, is magnified and fallacious.
On the con:rary, iQ my judgment, greater caution will be exercised and few
mistakes will be made and few if any increases of charity cases will occur.
Unfortunately, Masonry is not a cheap organization financially. And how
often, today, the "Perfect Youth" is admitted with a lack of proper considera.tion and inves'. igation as to the monetary status of the applicant, and then
through adverse and unforeseen circumstances this bro:her later becomes a
financial liability to the Lodge.
Also, I do not share the opinion of some conformists that if the bars are
lowered in one particular, that the ice will be broken and anything may happen
to our Old Charges and Landmarks and that the whole Masonic structure will
crumble.
I have more faith in the wisdom and judgment pf the craft and this has not
happened in Michigan in the thirty-four years that we have left this whole
matter in the hands of the Constituent Lodges.

702

' PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Some jurisdictions leave this problem to the judgment of the Worshipful
Master, the Grand Lodge or to the Grand Master, who may issue a special
dispensation, but personally I think that the subordinate Lodge is in the best
position to judge of the merits or demerits of the case.
What happens if a maimed brother from a liberal jurisdiction wishes to
visit a Lodge in another jurisdiction which maintains a strict regulation for
admission of candidates? If the latter jurisdiction is consistent the maimed
visitor should be refused a seat in the Lodge, and is this just?
On the other hand, if the brother be admitted to a seat in Lodge, is not the
rigid jurisdiction sanctioning the rules of the liberal jurisdiction. and discriminating against their own like material? , In which case the jurisdiction
with relaxed requirements is the great leveler and really governs or should
govern.
What also will happen to the brother who was sound physically when he
entered the U. S. Service, as of course he must be, and he returns to his
Lodge with the loss of an arm, leg or eyesight? Will he be denied a seat in
his Lodge? Michigan makes no exception in favor of service men who have
been maimed in war, thus pity and sympathy can and will not enter into consideration.
I personally know of many maimed Masonic brothers with the loss of an
arm, hand, foot and even complete loss of :vision, but not one is a financial
burden to the craft, nor is he ever apt to become one.
One of these is a judge in Detroit. He is a most ardent and well-informed
craftsman and also an able jurist, respected by all who know him. Our own
President would of necessity be debarred from joining any Masonic body today
that strictly enforced physical perfection as one of 'the qualifications of becoming a Master Mason. These brothers then are fine, active and useful. And
my observations often reveal that of two men of equal attainment, the one
who has overcome physical handicaps is often more to be admired, encouraged
and admitted into any sphere he may seek, than the one who has had no obstacle or handicap to surmount. Adverse conditions bring out one's iatent powers.
On topic 4 the Grand Master of Wisconsin, Louis D. Potter, spoke in
part as follows:
While there is universal disagreement among the writers who have made
lists and the Grand Lodges which have adop~ed lists and none agree as to
every one listed nearly all agree that there are "Landmarks." To determine if
there is any general agreement among the Grand Lodges of the United States
of America on any of the so-called "Landmarks," I .took Mackey's list, as it
is the list most generally used in this country, and compared it with the lists of
the Grand Lodges that use the old charges. This study ' shows considerable
agreement among our Grand Lodges on some of the "Landmarks."
From this study it seems that the following list at least would be accepted
as Ancient Landmarks.
1. A belief in God.
2. A "Book of the Law" constitutes an indispensable part of the furniture
of every Lodge.
3. The legend of the third degree.
4. Secrecy.
5. The symbolism of the operative art.
6. That a .Mason must be a man, free-born---of good moral report and of
mature age.
7. That the Landmarks cannot be changed.

British Columbia, 1944 (Grand Chaplain):
As we · gather for the seventy-third Annual Communication of the
Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Antient, Free and Accepted Masons
of British Columbia, may I salute your tremendous possibilities, for I
believe that the future will hail the present as one of the great turningpoints of history. But first-may I give you a text from the Volume
of the Sacred Law-from the · pr.ophet Am.os, Chapter VII, verse 8:
"And the Lord said unto me, Amos, what seeth thou?
And I said, a plumbline."
The voice, spoken through the prophet, is the voice of the Great Archi.tect of the Universe in righteous anger. In the vision of the prophet,
there stands on the walls of a nation a man of steel, with a plumbline
in His hand. And note well, it is the Great Architect of the Universe
that holds the plumbline.
God was sick to nausea by the wickedness of man. So, with the
plumb in His hand, He is about to put their civilization to the test- and,
as a w~ll that is out of the straight is condemned by the builder, so a
people out of straight will be condemned by the Great Architect of the
Universe. He will tolerate no wall that does not conform to His standard;
it must be thrown down in orde; to be rebuilt.
The picture of the vision, of course, is not a pleasant one". But neither
is it pleasant to see the toppling of the walls of a civilization built out
of plumb. · Prevention is always better than cure. Therefore, as the
level teaches unity in diversity and equality in difference-so the plumb
is a symbol of rectitude of conduct, integrity of life, and that uprightness
of moral character which makes a good and just man. And, by the same
token~ makes a good and just civilization. For a civilization, after all,
is the sum total of its manhood and womanhood. Let us look at a wall
erected by a good Freemason, built to be plumb. Listen to this:
"I desire solemnly to call my people to prayer and dedication, not
unmindful of our shortcomings, not to ask that our will be done, but
that we may be enabled to do the will of God. God has used our nation
and empire for the fulfilling of His divine purpose. I ask of my people,
during the crisis, a contimtous and widespread prayer. We can most
effectively enter into the sufferings of subjugated Europe by prayer. We
can sustain our sailors, soldiers and airmen, who go forth to set the
captive free, by prayer. Keep vigil with these men. At this historic
moment not one of us is too busy, too young or too old to keep worldwide vigil of prayer as the great crusade sets forth. If from every
place of worship, from home and factory, from men and women of all
ages and many races and occupations, our intercessions rise, then, please
God, both now and in future not remote, the predictions of an ancient
psalm may be fulfi lled: 'The Lord will give strength unto His people;
the Lord will give His people the blessing of peace.'"
Only a king who possesses the qualities which are represented in our
symbolism by the level and the square and the plumb could talk like
that. We need have no fear of any civilization governed and ruled by
men of this quality or character.
As with individuals, so also with nations. How could such a crazy
structure as Nazi-ism survive? It could not, for it was jerry-built, built

706

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

on lies and slavery. They had forgotten soµiething. They had forgotten
that the plumbline is in the hand of the Great Architect of the Universe.
Of course, the whole structure had to be destroyed. We are witnessing
its downfall. However, be that is it may, this morning we ar~ not .so
much concerned to condemn another civilization as to discover the flaws
within our own and remedy' them. _
Brethren, who can doubt that there are flaws in our own social order
which need the combined Masonic mind intelligently focused upon them?

mation of the influence of countless individuals which will determine future
polides of nations, and the future course of civilization. ~n infor~ed and
watchful public1 imbued with the spirit of true constructive service, cannot be long m isled by the most crafty and designing of politicians or
the most convincing of dishonest and ruthless demagogues. In the end,
therefore, we hold our fate and the fate of the institution of Freemasonry
in our own hands. If we are alert and intelligent, industrious, courageous
and aggresive, we will be victorious against the evil genius '."hich threatens us and everything for which we stand. If we are lazy, supme, cowardly
and without the qualities of leadership, we will aid and abet the decline
of our institution, the dispersal of our numbers, and the destruction of
everything we value, in our own country arid in the world. This terrible
responsibility is with us, and with those who follow in our footsteps. Ours
will be the respon~ibility if we fail and are .swallowed up in the final hol?caust which will destroy all justice, all liberty, all decency. And ours will
be the glory forever if we triumph.

Colorado, 1944 (Grand Master):
Freemasonry does not attempt to solve the specific problems of a
nation, a state, nor those of a community. It should not assume, nor
should it undertake to do the work which primarily belongs to the church,
the home, or the school. It is not a Y. M. C. A.; it is not a welfare
organization. It should not attempt to duplicate the work being done by
organized · charities or by governmental agencies. It should first contribute to the relief of worthy distressed brother Master Masons, their

In. th; Preamble to the Constitution of the Grand Lodge will be found
the following:
"Provided, always, That the ancient landmarks of the Fraternity be held
inviolate."
A discussion of the subject, therefore, naturally ?ivid~s itself into two
parts; ( 1), whether the proposal to abol~sh .the qualifications quoted from
Section 106 is a violation of the Consblutton of the Grand Lodge, and
(Z), whether such abolishment is for the advantage of the Craft.
. .
The Grand Lodge has the same right to amend or repeal any prov1s1on
of the by-laws that it had to enact it, provided that the Grand Lodge Constitution is not thereby violated.
. Whether abolishment would be violation of the Constitution d~pends
on whether or not the standard is a "landmark." With the exceptto~ of
the extract from the preamble quoted, we do not find the landmarks defined either in the Constitution or in the By-Laws of the Grand Lodge. W e
do not find that this Grand Lodge ever has defined the landmarks ... Th~
substance of some of them is contained in out "Standards. of R~cogmtton.
In the digest of the decisions of the Grand Masters published m 1.928, we
find but one under this head. It was decided by the Grand Master m office
in 1858 that "belief in the Holy Bible is a landmark."
Presumptively the disqualification found in Section 106 is derived from
the landmarks. In additibn to this one, there are undoubtedly others so
derived which are not enumerated either in the Constitution or By-Laws,
some df which are that the candidate must be a man, free-born, and of
mature age. A woman, a slave, a young man i? nonag~, and an ~ld ~an
in dotage cannot be accepted, as everyone admits; an.d 1f the ~ualificat.1on
under consideration is a landmark, neither can a candidate havmg p~ys1cal
imperfections which impair his ability to support himself an~ fa1?1ly, or
by reason of which he is unable to conform to all of our peculiar rites and
ceremonies.
- It has been stated that these qualifications really arise from the very
nature of the. Masonic institution, and from its symbolic teachings, and
have always existed as landmarks.
This landmark is the eighteenth of twenty-five computed, arranged
and published by Dr. Albert G. Mackey in 1856.
There has been objection to the arrangement and subj~ct matter of
Dr. Mackey's landmarks by many Masonic scholars. It seems in order to
determine the importance of landmarks in the structure of Masonic law.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The component parts of our Masonic law have been stated to be as
follows :
1. The Ancient Landmarks.
2. The Constitution of the Grand Lodge.
3. The By-Laws of the Grand Lodge.
4. The ancient regulations and usages of Masonry.
5. The By-Laws of a subordinate Lodge.
These take precedence in the order above enumerated. Implicit obedie.nce must be given thereto by all Lodges and Freemasons in this jurisdiction.

counts numerous instances of such violations, yet in every case such action
results in something different from that pure and unimpaired Masonry
handed down by the fathers.
As a Grand Lodge has no power to enact a landmark, so has it no
power to abolish or detract from one. Being supreme in its own jurisdiction, it may make or alter regulations, edicts, ·o r its own constitution at
will, always provided the old landmarks be carefully preserved. In the
early proceedings of this Grand Lodge, in Grand Masters' reports, and
in . many committee ·reports, we hear these words frequently repeated :
"Remove not the ancient landmarks, w hich thy fathers have set."
You will note that our ancient brethren revered and obeyed t he land. marks and repeatedly used the word "strictly" in connection with their
construction and interpretation. There , can then be no confusion caused
by any uncertainty of our duty to revere 'a nd obey a landmark; any possible confusion of our Masonic duty must be caused by inability to recognize a rule of action as a landmark or if it is so determined by the interpretation placed upon the language used. When we determine that a
given rule of action is a landmark, we must admit that h is at once the
highest form of Masonic law and is an unalterable code governing the,
actions of Masons, Lodges, and Grand Lodges.
Let us examine in detail Dr. Mackey' s eigh teenth landmark and determine whether or not it really is a landmark. Its wording is as . follows :
"He should be a man, unmutilated, freeborn, and of mature age." In view
of the difference of opinion that exists among Masonic scholars, it is
deemed advisable to trace this rule of action not only through our own
records but back of Dr. Mackey's publication to the earliest known records.
So far as your committee is aware there has been no controversy · over
any portion of this rule except the word "unmutilated" and what it
implies. We do not question that a candidate must be a man, freeborn,
and of mature age. These qualifications are adhered to in all jurisdictions. We do not admit women, old men in dotage, young men under age,
atheists, madmen, or fools.
Now let us examine the authority which Dr. Mackey undoubtedly
consulted on establishing his landmark. First : Three well known books
written shortly after the Grand Lodge of England was formed purporting to assemble the ancient charges, usages, customs, history and traditions of Masonry in published form. These all insist that candidates must
be a man, freeborn, hale, sound and unmutilated. The books are I-Anderson's Constitutions ('1723 ) Second edition 0738). 2-Preston's Illustrations (1722). 3-Dermott'l> Ahiman Rezon (1756) Second edition (1764).
Second: Certain old manuscripts used by the craft prior to the formation of the Grand Lodge of E ngland. By these manuscripts Masonic
scholars have traced the history of Masonry through the years until its
beginning is lost in the mists of antiquity. We quote from them as they
p er tain to the subject of physical r equirements.
1. Ancient Charge to the Lodge of Antiquity in London, written during the reign of J am es the Second: "That he be made able in a ll degrees;
that he is freeborn, of good kindred, true, and no bondsman, and that he
have his right limbs as a man ought to have. And that the prentis be
freeborn, and of limbs whole as a man ought to be, and no bastard."
2. Regulation made in General Assembly, December 27, 1663, Harry
Jermyn, Earl of St. Albans, Grand Master : "That no person hereafter
shall be accepted a Free Mason, but such as are of able body, honest
parentage, good reputation, and an obs~rver of the laws of the land."

Roscoe Pound, in his Masonic Jurisprudence separates Masonic law
into three types of rules:
·
'
1. The Landmarks.
2. Masonic Common Law.
3. Masonic Legisl~tion.
The above are listed in th~ ~rder of their precedence and importance.
He defines landmarks as follows:
"~y la?dmarks in Freemasonry we are generally supposed to "mean
certain universal, unalterable, and unrepealable fundamentals which have
existed from t~me imm~morial and are so thoroughly a part of Masonry
that no Masomc authority may derogate from them or do aught but maintain ·them."

He, however, does not c~nsider the requirement as to physical qualification a landmark.
Dr. Albert" G. Mackey offers a threefold division of Masonic law as
follows :
1. Landmarks.
2. General Regulations.
3. Local Regulations.
He explains that the landmarks are the unwritten laws or customs
of Masonry, while the regulations are the written law enacted by Masonic
authority and may be general or local. He defines landmarks as " those
ancient, and. therefore ~niversal customs of the craft, which either gradually grew mto <:'perahon as rules of action, or if once enacted by any
compe.tent. a~th.onty, were enacted at a period so remote, that no account
of their o_ngm is to be found in the records of history. Both the enactors
and the time of the enactment have passed away from the record, and the
landmarks are therefore of higher antiquity than memory or history can
re~ch. A cust?m or rule of action to constitute a landtnark must have
existed from time whereof the memory of man runneth not to the contrary."

Most, if not all, Masonic writers, scholars and leaders are agreed : that
1. Landmarks are the highest form of Masonic law.
2. They are fundamental, universal, of great antiquity and like the
laws of the Medes and Persians, unchangeable.
,

The~e are many different opinions as to just which rules are landmarks
and which are ~ot. It is 'evident, however, that landmarks do exist. They
are the recogmz~d fundamentals which give the fraternity its Masonic
character and which cannot be .changed without destroying that character.
!hey c?eck hasty and hysterical legislation as well as tending to prevent
~nnova~1ons. A Grand Lodge cannot abolish a landmark, though it is not
1mposs1ble for a Grand Lodge to violate one. Recent Masonic history re-

3. Constitution of the Grand Lodge of M<1-ssachusetts, published June
25, 1798, and signed, among others, by Paul Revere: "Every person desiring admission must also be upright in body, not deformed or dismembered, at the time of making; but of hale and entire limbs, as a man
ought to be."
·
4. Harlien Manuscript,' written in the 17th Century and now in possession of the British Museum: "That no person shall be act:epted a Free
Mason but such as are of able body, honest parentage, reputation, and

oldest Masonic Manuscript known to exist, now in possession of the

6. Buchanan Manuscript 17th Century. Gould's History of Free
