he ought to be."
These Manuscripts and Constitutions were evidently the outgrowth
of earlier regulations governing the craft when knowledge was handed
down from mouth to ear, before printing or even writing came into common use. They prove beyond any doubt that it has been a requirement
from time immemorial that a candidate be a man, freeborn, and unmutilated. They also show that the rule as to physical requirements conforms to both Pound's and Mackey's definition of a landmark.
It is true that some Grand Lodges do not recogn,ize the rule that
a candidate must be unmutilated, as a landmark; others no longer strictly
construe it and still others have by decree attempted to abolish it entirely,
substituting in its place a modern, streamlined regulation permitting its
Lodges to initiate material with varying degi:ees of physical imperfections
and thus swelling membership.
·
A Grand Lodge has no more right to change an ancient landmark
than has a state to change a provision of the Constitution of the United
States. This question is so clear and indisputable, that your committee
deems it unnecessary to argue the same at length, but will make a few
citations from Masonic law and the teachings of the fathers.
One of the ancient landmarks provides: These landmarks can never
be changed, nothing can be subtracted froni them; nothing can be added
to them; not the slightest modification can be made to them. It is quite
clear that the order against removing or altering the landmarks was
universally observed in all ages of the craft. A Brother installed Master
of a Lodge, is obligated that he admits it. is not in the power of any man
or body of men, to make innovations in the body of Masonry. The teach·
ings of the fathers give tlte following important command and solemn
injunction: "Remove not the ancient landmarks which thy fathers have
set." It is our duty, by our obligations, to transmit to our successors the
landmarks of the order as we received them from our predecessors. It
is only by the observance of and obedience to the ancient landmarks,
the established Masonic law, and the imperative command and solemn
injunction of the fathers, that the excellent tenets of our institution have
l!een transmitted from generation to generation, through a succession of
a.g es, pure and unimpaired.
If the landmarks were set aside and each Lodge determined for itself
what constituted physical disability, each Lodge would have its own rules.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

717

In one Lodge it would be held that a wooden leg is no disability; in another that it is; in one Lodge that a leg six inches short is no disability;
in another, that it is; and so on as to different degrees of di'Sability that
may arise.
The recognition of the doctrine, that a Grand Lodge can change or
modify the ancient landmarks, will produce · discord and confusion between the brethren, between Lodges, and between Grand Lodge and
Lodges; its tendency will be to lessen the influence of the Grand Lodge;
lessen it in the estimation and respect of the craft. The intelligent and
conscientious member of a Lodge will be placed in this dilemma; his
duty, as a rule, is to obey the edicts of the Grand Lodge. The universal
Masonic law says that he must obey the ancient landmarks; that these
landmarks can never be changed. Which must he obey? There can be
but one answer. He must obey the ancient landmarks, the great Constitution of Masonry, throughout the whole world.
An edict of a Grand Lodge is no edict, so far as it conflicts with,
changes or modifies any of the' ancient landmarks. It is no more an
edict than is an act of the State Legislature that conflicts with, changes
or modifies a provision of the Constitution of the State or of the United
States.
If a Grand Lodge can change the landmark as to physical qualification
and say that a cripple can be made a Mason, it necessarily follows. that ~t
can also change the landmarks, and provide that youths, old men m their
dotage, women, etc., can be made Masons. Once recognize th.e doct~ine,
where will it :-c:~nd? The only safeguard is to strictly adhere to the ancient
landmarks of the order; the ancient, universal, established Masonic Law
of the Institution, strictly obey and pr~serve the teachings of the fathers;
"remove not the ancient landmarks, which thy fathers have set."
One of 'the greatest symb~lisms in Masonry is the human body, the
greatest handiwork of God. If our .s ymbols are to mean anything we must
not forsake the landmarks of our fathers. It cannot be shown that any
material benefit to Masonry will accrue if the blind, the lame, arid the
halt are permitted to petition. If we consider, as we all should, the welfare of ]\fasonry, we must agree that the requirements for membership
should be elevated rather than lowered.
The quality of man1iood, not the quantity, should govern our decisions. We already have tpo many mere members. Masonry should not
be conferred on any man as a special favor nor can any man demand
admission as a right. Masonry has a reputation to maintain a~ a~mi?g
at the very best in human life. We cannot open avenues that will mv1~e
or allow reflections upon the fundamentals and groundwork. Masonry is
an exclusive organization. ·our candidates ought to be as· nearly perfect,
not only physically but mentally, as possible. In the past our bes.t men
have eagerly sought the privilege of membership. Let us see to 1t that
no act of ours shall tend to lower the esteem which all, friend and foe
alike, accord our Fraternity. ·
It is true that a seeming injustice may be done to many good men
because of a slight maim but let us remember, that every rule works hardships on someone. The greater benefit to the greater number justifies it.
Our fathers never intended Masonry to be open to the lame, the halt, or
the blind. If we in our wisdom, or rather lack of wisdom, lower the bars,
the effect will be to cheapen rather than to enhance the value of membership. If we modernize the Masonry handed down to us through the

718

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

generations we shall in turn hand down something to our children but it
will not be pure and unimpaired Freemasonry.
Your committee is of the opinion that Masonic law is based upon
and closely interwoven with the landmarks as published in the Constitution, Laws and Edicts. That continuous use and recognition of the
eighteenth landmark from the very beginning of this Grand Lodge, together· with its unabridged and unbroken descent from ancient to modern
times, clearly establish it as a landmark and as such beyond the power
of any man or body of men to modify or change.
Much of the · above has been quoted from the Report of a Special
Committee on the Eighteenth Landmark found in the Proceedings of the
Grand Lodge A:.F:. &A:.M:. of Wisconsin for the year 1938, and reprinted in the Report on Foreign Correspondence of . this Grand Lodge,
Proceedings 1939, pp. 474 and following.
2. Is Abolishment for the Advantage of the Craft?
In addition to what has been said above, we think that the greatest
good for the greatest number should prevail.
A brother who has· violated Masonic law is not expelled or otherwise
dealt with to punish him, but for the good of the fraternity.
A candidate who cannot meet physical qualifications, and to whom
we are as yet under no fraternal obligation, is excluded for the same
reason, for the good of the fraternity.
A candidate whose ability to support himself and family is impaired,
or who is unable to conform to all of our peculiar rites and ceremonies,
should be excluded. The founders of the Grand Lodge wrote a reasonable
provision into Section 106. It is reasonable because its phraseology leaves
no pretext for trifling objections, but does retain this qualification as
for the best interests of the fraternity. The reasons for the qualifications
are as valid now as when our Grand Lodge was established.
Our peculiar constitution, forms and ceremonies are essential to the
institution of Masonry and differentiate it from all other fraternal organizations. Ours is the prototype. The others .are imitators. The passion
for streamlining, for standardization and for uniformity, one institution
with artother, should have no appeal to the Masonic organization.
It is as important to the speculative craft as it was to the operative
craft to receive no apprentice whose physical condition impairs his ability
to work and support himself and his family, and who thus will become a
burden ori the Lodge. ·

PHYSICAL QUALIFICATIONS
So many brilliant arguments, pro and con, appear in the different Proceedings and in the record of the Conference of Grand Masters as to leave
the rational thinking mind more than a little confused. We cite one or
two of the arguments and the action of many Grand Lodges.
The "Perfect Youth" theory still has its resolute defenders, but it is
safe to say that this theory is challenged today as never before, not even
in the more emotional phases of previous wars. Grand Master Mohr of
. Illinois took perhaps the most advanced stand on this question in his annual address to Grand Lodge, reiterating his suggestion of the year before
that "we '.throw ~ off the ·yoke of the Middle Ages . . . with the simple
statement tha,t in Illinois moral fibre alone can make a Mason." He fol';\oiwi:~ . :with this j mpaasioned appeal:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

719

"Since then a silent parade, unannounced, unheralded, and largely unseen, is gradually wending its way from the far flung battlefields of the
world to hospitals in America. They are the casualties from the great
conflagration of war. Some of these men can never exchange grips-they
have an arm or a hand buried in North Africa ; some can never approach
the East in required form-they left a foot or a leg in the South Pacific;
some can only ask for light but never receive it-fiendish war has robbed
them of their most valuable sense. These men have most truly placed a
sacrifice on the altar of freedom. It is done for us. We cannot demand
heroism today and ignore it tomorrow. Many of these men share our
blood and have a right to turn to Freemasonry for warmth and comfort
and fellowship as.their legacy in life. What more can they do-my fellow
Americans-to win our respect? Do not remove one moral test, but cast
aside forever this meaningless prerequisite of physical qualification. Strike
out this portion of our Code and set up proudly, as the banner of this
Grand Lodge, that we search a man's soul and his soul alone, to discover
his Masonic fitness."
Subsequently the Committee on Legislation recommended, and the
Illinois Grand Lodge unanimously adopted, an amendment to the Code
which reads as follows:
"277. Every candidate applying for the degrees in Masonry must have
the senses of a man, especially those of hearing, seeing and feeling; be a
believer in God, and capable of readii;ig and writing in English."
That is a sweeping departure from conventional practice on this subject. A speculative person would naturally inquire how those three verbal
nouns are to be interpreted. As, for example, what constitutes "hearing"?
Is it ability to hear without artificial aids? If not, what degree of deafness
is legitimate, what degree proscribed, and who is to determine in any
given instance? What degree of "seeing" is lawful? Enough to tell light
from dark, with or without lenses, or enough to tell from west of the Altar
whether a man in the East is, or is not, wearing a hat? If hearing be
poor and seeing be indifferent, what degree of "feelin g" is required? The
cheekbone is said to be one of our most delicate organs of feeling. These
are questions, however, which the Grand Lodge of Illinois in its wisdom
will . doubtless answer to the satisfaction of itself and its Brethren. We
suggest them with no thought whatever of criticism, but only by way of
showing what delicate considerations are sometimes involved in the laying
down of basic definitions.
The Grand Lodge of Maine has taken quite a contrary position which
it is only fair to set down in contrast with the foregoing. Grand Master
Hadley brought the matter up in his Annual Address. Saying it believed
that Maine had already gone as far as possible ''in a liberal interpretation
of the Ancient Landmarks," the Committee on Jurisprudence ruled as
follows:
"The question therefore involves more than a denial of the privileges
of Masonry to those who, under .the Ancient Landmarks, through no
fault of their own are unable to meet its requirements. There are many
other institutions where they can be of service to their fellow men, and no
m~n! however worthy, has an inherent r ight to bec.o me a Mason. It is a
privilege that he may secure only under the Ancient Landmarks and
customs of the Fraternity. If he cannot meet those requirements and
the Ancient Landmarks are changed for his accommodation, he may' be a
member of an organization, but it will not be Masonry. A.s honorable men
and. Masons intrusted with the care and management of our ancient and

720

honorable institution, we are under solemn oath to. stri~tly comply with
all ancient Masonic usages and transmit them ummpaired to our successors. It is not within our power to change them, even were we convinced that it is advisable so to do."
In Nebraska a Special Committee has been appointed to study this
matter and report at a later Communication whether it is desir~ble to
make the existing rule "less stringent in view of the many soldiers r~­
turning from the war with maims." Grand Master Kurk had asked m

'You were good enough to fight to preserve the principles of democracy
that Freemasonry might continue, but you are not good enough to become
one of us?'" In South Carolina Grand Master Collins raised the question
thus:
"F;,om the ·early days of Freemasonry to the present time many Grand
Lodges have adhered to what is known as the 'Perfect Youth' theory. The
idea behind this theory was that in order to become a Mason a man must
be physically perfect to all outward appearances. It is easy for us to u~­
derstand the necessity for this when practically all men had to earn their
living by manual labor. As civilization advanced and many means of
earning a livelihood developed, it became less and less necessary for one
to earn a livelihood by manual labor. And, too, as Masonry became more
and. i;nore a speculative art rather than an operative art, there was less
and' less reason to adhere to the 'Perfect Youth' theory. We know that it is
impossible to judge accurately as to•the soundness of one's physical body
by outward appearance . . . . Already there are coming back into our midst
fine young men who have suffered the loss of a limb or some physical
deformity in the defense of our country. . . . Is it worthy of Freemasonry
to deny to these men who have borne the burden of the battle the warmth
and fellowship they might have as members of the Craft? Is Freemasonry
to penalize patriotism? I hope not."
The report of the Committee on · Jurisprudence on this section of the
Grand Master's Address was sharp; "We recommend disapproval of any

Nebraska, 1944 (Grand Master):

The theory of the perfect youth is in itself a symbol that is worthy of

These boys are fighting for the principles of Masonry. What is going

forces of the United States, who possessing .all the other necessary qualifications; btit who has suffered in battle against our enemies, the loss of
physical faculty, will be eligible to petition our Lodges regardless of that
condition. We cannot demand heroism today and ignore it tomorrow.
Do not remove one moral test, but open our doors to those men who
have defended your liberties, at such terrible sacrifice to themselves. Even
with all the modern devices to enable them to function, there is still a
great and lasting effect. upon them. The number will never be so great
as to endanger ou'r charitable institutions, even though some of them
may be forced to reside there.

South Carolina, 1944 (Grand Master):
According to our present law it is very difficult to know where to
draw the line in trying to determine whether or not a person is physically
eligible. This is true of many cases presented to the Grand Master. It is
also true that many very questionable cases are never brought to the
attention of the Grand Master. Consequently Lodges have received candidates with very varying degrees of physical imperfections.
We are taught that a man is first prepared to be made a Mason in his
heart. In my opinion he is prepared there first, last and always. If he
is not prepared in his heart it makes little difference that he has a perfect
physical body. Masonry is a thing of the soul. Character and character
alone counts. It has been a source of disappointment to me that some
of the most honorable and upright men of my acquaintance have been
denied the privileges of Freemasonry, and that Freemasonry base beeen
deprived of their fine leadership simply because they had had the misfortune to have lost a limb or suffered some other physical deformity.
Already there are coming' back into our midst fine young men who have
suffered the loss of a limb or some physical deformity in the defense
of our country. There will no doubt be more. Is Freemasonry to say to
these returning soldiers, "Yes, you were good enough to go out and fight,
bleed and suffer to defen? the principles and ideals of Freemasonry, but
because you have lost a hmb or an eye or some other part of your body
you are not fit to take your place as one of us"? I? it worthy of Freemasonry to deny to these men who shall have borne the burden of battle
the warmth and 'fellowship they might have as members of the craft?
Is Freemasonry to penalize patriotism? I hope not.

Vermont, 1944 (Correspondence Committee):
We have been gratifyingly impressed with tendencies here and there
to bring Masonry into line wtih modern times, but the balance of power is
still strongly in favor of the position that the only good thing in Masonry
is the old thing, and because it is old it must be good.
Some entering wedges, however, have been driven home to help explode that ancient and outmoded requirement of physical perfection in
candidates, and several Grand Lodges have had the courage to declare

to declare that even an "Ancient Landmark" might safely be reinterpreted
in the light of generally accepted changing world conditions.

Wisconsin, 1944 (Correspondence Committ;ee):
There is evident much agitation to construe the Eighteenth Landmark
more leniently for the benefit of soldiers who are returning from the war
maimed and crippled. A recent poll by the Masonic Service Association
disclosed that a majority of those asked for their views were in favor
of easing up on the rule. This agitation and sentiment are not peculiar
to this war alone. The same thing happened after the Civil War, the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

725

Spanish war and the last war. Proponents of the idea of either doing
away entirely with the Landmark or so changing its provisions as to make
it virtually of no effect, are probably actuated by a desire to do something for the soldiers as a mark of appreciation for what they have done
for their country. On this basis the proponents of a continuance of the
rigid rule are placed at a decided disadvantage, since it makes them
seem insensible to the obligation we owe to those who hav~ been maimed
while fighting for us.
Wisconsin, through the century just closed, has steadfastly adhered
to the principle that physical perfection is a Landmark and, as such, is
beyond the power of this or any other generation of Masons to change.
In this summation we find complete vindication of our conservatism.
The founders and the forefathers who gave us Masonry were wise men,
otherwise the system would never have stood the test of time as it has.
The moment we begin to whittle away at the foundations, we begin to
undo the work of our predecessors. We are transitory tenants of this
structure. It is not ours to do with what we will.

Following up the passing of this resolution, I wrote you a letter January 12, 1943, urging every brother and especially every officer of the
Lodges, every member of a committee, every district lecturer and every
Grand Lodge officer, to bear that resolution in mind at all times and
show by his effective work as a Mason that he has done so. I also urged
every Lodge without such to appoint an active committee to further this
work at once and urged every Mason to ·assist such committee to the
utmost of his ability in this work.
Therefore, it is earnestly insisted that the three principal officers of
each subordinate Lodge by and with the aid of the secretary of such
Lodge, make a concerted effort at once to secure the reinstatement of
worthy members suspended N. P. D.
I know of nothing in our Constitution and Edicts which prevents such
worthy members suspended N. P. D. from being approached and solicited
to reinstate as members of their respective subordinate Lodges. Unfortunately, during the depression that followed World War I, a great
many good Masons did become suspended N. P. D. I feel that this is a
great field for constructive effort by all. I am not unmindful that a
great many of the Lodges have inaugurated a movement along this line
· and a great many members have been reinstated who were suspended
N. P. D., but let me urge you, and especially every secretary of every
subordinate Lodge, to check all the old records where members were
suspended N. P. D. and communicate with those whom it is determined
are worthy of being reinstated, with a view of getting them back into the
Order, where this has not been done.

New Mexico, 1944 (Grand Master):
It often happens that the brother who is appointed by an incoming
Master to a place at the end of the line is advanced by succeeding Masters
until he reaches the place of Senior Deacon. When a Master starts a
brother in the line, he should keep in mind that he is starting a brother
who may in due time preside in the East. The mere holding of an appointive position constitutes no claim to advancement. It is incumbent
upon a Master .to consider well the best interests of his Lodge when he
~akes his appointments. After a Mason is once elected to the station of
Junior Warden, he usually becomes Master two years later, since the
brethren are usually reluctant to refuse advancement to a brother who has
progressed so far, but here also the best interests of a Lodge transcend
consideration of sparing the feelings of an individual brother. The choice
of a Junior Warden is exceedingly important for the future welfare of a
Lodge, and that officer should be elected, not because ~e has been advanced by several Masters to the position of Senior Deacon, but he should
be chosen upon the basis of his qualifications and upon that basis only.

Washington, 1944 (Grand Orator):
Peace lay over the land of old Judea, where for seven years no cloud
had -0bscured the deep cerulean sky. High on the slopes of Mt. Moriah
rose that sublime structure which multitudinous workmen, in harmony and
without confusion, had wrought near to completion. ·Pride glowed in the
breast of Solomon King of Israel as with practised eye he surveyed its
stately lines, and a pride greater still . pervaded his inmost being as he
contemplated that nobler temple not built with hands-the unison of
spir.i t he had wrought within his workmen. Exaltation, too, was his as he
reviewed how he, with his two Grand Masters, had by precept and example inspired in these simple workmen a desire ,to cre~te here an
earthly perfection, and had instilled into them that spirit of em.ulative
competition which should not only unite hand and mind and soul into
one master-craftsman, but should also bind them as men into one sacred
brotherhood that neither envy, discord, nor confusion could disrupt.
The temple was almost completed. His work was almost done. His
pride seemed justified.
Joy, too, filled the breast of Hiram Abif, the widow's son of the Tribe
of Naphtali, as he stood in the gateway of the temple at high tw~lve and
viewed the beauty which was the product of his artist hand and brain. Joy,
too, expanded his spirit as he saw in that visible beauty of carved wood
'and stone the symbolic beauty of, men's minds and souls wrought to the
finer beauty of human sympathy and love. Humility flooded his spirit
as he knelt before his Lord to render thanks for so much already achieved,
and fidelity to his self-imposed trust streO:gthened his heart as he arose
with conviction of so much still to do.
Yet even in that hour of pride and joy, when divine perfection seemed
almost to be attained on earth, there was for both these men to be disillusionment. The flaw appeared in the temple wall. The rift appeared
within the .human soul as fifteen men joined in vile conspiracy, their eyes
blinded to designs upon the trestle board, tl'leir minds uncomprehending
of the Master's high ideals, their ears alone attuned to the illusive potency
of words.
No need to recount here the course of that conspiracy. No need here
to tell of threats, of blows, of death. No need to here set down the tale
of flight, discovery, and execution. But let generations yet unborn record
that twelve recanted.
And of these twelve the legend says but little. Their names are not
set forth. Their travels and achievement occupy a short few lines. In all
the episode they walk subordinately, overshadowed by the .triple tragedy of
disappointment, death, and disillusion. Nor tells the story of that long
night of waiting, or the bitter dawn. What agonies their tortured souls
passed through we can but guess.
Yet this w e know. Theirs not the glory of position. Theirs not the
power and control of command. Theirs not the consummating leadership
of victory. Theirs not the immortality of sacrifice or triumph. Theirs the
footsore, weary travel. Theirs the desparate struggle of the capture under
no encouraging eyes. Theirs the mute standing by the gr aveside to see
the spirit of the Master raised by others to eternal life. Theirs, however,
the realization that not by word alone, not by strong grip only, but by
g rasp of principle and comprehension of ideal is mastery obtained. Theirs
only the soul-cleansing agony of recantation-renunciation of a lie.

In these forgotten twelve lies, for a modern world, the deep significance
of this drama. For seven long .years they had seen the master-craftsmen
moving to and_ fro, serene in their knowledge, sure in their skill, drawing
high praise and recompense from the Grand Master. And they had deemed
that rank an eminence to be attained. But work was hard and time was
fleeting, and forgetful by what persistent application, by what grueling
study they themselves had risen frorn entered apprentices to fellowcra,fts,
they judged the power of Master to be already rightly theirs. Doubted
that aught but secret signs and words well-guarded deprived them of their
due, and doubting judged the goal already won. And doubt bred envy,
and envy bred conspiracy to strike and win by force the deferred honor
in the easy way. For in the "word" they thought they saw the power.
Saw not the man that gave the word its strength. Saw not the spirit
which gave the word its glory. Saw not beyond the outward seeming,
into the inner heart of these. So we have doubted, grown in envy, deplored behavior not our own, yet failed to see within ourselves the very
faults we have condemned.
Yet even as the time approached when murder should be done, some
long forgotten lore welled up from deep within their work-numbed brains,
and knowledge, lost through toilsome years, seemed half to say the way
was wrong. 'And through the night perplexing doubts stirred dim remembrance how they, through study and through craftsman's skill, had risen
slow to what they were. And hope arose that by these means they might
so rise to equal him who in their thoughts stood as the temple's architect.
And. with that hope fell from their eyes the scales that blinded them to
light. For then they learned the inward truth which marks the Master
from the craft-that only can the word have power wheri spoken by a
man of strength. That strength is not brute force of men, but power
of spirit and of mind.
In this our generation, as in that, me~ seek to rely upon the potency of
words to cure their ills, on mystic formulae to salve the sores their errors
cause. As they, so we delude ourselves into believing that in a word some
secret power resides. As they, so we mislead ourselves by the conviction
that by a label we can elevate or can condemn. As they, so we hope that
in a phrase lies power to create the substance of desire. Eager for freedom
in ourselves, we have forgot that the word "Aryan" can not make an
ignoble people noble, the word "Slav" can not make a people who love
their homeland cowardly, the word "democracy" can not make an unwilling people free, tbe word " Mason" can not make a mannikin a man.
By contemptuous terms and opprobrious 'epithet we seek to dismiss false
prophets of new order s, while hugging to our breasts the very her esies
that in them we condemn. By palliative phrase we seek to make accept.able the nauseous theories of ancient doctrines long since r ejected. Like
the conspirators within the temple we think that by assault upon a man
fancied ills can be cured, supposed wrongs righte~, undeserved honors
gained, ways to peace and prosperity made secure, the laurel crowri of
man's ultimate triumph bound firm upon our brows.

the committee reports on the subject, those who are impressed with the
Masonic principles seek and find and benefit, the others just join and remain members on the roll.

Oregon, 1944 (Grand Master):
We have all heard the expression, "Once a Mason, always a Mason,''
and I subscribe to that theory. The trouble is that some members who
are initiated, passed and raised, are not really "made" Masons in spirit,
but in name only. They are "escorted" through the ceremonies of the
three degrees, but never really pass the "Northeast Corner."
After the influx of candidates into our order following World War
No. 1, a great .many lost interest and dropped out. It was thought by
some that we were not careful enough in making our examinations and
that unworthy men were admitted. I do not agree with that theory. I
feel that we did not sufficiently impress them, and that they were never
really initiated, in the true sense of the word.
Quebec, 1944 (Past Grand Master):
No doubt we have all at times met Masons who have not proceeded
beyond the third degree, who in a half apologetic manner have made
some statement such as this, "I haven't gone far in Masonry, I am only
a 'blue' Lodge Mason." A brother who makes such a remark, I think,
should be given the assurance that he has no cause to harbour any feeling
of inferiority as compared with others in that he is only a Master Mason.
He should be assured that the entire essence of Freemasonry is embodied
in the first three degrees. We may take all the so-called higher degrees
we will, study to our heart's content, and then after we have quietly
thought it all over, what will we find? We will fail to discover any
Masonic principle which is not inculcated in the lessons of the first three
degrees. Therein are to be found all the fundamental teachings of Freemasonry. The subsequent degrees, in fact, serve only to elaborate the
lessons of symbolic Freemasonry. These so-called higher orders are in
the nature of graduate schools in which the lessons of craft Masonry,
necessarily given in condensed form, are further explained and expanded
by methods which appeal to the eye and ear, through symbolism, drama
and allegory. It is a worthy ambition on the part of any Mason to desire to improve his Masonic knowledge. He is enjoined to do so at the
very inception. These advanced courses of instruction afford him the
opportunity, but in so pursuing his studies he should not forget that the
craft Lodge is the keystone of Masonry and demands his first allegiance.

Connecticut, 1944 (Proceedings):
On the evening of May 27, Hiram Lodge No .. 1 sppn~ored a ChineseAmerican night. A group of Chinese Masons, under the leadership of
Dr. Joe Woon ' Lum, exemplified,. in the English language, the Master
Mason degree. · Never have I seen the drama of the Widow's Son portrayed more beautifully. These Chinese Masons were members of Amity

to this country, and are now practicing their chosen vocations among us.
The dignity and sincerity of their ritualistic work set a standard that we
may well s_trive to emulate, and as we knelt about a common altar, with
these followers of Confucius, the conviction became more vivid that
Masonry, in its broader aspec'ts, has no boundaries and that our belief in
the existence of a Supreme Being is the foundation, upon which the great
superstructure of Masonry is erected.

The sub-committee felt that they should develop to the full extent the
facilities offered by the Masonic Boys' Home Trust, which had capital of

·
Instituted many years ago by Brother · Frederick S. Potter, who stipulated that there should be a committee of management .consisting of
• himself and several others. Brother Potter died, and for the past six or
seven years no committee had been functioning in charge of the home,
Brother Nicholson had shouldered the whole responsibility and kept the
accounts. The funds were growing at the rate of between £1,800 and

Quebec; 1944 (Committee Report):
Your Committee on Rites and Ceremonies beg to report they have
fully considered an amendment to the charge to the candidate in the
first degree and recommend that the following words, at the end of the
second paragraph on page 34 of the Ritual be. eliminated:
"and above all, by never losing sight of the allegiance due the Sovereig11
of your native land; ever remembering that nature has implanted in your
breast a sacred and indissoluble attachment to that country from which you
derived your birth and infant nuture."
You committee consider that the preceding words of this paragraph
sufficieJJtly covers the loyalty of the candidate and which reads as follows:
"by paying due obedience to the laws of any state which may for a
time become the place of your residence or afford you its protection"
South Australia, 1944 (Board of General Purposes):
In the board's report presented at the annual comm"unication last year
was included under the heading "Emergency Directions," a clause relating
to thq dress which the Grand Master had approved as prop.e r to be worn
during this period of emergency.
·
From reports received, it would appear that there is a misinterpretation
of the words "street clothes,'' although it was considered that the description would be quite understood as meaning a suit of clothes in its literal
sense, which, ~s the adjective implies, would be normally worn in the
street.
It was never expected that such a misconstruction would be placed on
the words as to include what are known as sports clothes, nor, as in one
instance it was recorded that the Brethren might discard their coats on a
warm evening.
South Dakota, 1944 (Grand Master):
Your Grand Master and Grand Secretary had as their guest Rear Admiral· and Brother Thomas L. Gatch, former captain of the battleship
South Dakota. I had two reasons for inviting Brother Gatch as our ·guest.
The first was that Brother Gatch had command of the battleship
named after our great state. The second was that my son Bill served under Brother Gatch in the Southwest Pacific when the South Dakota gained
the name of the "Battleship X." Brother Gatch has his Masonic membership in Salem, Oregon and his Grandfather Gatch was Grand Master of
Masons in Oregon in 1873. We found the admiral a very fine gentleman.
When the chairman of the meeting, Grand Master Stephens of Ohio,
announced the presence of Admiral Gatch, he said "We are happy to
have Rear Admiral Gatch, the former captain of the steamship South
Dakota with us this evening." When Admiral King passed our table, he
reached out his hand and · shook hands with Gatch and said "Hello
Steamboat Bill. How are you?"

HISTORICAL
Alberta, 1944 (Guest Speaker):
In 1660 came the restoration of the monarchy. This meant the fall of
Puritahism, the breaking of the power that did struggle for moral standards. The flood-gates of. looseness and licentiousness were thrown wide
open. The latter days of the century were marked by further conflict
between King and Parliament and by severe religious intolerance. Then

j
736

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

came Monmouth's Rebellion and the accession of James II. At last, near
the end of the century, England once again took a monarch off the
'throne and invited William of Orange and Mary to assume the sovereign,ty.
With the turn of the century there was hope of better things. In 1707
came the active union of England and Scotland. Perfectly true, there
were still wars abroad and.difficulties and depressions at home but a new
day had dawned and men were loo.k ing forward to a better standard of
living and a better level of citizenship. In such an hour men felt that
Freemasonry had in it not only that which would make a definite contribution to the spirit of freedom and constitutional liberty but would help
establish a new order, a day of better moral and social conditions.
Freemasonry, we know, is a beautiful system of morality, and for the
development of a nobler type of citizenship it has exceptional advantages.
It is possible, after all, to see why this Guild of Masons as an operative
craft should have perpetuated itself in a philosophic and speculative
institution into a system devoted to the ouilding of character more than
to the erection of material structures. There is, I think, no room for
doubt that thjs operative craft did project itself into the speculative system
of Freemasonry. It is the one craft out of the Middle Ages ·.t hat did
so continue. I believe it is generally recognized by students of sociology
that the medieval trade guilds did not as a rule continue their existence.
The modern trade union is not a projection of these guilds but is described rather as a movement created by the industrial revolution. One
guild did project itself, that of the Masons. For this I say there are
reasons. One of these is that for centuries it has been associated with
the erection of man's great cathedrals and churches, the institutions that
represent the highest aspirations and endeavors of the human soul. Another reason is the fact that the tools of the builder are called by those
names which are also the terms of our moral life-the square, the level,
the plumb, the compasses-are all moral terms. 'They are words of
·ethical significance. Our language has so developed. There are no other
adequate symbols nor words to express the ideas of uprightness and rectitude of conduct, of self control and the due restraint of human passions
of the holding of behavior within its proper bounds. Natural enough
that this society should undergo this very transition with which we are
acquainted, a transition from an operative trade to become a speculative
or philosophic society. Freemasonry then could launch itself on to the
world as the bearer of a philosophy of life, the promoter of worthy standards of good citizenship.
Deiaware, 1944 (Committee on History):
A book entitled "The History of Free Masonry in Tennessee 1789-1943"
was received from the Grand Lodge of Tennessee. As you read through
this book you come across the names of those who were high in the
Masonic order of that state: John Sevier, first governor of Tennessee,
Andrew Jackson, sixth Grand Master of Tennessee, and seventh President
of the United States, James K. Polk and Andrew Johnson, Presidents
of the United States, Sam Houston, one-time Governor of Tennessee and
liberator of Texas, and many others too numerous to mention. Andrew
Jackson was elected Grand Master of Tennessee spontaneously from the
floor at the meeting of the Grand Lodge in 1822 and at the tii:ne was
probably the most popular man in the country. Just two years later he ,
ran for President, captured the popular vote, but on account of a tie in
the electoral college, the election was thrown into congress and John
Quincy Adams was declared elected.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

737

In 1828 Jackson was elected and serve~ for eight years. One of his
most noteworthy achievements was the paying off of the public debt.
General Albert Pike, the eminent sch olar, jurist! warrior and statesman
was the founder of the Scottish Rite Masonry in Tennessee. He was
probably the most profound student and Masonic writer of the last century.
